…

“Mydeimos,” the thin one said again.

Mydeimos. That high, firm voice.

Mydei. That low, soft voice.

These five knew something. Knew him or those voices.

So he gave them those two words burrowed somewhere deeper than his mind or body. Aedes Elysiae.

When Mydei finally emerges from the Sea of Souls after nine harsh winters, the most precious thing in the world to him isn’t his name, his body or his life. But two words he can’t remember the origin of: Aedes Elysiae.

As the years pass in exile, he finds himself plagued by knowledge that comes from the same maybe-past or maybe-future that wasn’t quite Mydei’s and yet was.

It took four years for him to stumble across Aedes Elysiae, a boy that calls the place home, and why those words were engraved upon his soul.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
The world was dark and murky. It had been for as long as he’d known it. It clung to him in a stagnant weight that never shifted on its own but always dragged him back whenever he moved and buffeted him with the movements of something coming towards him.

They came for him often. Blurry figures that moved through the world with an ease he didn’t have. They lashed out faster than he could dodge, caught any weak hits he threw at them, and retaliated with tears everywhere they could reach and cracks deep in his body.

When they lost interest and discarded him to sink, those cracks and tears were the closest things he had to warmth.

Warmth. A bright light. A gentle voice that held him and didn’t want to hurt him.

The whole world was nothing but darkness and pain but, somehow, he knew of these things from beyond it.

Sometimes, when his body was still putting itself back together, it almost felt like he was somewhere else. Like there was something at his back. Hard or soft, it didn’t matter, just that he wasn’t sinking anymore. Like there was someone beside him.

Often times, the voice was higher but firm when it spoke to him in words he couldn’t understand but knew the meaning of. Fight with all his strength, endure any hardship, never waver. Other times, the voice was deeper but softer when it told him with certainty that he could survive anything.

So when he felt his body sway, he tensed. His fingers and toes curled, returned from the burning pain to the cold world and his own control. He opened his eyes and they stung with their newness but he could see again and dodged the lunging dark shadow.

Another one swung in his peripheral vision but he couldn’t stop his own momentum in time to dodge that too. He could only throw his hands and grapple it the same way it grabbed at him.

Soft. Slippery. But he clawed in and felt it puncture. The tentacle thrashed and more snapped around his arm. Yanking. His fingers creaked with their hold in the wound, on the brink of breaking with the force of fighting the creature’s pull. If he let go and it wrenched his arms apart then he would lost them again.

Colour spread beneath his fingers. A dark blot that blocked his view. But he didn’t stop. A tentacle dove for his neck and the snap he had once felt still echoed in his ears. He jerked his head down, opened his mouth and snapped his jaw closed.

The creature spasmed around him, under his fingers, between his teeth. It clenched and unclenched in raw panic as a foul taste filled his mouth and he bit harder anyway.

It shot off. He didn’t know where they were going but it thrashed in eagerness to get rid of him. He dug his nails and his fangs in and didn’t waver. Never. He would do better than survive. He would kill this thing.

But then something changed. Pressure and coldness. It was different. Lessened and warmer.

He wrenched his head back and any resistance was torn away. Something cracked in his chest this time when it shuddered in pain and crushed him.

His hand slipped and it felt the loss of his two footholds because it flung him away.

He flew backwards and—

And hit something.

Under his feet, his back. It moved when he pushed against it. Unhelpful but better than the nothingness he was used to. It was like the gold around his neck and in his mind alongside a deep voice. But dulled. It fell apart into chunks, then smaller, when he dug his fingers in.

Everything was brighter around him. Easier to see. His eyes didn’t feel as if they would burst in his head even as they stung.

The creature was more than a dark blur. Its tentacles flowed against the water, pushing smoothly and quickly as a pair of big eyes darker than the world he knew stared at him. Circling him but not attacking. The stump of the tentacle he had ripped free flailed. It was nervous.

The light dimmed. There was something above them. Another dark shape, rounded on either side until it met at a sharp point at the top and bottom.

It didn’t seem to notice the two of them. If it did, the creature’s bleeding wound should make it the primary target while he escaped or lurked to finish off the injured victor.

The creature looked at him and he dug his toes into the thing beneath him in preparation. It was coming again.

Then it darted straight up.

It was injured and it would rather take that unknown creature above them than him? He was smaller and weak than anything else in this murky world.

The tentacled creature smacked the newcomer and it… it rolled over immediately. Two more shapes appeared. Extra limbs?

But he watched the back and forth of their bodies, bobbing, and he knew the shape of them. It was the same every time he looked down at himself.

They were like him.

He kicked off and sped through the water. The tentacles grabbed hold of them and they struggled uselessly. They didn’t even try to dig their fingers in, stamp their feet or use their teeth. They just flailed around. Weaker. Both of them weaker than him.

A tentacle flicked at him but he dodged. Easier than before. There was less dragging him down up here.

He whipped his head round, seized it, and bit hard. The tentacles writhed but he grit harder, gripped harder, and tore.

Not a blink later and he threw it away, launching himself at the two trapped prey. One of them had stopped moving. The creature tried to flee but it was too late and he sank his finger, toes, teeth in to free the one still moving.

He pried them free. They stared with wide, glassy eyes. He didn’t have time to get them to safety. Were they so weak they would just accept death and not even try to flee?

He darted for the next prey and the creature swung them out of the way but he closed the distance easily. While he was quicker, the creature was slower up here and he snatched it before it could curl away from him.

He tore it as mercilessly as the rest and flung the unconscious one at the motionless one. That seemed to finally spur them into action as they caught their ally and dragged them up, up, up with them.

He didn’t bother watching where they went as he lunged for the creature again and ripped it to shreds with the same viciousness done to him.

Only when it was reduce to a mess of floating limbs, twitching like they could still escape, did he wade out of the mess.

That strangely round and pointed shadow was gone. So were the two creature that looked like him. No sign of where they had gone. So they could flee just fine after all. But for beings as weak as them to survive all this time… how? Where had they gone?

He dropped the creature’s head and let it sink back into the depths. He tipped his head back. It was warmer up here. A bright light came from above and he thought of blue, white and gold and reached for it.

His hand broke through first. The weight he thought lessened suddenly vanished completely.

His head passed through next and—

Hot. Cold. Pressing down on his skin and blowing against it. Noises in his ears. His chest ached and spasmed, rough sounds and something else trickling out of his mouth and merging into everything around him.

There were more things in the distance. Everything new and unknown and dangerous but if those two weak being could survive up here then he would be fine.

He paddled towards where the thing surrounding him ended and merged into something gold like what he’d found underfoot earlier.

Small things darted below him and shadows passed overhead. But nothing ever attacked. They only ran away. Everything up here was weak.

Eventually his feet touched something solid again. It still broke apart and moved every time he tried to push off but it was enough for him to stumble the rest of the way. When that weight finally let go of his ankles, he collapsed onto his back and didn’t move.

His body ached. Not in the way of limbs ripped free and growing back. This was different but still so familiar.

It was blue with a bright light above him. Closer now than when he was weighed down. He reached for it again and the warmth gathered in his hand.

The hardness at his back. The burn in his nose even without blood or injury. The… sky and the sun. Like he had seen them before. Like he had laid here to see them before.

His hand was too heavy to hold and it dropped beside him. His eyes followed, slipping closed and even then the world was less dark than it had been his entire life.

There was one thing left on his mind. Two words. The only things that never left him no matter how many times he sank into darkness and reemerged.

They were all he had even when he opened his eyes not on something hard —but soft. The light and warmth were different now. They didn’t come from the dark thing that had replaced the sky and joined with the four solid things all around him. It was somewhere beside him, in a colour that reminded him of the marks on his body and not the sun.

But he didn’t entrust those words to the being he found when he emerged from a lighter, easier darkness than what usually consumed him when he closed his eyes. The being was one of the two he had saved from the creature and it made all sorts of noises he couldn’t understand. It bared its teeth but didn’t bite. A warning?

Now that the former prey was safe again, there was no reason to assume it wouldn’t attack him too. They were both alone but weak things usually attacked in numbers, using trickery and force to overwhelm him. So when it wasn’t looking he snuck away and ran before its allies could arrive.

Unlike in that cold and darkness, his movements were free of that clinging drag and there were lots of places to hide. The beings who looked like him came to search when they realised he escaped. But they were easy to evade in the tall golden stalks.

When the sky began to darken, the rustling and shouting stopped. It was quiet again except his own breathing. He could occasionally hear things moving but they were just as hidden as him and nothing ever approached him as he crawled further away from those things that looked like him.

The sky lightened and darkened as he roamed. The gold stalks thinned and disappeared quickly but he found more shelter, more hiding places, with ease. If he heard the loud noise of something bigger, stronger than him, he ducked out into the open where they didn’t prowl. If he saw a thing that looked like him out on the open paths then he wove his way into the green.

He was right when he assumed that everything was weak up here. The most anything did was scratch and bite him. No missing fingers or hands, toes or feet, or eyes. No crunch or snap when they grabbed him. And they crumpled easily in his hands before he ripped into them with his teeth.

And still those two words followed him. He mouthed them to himself with every step, every bite, every gaze up at the sun as it rose, held and sank again three times.

It was when the sunlight accompanied him that fourth time, some of those beings that looked like him finally chose him as their prey. There were five of them, hunting him in a group. They were smarter and stronger than the ones he first encountered.

He tried to lose them by winding in and out of every obstacle or hiding spot he could find. He was smaller and quicker and quieter. Every new corner he turned, it was like he’d seen it all before. He knew where to drop, where to jump, where to slow down and speed up. They were persistent but so was he.

It took another two rises of the sun before they cornered him.

It was his mistake. He’d fallen into a ditch trying to make a tricky jump from one ridge to another, hoping it would be enough to lose them for good.

His leg snapped and burned in a way he hadn’t felt since before he had slain that tentacle creature. He ignored it and clawed his way up. It would take them time to get to him safely. He would need to be somewhere else before they found a way down.

When he finally emerged from that pit, the five of them were already waiting.

He bared his teeth at them and bent low to the ground. That thin one looked like the easiest to kill but he had seen how well it moved. Either way, he had to take that one first.

“Mydeimos.”

Mydeimos. He knew that word. Except for those two voices that held him together in the depths, it was the first time anything had ever made a sound he could understand.

The thin one’s lips curved upwards, not baring teeth, and lowered himself. Not low and ready to pound, but to one knee. And then he tilted his head and exposed his neck.

The other four followed.

“Mydeimos,” the thin one said again.

Mydeimos. That high, firm voice.

Mydei. That low, soft voice.

These five knew something. Knew him or those voices.

So he gave them those two words burrowed somewhere deeper than his mind or body. Aedes Elysiae.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei finally hears rumours of Aedes Elysiae and follows them to a wheat farming village.

Chapter Notes

In the fourth year of Mydei’s exile, he was assailed by the image of poisoned arrows. It came to him in dreams, conversation, thoughts. Unbidden but always lurking to strike when he least expected the assault. When Perdikkas asked him one night where the Kremnoan detachment would be marching to next, Mydei blinked at the fletching in his stomach and back only he could see. He only had one answer: not Ladon.

None of his warriors questioned the command. They cheered, hoisted their honey brew high and returned to their songs from a home everyone shared and longed for except him.

They wandered the wilds without much direction. Disregarding, the military discipline, the detachment was a group of mere exiles, so their days were spent following the rust scented winds and their nights wiled away on food, drink and music.

The town they ended up in had a name but not one any would care to map. It was too far from any major city-states that none had even claimed the territory their own and, something Mydei concluded with a brief glimpse over the market stalls, produced nothing of real value. It was a mundane place. Perfect for a brief respite and resupply.

He shadowed Krateros as the man negotiated with the town’s blacksmith. The detachment’s weapons were beginning to wear down. They needed repairs or replacements but enlisting the services of some unknown blacksmith in an unknown town wasn’t enough.

Kremnos had its own forging techniques that had been taken into exile with the detachment. The quality of the materials and the forge wouldn’t be up to par but it was better than nothing.

“They’re willing to allow us to rent their forges but only at night,” Krateros summarised for him while the blacksmith got back to work.

Mydei grunted. They had spoken in common tongue but he couldn’t understand the blacksmith’s accent and gotten lost too quickly. No matter Mydei’s thoughts or emotions, his face rested in a look of quiet anger. It did well to hide his confusion even if it drew the ire of strangers who didn’t appreciate being looked down upon by a child.

But Krateros, despite being a relatively recent member of the detachment, choosing self-imposed exile to seek them out across Amphoreus and finally join them half a year back, was responsible for the bulk of Mydei’s education. He had observed Mydei’s father for many years, and his mother many more, so he had honed a talent for reading the opaque.

“Tell the others when we get back.”

There were still supplies they needed to pick up. Primarily grain and honey brew. The detachment could weather any storm without complaint so long as they had those two things and one more: steel.

They hadn’t moved far from the blacksmith when Mydei caught sight of another stall. A fletcher.

The arrows loosed overhead. Mydei sucked in a harsh breath.

Krateros paused at the sound but only considered the bundles of well-crafted arrows. “Arrows… Ptolemy mentioned they would be in need sooner rather than later.”

Mydei watched his teacher approach the stall and forced himself to follow. The fletcher had the same accent, so there was nothing to distract Mydei from the… thoughts, memories, foresights. A future that had already happened in the past.

They walked away from the stall with a bundle of arrows wrapped inside waxed leather. Mydei eyed the feathered ends and saw them coloured red.

“Teacher?”

“What is it, Your Highness?”

It wasn’t as though Mydei knew everything. Only feelings of familiarity like he had seen or done these things before. Vague recollections of conversations, hazy images of scenery. But he didn’t recall this town.

“Do you think Fate can be defied?”

It was a silly question, he knew it was before it had even left his mind, but Krateros had lived long enough to mask the disbelief.

“Your Highness, of course not.”

Mydei let his face rest in its anger and not disappointment.

And Krateros didn’t notice as he gazed at the sky, seeking out the silhouette of a mobile fortress. “But fear not, your father was bewitched by traitors and led astray. It was false prophecy fed to him. Not the will of the Titans. When you reclaim the throne, you will bring the thousand year Kremnoan dynasty to new heights of glory with that blessed body of steel.”

Mydei hummed and tugged at his chlamys hung over his head. He knew that prophecy. Krateros explained every word to him not long after he joined, as he regaled to Mydei the relationship between his parents and how things had ended so twisted. But that wasn’t the foretold future Mydei was interested in.

What if a prophecy came from something that wasn’t a malignant mortal nor a Titan? Something… beyond even Fate? Then surely, if he put his faith in that knowledge…

Across the street, Hephaestion smiled at a travelling merchant who possessed some of the only interesting wares in town.

“Krateros, return to the encampment.”

With a brief glance between Mydei and Hephaestion, Krateros knew Mydei would be in safe hands and took his leave. Mydei lurked in the shadows between buildings as Hephaestion revealed an intricate bronze mirror they had pillaged from a small army. It had flown a flag Mydei hadn’t cared for beyond the spoils, knowing it originated from neither Ladon nor Kremnos. The men were so poorly trained, the army crumbled at the first strike of their Kremnoan formation.

The travelling merchant’s eyes widened, practically sparkling in the reflection, and his mouth opened, looked once over Hephaestion, closed again. He handed over the coins at the price Hephaestion had set, along with the herbs Perdikkas had been searching for, picked and preserved from somewhere near Tretos.

Mydei’s lip curled and he tugged his hood as far down as he could before pushing off the wall. Hephaestion had chosen well. The merchant knew enough to recognise that Hephaestion was likely a member of the nameless warrior exiles that used Kremnoan techniques without bearing its flag.

Then remembered that bartering was considered offensive amongst Kremnoans—only the owner could decided the worth of their own possessions or labour. It was only up to others whether they accepted the product or sought better prices elsewhere. But never to barter—and so he accepted the given rate.

When Hephaestion saw Mydei approach, he smiled and met him halfway, dropping the pouch of coins into Mydei’s palm.

He weighed it and arched a brow, choosing the harsh sounds of Kremnoan over the smoother common tongue. “It was just pretty bronze.”

Hephaestion laughed. “My dear friend, it’s less the item itself people like that man take interest in. Its value is the life that object has led. He can have it appraised but the story he’ll tell all his guests is that it came straight from the spoils of that nameless army making itself known across the land.”

He tossed the pouch up, coins rattling, and caught it again. So he paid for pretty words instead. “If he had won it himself, only then would there be a story worth passing from the host onto a guest.”

Hephaestion raised a hand and Mydei tossed the coins back to him. “It will make a good conversation piece for that Okheman merchant on the savageness of the Kremnoan people.”

Long fair hair neatly tied back. A golden hoop in each ear. A slender face and body. Clothes as clean as could be reasonably expected while constantly on the move. Hephaestion was far from a savage.

Now, Mydei on the other hand. There was a reason he kept his hood up and refrained from speaking with the merchants. His body was still short and thin after nine years of malnourishment. At thirteen he still bore the stature of a child but a merchant from another minor town, only important as a distant territory of a larger city-state, had startled so badly at the sight of his tattoos it alerted the city guards.

His grasp of the common tongue had been poor at the time, not long enough after he emerged from the Sea of Souls for him to answer in more complex language even if he somewhat understood it. There had been numerous questions about his past crimes to warrant an identifier on his face at such a young age.

But he was such a pitiable sight the city guards turned to other ideas: kidnapping, slavery, the unsavoury unknown warriors so clearly Kremnoan. When they tried to “rescue him”, he bit one of them, clawed at the other’s face, and slipped away. He’s certain that encounter was made into another story of Kremnoan barbarism.

“I believe I saw some pomegranates in the arms of a woman who passed us by earlier,” Hephaestion said. “Shall we, Mydeimos? And on the way we can discuss our troubles.”

He frowned but Hephaestion had already turned his back. “What troubles could I possibly have to share?”

“Mydeimos, if someone of your status wishes to lie then they must take care to do it well.”

His frown deepened, accompanied by a twitch of his brow. He could accept Krateros referring to him as Your Highness or Crown Prince, but never liked how Hephaestion would mention his supposed status. The Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos? He was birthed more from the Sea of Souls than any human city. They were all companions in their shared exile: what difference did status make?

Everything. He knew that. The only reason his five friends had expended the effort to pluck him from a feral life in the wilderness was because of that status. One they caught wind of in a rumour about a child emerging from the sea and slaying with bare hands the sea monster that had so troubled the fishermen. That child’s most distinctive features were the mane and eyes of a solitary lion, and jewellery of blue and gold.

While lacking a formal education, the one provided by the Kremnoan detachment and then Krateros was as close as numerous exiles could come to preparing him for kingship. The king that would lead them home and restore glory to Castrum Kremnos.

“I’m not lying,” he lied.

Hephaestion glanced back, an amused crinkle at his eyes. “Of course not, Mydeimos. Then, as one loyal soldier under your command, I beseech you to explain your sudden aversion to Ladon.”

They both knew Hephaestion was a lot more than that. A subordinate who marched on Mydei’s orders, a comrade who shared food and drink and toasts with Mydei, a teacher in whatever Mydei could learn from him. A friend, his dearest one, and a confidant.

But when Hephaestion asked why he was so attached to the words Aedes Elysiae and where he first heard them, even he was not privy to an answer.

In part because Mydei didn’t know himself. Didn’t know how to explain the feeling that he had already seen and done this. Not everything down to the

finely woven threads, but the tapestry each one came together to create felt like it had been draped over his shoulders once before.

Hephaestion shortened his steps on legs far longer than Mydei’s, slowing to his side so they could speak more lowly between themselves. “The Kremnoan detachment harbours no doubts. Your judgement has never led us astray—it’s the mark of a born warrior, and a worthy king.”

Mydei kissed his teeth. “They coat their weapons with poison. We shouldn’t throw lives at those who fight so dishonourably.”

Hephaestion’s brows rose. “Poison? I’ve never heard of Ladon using such underhanded tactics. Where did you hear such a thing?”

Mydei tugged his hood over his eyes.

“Forget I asked,” Hephaestion relented, knowing Mydei could stay silent for days, weeks, on end if he wanted. It was more difficult for him to speak than refrain after nine years of silence. “Is that what concerns you so that you’ve been tossing and turning every night in your cot like a newborn?”

That was an exaggeration. Sometimes Mydei had restless nights, as all warriors who had spilled life and guts into the soil did. His rest just happened to be plagued by thoughts of a lightless abyss where monsters and the dead grappled at him knowing he didn’t belong. If not that, then a dream about unimaginable pain through his back from the blade stained gold as it pierced through his chest.

Even as he told himself there was nothing to be embarrassed about, he turned away his burning face.

Hephaestion chuckled. “Feel reassured, so long as we have Perdikkas by our side, no warrior of yours will succumb to poison or ailments.”

Mydei peeked out the corner of his eye to find Hephaestion already watching; a hand over his heart in a show of sincerity that Mydei found in his smile and creased eyes. A gesture to his weak heart and health. But he

still stood tall and able thanks, in part, to Perdikkas’ concoctions as well as his one tenacity.

But sincerity wasn’t the same as truth.

The truth was that Mydei knew the colour Perdikkas’ skin would turn when all the blood rushed out the wounds in his stomach. Then how that pale skin would green and yellow when the poison spread through him. The shaking, the cold sweats, the convulsions.

At some point, his pained cries would dwindle away into nothing more than harsh pants and crazed mumbles. On his very death bed, as Mydei clutched a hand that lacked the strength to do more than twitch, Perdikkas found the strength to bestow his parting words.

Mydeimos, do not mourn. I have achieved honour by bestowing a noble death upon the enemy.

Except Mydei had mourned, would mourn, was mourning for one of his dearest friends that was still alive. Perdikkas greeted him every morning, sang Kremnoan folk songs in harmony with him, checked him for injuries knowing they would heal perfectly every time. And he would do everything to keep it that way.

Just as he would never allow Leonnius to have his legs cut off and body disappear in a bottomless swamp. Ptolemy to be crushed by rebels in the snow covered city. Peucesta to martyr himself for their retreat. Hephaestion to fall ill after ten years in exile and finally succumb. The visions that tormented him every night was knowledge for him to use and emerge victorious. Not for honour nor glory but for the sake of a future where the six of them together might live without being dogged by Strife eager to end them.

Footsteps thundered across the ground and Mydei twisted his body to dodge out the path of whatever idiot was sprinting through the market place at full speed.

“Mydeimos! Hephaestion!”

He groaned. It was one of his idiots.

Leonnius sprinted past, then did a double take when he noticed Hephaestion’s distinct hair. The speed of the detachment’s fastest runner meant he was already a good ten steps away but he spun on his toes with hardly any momentum lost.

The two of them shuffled over to the side of the road, Hephaestion showing an apologetic smile to all the bystanders who had nothing better to do than stare, and Leonnius skidded to a halt.

There was no telling how far and how fast Leonnius had run. Many of the detachment had scattered to sell or trade their spoils for supplies. If he recalled correctly, Leonnius had gone with Peucesta to exchange an ivory carved flute for some gold, yet Peucesta was nowhere to be seen.

“Is there an emergency?” Mydei asked. There was no other reason for Leonnius to leave Peucesta behind and appear so suddenly.

Leonnius took one deep inhale to catch his breath and then spoke in a level voice untouched by exhaustion, “We found it.”

Found it. They found it. And he knew with absolutely certainty what it was.

Hephaestion grasped Leonnius’ shoulders with urgency for a nonexistent emergency instead of celebration. “Found what?”

Leonnius opened his mouth but Mydei got their first as he breathed:

“Aedes Elysiae.”

Just the word brought a warmth up the back of his throat, dripping from the tip of his tongue, like he had swallowed pure sunlight.

Hephaestion shook Leonnius by the shoulders. “Explain yourself. And where is Peucesta?”

They had traded the ivory flute and been purchasing grain. Peucesta was a man of few words but his skill with their craft and rhythm were undeniable.

If Mydei wanted information then Hephaestion and Peucesta were his first choices.

And the detachment had made it their secondary mission to discover the meaning of the words Aedes Elysiae. They assumed the words were passed onto Mydei from the Sea of Souls, so they must have been of the utmost importance.

A person? A skilled warrior or tactician or physician? Only Kremnoans were permitted to join the detachment but there was unspoken agreement that an exception could be made for another gift from the Sea of Souls, second only to Mydei’s immortal body.

Not even Mydei knew what the words meant. He only knew that the very thought of them brought images of something brighter than the sun. Of white, blue and gold. That his heart ached and his body very nearly trembled with the urge to move, to search, to reach and unmask this unknown.

“It’s a small village not far from here. Two days march westward,” Leonnius recounted. “Touches the coast but the only thing it’s known for is wheat.”

It wasn’t a person but a place. Mydei felt something in his chest twist but…

Wheat. Yes, that was right. It settled into his mind comfortably, as though it had always been there, washing mud from metal in a river until the water ran clear and revealed the truth beneath the grime. Golden in colour; warm under the sunlight.

When they returned to the encampment, Mydei had one order: march westward, for Aedes Elysiae. The detachment cheered and split into two parties. Those who would follow Mydei and those who would stay behind to utilise the forges before marching to Aedes Elysiae under Krateros.

That night around the campfire, a new air of anticipation came with every cheer and song. Mydei turned the meat, a boar hunted from the wilds by Ptolemy, on the spit while the others engaged in drunken revelry. If he

didn’t watch it then it would undoubtedly burn, or the seasoning would fail to bring out the meat’s full flavour.

Above the cheer and song of the others, Peucesta strummed his lyre and sang an old epic about ancient heroes while the rest of them listened. The metre changed as the tale of heroism cooled into one of lovers.

Despite the playful mockery of the pink tinge Mydei preferred to his drinks, Hephaestion passed him a half-full chalice alongside a pot of goat’s milk. “Nervous?”

He mixed the two together, swirling them as the red began to lighten. “Why would I be?”

Hephaestion hummed and the firelight added colour to his face that only made Mydei think of his feverish skin on a sickbed. “It could be anything, or it could be nothing.”

None of them wished for Mydei to be disappointed. He was their crown prince, their would-be-king, the one who gave them commands and charged into battle at the lead with his infallible body and would one day take them home.

But he was also a child. As much as he loathed his malnourished body yet to recover from those long nine winters and wished it would grow sooner rather than later. A child they had raised and were still raising with their own rough hands. What father, brother, uncle wanted to see their child crushed?

He watched the boar brown over the fire, fat dripping onto the loaves he had set underneath. “Whatever comes, I will not falter.”

Hephaestion didn’t say anything more. He simply raised his chalice. The other four noticed and paused their merry making to lift theirs. Mydei did the same, the metal clinking together, and they threw their drinks back as one. It was a promise to stay by one another’s side through all hardships.

A voice he hadn’t heard in many years came to him in his sleep. One that had once told him how he could doubtlessly survive any challenge the world threw at him. Now it whispered to him in a voice like the sea breeze through the wheat fields.

Two full days march was conservative. Halfway through the second day, the green forests flattened to fields and from the plains golden wheat sprung abundant. It was almost endless.

Leonnius returned from scouting ahead and announced that the village was only an hour or so ahead. The sight of a fully equipped army, especially with the rumours flying faster than their feet could carry them through Amphoreus’ wilds, would… frighten those poor villagers, so Mydei ordered everyone to set up camp again despite the early hour.

It was better than being met with the best siege defence the place could muster. Strife begets Strife and Mydei would prefer peace where it could be found

While the others set up the tents and dug fire pits, Mydei climbed up a nearby tree and settled on its branches to keep watch. Ahead, the flats dipped into a valley and supposedly that was where Aedes Elysiae rested.

He didn’t know what awaited him there. A small, sleepy town? One that grew wheat instead of warriors. Why had the name of such a place been imprinted onto him by the Sea of Souls or something beyond it?

So deeply engraved into his soul that even the knowledge of it ahead of him, like the sun beginning to break over the horizon, filled him with an indescribable feeling. Every breath was heavy and light, his body tense and relaxed, his mind full and empty at once.

A sharp whistle pulled his gaze to the ground. Ptolemy grinned at him, a strung bow and quiver over his shoulder, a coil of rope in his hands. “Are you coming down, Mydeimos? We’re holding a contest over the game hunt.”

Mydei nodded and swung himself down, holding his weight as he dangled for a heartbeat before falling the rest of the way. He shook the splinters off his gauntlets.

Other people hunted with bows or spears—although Ptolemy excelled in traps. Ones he only needed to read about before he could recreate each knot and length of rope flawlessly—but Mydei preferred to hunt with his hands, gauntleted or bare. His body was his best weapon.

Ptolemy cocked his head. His grin grew and he leaned down, cupping his mouth conspiratorially. “Or you could take the opportunity to go off on your own.”

Mydei languidly blinked at him and recounted, “All members of the detachment are to travel in pairs.”

If someone were ambushed or injured, their chances of survival drastically increased if at least one other person was at their side. Whether it was game hunting in the wilderness filled with lurking predators, restocking supplies in nearby towns that may become hostile on a coin toss, or even going down to the nearest water source to bathe. The exception was Leonnius’ fast feet serving as their most reliable messenger.

Ptolemy rolled his eyes, amused. “I doubt this little place is harbouring anything that could bring serious harm to you, Mydeimos. Either you disappear now so I know how long you’ve been gone and where. Or you can disappear later when no one will know.”

He wanted to defend his honour. He wasn’t going to… but he faltered. Maybe he was. Maybe he wouldn’t have been able to shake off the allure of Aedes Elysiae and whatever he may find there, calling to him like a siren lured a father to throw his child to the sea. Maybe he would have left everything behind and disappeared without a word to anyone.

Thrown away the weight of their expectations and his responsibilities and ran for the thing that had captured his interests. Captivated him so completely with sweetness warmed gold by the sun.

Then Ptolemy smiled and laughed through his nose. “Besides, some things are best experienced on your own.”

And Mydei gazed off towards that horizon again. There was a word for this feeling; he was certain. But all he could recall was Peucesta’s songs about a warrior who sailed across the West Wind to retrieve their lover.

“I’ll be back,” he promised.

Ptolemy handed him a dagger as a precaution. “Before evening begins to welcome the night.”

Mydei strapped the weapon to his thigh, hiding it beneath his tunic. “If I fail to return…”

“I’ll ensure we try peaceful means before Hephaestion burns the village down searching for you.”

Mydei nodded but didn’t turn to leave immediately. He stared at Ptolemy, watching him back expectantly, and shifted his weight between his feet. “Thank you.”

His smile softened and he raised an imaginary cup. “May triumph be yours, Mydeimos. Whatever form that triumph takes in your next battle.”

Then he was off. The wheat stalks scratched at his bare legs as he ran, pushing them aside and weaving through the gaps. It didn’t bring any pain. If anything, it was sheer relief that pulsed through him, a companion to the anticipation racing in his ears. The heat of the sun overhead, the harshness of the grain, the wind in his ears that smelled of the fields and the salty sea —they were all reminders that this was real.

Aedes Elysiae. Not just a perfect, peaceful place his mind conjured for him amidst the darkness of the Sea of Souls. Finally, finally, he would be able to see it with his own eyes and settle the endless yearning for something he had never known but still knew that had made a home in his chest these past thirteen years.

There was a break in the wheat ahead of him. He could see where it had been disturbed. Parted and kept as such by something.

When he looked down, a pair of blue eyes gazed at him from beneath white lashes. A young boy but older than himself. Taller, well-fed, broad shoulders and muscles suited to a real sword and not the wooden one resting on the ground as languidly as its wielder.

Mydei met the stunned, wide eyes of that boy and something in his chest caved. It shattered like glass and rained down like stars and new words emerged from the cracks.

The love of my life and the one to end.
