chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon introduce themselves to each other properly and almost immediately start a duel.

Chapter Notes

Neither moved. Mydei’s heart raced, breath quick, like he never stopped running and he searched the boy’s face for even a hint that he was feeling the same things tearing through Mydei. It was the same way he tore through obstacles, whether monsters or human: bloody, brutal, teeth and fangs bared.

Nothing. No anticipation and relief and exhilaration shaking hands and flushing skin and dilating pupils. Just a confused scrunch of the boy’s nose.

Mydei deepened his breaths and wrangled his heart back under control with the efficiency of any good warrior. It wasn’t disappointment. It wasn’t. He never had any expectations for what Aedes Elysiae might hold. Mydei was good at adapting and it was time for him to adapt.

The boy pushed himself to his feet. Mydei wasn’t wrong. He was a lot taller than Mydei’s malnourished stature, yet it didn’t feel like the boy loomed over him, leered down at him, when he smiled.

“Hello, I’ve never seen you around here before. Are you lost?”

He had a nice voice. Still youthful, high and a bit whiny, but it balanced out with a certain softness like the wheat swaying in the wind. Carefree, relaxed and flexible. Mydei didn’t recognise the boy’s voice as one of two.

Mydei’s hands curled into fists at his side and he knew his face rested in that stony anger, despite his true feelings, but he couldn’t bring himself to

change it. “No.”

“It’s okay to admit you are,” the boy encouraged brightly, seemingly oblivious to the metal claws on Mydei’s fingertips even as it creaked. He hadn’t cleaned them properly. “Where are your parents?”

“I don’t have any.”

“Oh… so who do you live with? Do you know where you live?”

“I roam around.”

It was clear none of those were the answers the boy wanted. His face had become increasingly sullen the more short, sharp replies Mydei gave him.

“Your legs must be tired then.” The boy sat back down and patted the dirt next to him. “Come rest for a bit. What’s your name?”

There was no one else hiding in the wheat fields. Mydei would have noticed them already. It was just him and this boy he apparently had loved and would love and already loves with the way his heart made itself known against his chest. This boy staring up at him so earnestly, practically pleading with him to accept his invitation.

Apparently his heavy plates of jewellery and red tattoos didn’t scare him. No fear; although, a glimpse of Mydei on the battlefield might change that.

He crossed the last couple steps and sat down. “Mydeimos.”

“I’m Phainon.”

That name, too, slid into place. Something always known yet not remembered. But it wasn’t quite right when Mydei watched Phainon stick out a hand. Mydei clacked his claws at him but he didn’t even blink, just kept his hand out until Mydei shook it.

“Nice to meet you, Mydei.”

Only one person, if a voice in his head could even be called that, had ever used that name.

His eyes widened and he turned away, snatching his hand back. “That’s not my name.”

“Sure,” he chirped back, undeterred by Mydei’s rough edges. “But your name’s long. Besides, Mydei is a lot cuter than Mydeimos so it suits you more!”

Mydei replayed the words in his mind, wondered if he had misheard among Phainon’s accent and quick speech, two traits he usually disliked. When it was clear he hadn’t, whipped his head to Phainon. “Cute?”

He nodded with a giant grin. “You remind me of my friend’s cat. Livia. That’s my friend, not her cat. She has eyes like yours—“

“I’m a boy,” Mydei clarified, just in case. He shouldn’t need to but Phainon seemed like an idiot.

“I know! But her eyes and fur are the same colour as yours. Plus, she’s always hissing at Big Snowy,” Phainon rambled away, one hand raised and curled like a cat’s claws and Mydei glanced down at his own gauntlets. “That’s my dog. I think you’d like him. He’s very big and fluffy. Would you like to meet him? He’s very good at finding me so if I call him I bet he’ll come running right away.”

“Do you always speak this much?” Mydei asked because he couldn’t imagine saying so many words in such quick succession.

He stopped mid-breath, closed his lips, and smiled sheepishly. “Sorry, that must have been annoying.”

Mydei shrugged. “Not really.”

After all, Phainon had a nice voice. Despite speaking in common with an obvious accent, Mydei found he could understand with ease. Every syllable of his easy cadence sank right in. Kremnoans were usually ones for shorter

words, or better yet actions, over extraneous chatter or persuasions. But Mydei wasn’t averse to Phainon’s ramblings. He actually enjoyed listening to him.

Is that why he falls in love with him? Because he has a nice voice? That thought didn’t fit, displaced where the right ones interlocked their joints into a steady framework. Unless the maybe-past, maybe-future version of Mydei was surprisingly shallow for a pretty boy and pretty voice, there had to be more.

He pointed at the wooden sword between them. “Do you know how to use that?”

He couldn’t imagine entrusting himself to someone who couldn’t defend themselves. It didn’t have to be a sword, if not his gauntlets then Mydei was partial to a spear, even a bow and arrow would suffice. But if the sword was Phainon’s then Mydei could only assume he knew how to use it. Or else he was just a kid playing pretend and what could they ever have in common?

Phainon picked it up and swung it at some invisible foe in front of him. “Of course. I’m going to train to become a hero and protect everyone.”

Mydei rolled his eyes. “Heroes aren’t real.”

Phainon’s smile never wavered. “Maybe you just haven’t met one yet.”

Everyone assumed he would meet one in Aedes Elysiae. Some part of Mydei did, too. The same one whose voice murmured in his ear in the darkness and despair, blazing like the sun, to keep going. That someone would have all the answers about Mydei’s strange mind, would understand him and guide him to subvert that Fate.

The simple tunic, the wooden sword, the carefree smile. Mydei knew Phainon wasn’t that hero even if he was something. And that made Mydei just as curious. He may as well try to understand what exactly he was meant to uncover in Aedes Elysiae and why. What Phainon was to him—a lover, a murderer—and why.

He knew the Kremnoan detachment, all its exiles, and Castrum Kremnos itself was his responsibility and nobody else’s. It had been a foolish hope. A dream, a wish, more than a reality he thought he could grasp.

“You have to be strong,” Mydei said quietly, “if you want to protect everyone.”

Phainon nodded, surprisingly somber even if his smile didn’t change. “That’s why I’m planning to go to Castrum Kremnos to train.”

Wooden sword. Carefree smile. A proclivity for words.

“They’ll laugh you away at the gates.”

Phainon chuckled. “Then I must have told a pretty funny joke.”

He didn’t dignify that with a proper response and Phainon scratched his cheek at the judgemental silence and unimpressed stare.

Mydei showed some mercy when he asked, “How old are you?”

“Fifteen.”

Kremnoans began formal military training younger than that, closer to Mydei’s age than Phainon’s. But the informal training began the moment they could hold anything in their little hands.

Their hands grew clutched around a child’s sword, a dagger, a spear and their legs grew to hold the weight. As soon as they learned to walk, they learned to run with a weapon dulled just enough not to hurt. If they couldn’t survive a night in the wilderness by the time they were seven, then that death was only an inevitability brought quicker to spare the family’s honour and resources.

If Phainon went to Castrum Kremnos, not only would the guards laugh him away, they may even bring a child to throw him out.

“How old are you?” Phainon asked.

“Thirteen.”

Phainon squinted. “You know, there’s nothing wrong with being younger.”

“I’m not lying.”

“But you’re so…” Something crossed his features and he shook his head. “Never mind.”

“What?” Mydei asked. Sharp, lips pulled back like a feral dog gave warning.

“What?” Phainon asked. Just confused and not condescending.

Mydei pressed anyway, “You were going to say I’m something. What was it?”

“It was nothing. I was wrong.”

“It can’t be both. So tell me.”

Phainon swallowed, hands pulling at the grass, and braced himself. “… small.”

So the apparent love of his life was not only an idiot, but thought Mydei was small. Weak. A child and nothing more.

The love of my life and the one to end. The knowledge that Phainon would kill him one day didn’t faze Mydei. There were many reasons someone Mydei loved might come to cross blades with him. Life and battlefields shared many things; first and foremost was their unpredictability. It could be as simple as a conflict of interest. It could be as likely as Mydei finally going mad like his father and needing to be put down.

But if Phainon was someone worthy of having Mydei’s back and bestowed the honour of taking Mydei’s life one day, then that would be because they were equals.

“Stand up.”

Phainon tilted his head but was already halfway to this feet. “Why? Where are we going?”

“Nowhere. Pick up your sword.”

That finally brought some hesitance, glancing between Mydei and the wooden sword he had left on the ground. “Well…”

Mydei scoffed. “You insulted me, so now I have to defend my honour.”

Phainon just stared as Mydei rolled his wrists and ankles to loosen the joints. “I’m not fighting you. I don’t even have a spare sword for you to use.”

Mydei clacked his claws at him.

Phainon considered them for a moment but it wasn’t with approval. “Those look sharp. Who gave them to you?”

Mydei stretched his biceps and shoulders, then slid his weight to feel the stretch in his calves too. “Don’t worry, I won’t aim to kill.”

Phainon kept staring. “You’re serious.”

To prove how serious he was, Mydei lunged. Phainon yelped and dodged the first swipe. Not bad. He was fairly fast, graceful when he used the momentum to bend low and swipe his sword up without stumbling. Instead he straightened and twisted at once so the two of them were face-to-face.

Good reflexes. Quick recovery. His stance balanced his weight, mindful of the uneven ground, and would let him respond to Mydei’s next attack. He could admit it was better than he expected but his eye twitched when he realised Phainon was staying on the passive defensive.

Fine. Mydei would make him realise that wasn’t enough.

Mydei bent low and pounced. Phainon’s weapon gave him a range advantage but Mydei had always been fast, slippery, body honed to move in

water weighted with dread and Death. Air and solid ground was nothing. They were a boon.

It was the one advantage of his small body. He easily dodged Phainon’s sword—decent swing. If it connected it would hurt on a lesser man—and closed the distance in a blink. Phainon’s eyes widened at the claws surging from below for his throat.

He threw his head back and twisted his body. His shoulder took the brunt of the hit. No blood. Mydei wasn’t interested in that. Just some torn fabric.

Then he jabbed his elbow at Mydei’s chest and he barely caught it with his free hand. He threw Phainon back, already searching for his next angle of attack, while Phainon was already opening the distance again. Retreating.

Except it wasn’t a retreat.

His sword arced. Mydei dropped low and felt it skim past the top of his head. He straightened just in time to jerk out the way of a slash. Phainon had abandoned the defensive just when Mydei was preparing to exploit it.

Phainon pressed the advantage and Mydei deflected his blows. He kept speeding up without sacrificing strength. As though every swing brought momentum he carried forward into the next step, the next attack.

Mydei tried to close the distance again, slip into range, but Phainon was watching his routes in with an eerie focus in his eyes. He was so steady as he closed in for another hit. Face set and hands sturdy and base even. An immovable object against Mydei’s unstoppable force.

He showed his hand too early. He was too eager and paid the price. Usually his opponents were stupid and dead or smart and retreating.

If he were going for the kill—

Mydei changed tactics and aimed to grab Phainon’s sword on the next attack. But Phainon twisted the blade, pulled it free and angled for Mydei’s

hands. Already gone because Mydei needed to be faster, stronger, better to match Phainon.

If Mydei were going for the kill… that would mean Phainon was too. This was just play fighting, no different from dogs pulling each other’s tails. It wasn’t that they got lost in the violence as their attacks came harder, quicker, closer to something deadly or at least seriously injurious.

Every attack, dodge, parry was proof of their skill and a taunt. Better. Be better if you want to win. So they did better.

But Mydei felt a sudden rush for battle. A real hunger for it. One he had never felt before. It couldn’t be just any battle. It had to be theirs. Both of them at the height of their power, clashing with a thirst for victory and intent to kill that couldn’t be sated by any other.

He needed to know what it would feel like when it was a real sword in Phainon’s hands. To bleed on it and draw his blood in turn.

Yes, of course this would be the man worthy of his back. Not only one of Mydei’s many thousands of lives but the one life.

But not yet. For now, Mydei still needed to win.

He took the next hit to his stomach. Phainon’s eyes widened and his grip faltered. Mydei should have been able to dodge that. He should have.

He didn’t because it let him grab Phainon’s blade and yank it from his hold. Disarmed and still stunned, Mydei easily tackled him to the ground.

The impact winded Phainon and he choked on a breath but still scrabbled at Mydei with surprising strength left in his fingers. It was pointless. Mydei excelled at hand-to-hand combat and had him pinned by the wrists in seconds.

He sneered down at him. “Yield.”

Phainon’s fingers clenched, muscles flexing in Mydei’s hands, as he tested the give. There wasn’t any.

He tried again anyway and his face was flushed, chest rising and falling in harsh pants, but he grinned with the same flash of teeth as Mydei’s own. “You don’t fight like a thirteen year old. Maybe you lied about your age after all and you’re actually a very short adult.”

“You still have energy for pathetic jokes?”

Mydei didn’t dare move even one of his hands from Phainon’s wrists, pinned above his head. He was too strong and would break free in an instant. Instead, he dug a knee into Phainon’s chest and watched him wheeze.

He still managed a strained laugh. “Do you always get riled up at pathetic things?”

“No.” He leaned more weight onto Phainon’s wrists, his chest. He could handle it and let Mydei come closer. “I usually kill them.”

His smile only grew. “So I’m the exception. I’m flattered.”

“At least you know what you are.”

“Flattered?”

“Pathetic.”

“Oh, Mydei, if I was so pathetic, would I be able to do this?”

Mydei realised his mistake the moment Phainon’s weight shifted beneath him but it was too late. Phainon snapped his hips and twisted his torso and Mydei’s one knee on solid ground wasn’t enough to stop Phainon from throwing them both.

If they had been on stable ground then Mydei would have been able to recover. Unfortunately, they were on the side of a hill.

He was weightless for a moment and he used it to latch his hands behind his head and tuck his body. Then he hit the ground and kept hitting it all the

way down. He only clenched his teeth and curled up tighter as the compact soil beat aches and bruises into his body.

By the time he slammed into flat ground, his whole body protested in a way even the toughest battles couldn’t manage. He was usually ready for those hits.

He didn’t bother moving. He sprawled on his back and the only reason he knew he was still alive was his heart thundering in his head to the same rhythm he had tumbled.

Phainon laughed, laughed, beside him. “Haven’t done that in a while. Mydei?” Rustling as Phainon moved. “Mydei? Are you all right?”

He sounded genuinely nervous even after Mydei had proved himself by wrestling him to the ground. Maybe this was just how Phainon was. Concerned over the smallest things.

He kept his eyes closed. “I’m fine.”

“Can you… did it hurt?”

That level of pain was nothing. He could already feel his body healing it away. “Forget it.”

More rustling, closer this time, before the warmth of the sun vanished over his torso. Mydei opened his eyes to Phainon hovering over him, lips thin and eyes downturned.

“Sorry,” Phainon said so sincerely Mydei half-expected his bottom lip to tremble under the weight of his guilt. “I didn’t mean to hurt you. At all.”

That was obvious from the way they were fighting but Mydei nodded anyway. “I know.”

“Where does it hurt?”

“I’m fine now.”

Phainon’s hands hovered uselessly, not sure when to poke and prod but needing to do something. “You don’t have to keep lying to me.”

“I never lied to you.”

Phainon’s expression only became more grave. “You tucked up, didn’t you? When we fell. I thought you’d roll flat. I—“

“I don’t want to hear apologies,” Mydei snapped. He sat up, pushing Phainon away with a hand against his chest. “I challenged you to the duel so save your pity for something more pitiful.”

Phainon searched his face for something, probably pain, but if a tumble down a hillside were enough for Mydei to curl up and cry then he would’ve died a thousand more deaths by now. Pain was a friend even older than Death.

When he found nothing, he relaxed with a harsh exhale. “You’re right.” His breath caught in his nose and Mydei only realised it was amusement when Phainon raised a fist to his mouth and laughed. “But really? Taking that hit to your stomach? Are you out of your mind?”

If Phainon thought that was crazy it was only because he hadn’t seen Mydei do it on a real battlefield. No matter how battle hardened the enemy, a child being impaled on their weapon only to grab it and yank the weapon closer —when most adults would be a choking, cooling corpse—was enough to disarm anyone.

A blunt hit to the stomach was nothing. Never mind that the force of Phainon’s swing could do more than wind a man who tried to bear the same hit. They would spit blood.

“It worked,” Mydei grumbled and his body didn’t protest anymore when flopped onto his back again. “But what kind of underhanded tactic involves rolling down a hill.”

He didn’t really mean that. If it were pure chance then maybe. But Phainon had kept a keen sense of his surroundings and known what he was doing

when he goaded Mydei off balance and threw them. Mydei just wanted to poke and prod a little. It was childish but Phainon didn’t seem to mind.

“It worked,” Phainon threw the words back at him, laying down on his side. “So who won?”

“Do you really need to ask that?”

“It’s better to be on the same page.”

Mydei muttered some Kremnoan curses under his breath before he spat, “You. ”

Phainon preened. “That’s right. Which means I get to claim my prize.”

“The spoils have to be agreed upon before the duel.”

“Wha—you’re saying I don’t get anything?”

Mydei glanced out his eye at Phainon’s frown. He sighed and rolled onto his side too. “I’m saying it depends on what you ask for.”

Phainon’s smile returned like clouds blown away to once again reveal the sun. “Then come home with me.”

“What?”

“Come home with me,” Phainon repeated, just as casual and shameless as the first time. As though Mydei hadn’t heard him when the issue was that he definitely had. “My parents won’t mind. My dad went fishing this morning so my mum should be cooking fish for dinner. I’ll ask them to let you stay.”

He was almost afraid to ask. “The night?”

Phainon stared at him, dumbfounded, like Mydei was the fool. “As long as you need.”

How was he supposed to reconcile the warrior he had traded blows against with the fool staring at him with such wide, hopeful eyes at the idea of what? Providing Mydei a warm meal and place to sleep.

“I don’t need that.”

Mydei didn’t need Phainon’s home. Even if Mydei didn’t have parents or a house to return to, he had a home of his own. People who cared about him. People he swore he would give everything to protect. People who would worry if he went missing.

He jolted upright. What colour was the sky? “I have to go.”

“Wha—Mydei, come back!”

Phainon scrambled to his feet but Mydei climbed the hill on all fours and was already halfway up.

“Mydei, there are wolves out there at night.”

He could snap a wolf’s neck with his bare hands. Wild animals generally knew better than to approach the numerous campfires and rambunctious people but, on the rare occasion some were too bold, hungry or feral, they had night guards on duty in case.

“So don’t follow me,” Mydei called back, hauling himself up the crest of the hill.

He was about to sprint off when he noticed something wooden on the ground and snatched it up.

Phainon was, of course, following him, and rather quickly. But he was forced to stop and catch the wooden sword Mydei threw right at his head.

“I would never withhold your rightfully won spoils,” Mydei announced while Phainon stared up at him, the wind stirring his sweaty bangs and fresh exertion colouring his cheeks. “So I’ll come back tomorrow.”

Then he turned and ran and didn’t stop running until he reached the Kremnoan encampment. He had wheat in his hair, mud and grass stains on his clothes, new scuffs on his gauntlets.

But Hephaestion, pacing by the main fire while Ptolemy knelt looking thoroughly scolded, took one look at him and the anxiety was replaced by three words.

You look happy.

Chapter End Notes

Brat Mydei and Brat Phainon. They’re just different types of bratty and both insanely fun to write when they’re both so silly.

Don’t have much to rant about this chapter but

chapters.title: Chapter 4
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon gives Mydei a personal tour of Aedes Elysiae.

Chapter Notes

The next day, the entire detachment was practically fighting to be one of the few allowed to venture into Aedes Elysiae. Not because they needed a resupply—they were just nosy. When everyone pestered Mydei over honey brew and a campfire about the place and he refused to say a word, their curiosity had surged into something insatiable.

No one asked if he found what he was looking for. Hephaestion’s word had become law the moment it was uttered: Mydei returned from Aedes Elysiae happy.

The grin on Perdikkas’ face that morning foretold trouble and Mydei tried to ditch the others on the way. But Leonnius’ feet were as quick as his tongue would be when it came to spreading the gossip. No matter how he ducked, wove and circled through the wheat fields, he failed to lose Leonnius before he arrived at the hill.

While Phainon had been relaxed dozing in the field the day prior, that morning he had taken to pacing back and forth while nibbling at his thumbnail. As soon as he heard the wheat rustle, his head jerked up to Mydei.

He beamed and strode over. “Mydei! You really came back. Not that I doubted your word, of course, but…”

From the wheat moving behind him and the warm body just treading the edge of a polite distance, Mydei knew Leonnius had caught up.

Phainon glanced between the two and his smile didn’t change but it was somehow more fixed than before. “Is this your brother?”

“No.”

“Uncle?”

Mydei arched a brow that, compared to Leonnius’ was rather thin. Leonnius also possessed a larger nose worn well upon his longer face. Unlike Mydei’s untamed mane, his soft hair was cut short and perfectly coiffed, untouched by the wind he ran upon. The two of them looked nothing alike.

“No.”

Leonnius laughed and showed some mercy, “I’m a friend. A brother in arms.”

Phainon looked from Leonnius to Mydei with that stiff smile. Mydei didn’t realise he could express emotions that weren’t carefree joy, a warrior’s focus, and needless anxiety. Certainly not something so complex.

“Mydei, come over here. I wanted to show you something but you ran off yesterday.”

The only thing Phainon wanted to show Mydei the day prior was his home . And now that he had used that nickname—one Mydei has heard and kept close to his heart next to Aedes Elysiae—it would undoubtedly spread through the encampment.

Mydei’s brows furrowed, nocking an argument to loose.

But then Phainon added a soft, “Please.”

Mydei sighed and went to his side. The sun glinted off him and that was what it took for Mydei to realise the sword strapped to Phainon’s waist wasn’t a wooden plaything wielded with deadly precision—it was real.

Phainon unsheathed it and levelled it at Leonnius in one smooth motion. “What could an older man want with a young boy.”

Leonnius didn’t even blink. His demeanour switched as effortlessly as Mydei’s, assessing the new threat, but he still whistled playfully. “Speak for yourself.”

Age lost a lot of its meaning in the detachment, just as it did in Castrum Kremnos. What did age matter compared to an individual’s skill and the camaraderie fed blood and Strife on the battlefield. If Mydei wanted, he could sweep Leonnius off his swift feet and have his hands around his throat with hardly any blows taken.

“Why does he have so many tattoos?” Phainon pressed, any warmth used to temper the edge of his voice and then extinguished to leave it cold and cutting. “He’s underfed. Why does he need weapons for hands?”

Perhaps Mydei’s penchant for short answers and little explanation had finally done more harm than good.

Leonnius glanced at Mydei but he shrugged and then, after a moment, gave a subtle thumbs up hidden from Phainon’s view. The sword sheathed at Leonnius’ hip was to remain that way. Mydei didn’t need rescue; he didn’t need slaughter in his name.

“Heard wind of that flagless army roaming Amphoreus?” Leonnius crooned.

“The one that uses Kremnoan tactics.”

His smile widened like he was a heartbeat from a glorious kill on the battlefield. “That’s us.”

Phainon’s blade didn’t waver. He only firmed his stance. “Do you make a habit of taking in young boys with no home and no parents.”

Mydei motioned for Leonnius to make himself less offensive but his grin grew to show the subtle dip in each of his cheeks. Mydei would get him back for this and all the rumours he was doubtless concocting in his mind already.

“Not at all. Mydeimos is just special.”

Mydei glared and Leonnius pretended not to notice.

Phainon’s grip whitened, trembling for the shortest moment before he regained enough composure to quell it. But his lips pulled in real anger. Somehow it didn’t appear out of place. “You’re sick.”

“That’s enough!” Mydei barked and he smacked the back of Phainon’s head. He didn’t stumble but he did falter enough to look at Mydei. “I’m here to honour your victory. Don’t waste my time by dragging me into pointless squabbles.”

“What’s so pointless about your wellbeing?”

Leonnius practically purred,  “How cute. He cares about your body, Mydeimos.”

Mydei spat every Kremnoan curse he knew but Leonnius only cackled. When Mydei raised a clenched fist it was a reminder of the punishment to come. He was too far away at the moment and if Mydei lunged at him, he feared Phainon would join him to cut Leonnius down when Mydei only meant to give him a thorough beating. Leonnius still needed function in his legs to fulfil his role as a messenger.

Mydei didn’t bother to soften his anger when he rounded on Phainon. “Get out of your own head. Do I look in need of rescue?”

“But Mydei…”

He crossed his arms, squared his shoulders and tipped his chin back as he drew his voice from below his chest. “Leonnius is one of my dearest companions. Someone who has been by my side for years. Now, if you don’t want to claim your spoils then I’ll leave and I won’t be coming back to waste any more of my time.”

His grip tightened around his sword, as though he were prepared to launch himself at Leonnius on his own. It would’ve been quite the show at least,

and a chance for Phainon to win his respect.

But he relented with a sigh and sheathed his sword. “I trust you, Mydei.”

Mydei forced himself not to smile. “Then get moving. You too,” he ordered Leonnius with a jerk of his head.

Leonnius raised both hands in surrender, a false one despite the speed he disappeared. He was just itching to get back to the others and wag his tongue.

Head bowed, Phainon peered at Mydei through his lashes. He somehow perfectly balanced a look that was at once throughly chastised and yet gave no indication he wouldn’t do the same thing again. Like a dog who had stolen someone’s dinner and only licked its lips when caught.

Mydei huffed. “He was messing with you. Empty your head of his words.”

“Yeah,” Phainon agreed, sullen.

Mydei wasn’t good at comforting others beyond food, drink and battle. He shuffled between his feet and clacked his claws at his side.

But then Phainon shook his head and slapped his cheeks, red and stinging when he grinned. “Come on, let me show you around.”

“I thought you were taking me to your home.”

He laughed and swept a broad hand to the wheat fields, the sky, and the village down below. “Aedes Elysiae is my home.”

It was apparent how at home Phainon felt as he guided Mydei down the worn and winding village paths. He waved at everyone he saw and, no matter what they were doing, their faces lit up as they returned the greeting. Despite Mydei being nothing more than a stranger in their close community, the amicability they showed Phainon extended to Mydei at his side.

Although, they weren’t openly hostile to outsiders. While Phainon took him around the small marketplace—asking if he was hungry, when the last time he ate was, what his favourite foods were—Mydei noticed Hephaestion and Perdikkas purchase some food and local herbs.

Mydei knew Leonnius’ slander had already reached them because Perdikkas elbowed Hephaestion and they both grinned knowingly at him. Perdikkas mouthed something uncouth in Kremnoan and Mydei gave a gesture right back even as Hephaestion rolled his eyes at them for it.

“It’s harvest season,” Phainon explained as he passed a fig, given for free but Phainon insisted he check the young woman’s roof in exchange, “so everyone is busy. This is the school but lessons are cancelled until the harvest is over.”

The building was hardly any different from the homes they had passed. White walls and wooden frames dulled by time but not rotted by it. The only distinguishing feature was the small outdoor platform. There was no training ground.

“Can you read, Mydei?” Phainon asked, honestly curious instead of insulting.

He scoffed anyway. “Of course I can read.”

“Really? What about writing?”

“I’m not a fool.”

“Well, since you’re…” he glanced around and then dipped his head to speak lowly between them. “You can speak Kremnoan, too, right? Not just in common.”

If he were a prince who couldn’t speak, read and write his native tongue then he wouldn’t be a prince at all. He answered with an unimpressed look.

Phainon chuckled. “I get the message.“

He prepared to take them up a slope but Mydei tapped his arm and pointed behind them.

“What’s that statue?”

A hooded figure with clasped hands. Slender and grey with things left at the base as it stood watch over the village.

“That’s a statue of Oronyx, the Titan of Time. They protect the village.”

Mydei gazed up at the faceless statue but he knew he could lay down offerings, sat on his knees and clasped his hands, and none of his prayers would be answered. He had tried that already when the detachment first told him about the Titans.

He wanted to know what the meaning behind these thoughts and feelings and memories that weren’t his own yet were. He wanted to know who or what gave them to him. He wanted to know why him and seemingly no one else. Nothing ever answered.

But the statue of Oronyx gazing across every small corner of the village made some sense. Everything about Aedes Elysiae was so old and simple. Untouched by the rest of the world as the golden wheat and the vibrant leaves swayed to their own rhythm. In a way, Aedes Elysiae felt timeless.

Up the hill was the Sacramental Courtyard dedicated to Oronyx. Phainon tried to take Mydei inside but he refused at the sight of high walls and only one, maybe two if there was another he couldn’t see, exit.

Phainon pursed his lips thoughtfully and his searching gaze settled on the small pier built above the pond. “Get on.”

Mydei assumed he didn’t mean just the pier but the small wooden plank strung from a tree listing over the pond. “Why?”

“It’s fun.” Phainon insisted, a hand at his back to guide him over and down. “I use it all the time with Cyrene.”

Mydei gripped the ropes. “Who’s Cyrene?”

“My best friend,” Phainon said and pushed.

The swing swayed just a little. Phainon’s hands hardly left Mydei’s back before the warmth of them returned again for another push. Mydei went a little faster, a little higher, that time.

“You should meet her later. She’s in the courtyard with the elders right now. They’re preparing to send her to Janusopolis to become a real priest of Oronyx. That’s when I’ll leave, too, for Castrum Kremnos.”

He snorted, leaning back on the downswing to pick up more speed. “Good luck finding it. It’s a sky fortress. It always moves.”

Phainon caught him and pushed him again. “Wow, so that’s true. But I heard it always docks for the Kremnos Festival so the best warriors from all over Amphoreus can board. Have you ever seen a Kremnos Festival, Mydei? What’s it like?”

Mydei kicked his legs on the upswing. He was starting to gain some real height. “No.”

“Oh.”

Mydei stared up at the sky, growing near and then further and then even nearer again. If he let go, it felt as though he could soar.

“Higher,” he demanded.

Phainon chuckled and pushed him harder. The wind blew past his face, ruffling his hair, and his stomach dropped as he rose. He unclenched one hand and reached out for the sun.

A loud bark just to Mydei’s left and his body instinctively prepared for a fight. Unfortunately, that meant his hands flew to defend his torso just as he

reached the peak of his swing.

“No, Mydei! Don’t let—“

Too late. Mydei was thrown from the swing and flew into the air where he hung weightless for one moment. He could see the sun glistening off the wheat fields, the sea in the distance, the pond right at his feet.

Then he crashed into the water.

It was shallow and did little to soften the fall even as he went boneless and hit the pond bed with the meat of his thigh and shoulder, hands around his head.

A splash and the water lapped at him as it moved. Phainon dropped to his knees and placed a hand on his shoulder, his back. “Mydei, are you hurt?”

His shoulder scraped a little on impact but it hadn’t popped. He catalogued his body for scrapes, bruises or aches.

“No.”

Another bark and then a splash. Mydei watched a fluffy white dog bound through the water towards them at full speed and it didn’t slow even as the distance rapidly shrank to nothing. The closer it came, the bigger it got.

“Snowy!” Phainon demanded attention but the dog didn’t hesitate before it threw itself at Mydei.

Mydei fell backwards into the water as the dog’s paws slammed against his chest and its tongue came for his face. It was moving too much, squirming and barking and slobbering all over him. He didn’t want to hurt it by grabbing with his claws so he held his breath, closed his eyes and kept perfectly still.

None of the strays Hephaestion chose to nurture were ever so boisterous and friendly. They usually showed their affection in smaller ways, curling up beside Mydei while he slept or following him around the camp.

“Yes, Snowy, you’ve said hello. Now get off him. You’re heavy.”

The weight lifted off his chest and Mydei dragged a handful of water down his face before opening his eyes. One of Phainon’s arms was wrapped around the dog’s middle, pinning it to his body and leaving its legs to dangle, while the other hand scratched behind its ear. The two of them looked remarkably similar.

Phainon smiled sheepishly. “He got a bit too excited.”

“I noticed.”

“He still thinks he’s a small dog.”

A quiet sound caught his ear. High and muffled. Mydei looked towards the courtyard.

On the upper levels, a head of pink hair leaned out the window. A girl stared at them drenched in the pond and cupped her mouth but the gesture did little to hide her laughter.

“Cyrene!” Phainon called when he noticed where Mydei was looking, raising both arms over his head and waving.

She waved back. “Phainon! Introduce me to your new friend later! I’ll do him an oracle reading.” Her head suddenly whipped around and any amusement fell from her face. “Got to go!”

She ducked back into the building, likely caught shirking her duties.

They clambered out the pond and Snowy danced at Mydei’s feet as they wrung their clothes out.

“Good thing the sun’s out,” Phainon said, bent at the waist and squeezing the fabric around his thighs. “Should help us dry quicker.”

Only Phainon’s lower half was soaked from where he waded ankle deep in the pond and then dropped to his knees. Mydei wasn’t so lucky and had

shouldered his way out of his tunic to wring it to the side. Snowy innocently lapped at the water as it fell.

“You really don’t have any injuries.”

Mydei twisted harder, mindful of his claws. “Why would I?”

“No reason,” he said with a shake of his head but he sounded relieved. “Although, you have a lot of tattoos. Are those some kind of Kremnoan tradition?”

“No.”

“So they’re just for you? Where does a kid even get those kind of ideas?”

“Stop calling me a kid. I’m only two years younger than you.”

“A lot shorter though.”

Mydei glared. “I won’t look shorter when I knock you to the ground.”

Phainon practically perked up at the offer to spar. “I’ll hold you to that. But I’m still claiming my prize. Speaking of, I thought of a better idea than standing around waiting to dry off. Come on, we’ll hit two birds with one stone.”

They closed the loop around the small village by walking down the hill, passing a scarecrow wearing familiar colours but when Mydei pointed at it Phainon only laughed and blamed Cyrene. The wind blew from the coast, tasting of sea salt, and followed them back into the village streets. It rang the wind chime above the entrance to a house no different from the rest.

“This is my home,” Phainon announced with a little chuckle and a scratch at the back of his head. “Come inside and I’ll find you a change of clothes.“

It was small. As he peered around the main room, Mydei guessed at two additional rooms.  Phainon hadn’t mentioned any siblings; only a mother, father and dog, so they likely shared a bedchamber and one or two

mattresses. With the scent wafting through the air, the other room must be an indoor kitchen.

It was more spacious than the tents that could be shared between seven members of the detachment at a time. More sturdy against the elements.

A woman emerged from the room to the left, hair a mix between an aging grey and a recognisable white. “Phainon? What are you doing ba—you’re wet!” Two hands turned Phainon around and shoved him back towards the door, which meant right into Mydei. “Out! You’ll track water through the house.”

“B-but mum,” Phainon protested as he tried to dodge Mydei and stumbled over his own feet. Mydei side-stepped. “Mydei needs a change of clothes.”

She paused. “Mydei? That Mydei?”

“Yeah!”

The woman finally looked past Phainon and noticed Mydei’s short stature hidden behind him. Her face softened. “Hello.”

“Hello, ma’am.”

Phainon’s head whipped around with wide eyes and Mydei squinted back at him. Of course he knew how to be polite if he wanted. This was Phainon’s mother.

“Oh you’re soaked through, you poor dear.” She hurried towards him and he held himself perfectly still against instincts trained to flinch away, letting her lay a hand on his shoulder. “What has Phainon done to you.”

“I got wet too, you know.”

“I know. I can see you dripping on the floor.” A hand on each of their backs guided them out the door. “Go wait outside in the sun while I get a change of clothes. I’ll look through Phainon’s old ones for you.”

“Thank you, ma’am.”

She chuckled. “No need for that. Just call me Audata. Any friend of Phainon’s is a welcome guest.”

Beside the house was an area for storing sacks of grain and a bench to rest between the heavy labour. Snowy curled up at their feet as they sat and waited for Audata to come get them.

Mydei kicked his sandals across the dirt. “Your mum is nice.”

She offered him clothes and friendly touches despite dripping a mess across her floor, his unkempt appearance and the mark on his cheek that usually earned at least a suspicious second glance.

Phainon grinned and nodded his head vigorously. “My mum’s the best.”

“My mum…” He gripped the bench tight, claws chipping at wood but he couldn’t bring himself to let go. “My mum was too.”

When was the last time Mydei had ever spoken about his mother? The detachment had told him a few things here or there—a fierce warrior, the first to stand against his father’s tyranny, a valorous death—but Krateros was the only who could claim to know her. Even so, Mydei never asked about the woman he would never get to meet himself.

Phainon didn’t look at him, only leaning back on his palms and gazing into the distance. But Mydei knew was listening when Phainon’s foot bumped against his calf.

“My dad didn’t want me.”

Because wasn’t that the truth? Beneath all the grand prophecy, the right to rule, the legacy of Castrum Kremnos and the Titan of Strife, his father simply… hadn’t wanted Mydei enough to keep him.

He swallowed and kept his voice even, “She died trying to protect me.”

Phainon didn’t say anything but he slid closer, until their thighs were almost touching. But it was up to Mydei to decide whether they were or they

weren’t. Mydei pressed their sides together and they both watched the birds soar past the clouds and the sun across the horizon.

Much closer than the sky, a pink figure bobbed down the hill. One Mydei had only seen once from a distance but recognised enough as Cyrene hurried down the hill of the Sacramental Courtyard.

“There you are,” she panted when she finally arrived, dabbing her sleeve at the sweat on her brow. Her other arm pinned something to her side. “I finished my lessons. I’m Cyrene. It’s a pleasure to meet you officially.”

“Mydeimos.”

She slid onto the bench between Mydei and the edge. Snowy greeted her with a butt of his nose against her leg and she giggled, petting his head. “So what has Phainon told you about me?”

Phainon laughed but it pulled over a certain nervousness. “I haven’t gotten around to any of those stories yet.”

“Good. If your new friend is going to hear stories about me, they should come from me.”

“And if those stories of yours happen to involve me too? Probably doing something embarrassing?”

“Time preserves all. Even your most embarrassing moments.”

“Right… and would time happen to go by any other names?”

Cyrene smiled, innocent and mischievous and Mydei understood why the two of them got along so well. But she was really sitting too close to him. He might have moved away already but he was trapped between Phainon and Cyrene. Phainon also called her his best friend so Mydei didn’t want to stir trouble by offending her.

However, Phainon pulled away from Mydei’s side, shuffling down the bench. Mydei kept his breathing even instead of sighing with relief as he shifted into the newly opened gap.

Cyrene plucked the thing from under her arm and held it out to him. “Have you ever done an oracle reading, Mydei?” He shook his head and she opened the pages, pulling out a card from each page. “That’s all right. It’s actually quite simple. Just close your eyes, open your heart and pick a card. It’ll tell you your future.”

She held the cards out to him face down that supposedly held his future. He closed his eyes. It was just a silly game between children. There was no reason to put weight on what picture he happened to choose.

But he still thought of the future he wanted over the future he knew, somewhere in his mind, his soul, would come to pass. Had passed before. A future where his five dearest friends lived to see him become king and lead their people to a brighter future. A future where Phainon was with him until the end brought about by steel stained gold and Mydei wouldn’t begrudge him for it.

“The Ruler.”

His eyes opened. He hadn’t realised he’d chosen a card, let alone that Cyrene had taken it from him.

Phainon rested on Mydei’s shoulder as he leaned in for a glimpse. “What does that one mean?”

“It stands for discipline, authority and glory, but frequently also points to isolation and warfare,” Cyrene explained with a small frown, looking between Mydei and the card.

He huffed a laugh. “Seems pretty accurate.”

“No it doesn’t!” Phainon protested right in Mydei’s ear. He flinched but Phainon kept going, “Isolation? So Mydei’s going to be alone.”

“A ruler directs their will down onto the people,” Mydei recited from his lessons with Krateros. He kicked the ground. “Of course, the ruler has to be alone at the top.”

“That’s not true at all. I-I mean—“ he sputtered for some kind of argument, “—kings have queens, right? They have someone who rules beside them. So they’re not completely alone. And Mydei has me now.”

“Haikas,” Mydei hissed, face burning while Phainon only looked at him so painfully earnest and hurt at the idea of Mydei being alone. As though he hadn’t spent nine years completely alone. “Do you ever think before you speak.”

“At least you know it comes from the heart.”

“It certainly doesn’t come from your brain.”

His lips thinned, more sulky than angry. “Cyrene, show him my card.”

“If you wish.” She searched through her deck and pulled one card between her index and middle finger, flipping it to face them. “The Deliverer.”

Deliverer. That word sank in and, more than the name Phainon, Mydei knew it was right.

“According to the tripartite prophecy, this card means absolute harmony and perfection.” Phainon preened and Mydei rolled his eyes but didn’t interrupt Cyrene’s explanation. “In fact, it’s the only oracle without a dark side. It’s the card of someone destined to bear the wishes of many, and answer the world’s call.”

“See.” Phainon gathered Mydei’s hands in his. Warm, calloused along his palms and fingertips from a sickle and a sword. If Mydei just stretched out his curled fingers it would look like a prayer. “So tell me your wish, Mydei.”

“My wish.”

It was on the tip of his tongue. The feeling that something, everything, had happened before. This knowledge he couldn’t explain. The insane fact that Mydei had known him—known Phainon. Known the Deliverer—before he had even known the sun.

That his friends were fated to perish. That he was destined to die. That this feeling in his chest when he stared into Phainon’s bright, desperate eyes and felt his hands, sharp metal edges and all, cradled inside Phainon’s was in some way some Mydei’s  love.

Love like the kind that would kill his friends. Had killed his mother. Had and would kill Mydei too.

He turned away like that would free him from Phainon’s sincerity ingrained in his mind. “It’s not something anyone else can grant. I have to do it on my own.”

“Then I’ll do everything in my power to help.”

“You don’t even know me.”

“Of course I do. You’re my friend. If I can’t grant the wishes of the people I care most about then what’s the point.”

It was that face again. Still tormentingly earnest but also set with determination. The expression of a warrior prepared for battle.

“Boys?”

They both looked to the entrance of the house. Audata stared back, darting between both of them and their joined hands before sliding away. “Oh, and Cyrene joined you.”

“Hi, Audata. I was just leaving,” she said, book flipping closed so she could jump to her feet. “I promised dad I’d help out with the cleaning today.”

“Tell your parents I said hello.”

“Will do.”

When Audata invited them back inside, she had a change of clothes prepared for the both of them in the main room. Mydei was accustomed to a lack of privacy in the detachment so he had no qualms stripping out of his tunic and tugging Phainon’s over his head.

It fit well. The clothes were still in good condition even if they smelled as though they had been in storage for a while. It had been well worn and well repaired, based on the added patches and stitches.

Light blue and white weren’t the colours Mydei usually wore. Black and red was more practical: they needed less thorough scrubbing when dirt and blood was less visible.

Mydei turned to find Phainon already watching and he raised his arms. “How do I look?”

Phainon blinked and then stepped closer. “Here, let me help you.”

With what? Mydei didn’t have time to ask because Phainon’s hands were already on his shoulders. He plucked at the fabric, shifting it around, brushing it down for invisible dust.

Mydei glanced across the room at Audata. She was stitching up the shoulder on clothes he recognised as Phainon’s. The exact ones he tore yesterday during their duel. He felt a little guilty and accepted it was well deserved when his pleading eyes were only met with her amused smile.

He took a step back, looked Mydei up and down, and nodded to himself. “You look good. Come on, there’s still one last place I want to show you. Bye, mum.”

“Bye, Audata.”

“Oh, Mydei, will you be joining us for dinner?” When Mydei shook his head, she sighed and lamented, “That’s too bad. Feel free to come back another day.”

Mydei didn’t know how many another day’s he had in Aedes Elysiae. Until Krateros and the rest of the detachment had finished repairing weapons and rejoined the rest of them at least. The detachment were wanders by choice and by nature. Even if they were exiles, they were still Kremnoan. They sought out battle, spoils, honour like others sought out peace in a sleepy village only known for its wheat.

“I-“

“He will. I’ll be back for dinner, mum,” Phainon practically sang and looped his arm around Mydei’s to drag him out the door.

They ended up back at the shore. The fishermen invited Phainon onto the pier but he waved them off in favour of a private spot: a grassy bank sequestered away from view by the trees and shrubs.

Phainon kicked off his shoes and dipped his feet into the water. “How long have you been with the army?”

“Four years.”

Mydei knew he was silently doing the calculations—that Mydei was only nine years old when he joined—but his strange protectiveness flash like steel again.

He plucked some grass and let the wind take it away across the sea. He leaned forward like he could follow. “You must have seen a lot of Amphoreus.”

“I’ve wandered around.”

Phainon propped his elbow on his knee and rested his head against his knuckles, the sunlight reaching across the water to illuminate his hair, his eyes, and his smile aimed solely at Mydei. “There’s a whole world outside of Aedes Elysiae. Can you tell me about it.”

Mydei didn’t tell him about the lightless abyss, the monsters, the dead and a prophecy. But he did tell him about the Kremnoan detachment and every member that had passed through its ranks. By name, by lineage, by the battles they had fought together.

Phainon listened, enraptured, and Mydei told him more and more about the history that blew on the ends of their empty flag. He wanted him to know. To understand. The same way Phainon had shown him around a small town

encircled in golden fields, Mydei took Phainon’s hand and led him right through his home and into his heart where he could choose to stay or leave.

Chapter End Notes

Endless dog metaphors with Phainon. He’s a big white puppy and I will never see him as anything else.
