chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Whether it’s discontent in the detachment or the black tide itself, Mydei solves his problems the best way he knows how: with his fists.

Chapter Notes

Two weeks passed in Aedes Elysiae. He had kicked off his sandals and competed with Phainon to wrangle fish from the river, eaten at Phainon’s home with his mother and father, had fallen asleep languishing in the wheat fields and woken up with flowers in his hair and Phainon half-curled around him.

That morning, he knew Phainon had something planned about… fairies. Whatever that meant. Phainon declared that Mydei just had to meet them because then it would be a secret shared just between him, Phainon and Cyrene.

But Mydei returned from Aedes Elysiae the night before to a figure stood guard outside his tent. He doubted a hostile party could breach the night watch but he still clacked his claws at his side.

Only when he came closer did he recognise the well-groomed facial hair and familiar armour.

“Krateros.”

He bowed his head. “Your Highness. This is a late return.”

At first, Mydei had consistently returned to the encampment before the evening darkened into night. But as the days passed and nothing hostile reared its head to disrupt the peace of Aedes Elysiae, it felt safe enough to return later.

“I can take care of myself,” he reminded him as he pushed into his tent.

Since they had stayed in the area so long, extra tents had been set up so everyone could have more space. Mydei’s was private.

He had joined Phainon’s parents for dinner again. Mydei thought he had a big appetite but Phainon’s parents had been concerned and insisted he feel no shame in eating everything he needed. One glance at Phainon inhaling his food explained their… skewed perception of a child’s appetite.

“Of course,” Krateros agreed and followed Mydei in, which meant he wasn’t just waiting to make sure Mydei returned safely. He had more to say. “But there are other things Your Highness is responsible for taking care of.”

Mydei stripped out of his clothes for a cleaner set. Still suited for combat; gauntlets still on. “Speak plainly, Krateros. Anything else doesn’t suit you.”

Krateros’ face was grave. “The detachment is restless.”

Mydei’s hands paused pulling his tunic into place. There were a lot of questions he could ask but that would just be… feigning ignorance.

Of course Mydei had noticed something was off. It started when Krateros’ men rejoined them after six days in Aedes Elysiae and they asked the question Mydei’s men had not yet asked: what now?

Every warrior appreciated a reprieve every now and again to recuperate their muscles, care for their spoils, and repair their weapons ready for the next battle. Anytime they set up camp somewhere peaceful for a little longer than usual, it was an excuse to make merry through the night and wake with the realisation of what a terrible decision that was, only to do it again that same night.

But that was just the problem. It had been two weeks and the Kremnoan detachment hadn’t gained new direction.

Aedes Elysiae had been found but for what was unclear. The prince’s happiness? As fond as they all were of Mydei, that meant little if his happiness was tied to a small wheat farming village in some forgotten corner of Amphoreus.

The seeds of unease had quickly taken root in fertile soil. Kremnoans may not have been as savage as the rumours liked to portray them, but they were still undeniably warriors. They needed battle for more than honour, glory or the thrill of victory—they needed it like a blade needed a whetstone. It kept them sharp, capable and competent for the next inevitable battle. It was the difference between lying defeated in the dirt or trampling the dead underfoot.

Prolonged peace made them anxious, especially when the future was so murky. Mydei meant it when he regaled Phainon with tales of the detachment and called it his home. But, much like Castrum Kremnos where they all came from, if Mydei tried to settle on the earth in one place for too long then his home would move on without him.

“I’ll deal with it,” Mydei’s promised.

He had known but hadn’t addressed it—he simply hadn’t found a good time to tell Phainon he would be leaving and maybe, just maybe, asking him to leave everything behind. To join the detachment instead of seeking out Castrum Kremnos—but the choice was taken from him when he was awoken that morning by a scuffle in the camp.

Fights weren’t uncommon in the detachment. They were all grown men who slept with their hands on their weapons, shared extremely close quarters, and had hardly any company except for each other. The tiresome life in exile sometimes wore their patience thin and mere words were taken as slights that had to be refuted with fists.

But all they had in the wilds of Amphoreus was each other. If they didn’t have that, then spoils, honour, glory was meaningless—they had nothing.

At least half the encampment could found in the brawling throng. It was all movement: the flash of weapons, blur of bare skin, the spray of blood. He

could hardly see beyond the outmost layers of the mob. His five companions were nowhere to be seen.

If he dove in he would just be another drop of water in a storming ocean. The longer he let them beat each other the higher the risk of real injury, even death.

He inhaled until his lungs couldn’t expand any further. Then he unleashed it all to scream the war cry that led them all into battle on his heels.

The fighting stopped and everyone turned to him. Ingrained discipline winning over the adrenaline.

“Fall in line! And explain yourselves!”

The crowd parted and confirmed his suspicions. At the centre was Hephaestion, bloody nose and hair unkempt, and the rest of his friends in similar states nearby. He didn’t spare them a second glance as everyone separated into lines loosely mimicking their battle formation.

A spar had gotten out of hand. Not unusual in itself but neither participant had backed down when first blood was spilled. And the rest of the detachment hadn’t stepped in to prevent any serious injuries, but had goaded them on.

When Hephaestion intervened, Mydei’s name was dragged in and the fight sparked anew. No longer an outlet for tensions but a two sided conflict. The Crown Prince grown soft over a boy.

He couldn’t put it off any longer. Aedes Elysiae welcomed him with open arms and he had fallen into peaceful slumber hoping it could keep him away from the rest of Amphoreus in blissful ignorance. This was the price. His home splintered and he had driven the wedge in with his own hand.

He raised a fist high in the air. “We’ll be marching on tomorrow. Wherever the rust scented winds of Amphoreus take us!”

The men cheered but he didn’t miss the skepticism on some of their faces. That was fine. He had squandered their trust with softness and indecision. It was only right for him to win it back.

“If anyone sees fit, I welcome any and all to challenge me in combat for the right to decide the detachment’s fate! Our very own Kremnos Festival!”

That sparked their resolve anew in a rush of cheers roaring like the fires of Strife.

Hypatos was the first to step forward. He was one of the oldest detachment members and one of the most outspoken about Kremnoan values.

Mydei had only just roused from sleep but he spent all nights in his tunic and gauntlets so he was ready for combat at a moments notice. All he needed was some stretches to shake off the last of his lethargy.

Hephaestion nursed his bloody nose while Perdikkas slathered his wounds with salve and bandaged them. Peucesta handed Mydei some grilled meat skewers for a meal, a little charred at the edges due to the distraction, and Ptolemy poured him a chalice of pomegranate juice. Leonnius had disappeared with a message for Phainon: an apology that Mydei wouldn’t be able to make their meeting.

“Are you certain about this, Mydeimos?” Hephaestion asked in a nasally voice.

He rolled his wrists. “Afraid I’ll lose?”

Ptolemy barked a laugh and poured another chalice of pomegranate juice for Perdikkas. “Mydeimos The Undying? Who would worry about you over your opponent?”

“It’s only until first blood,” he grumbled. Not death.

“All the more reason to make that blood count,” Ptolemy said with the same grin he wore while reading the exploits of past battles, and Peucesta nodded his agreement.

The others laughed but Hephaestion’s lips were thin. Of course Mydei knew what Hephaestion’s unspoken question had actually been. Was he certain about leaving Aedes Elysiae?

Out of all his five friends, Hephaestion was the dearest to him. His closet confidant. The others would have been able to deduce it easily enough that Mydei enjoyed spending time in Aedes Elysiae and was eager to meet with Phainon. But only Hephaestion could take one look at him mussed with dirt, wheat and grass, his face still flushed but not from the exertion of the sprint, and know he was happy.

“I am,” he said unbidden and the others stopped laughing at the song Peucesta was reciting about Hypatos’ inevitable downfall. “I am certain that this is the right decision for our future.”

Hephaestion’s eyes, softened with affection for a child that was finally happy, hardened again with the dedication to his prince. He raised his chalice of honey brew.

The other four followed and chanted as one: “May victory ever be yours, Mydeimos.”

Hypatos’ weapon of choice was a spear. He was adept with a sword but he had been one of the men to teach Mydei how to wield a spear. Now he brandished one against Mydei.

This duel would have to be quick. He didn’t know how many other challengers he would have afterwards. A swift victory would conserve his energy and send a clear message to the others. They let him lead while they followed out of birthright and reverence to his immortal body, but he could earn it just the same.

He charged first and darted at the very tip of Hypatos’ range. Like any Kremnoan, his weapon was an extension of his body. He knew the length of his spear just as he knew the length of his arm and didn’t waste the energy going for a hit he couldn’t land.

Instead, he worked on closing that remaining sliver of distance with small but certain steps and only jabbed to keep Mydei from breaching the edge of his range.

The duel wouldn’t be decided by first blood, but whether Mydei could breach Hypatos’ defences. Once Mydei was in, it would be much more difficult for him to defend himself. He could end him in an instant.

But Mydei had another advantage. Hypatos was one of the oldest members from a group of exiles that gathered long before Mydei was plucked out the woods like a feral dog. His age was beginning to set in and his Kremnoan discipline kept his body in fighting condition. But his age showed in his slightly hindered reflexes and less tricky manoeuvres.

Mydei dodged his jab and feinted that he was about to press an attack only to draw back again when Hypatos saw his bluff and blocked against a potential blow. Then he countered into Mydei’s open side.

One he had left exposed. He let the blade barely avoid skimming his torso. Then he snapped his arm shut around the polearm right below the blade and pinned it to his side. A risky, ridiculous tactic no would pull in the heat of battle. Except Mydei who didn’t fear blood nor Death.

He grabbed the staff and yanked with strength far greater this his small body. Hypatos was a better warrior than to let go but his grip faltered just enough. Mydei dropped the weapon and charged in.

There was nothing Hypatos could do. Mydei was too close, too fast, for him to bring the spear back into the new range of combat. Mydei thrust his claw at Hypatos’ face and his eyes closed with acceptance.

Metal scraped skin and red beaded from the surface. Hypatos opened his eyes and his fingers hesitated before they grazed the thin cut on his cheek, smearing blood.

Mydei stepped back and faced the crowd. “Who’s next?”

Kyros. Agathon. Polydorus. The list went on of warriors who stood tall against him only to spill their mortal blood and be knocked low.

The crowd roared, chalices clacking and coins rattling. People offered him food and drink between rounds. The purpose of the duels had been all but forgotten by the thrill of a good fight. Feats of strength that demanded their respect, their subordination, their loyalty. This was a Kremnos Festival and who better to emerge victorious than Mydei.

It was so loud Mydei was almost too overwhelmed to notice the sudden smell of Death. It appeared rapidly, unexpectedly, surging like the tide and clinging onto him, dragging him into the lightless depths.

“Mydeimos!” Leonnius pushed through the onlookers marking the edge of the arena. “It’s Aedes Elysiae. The whole village is being consumed by flames and monsters of the black tide.”

Aedes Elysiae.

Phainon.

“Everyone prepare for battle!”

The detachment scattered to gather their equipment. Mydei was already equipped and limber but he could only stand there, arms crossed and claws digging into flesh.

If Mydei had met Phainon like he intended, then they would have been together when the black tide arrived. They could have fought side by side, guarded each other’s weaknesses, come back alive.

His grip tightened. No. No that wasn’t right. Phainon was alive. He had to be. Mydei knew that he survived this so they could meet again in the future.

But he also knew that the two of them were never supposed to meet so young. A scale, an oracle card, a signet ring. The sun and moon exchanging places ten times to witness their duel.

Mydei wasn’t supposed to know the words Aedes Elysiae but knew them anyway. And what if that was the difference between life and death? What if Phainon died because of him.

“I’m going ahead.”

His feet pointed towards golden wheat fields set ablaze and a sun swallowed by the black tide.

Perdikkas stepped forward to protest but didn’t dare grab him, “Mydeimos —“

“Prioritise your lives and evacuate the villagers!”

The detachment had faced the black tide before. It was an inevitability of wandering the outskirts of Amphoreus, skimming along all the cracks where the black tide seeped through and stained all living things with the touch of not only Death but total annihilation.

They knew the procedure and charged in with caution and control—but not fear.

Not like Mydei. He was always fearful when black tide came. Not for himself but for a comrade too swept up in the fervour of battle, venturing too far into the tide, and getting swept away only to be spat back out an unrecognisable monster. One Mydei would take the responsibility of putting down.

The fields no longer smelled like wheat and sea salt. Every gust of wind mocked him, carrying embers and anguish that bloodied the sky the further he ran.

The hill Phainon liked to hide on and had shared with Mydei was empty. The schoolhouse was ablaze. The marketplace was gouged open. The statue of Oronyx and the Sacramental Courtyard had crumbled as the Titan of Time abandoned the village.

A shrill cry rattled like a death throe and he spun, thrusting his palm out. He caught a creature of the black tide by the jaw. Short and thin. Limbs grotesquely pulled longer than its body and stretched enough for orange to pulse through blackened skin.

It shrieked and charged at him again on clumsy limbs. The same way a child stumbled when they first learned to walk. He grit his teeth and grappled at its body. Its head swayed on its gangly neck and a low voice chittering grated on his ears. He needed to keep it away before it corroded him too.

He swung it round and knocked it to the ground. Feet on its back, he grabbed its head and pulled until a sickening crack echoed in his ears and the head came free and body fell limp. He tossed it aside and kept going.

The house he had shared a meal in with Phainon’s family, changed in with old clothes Phainon worried himself over, napped in upon a thin cot he shared with Phainon—it was already a cremated husk of ash and memories. The wind chime rattled out a hollow welcome.

Phainon was still nowhere to be found.

Another scream, a human one, rang through the air. High, female. Followed by a rough bark Mydei knew anywhere.

He raced for the coast. There, cornered on the pier. Audata, Hieronymus and Snowy. Three creatures of the black tide. Audata held Snowy back by the collar while Hieronymus’ shaky hands raised a sickle.

Mydei launched himself forward and slammed his feet into one creature’s back. It flew off the pier into the water and sank into the sea dyed red.

The other two creatures rounded on him but he was already reaching for one and it had hardly finished turning before his claws were around its throat. He swept its legs out and jerked his arm back, tearing out its jugular in a putrid spray of rot.

One left and it was already swinging at him. No time to dodge. He whipped his hand up and the blade growing from its arms like distended bone and mutilated flesh clashed against his gauntlets.

He winced as it nicked skin further up his forearm. The skin would soon blacken. The injury was small enough he didn’t need to worry about corruption.

He reeled his other arm back and punched the creature in the chest. It didn’t stumble but it jolted back just enough for him to slip out from under its blade.

He snagged Hieronymus’ sickle and dodged the creature’s next attack. He closed the distance and looped the sickle around the back of its neck. When he pulled, the head came clean off.

Three creatures dead. Three civilians behind him. Audata and Hieronymus gaped at him. He flicked the evidence of the Black Tide from the metal and flipped the hilt for Hieronymus to grasp. Audata fell to her knees, catching herself on Snowy’s big back, with a dry sob.

“Where’s Phainon?” Mydei asked and motioned again for Hieronymus to take the sickle. It was hardly a weapon but better than nothing.

Hieronymus’ hands still trembled but his eyes widened with alarm rather than the fear of death. “He-he isn’t with you?“

“I…” He clacked his gauntlets. “I missed our meeting.”

“He could be anywhere!” Audata wailed and her hand grappled at the air, too weak to reach for Hieronymus’ leg right beside her. “Our boy. Oh my boy. What if—what if—“

“Phainon’s strong,” he interrupted, voice too hard for much reassurance but the two parents looked at him for it anyway.

Audata’s eyes glistened with more tears to shed, heedless of all that had already fallen. “He is but… but he’s just a boy. He’s never even left home

and—“ another broken sob.

Mydei wondered if his mother would’ve cried like this for him, if she hadn’t died before he had been thrown away to drown in Death.

“I’ll find him.”

It was a ridiculous thing to promise. Amongst all the blood and smoke and abominations, that he would find a single person. Alive, uncorrupted.

But it was Phainon.

And his parents looked at Mydei with hope.

He led them to the edge of the village and told them to run east where they would eventually meet with his army. Then he dove back into the calamity.

There were likely still civilians trapped in corners he couldn’t find but he couldn’t hope to hunt them all down before the black tide did. So he did the next best thing.

At the top of the hill, stood in front of the Sacramental Courtyard, he let loose a war cry. It erupted from his stomach, roaring across the valley, and daring all to come face him and just try to steal a life even the Hand of Shadow could not.

He backed into the Sacramental Courtyard. Before everything could arrive, he tipped the bookshelves to block each of the side entrances. He couldn’t let himself get swarmed. He needed to funnel them in. A small crack between the top of the archways and the bookshelves meant he could slip through if he needed an escape.

The black tide surged to meet him. The creatures flooded in through the main entrance and Mydei tore his way through with hands, feet and teeth when necessary. It was almost nostalgic to taste a monstrous Death in his mouth and feel it rend as it collided with his immortal body.

The successive duels from that morning had diminished his energy but he was still a force to be reckoned with on the battlefield. Even if his senses

were slightly dulled and his reflexes slightly slowed, he was still leagues above the black tide.

He wrenched a creature’s arms behind its back and kicked. Its body flew into a group of other creature charging towards him and knocked them aside. He swung the severed arm still in his grasp at another creature before he tossed it aside with a battle cry, preparing to dive back with his hands.

A shadow drifted over the courtyard.

He looked up. Thoughts, visions, memories surged through his mind and his back burned under the weight of it.

The figure was cloaked in black and masked in gold but Mydei could still feel its gaze pricking him. Stabbing him the same as that corroded great sword in its hand.

It tipped its head. Mydei took a single step.

A black blade ripped through his chest. He choked on gold spluttering past his lips. The blade of a black tide creature pulled free and he collapsed to the ground.

Through the cold waters of the Sea of Souls washing over him, he thought he heard someone call his name.

Mydeimos. When he was a child adrift and alone he hadn’t known that voice. Now he knew beyond any doubt that it was Gorgo, his mother, who had accompanied him all these years. Stand up. There are still great things for you to accomplish.

The Sea of Souls was so cold. But it was also peaceful outside of that abyss he had fallen into after he was born. Not the lull of a warm place, but the cold silence turned his mind sluggish and his soul lethargic. Rest, it told him. Stay here. Forget the Strife that comes with living.

Mydei. And he hadn’t known that voice either back then. Still, for the longest time, hadn’t known even when the tales of his mother had filled him

with such certainty for the first voice. But the more he heard that name spoken to him everyday—overjoyed, sulky, outraged. In tears, in laughter, in fondness—the more certain he was. Let’s meet again.

The first thing he saw when he opened his eyes was white. A beacon in the smoke and shadow, gleaming more than even the blade arcing through the air.

Phainon. His face twisted in anguish and crowned in gold. Gold. His blade an unending source of destruction against the decimation of his sleepy, sunbathed existence. His back wide and strong where he positioned himself like a bulwark between Mydei’s prone body and the black tide coming to devour it.

Mydei coughed wetly and spat gold—the same gold coursing through Phainon’s veins—across the floor. He rolled onto his front and his body was still sluggish when he pushed himself onto his feet.

Phainon’s sword was locked with a black tide creature. He couldn’t break away even as another creature aimed for his exposed side. Mydei whipped a fist across its face.

Phainon’s head snapped around like he had been struck. “M-Mydei!”

“Focus!” he snarled back and grabbed the creature still reeling from the punch. He tossed it at the creature Phainon was still caught in battle with.

Phainon’s gaze was still filled with too emotions to disentangle. But they were all locked behind a steely resolve and he nodded, raising his weapon ready.

They moved in sync to stand back to back.

The black tide was no match for them. It had struggled when they were alone but together they were unstoppable.

They fought beside each other, opening avenues for a new offensive, covering each other’s weak points, and Mydei had never truly understood

the thrill Strife could bring until now. It wasn’t just fuel to strike harder, faster, to wrestle for glory and emerge victorious. It was a bulwark. A protector.

Mydei thought the epitome of combat would be the day him and Phainon clashed as incontestable equals, consumed by thoughts of victory. He was wrong.

This—moving in sync like the tide pushed and pulled, like the seasons handed over their reign to the next, like the sun and moon cycled—it was addictive. He wanted more. He wanted it to never end.

A klaxon boomed over the valley and signalled the arrival of the Kremnoan detachment.

Mydei dashed for the side exit and Phainon even didn’t ask before he followed. They hopped over the bookcase, a tighter squeeze for Phainon than Mydei, and ran for the hill where a flag whipped in the wind.

The tight formation parted like a curtain to pull them in and closed around them again. Mydei panted from exhaustion as the detachment pushed the two of them to the back lines but he fumbled behind him with a clumsy hand that could hardly remember to be gentle after such violence.

Phainon took Mydei’s hand and Mydei could face ahead knowing Phainon was right behind him.

Word had travelled faster than the two of them and Perdikkas already had a bottle uncorked. It was one of the most valuable items in the detachment’s possession and only two people had the right to so much as touch it: Mydei and Perdikkas.

“Wounds?” Perdikkas asked immediately.

Mydei stripped his clothes and gauntlets and tossed them aside. He looked at Phainon expectantly and his hands fumbled but he began to do the same. Their clothes were stained with the black tide and someone came to take them away, hands wrapped in ragged cloth, to be burned.

A few small cuts on his arms, his legs, and one across his forehead. There was also the wound through his chest. It had shrunken while he was pulled under the Sea of Souls. But where a normal wound would have already closed with only the thinnest fold of skin left behind that, too, would heal in a blink, the black tide kept the wound open. The blood sluggishly trickled down his torso.

Perdikkas cursed and tipped the contents of the bottle into a shallow dish. He dipped a roll of clean bandages in and soaked them through before winding them around Mydei’s chest.

The water was from a Temple of Phagousa. Blessed. It could cleanse the effects of the black tide assuming they weren’t so severe they twisted humanity to monstrosity. The detachment had taken them as spoils from an army of Phagousa followers. It would be near impossible get their hands on more.

“I found your parents and got them to safety. Snowy, too,” Mydei said as Perdikkas handed him a cloth dabbed in blessed water for Mydei to hold against his cuts.

Phainon still hadn’t moved. No reaction even as Perdikkas started wrapping his wounds. His eyes had never looked so dull.

He blinked unseeing at Mydei, then the words hit and his eyes widened. “My…”

He jerked forward and Mydei hardly had time to open his arms before Phainon fell into them and wrapped Mydei in his own.

“Thank you.” His voice cracked and his arms trembled where they had been so strong holding his blade. “Thank you.”

Mydei let the hold linger for a moment, knowing a single moment made all the difference in a patient’s recovery or a battle. Perdikkas was looking at him disapprovingly but Mydei couldn’t bring himself to shake Phainon off just yet.

Luckily, Phainon pulled back on his own and Perdikkas immediately went back to purifying his wounds.

They clothed themselves in spare garments. Mydei had his own set, smaller than the ones prepared for the rest of the detachment. Despite being several years younger, Phainon filled out the tunic in all but the slightest slack to the shoulders.

Mydei rifled through a chest beside the medical supplies until he found a small wooden box. He clicked the lid open and pulled out a fresh set of gauntlets. He slid his hands in and buckled until a hand caught his wrist.

“What are you doing?” Phainon demanded.

Mydei had no qualms about shaking him off now, testing his gauntlets with a curl and uncurl of his fingers. “Going back into battle.”

Gauntlets back on, Mydei stood to leave.

Phainon grabbed his shoulder and hissed, “Are you out of your mind?”

“Those are my men fighting on my orders.” Mydei tried to shrug him off but his grip was too tight and only tightened when he realised Mydei was trying to leave. “I can’t expect them to risk their lives while I wait in the back lines.”

Phainon’s grip dug in like he had claws to could gouge into Mydei’s flesh and hold him there. “You already died!”

And he finally noticed the tremor through that hand.

“I saw it.”

The look in Phainon’s eyes was haunted. The very same as warriors who swore they saw the ghosts of their comrades lingering on the battlefield. In their dreams.

“You-“ Phainon choked and his hand drifted down, large and calloused when it rested against Mydei’s chest. Above the still bleeding wound.

“Right here. You collapsed. Your eyes glassy. You weren’t breathing. Your heart stopped. Mydei…”

No one had ever looked at Mydei with such grief etched into their face. So overwhelming it surged from where it weighed heavy in Phainon’s chest right into Mydei’s squeezing lungs and clenching heart.

“You were dead,” Phainon whispered and he hadn’t realised the sheen of his dazed eyes had been tears until they spilled.

They cut through the ashen grime clinging to Phainon’s skin. Like a Blessing of Phagousa, it cleansed him of the mire and rot of battle. They glided over the curve of his cheeks, dipped under his jaw, down his neck to skin hidden under fabric or fell away to water the earth.

And Mydei was struck by how pretty Phainon looked in tears shed for him.

Then Phainon pulled his hands away and swiped at his eyes, his cheeks, wiping away his tears. It seemed for a moment that he was done but the tears renewed with a harsh sniff and he dropped his head into his hands.

Mydei’s tongue was heavy but he found the will to move it. “Find your parents. They’ll want to know you’re alive.”

“While you go into battle?” Phainon snapped but his anger was weakened by the teary waver of his voice. “I’m going with you.”

“No.”

He scowled. “So it’s all right for you to go but not me?”

“I don’t have time to explain,” he snarled back. “Just trust me.”

Phainon’s eyes stayed narrowed, skeptical, his lips bared in the beginnings of fangs. Then his face softened. The anger gave way and he looked Mydei up and down with renewed calmness.

He breathed a sound too rough to be a sigh, too tired to be anything else, as his whole body slumped. “Then go.”

Mydei turned to leave but something stopped him. He glanced back. Phainon was already watching him.

“Phainon…” Mydei clenched his hands at his side. “I’m sorry I missed our meeting.”

His eyes widened, blinking. His lips curled into the smallest smile and Mydei knew they would be okay. “Then make it up to me later.”

“I will,” he promised. “Let’s meet again.”

Then he took off and dove back into Strife to protect everything waiting behind him.

Chapter End Notes

If you saw the chapter count go up… no you didn’t. My first draft is a near flawless piece of writing with perfectly cut chapters and no added or seriously extended scenes.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei deals with the aftermath of the black tide.

Chapter Notes

There were immutable laws of combat within the detachment: avoid unnecessary cruelty, abide by Kremnoan military discipline, never leave comrades unguarded. To break such laws would incur punishment. Simple camaraderie wasn’t always enough to hold everyone together, from the crafty to the fools all with their own hidden desires that could arise at the most inconvenient moments, through every hardship.

But there was another unofficial one: Mydei was the first to change into battle and the last to return. Some loathed that he reversed such glory for himself but who among them could compete with his immortal body as the spear tip of the offensive that breached enemy lines.

The black tide wasn’t so simple. It couldn’t be purged or coerced into retreat by any death defying show that scattered regular armies. But the detachment fought to slow its incursion so the backline could retreat with the injured and civilians.

The numbing exertion of battle wasn’t anywhere near as exciting without Phainon at his back but the tear of corrupted flesh beneath his claws was an adequate outlet for the… fear and panic Mydei let consume him earlier. The moment he heard about the black tide ravaging Aedes Elysiae, he lost control of himself—his rationality, his military strategy, his leadership and responsibilities—when he should have known better. The detachment was his to lead, not simply command and vanish. Phainon was a worthy warrior who would have emerged scathed but alive.

Mydei channelled all his frustrations into his fist and ripped the head off a black tide creature. He picked up the body and threw it at an oncoming hoard, opening the way for his men nearby to descend with their shields up and spears out.

While his men fought in formations to watch over each other as they held the black tide, Mydei fought alone. He lashed out with the ferocity of a spear poised to end battles only to withdraw and find himself beside his comrades who needed him most, melding into their attack before he charged off again.

Ptolemy’s spear soared past Mydei’s head and impaled a black tide creature through the chest. Mydei grabbed the polearm and let the dead body slide itself off the spear tip. The dust hadn’t yet settled before Mydei tossed the weapon back to its rightful owner.

The black tide grounded the detachment’s cavalry. The horses’ bulky stature, speed and strength made them even more dangerous than humans once twisted by the black tide.

“Start moving the frontline back. Do not take risks to hold it,” Mydei commanded before he darted away to where he was needed and relay the same orders elsewhere.

When the klaxon sounded from beyond the horizon, the dying wails of the final black tide creatures almost drowned out the signal of the backline’s safety. But the second sound bellowed long and loud over the valley and a final third confirmation. The black tide had been suppressed for now but there was no telling when the next surge would bring more creatures to the surface. Mydei ordered a swift retreat.

The wheat fields were still ablaze but the travel worn path was wide enough to let them through with sweat and warmed skin instead of burns. Mydei brought up the rear as they blitzed down the trail faster than the flames or the black tide could follow. They didn’t stop until they passed the detachment’s backline cutting a firebreak through the long grass.

The evening sky was empty of clouds and relatively warm and dry. No rain to douse the fire. If the detachment were the only concern, they would have packed up and left at the sight of wildfires feasting on dry lands but it wasn’t an option with so many exhausted civilians and wounded warriors. A firebreak was the next best option.

The encampment had never been so full yet there was only one person Mydei ached to see. He wasn’t so reckless he would skip a medical examination and purification from Perdikkas—not when his thigh still throbbed where a black tide creature had burst from the debris of a fallen house and cut him deep—but his head swivelled as he searched the many familiar and unknown faces.

There. Running errands. Brow set and eyes shadowed with fatigue. Hands steady as he carried a basket of dirtied gauze to be properly disposed of, but stopped long enough to offer a reassuring hand to an injured civilian bandaged around one eye.

As though feeling Mydei’s gaze, Phainon glanced over. He took him all in, searching for blood and life on Mydei’s battered body. Then he smiled, nodded and they both parted ways.

Neither had time for a proper reunion. Mydei needed treatment and a strategy meeting. Phainon was doing everything he could to ease the burdens of the detachment and refugees. What had become of his friends, neighbours, home. The one he had taken Mydei’s hand and walked him through.

The medical tent was surrounded by those in need of treatment but Mydei was taken right inside. Leonnius had heard of their arrival and met Mydei there to take his message to Krateros, who arrived not long after Perdikkas had wrapped Mydei’s thigh in gauze dampened with Phagousa’s blessing. They were running low. Another problem he needed to deal with.

“Your Highness,” Krateros’s voice croaked from overuse and lack of water. Perdikkas poured him a glass and he threw it back in one swig as though it were honey brew.

“These are only minor injuries,” Mydei reassured him and Perdikkas raised a brow but didn’t argue over how the blade had gone clean through his thigh. “Tell me your report.”

“No Kremnoan casualties; seven major injuries. I’ve told the elders of Aedes Elysiae to draw up a census so they can track the alive, injured and dead.”

There was no category for missing when it came to the black tide. Only dead. A monster without its humanity was as good as a corpse.

The census was necessary to manage their resources. Even without exact numbers, they could continue to rely on the same water supply. The river would suffice for all of them. Once they were on the move, water skins would be more of an issue.

So would food. The detachment balanced rations with hunting and gathering. Either way, it would be a struggle to feed so many extra mouths. The civilians would only be with them for a few days, at most a week, but it was an issue of quantity.

“In the morning send Ptolemy’s cavalry to the nearest settlements,” Mydei ordered as he pulled a fresh tunic over his head.

Krateros stroked his beard. “I’ll order them to purchase supplies first, then warn them about the black tide’s closeness and the refugees about to move through the area.”

All garments touched by the black tide had to be burned; armour and weaponry cleansed in flames. Although Kremnoans possessed a certain laxity towards clothing, another reason to spit barbaric when they passed, Mydei could assume they had enough spare clothing to distribute since he failed to see any of the detachment running about the encampment naked.

“Injured and children take the tents. Our men will have to sort out exact arrangements between themselves. Everyone else sleeps rough.”

It was nightfall that finally lulled the chaos to rest. The civilians answered to the census in exchange for dinner rations before settling down to sleep. The detachment kept their distance from the campfires the villagers chose to cluster around but it was impossible to miss the quiet sobs that arose like the crack and snap of firewood under heat.

While Kremnoans honoured their dead with feasts and toasts to their valour, it was not the detachment plagued by loss. Of their bonds, their home and peaceful way of life. So the warriors allowed the villagers to mourn in silence and prepare themselves for the early morning departure.

Despite the protests from the detachment, Mydei gave his tent to a family of six. Instead, he lounged by one of the campfires along the edge of the encampment where Hephaestion joined him.

“Perdikkas told us the news.”

Mydei swirled the chalice of his preferred drink. An offering from Hephaestion, so Mydei had some idea that this conversation would go somewhere he didn’t appreciate. “Be more specific.”

“About that little friend of yours. The one who happens to bleed gold.”

Gold had contrasted against his eyes and his hair so beautifully.

Mydei took a sip. “Right.”

“Leonnius nearly fell flat on his face when he heard. Ptolemy and Peucesta are already composing verse about such a fated encounter. And I’m here asking you: did you know?”

“Not until the black tide spilled it from him.”

“And you asked him to join the detachment even so?”

Mydei grunted. “Never got around to it.”

“Mydeimos…” He sighed and shook his head, giving them both a chance to breathe as they drank from their cups; Hephaestion’s undiluted pomegranate

juice instead of the usual honey brew. It wasn’t a night for merry drinks. “He won’t be the one to ask.”

“I intend to,” Mydei argued around the rim of his chalice.

In his defence, he had. The timing had simply been poor. Mydei had been too swept up in the peace Phainon handed him freely, hiding away from his inevitable departure from Aedes Elysiae, before the consequences of his indecision brought duel after duel to keep the detachment together. Then the black tide.

“Will you act on those intentions?”

“Yes.”

Hephaestion stayed silent but waiting.  Until it became clear Mydei had nothing more to say and he arched a brow. “And yet?”

Mydei huffed. “And yet what?”

“Mydeimos, I have never seen the prospect of words frighten you so since you first learned to differentiate speech from noise.”

Mydei’s pride twinged but he hid it behind another long sip. It almost made it sound like Mydei was overwhelmed with cowardice.

”And yet,” Mydei relented sharply but he sighed and the edge to his voice softened, “he experienced his first loss today. He needs time.”

When members of the detachment were exiled by law, it took them time wandering alone to adjust to the loss of their home. When members of the detachment were exiled by choice, they had long prepared themselves for the same loss. Both groups still mourned that point of no return.

And who if not a warrior could appreciate the pain of witnessing life bleed out into nothingness for the very first time.

“His future is uncertain,” Hephaestion agreed with a considering tilt of his head, blond hair burning red in the firelight. “But is that not precisely the

perfect time to offer him something he can grasp hold of and take heart in.”

Mydei ran his thumb across the chalice’s smooth surface, then the lines of the emblem of Strife carved into the face.

Was it cowardice? If Phainon rejected his offer then he would accept it—of course he would. There was nothing else to do—but it would still ache every time he reminisced on their short time together. They only fought as allies instead of sparring partners once but Mydei knew there would never be anything like it again.

To ask while he was still reeling from such a devastating loss, wouldn’t that be the same as coercion? It was natural to seek out sympathetic comrades and stability during troubled times. But it wasn’t as though he had no other options. He still had the parents and his dog he adored, and his community he could follow if all he wanted was safety, stability and people who understood.

If Mydei truly trusted Phainon, he would trust him to follow the choice most true to himself. Even if that meant parting ways.

His mouth curled into a self-deprecating smile. “As always, you make excellent points Hephaestion. If you dressed more modestly and masked that accent, you might even pass as an Okheman with that tongue of yours.”

Hephaestion guffawed. “To be so insulted by you after offering my sincere advice. Would it be unwise to extend an offer of my company too?”

Mydei shook his head and his smile grew at his dearest friend. “Go rest. I assume you and the others managed to barter, strong arm and cheat your way into a tent for the night.”

Hephaestion read the dismissal—Mydei would rather be alone—and left with a wish for a pleasant rest. He must have relayed the news to their friends because none of them came with an offer to join him. It was only him as he swirled his chalice in hand and gazed at the night sky. The day’s smoke had blotted out all the stars.

The grass rustled under foot of something bigger than an animal and from the wrong direction to be the night watch. Only one person would be audacious enough to bother him.

Phainon stopped at the edge of the tarp, leaning into Mydei peripheral vision. “Mind if I join?”

He grunted his approval and Phainon lowered himself onto the edge of Mydei’s waxed tarp. Out the corner of his eye, Phainon winced at the pull of his exhausted muscles but he slowly laid down and breathed with relief when he was finally flat after being on his feet all day.

Mydei finished his pomegranate juice and set the chalice aside. He swiped the back of his hand across his mouth. “You should be resting. We have an early morning.”

They needed to get further away from the black tide as quickly as possible. If someone had ever been foolish yet intelligent, courageous yet reckless, enough to measure the exact speed of the black tide’s spread, they weren’t a member of the detachment. They could only assume it was swift and act accordingly.

Phainon tucked his hands behind his head. “Couldn’t sleep. What about you?”

He shrugged. “Couldn’t sleep.”

They both gazed at the same empty sky. Like every star meant to guide them had been snuffed out by the black tide as easily as blowing out a candle. Even the moon was dim and hazy.

“I’ve never seen so few stars in Aedes Elysiae,” Phainon mused, voice lower than Mydei had ever heard it. Too weighted to attempt his usual levity. “Although, it’s not really Aedes Elysiae anymore, is it?”

It was the nature of a wanderer that Mydei had never been attached to one place. The closest he’d ever come was Aedes Elysiae but that was put to an abrupt end. But there were other things Mydei knew how to hold onto. A

home constantly on the move. Nowhere and yet with him every step of the way.

“So long as you remember how the night sky looked from the wheat fields, that will be Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon stared at the sky, and Mydei hoped he was seeing stars, before he rolled onto his side. “You’re such a brute when you fight yet you say the most profound things.” There was almost humour there, if it weren’t so fragile. “Is that the mark of a good prince?”

Mydei took in the view one final time before he rolled, one arm braced under his head, so they were face to face. “Where did you hear that?”

The distance wasn’t much different than when they had laid flat side-by-side. If anything it was larger without the widths of their shoulders stretched across the tarp. But the space narrowed as they curled towards each other.

They had been closer before. Napped beside each other on a cot at Phainon’s house because Mydei was clearly exhausted after a night plagued by the past, or in the wheat fields after a good spar.

But it felt different when Phainon nuzzled his cheek against his tucked arm and watched Mydei, blue eyes almost alight beneath his lashes. There was a scabbed cut just above his brow, a patch of gauze on his cheek, and his skin was clean but his dirtied hair was still ashy.

Mydei wanted to reach out and learn whether his hands could be gentle enough to run along the cut without drawing fresh blood. But he gripped his forearm and waited for what came next.

Phainon shrugged, giving nothing away. “Around. Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos Mydeimos. I guess that oracle card was more literal than I thought.”

Mydei’s grip tightened but he didn’t look away. He owed it to Phainon to meet his eye when confronted with the fact he had been less than forthcoming about his identity. “So…”

“So?”

“What now?”

Phainon blinked. “What now?”

“That’s what…” Mydei exhaled. He couldn’t begrudge Phainon for being difficult. “That’s what I said.”

Phainon nuzzled his head against his arm again. His languid blink was heavy with sleep but he forced his eyes to stay open, if only half-lidded. “What do you want to happen?”

“Don’t do that.”

“Do what?”

Mydei’s face scrunched. “Defer to me. I thought we were…”

Friends. But he was friends with Hephaestion, Perdikkas, Leonnius, Ptolemy, Peucesta. They deferred to his judgement all the time. It was an inevitability when there were more titles to their relationship than friends; too many threads tangled together of what they were and did for each other. Friends, confidants, comrades. Teachers and student. Ruler and citizen.

With Phainon…

“Aren’t we friends,” he muttered in his arm, so childish it burned his ears. It wasn’t the same as his other dearest companions but he said friends and it sounded like more.

Either Phainon didn’t notice or he didn’t care because he smiled and stretched out a hand. Mydei squeezed his arm a final time and reached out. His gauntlets were sharp, deadly, but he was mindful of all the cutting edges when he twined their fingers together.

Phainon’s smiled, soft at the corners and the crease of his eyes. “We are.”

The burn in his ears spread lower and Mydei concentrated on keeping it out of his cheeks. “Good.”

Phainon was already half asleep and Mydei expected him to drift the rest of the way. He had a long day, and another come morning.

But his fingers twitched under Mydei’s hand and his lashes fluttered, eyes darting down when they had so steadfastly held Mydei’s own.

“What?” Mydei’s voice was low, word slurring together. Maybe he was closer to sleep than he thought too.

He shook his head, biting his lip. “Forget it.”

He shed the exhaustion with a few hard blinks. “Why? It’s bothering you.”

“You have enough troubles to deal with.”

“Without adding you to my burdens?” He let a little meanness, some mockery, seep through. “Stop assuming my limits. If I couldn’t handle it, I wouldn’t ask.”

Another flutter of his lashes as he briefly met Mydei’s eye only to glance away again but Mydei knew he had him.

“Cyrene…”

Mydei hadn’t hovered during the village census. He had delegated Krateros to interact with the village elders and ensure everything was organised for refugees while Mydei managed the detachment. But it was impossible not to notice a head of pink hair missing from the encampment.

He hadn’t known her very well beyond her devotion to Oronyx and her mischievous nature hidden behind an innocent smile. It was Phainon that connected them. But he thought they could have been friends, too, one day and it was all the possibilities of a future she wouldn’t have, one he failed to protect along side the others, that he mourned.

Mydei squeezed once and Phainon gripped tight in turn.

“We were together just that morning. How did she…” His teeth dug in harder than before, enough Mydei expected to see gold. He shook his head and scrunched his eyes shut. “I just can’t believe she’s…”

Another squeeze and Mydei felt his fingers relax again. He ran his thumb along the meat of Phainon’s thumb. “I’m sorry.”

If he made their meeting that morning, been there when the black tide struck, then maybe, just maybe, Phainon would still have best friend.

And he knew it never would have happened. He never would have abandoned the detachment in such a precarious state.

But if Mydei had been better? Done better as their leader? More attentive, more skilful, more mature and less selfish. Maybe he could have alleviated the unease before it erupted and still arrived to their meeting on time and walked away with everything still intact.

Weak and wet, Phainon laughed. “Why are you apologising? I talked to my mum and dad. They told me how you saved them. Snowy, too.”

“I was looking for you.”

But Phainon had been the one to find him in the Sacramental Courtyard. Golden blood pooling around a dead body.

Mydei tucked his legs tighter, almost to his chest. The wound had long since closed but he could still feel the trickle of blood down his chest as though it hadn’t. “I never wanted you to see that.”

“You dead?” He breathed a gutted, hollowed out laugh. “Yeah I never wanted to see that either.”

“You don’t have to pretend to be so glib.”

“I already cried in front of you today. Let me try to preserve some of my dignity.”

Mydei frowned and shuffled closer, just a little, like that minuscule distance would help him rip that mask right from Phainon’s face. It would be easier to speak in Kremnoan, the language could be more crude than common tongue but he found it easiest to express himself in, yet it would defeat the purpose if Phainon couldn’t understand. So Mydei worked his tired mind to translate the things he needed to say.

“You don’t need dignity. You need to mourn your loses and move forward.”

Phainon closed his eyes and inhaled deep, releasing a soft sigh. “Mourn, huh.” His lips thinned and his jaw tightened around a short, shaky inhale. “That black-robed swordsman, he brought the black tide to Aedes Elysiae. Everything I wanted to protect is gone. How am I supposed to move forward when he still lives?”

The two of them had become similar in ways Mydei would never wish upon anyone. Least of all Phainon. No matter how Phainon had let him pretend at playing house in Aedes Elysiae, as much as any sword or spear, his body of steel was forged for battle. Mydei’s jagged edges didn’t slot into a life of peace.

But peace fitted Phainon in the way peace fitted all lives untouched by Strife. Even more, it embraced him in endless wheat and the sea breeze. A carefree smile, an idealism, a sense of heroism.

Now every shadow upon Phainon’s face was burdened by all he had lost and sought retribution for. Like one final death would lift that darkness and make the sun rise warm and tranquil over the wheat fields again.

“Revenge is nothing more than an obligation of the living to the dead,” Mydei spoke low but firm.

That wasn’t the lesson Krateros had taught him, nor the expectations of the detachment—all of whom eagerly awaited for the day he claimed his father’s head. To them, revenge was a matter of honour and succession.

Yet Mydei struggled to see what honour or satisfaction could be found in the act. It was his duty as his mother’s son to avenge her and send the man

who murdered her down the Sea of Souls so she could confront him for herself. But he wouldn’t celebrate when his father was dead at his feet— hadn’t as far as the vague mural of memories told him—just mourned that it had been necessary at all.

He exhaled and could see his reflection held in Phainon’s eyes as he came so close their foreheads almost touched, words brushing skin as though he could force Phainon to take them all in. “But you bear responsibilities to those who still live, and to yourself.”

A shuddered breath and Phainon rolled onto his back, keeping their hands firmly intertwined but throwing the other arm over his eyes. “What does forward even mean? All I wanted was to protect my home. Protect and help everyone. Now I don’t know where to go from here.”

Mydei pinched his hand but Phainon’s arm didn’t move. He frowned and demanded sharply, “What are you talking about now?”

That got Phainon to uncover his eyes and roll his neck to meet Mydei’s glare. “Huh?”

He huffed and averted his eyes for a beat before he steeled himself to speak his next words to Phainon’s face. “You so arrogantly declared you would make my wishes come true. Wouldn’t the Deliverer have to stay by my side to make that happen?”

It took Phainon a few beats to understand but when he did his eyes blew wide. “Mydei…”

He swallowed the rest of the words down.

Mydei squinted. Would he really have to say it plainly before Phainon stopped doubting himself? “You have a place in the Kremnoan detachment. If that is what you want.”

None of the Kremnoans would refuse. They all knew that Phainon was the one the Sea of Souls, or wherever that knowledge had come from, had sent Mydei to find. Their patience had worn at the idea of Mydei choosing to

settle in a small wheat farming village for some boy rather than live up to the glory expected of the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos and their hope to return to a place they could proudly proclaim as home.

It was different if Phainon joined their life of wandering. And he had the skill to cut down any objections through a duel.

Phainon hadn’t stopped staring.

Mydei clenched the hand tucked behind his head but kept his expression carefully neutral. “Or you can seek out Okhema.” That was where they were recommending all the refugees flee to. “The holy city won’t turn a Chrysos Heir away. And you won’t have to fear another incursion of the black—“

Phainon jerked upright and Mydei hissed as his shoulder tugged in its socket but he didn’t have time to complain when Phainon’s hands landed on either side of his head.

There were no stars and no moon. Phainon’s face was cast entirely in darkness as he loomed over Mydei. But his eyes shone with all the stars plucked from the night sky above his home.

His smile stretched across his entire face. Happier than Mydei had ever seen. “I’ll come with you!”

The burn spread down to his cheeks, maybe even his neck, as he hoped the darkness was enough to hide it. “Oh.”

“Well, actually I will have to discuss it with my parents. They’re far from old but they aren’t young either. So it depends on their plans and the rest of the villagers but I would be a terrible son to abandon them if they have no one else to rely on—“

“Breathe.”

Phainon took a deep breath and it was too dark to confirm but Mydei thought he saw a slight tinge to his cheeks. So Phainon could absolutely see

his and that knowledge made his skin warm even further.

“But they want me to happy,” Phainon concluded quietly, an absolute fondness overwhelming his face. They was so close if Phainon leaned down any further his bangs would brush against Mydei’s forehead. “So will you tell me what your wish is?”

“No.”

“Then how am I supposed to make it come true?”

“Figure it out yourself, Deliverer.”

The name rolled off his tongue so naturally, even more so than the name Phainon.

He pouted and flopped to his side, thinking for a moment before a sly smirk returned. “Scared? Just because I fulfil your wish doesn’t mean I’ll leave.” His grin evened out into something sincere. “I’m staying, Mydei.”

Mydei laughed through his nose and felt his smile grow to match. “I know.”

A few moments passed. Then…

“So what’s a Chrysos Heir?”

Mydei waited for Phainon to laugh at his own joke but he only blinked expectantly at him as the silence dragged on.

After a brief explanation of Amphoreus’ history, probably butchered but Krateros and Ptolemy didn’t need to know, Phainon finally understood that there was a deeper meaning to his golden blood and it was time to rest.

In the morning, after two weeks that had passed like a blissful daydream only to end in a nightmare, the detachment packed up the encampment and prepared to set out.

While Phainon woke up and immediately disappeared to find his parents, Mydei checked through his belongings as he packed his tent. Nothing had

gone missing at the hands of the family he let use his tent that night. Luckily the parents had enough common sense and control of their children to realise it would do more harm than good.

The tent flap rustled and a head of white peeked in. “Mydei.”

Mydei’s heart quickened but he kept his expression in that neutral set most people interpreted as anger and sign to stay away, yet Phainon was so undeterred by. He had news but it was impossible for Mydei to read which kind. How did Phainon balance but boldness and sheepishness at once.

He motioned and Phainon stepped inside, both hands tucked behind his back, while Mydei asked, “What?”

“Here.”

Phainon revealed his hands. A chalice of pink tinged liquid and a bowl of porridge mixed with honey, pomegranate seeds and some herbs. Mydei recognised the touch of Hephaestion and Perdikkas. They knew he would scold them for adding unnecessary things when their rations were in such short supply as is.

But when Phainon presented them to him with a little smile, Mydei could only take both with a muttered thanks.

Then Phainon smiled abashedly. “I know how busy you must be but do you have any time to spare?”

Mydei swallowed a mouthful. “All right. For what?”

“I spoke with my parents.” Phainon fidgeted with his hands. Mydei had never seen Phainon fidget before but he only ate in silence to let him continue at his pace. “They decided to head to Okhema with a lot of the others, so they don’t need me to join them.”

Oh. Oh.

Phainon grinned and it was almost like the past day really was nothing but a nightmare and Phainon had awoken unchanged. “So I’ll be true to my word

and deliver your wish, Mydei.”

It was difficult to be dignified with a bowl of porridge in his hands so he exchanged it for the chalice.

He raised it high. “The Kremnoan detachment welcomes you.”

“I don’t have a cup.”

“I’m aware.” Mydei took a sip and then offered it to Phainon. “We share this one. To mark the beginnings of an alliance.”

Phainon took the chalice, stared at the pink contents with an almost amused twitch to his lips, then raised it high before taking a sip.

It was an old tradition. So old it used to be blood in that cup shared between two in an allusion to their new alliance honoured the same as blood ties.

“Oh.” Phainon blinked at the chalice. “This is good.”

Mydei’s smile grew. Finally, someone who could appreciate his good taste. “It’s pomegranate juice and goats milk. Have it if you like it so much.”

Phainon only took another sip, savouring the taste before he swallowed, and then passed it back to Mydei. “My parents want to thank you.”

His hand stopped midair, gruel slipping off his spoon back into the bowl. “Why?”

Phainon’s brows furrowed in confusion. “Because you saved their lives.”

Mydei stirred the porridge. “Huh.”

No ordinary person had ever thanked the Kremnoan detachment for something. Let alone Mydei personally.

He shrugged. “If they feel the need.”

Phainon brightened again. “Great. I’ll bring them to you.”

“Now?”

“Yeah!”

And then he was gone before Mydei could tell him that he wasn’t ready for Phainon’s parents to see him as anything other than the stray Phainon had picked up in the wheat fields.

Mydei cursed and quickly shovelled down the rest of his food and cleaned off his face. When Phainon still hadn’t returned, he occupied his hands by packing.

He had rolled up the mattress, locked up his spare set of gauntlets and was about to begin taking the tent down by the time Phainon pushed the flap aside again. He held the tent open for his parents and his dog.

Snowy bounded right up to Mydei and he quickly dropped to his knees before Snowy felt the need to lunge at his face. He happily rolled over and Mydei carefully ran his gauntlets across his belly.

Both Audata and Hieronymus looked better than the last time Mydei had seen them. But that would likely stay the lowest point of their lives for a long time. Hopefully until the end.

Their skin was pale with bruises under their eyes from a poor night’s rest and an early morning. The clothes intended for warriors were ill fitting on the bodies of two farmers.

Satisfied their condition was as good as could be expected, Mydei lowered his eyes back to Snowy. He moved his hands rhythmically, watching Snowy’s tail sweep side-to-side and ears twitch. It was soothing.

A pair of bent knees entered the top of his peripheral vision. It was Hieronymus’ hands—thick, darkened by long days in fields that no longer existed, wrinkled with the first signs of age—that joined his on Snowy’s belly and rubbed.

“Thank you,” Hieronymus said but his hands kept the same rhythm against Snowy’s ribs. “Thank you for saving us. For risking your life for us and our son.”

Another set of knees. Now Audata’s hands—thick from labour but fingers still more slender, suited for needlework as much as a sickle—joined to scratch at Snowy’s exposed side. “We want to be able to thank you properly, one day, with a meal. We hope you’ll join us.”

Mydei held his breath and waited for them to retract the offer, as though a Prince of Strife could ever be crammed into the rickety seat of a small wooden table to eat a simple harvest. But a warm thigh pressed against his as Phainon, dressed in the red and black of the Kremnoan detachment, ruffled Snowy’s neck and Mydei lifted his eyes. Audata and Hieronymus were already looking at him with the same warm smile they had given their son.

He immediately ducked his head again and promised, “I will.”

Snowy panted happily under the attention of four sets of hands joined together.

Chapter End Notes

Finally got to the “Phainon joins the Kremnoan detachment” part of this story. One of the two original premises of this story and it only took… 6 chapters…

If you see the chapter count suddenly jump again… I’m sorry. Next chapter was supposed to be 5 short-ish scenes in one chapter but uhhh they’re not very short-ish anymore. So now I’m debating splitting them into five chapters or keeping them in one chapter that’s just really really chunky. Like 15k to 20k chunky… I open a google doc and the words magically appear from the void.
