chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei is poisoned and Phainon takes care of him.

Chapter Notes

In Mydei’s fourth year of exile, the Kremnoan detachment encountered a waylaid army from Ladon. In the midst of battle, Mydei took a poisoned arrow to the chest meant for Perdikkas.

His body healed all wounds but poison was always a tricky task. He needed to either break it down or expel it. Much like the black tide, it sank into his flesh and blood where it slowed the recovery of his other wounds.

His body burned but he shivered under the fabric draped across his chest and his sweat ran cold. A wet cloth dabbed across his forehead and he tried to reach out a hand but barely managed to twitch his fingers into the cot.

The world was a blur. He couldn’t see beyond vague white blots and two specks of blue. He couldn’t hear over his blood rushing in his ears and leaving him lightheaded.

His mouth was dry, his throat parched, and he opened his mouth. Water, he wanted to ask, but it scratched the inside of his throat and caught there and if he tried to spit it out it would come with blood.

The person understood anyway. A hand slipped behind his back, sitting him upright enough for him to swallow when something cold pressed against his lips and tipped liquid into his mouth.

It was bitter. He gagged and tried to jerk away but the hand slid across his back, looping an arm around his waist that kept him firmly in place.

“I know,” a voice murmured and his heart quieted in his ears. “It tastes pretty awful. But it’ll help speed up the process. Can you swallow for me?”

The hand came back to rub gentle circles into Mydei’s back. When he finished drinking the decoction, it tugged him into something warm and solid. Someone’s side. The hand ran through his hair, pushing back his sweaty bangs.

“I have to change your bandages too,” the voice continued in a smooth, gentle cadence like mothers putting their child to sleep. “The arrow wounds haven’t healed up yet. But the bleeding’s staunched enough that even I can be trusted to watch over you.”

He felt himself being shifted around but he couldn’t bring his body to move. He was being a burden and not a prince—not a would-be king who would find the find a better path for his people—but his nose was full of the scent of wheat. He closed his eyes and breathed deeper until hints of sea salt came through.

Cold air hit his chest before something colder smeared across his skin. Then he was jostled again, almost rocking from side to side, as the bandages were wound back around his torso. After that, he was laid back down to rest. With the fingers scraping through his hair and that voice murmuring in his ear, he was asleep before the pain had a chance to fade.

When he woke up, it was Ptolemy with a book at his bedside and Krateros stood guard by the entrance and Mydei didn’t know if his chest ached from the remaining poison or the absence of two particular people.

“Mydeimos,” Ptolemy noticed the lucidity in Mydei’s eyes first and hurried to help him sit up. “How are you?”

There was still the dull ache where the arrows struck and his heart underneath. He was thirsty and lightheaded. His fingers took twice as much effort to curl and three times as much to lift the blanket.

“Fine,” he said. “Report what happened.”

Ptolemy glanced at Krateros and then retreated from the bedside. “I will fetch Perdikkas, and a hearty meal for you to replenish your strength.”

The burden on Mydei’s shoulders eased somewhat at the mention of Perdikkas: alive and healthy enough to treat Mydei as a patient for the same poison that would have sent anyone else down the Sea of Souls. But the sheer relief only made it more difficult to convince his body to cooperate as the sheer need to get up in search of a sick bed, patient pale and feverish and pained into incoherence, dissipated.

Krateros took up the empty position by the bedside. Shoulders back and armour polished of blood, always so rough yet dignified, as though the battle and Mydei’s injury never occurred and this meeting wasn’t in the medical tent.

“That boy,” Krateros said with barely concealed distaste, “noticed you were struck down and carried you to the backline with Perdikkas close behind. We sustained a few major injuries but most were minor and we defeated the enemy army.”

While Mydei’s face maintained a stony disposition, his hand unclenched around the mattress. No one died because of his mistake. When Ladon’s flag came over the horizon his rationality frayed and when he saw that archer take at Perdikkas it snapped completely. There must have been another way but Mydei’s emptied of anything except Perdikkas’ final farewell. Pure instinct screamed to throw his own immortal body forward.

Now Krateros’ face twisted with open disgust. “We recovered the antidote to their poison. To think Ladon would fall so far as to use such dishonourable tactics to claim an unearned victory.”

Mydei wanted to pinch the bridge of his nose and massage his forehead where he felt a headache building but his hand was too heavy to move. He needed to conserve his strength. “Who saw?”

“That boy—“

“He has a name,” Mydei interrupted and Krateros words fell silent between gaping lips.

This was the first time Mydei had ever interrupted him. He respected his experience and teachings too much. But the world was slowly beginning to spin and he initially refused to interfere in such a blatant show of favouritism—nothing Phainon ever achieved would earn him the detachment’s respect if he did—but he wouldn’t tolerate such disrespect now that Phainon had earned more.

“He risked his own life for a body he knew was immortal. Isn’t that the type of character and camaraderie Strife seeks to honour.”

“That is correct, Your Highness,” Krateros said but his expression spoke of more before his lips did, “But that boy is not Kremnoan by birthright.”

“And yet the Kremnoan detachment has chosen to honour him as such. As have I,” he pointedly reminded him. “So speak his name next time or I may have issue recalling who that boy is.”

Krateros cleared his throat. “Yes, Your Highness. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae —“ he had to switch to common tongue just for Phainon’s name before sinking back into the familiar harsh Kremnoan, “—laid his outermost garments over you and carried you on his back. If the enemy realised you had been struck down in a less temporary way than usual, they didn’t act on it.”

“And our men?”

“Some may have noticed your absence in the heat of battle but Hephaestion and Phainon of Aedes Elysiae rallied their morale.”

Mydei huffed a laugh. Peace suited Phainon like a well-worn cloak but he took to battle just the same as any Kremnoan. Perhaps better with that golden blood in his veins. “And now?”

“The detachment are eager to celebrate this victory with their prince.”

Careful not to betray the movement beneath the blanket, he slowly tested the clench of his hand. Still a little numb but nothing he couldn’t handle. Once he stood and his blood started pumping faster, his movement would come back quicker. It wouldn’t be seamless but the others would be too drunk to notice.

“I’ll offer them a toast once I’m out of a sick man’s clothes.”

Krateros turned to exit at the dismissal and give Mydei privacy to change. But the flap lifted before his hand could reach it and a head of white rushed passed him to the bedside.

“Mydei, you’re awake!” Phainon’s voice was too loud but Mydei withheld a flinch. “How do you feel? Do you need anything? Here let me get you some water.”

He reached for the jug of water by the bedside and a chalice.

“I have no need of it,” Mydei cut him off, heart quickening when he realised Krateros wasn’t leaving.

He watched the exchange but Mydei wasn’t certain if that was genuine curiosity or curiosity waiting for Phainon to finally reveal his true colours and stab Mydei through the back.

“Yes you do,” Phainon countered immediately, chalice already half full. “The only drinks you’ve had since you went down were those nasty decoctions prescribed by Perdikkas. You were feverish and sweating out the poison. You need water before anything else.”

With his declaration, he held the chalice out to Mydei. Eyes bright despite the shadows underneath from the hours of sleepless care he had given. Mydei was doomed.

He swallowed, as dry as Phainon had assumed, and unfurled his hand from the mattress. He suppressed every tremble when he reached for the chalice and Phainon didn’t notice anything amiss when he let go for Mydei to take it in hand. The cool weight spread through his palm and fingers.

The muscles spasmed. The chalice clattered to the floor. In the damning silence, Mydei shoved his hand back under the blanket.

Phainon stared at the water splashed up his calf and pooling under his sandals like it had betrayed him and not Mydei.

“Phainon—“

“Mydei, show me your hand?” He smiled when he asked but it lacked his usual carefree and easy warmth. A smile that bordered on a threat.

“My body is fine.”

“Then you should have no problem showing me how fine you are.”

Phainon wasn’t one to give up and Mydei could only lie so blatantly for so long as though the evidence weren’t right beneath their noses. Krateros could be just as stubborn. The two of them would get on well if Krateros could just let go of his prejudices.

He withdrew his hand from beneath the blanket. He didn’t have the strength left to stop the tremors when he dropped his wrist into Phainon’s awaiting palm.

His brows furrowed but it wasn’t with anger, more frustration like the twist of his mouth. “Mydei, you’re shaking.”

“Genius. I wouldn’t have noticed if you hadn’t said anything,” Mydei bit out.

Phainon didn’t flinch at the insult. He inspected Mydei’s hand with that same stricken expression, witnessing every pathetic tremble where his hands were steady enough to tear warrior’s hearts from their chests and monster’s heads from their shoulders.

“Ptolemy told me you woke up. Perdikkas insisted you would be fully recovered once you did,” Phainon mused lowly. He aligned their fingertips and stretched Mydei’s hand out. “So why are you clearly not yet recovered.”

“It’s nothing to be so concerned over,” Mydei said through clenched teeth and tried to wrench his hand back.

But Phainon’s fingers encircled his weak wrist and held as firm as his eyes pinning Mydei in place. “Mydei, you need more rest.”

He barked a laugh. “Don’t declare things you know nothing about. Who knows my body’s condition more than I?”

Phainon’s lips thinned and the frustration hardened under a layer of grim resolve, like this was another battlefield and Phainon would be the victor. The only warning was the squeeze around Mydei’s wrist before Phainon yanked him straight from the mattress.

Mydei wasn’t prepared. His legs buckled and the only thing that stopped him hitting the floor was Phainon. A hand in his. A hand around his waist. The world spun to the rhythm of his heart finally pumping hard and fast all the way up to his ears.

“My legs are asleep after being in a sick bed so long,” Mydei grumbled, eyes down at the floor where the water puddled and his feet would have gotten wet if he weren’t standing atop Phainon’s own.

Phainon sighed and his hands moved. From Mydei’s hand to around his shoulder. From his waist down to the back of his knees. Mydei’s eyes widened and he opened his mouth to protest but the dry air caught his throat and he coughed.

Phainon swept Mydei into his arms and lowered him back onto the mattress. No more agitation just… “Rest more, Mydei.”

Sorrow.

Mydei rolled his head away and glared at the tent wall. It had only been a few months since the last time Phainon was so close to being crushed by despair. Since then he had been nothing but smiles and cheery laughter, even when the rest of the detachment hazed him with teasings, the worst

chore rotation, and duels as a chance to elevate his status so long as he was good enough. He was.

Something as simple as the state of Mydei’s body shouldn’t have brought even a hint of that melancholy back.

A hand pressed into his, pushing it open with a thumb against his palm and massaging deep circles. It felt good.

Phainon lifted Mydei’s hand, still rubbing firm circles as Mydei’s limp fingers just brushed Phainon’s forehead. When he spoke, every soft sound caressed the skin of his palm. “Your body may be immortal but that doesn’t mean you don’t feel the pain of death.”

Ptolemy returned with Perdikkas and they both faltered at the entrance. Mydei scowled and jerked his head, telling them to come inside. Ptolemy placed the food down by the bedside before he retreated but, rather than leave, he stood guard by the entrance alongside Krateros.

No matter how Mydei emphasised to Perdikkas that his body had recovered, Phainon contradicted him with a wave of the empty chalice to the watery floor as evidence.

Worse still, Phainon insisted he wasn’t capable of holding anything—and Mydei hadn’t been able to prove him wrong when Phainon passed him a wooden spoon too small for his clumsy hands—so Mydei needed help.

Help eating and drinking.

Perdikkas noted Mydei’s symptoms down and scratched his head. “I admit, I fail to see why this poison has plagued you with so many more after-effects than usual.”

Mydei glowered at the spoon raised to his lips and the hand holding it but the person it was attached to didn’t retreat. How humiliating.

Mydei opened his mouth and Phainon pushed the spoon in before he could change his mind and close it again. Porridge flavoured with some figs, as

though the acidic sweetness could mask the bitter medicinal herbs mixed in.

He considered snapping the spoon in two with his teeth but then Phainon would start fretting about splinters in his mouth. What then? Would he feed him like a mother bird did her children. He shuddered at the thought.

“Shaking? Has your fever returned?” Perdikkas’ eyes widened with alarm and laid a hand against his forehead.

Mydei swallowed the mouthful. “No. My mind went somewhere unpleasant.”

He sighed with relief. “No fever or sweats. Fully lucid. Just some remaining weakness. I’ll study Ladon’s poison more in depth.”

Phainon set the bowl down in favour of the chalice, refilled to the brim with water and held it to Mydei’s mouth. Mydei opened his mouth and tipped his head back. The sooner this ended the better.

“There’s no need for that,” Phainon told Perdikkas with fake brightness.

Mydei almost spat the water at him.

Perdikkas’ brows creased. “What do you mean?”

Phainon took the chalice away and picked up the bowl again, mixing it together for another small spoonful while he ignored Mydei’s glare, one which inspired terror in anyone unfortunate enough to oppose him on the battlefield.

He smiled innocently at Perdikkas. “Mydei lied.”

“Haikas! Watch your mouth.”

The realisation hung so heavy he feared the tent would cave on top of them. Ptolemy quickly excused himself, probably off to inform the others of this recent revelation that Mydei’s body of steel wasn’t as reliable as they all thought. Every time he was struck down with poison, his flawless recovery was simply an act.

Perdikkas’ eyes darted across Mydei’s face and his body, even hidden beneath the blanket. Reassessing.

Krateros paled and took half a step forward before he stilled again. “Your Highness, to take such poor care of your own body…”

“Leave,” Mydei said coldly. When no one moved he thumped a hand against the bedding. “All of you! Dismissed!”

Only two people walked out the tent, Perdikkas promising he would return with another decoction and Krateros that he would keep the detachment from inquiring into his condition.

Mydei glared at the loose fist he couldn’t bring himself to move again. “That meant you, too.”

Phainon shrugged and lifted another spoonful. Mydei eyed it out the corner of his eye but didn’t move to take it. “I know. But I won’t walk away just because you tell me to.”

Insubordination was a terrible thing in an army. If everyone thought they could do anything they wanted then their formations would simply unravel at the seams.

But it was Phainon, a member of the detachment but so much more, so Mydei only tentatively opened his mouth and accepted another spoonful.

He chewed thoughtfully and swallowed. “I’m not so weak I need someone to take care of me.”

Phainon smiled, small and a brittle, eyes downturned at the bowl. “I’m aware. It’s not your weakness that I…” He continued stirring, seemingly forgetting that he was supposed to be feeding Mydei like he had so insisted, until he admitted in a shaky breath, “It’s mine. I’m weak, Mydei. That’s why I have to—to take care of you.”

I didn’t realise you were capable of being selfish. The words were right there on the tip of Mydei’s tongue. Sharp as always but meant to prod and

tease and then be brushed aside like usual. He didn’t say anything because he wasn’t certain if he could temper his prickliness enough for such acrid words, and he knew Phainon might never be so “selfish” again if he did.

“I’m still hungry,” Mydei said instead.

Phainon’s head perked up, all hopeful wide eyes and parted lips, then he nodded vigorously. “Here.”

Only once the bowl and chalice were empty did Phainon let him stand. It wasn’t a lie to say Mydei was fully recovered by that point but he didn’t object when Phainon helped him change into fresh garments.

Mydei’s hair was a mess from him tossing and turning in his sick bed but his unruly hair wasn’t an unusual sight, an untamed mane feeding into his epithet of the solitary lion. However, he couldn’t stand the braid loosened over his shoulder into a formless cluster of hair.

He unclasped the metal end and ran his fingers through, untangling and smoothing out the waves that came from how long it had spent braided tight. Phainon stared with such narrowed focus, it almost numbed Mydei’s fingers again.

“Can I help?” Phainon asked with a polite smile, as though he didn’t care either way but offered out of his sense of moral duty. Mydei arched a brow and Phainon swiftly defended himself, “I braid…ed hair before.”

Phainon’s brows pinched, baffled by himself. There were two people Mydei could imagine Phainon seated behind, running his fingers through their hair and laying the strands over each other: Audata and Cyrene.

Mydei suspected he would regret this but he turned to face him and tilted his head for easier access. “Only if you can make it passable.”

“Of course!”

The braid was not passable. It was not even a braid.

“Phainon…” Mydei interrupted partway through the fifth attempt. He didn’t need to check for himself; Phainon’s face told him all he needed to know.

He flushed darker. “I… don’t recall this being so difficult.”

“Is it possible—“

“No.”

That Phainon’s mother and best friend took pity on him. That was the only explanation for how the results could be so poor.

“Let me do it.”

“I just need some practice. Every good warrior needs a warmup.” His fingers slowed and he glanced away, his smile falling at the edges. “It’s been a long time.”

A kicked puppy.

Mydei sighed, “Another three attempts and no more.”

Resolve set Phainon’s features. That persistence, which served him so well on the battlefield, did nothing to prevent Mydei from undoing his hard work after his final attempt. He braided it himself while Phainon sulked and memorised the movement of his fingers, hands following along in his lap. Mydei let Phainon gather the ends and fix them in place with the metal clasp.

Only then did they rejoin the rest of the detachment. All of whom were none the wiser about Mydei’s moment of weakness when he raised a drink to victory with unshaken limbs and a clear mind.

When he gathered with his friends around the campfire, Krateros overseeing from a distance while pretending he wasn’t, there was no avoiding that they knew when they looked at Mydei differently, as well as Phainon at his side.

But it wasn’t a bad thing when Peucesta plucked at his strings with a song about a man apologising to his scorned lover and Hephaestion sent one of his dogs over with a low whistle. Ptolemy passed a drink mixed just to his liking, Perdikkas tossed herbs that burned sweet into the fire, and Leonnius lifted his chalice in their own private toast in common tongue so Phainon could follow along. Mydei downed his drink and it tasted sweeter than usual.

Chapter End Notes

Phainon used “puppy dog eyes”. It was super effective!

chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon get stuck out in the cold. Only one of them is good at handling it.

Chapter Notes

In Mydei’s fifth year of exile, a snowstorm ravaged through Aidonia for three full months. While skirmishes with a number of mercenaries had pushed them closer to Aidonia in the months prior, Mydei kept the detachment away from the main city and its surrounding territory. When the blizzard hit, they were settled outside a small village in Aidonia’s periphery.

The earth was frozen solid by the harsh winter and the villagers complained how they would ever be able to till it come the Months of Cultivation. There were no bottomless swamps for Leonnius to sink in.

The greatest threat was the cold. While they weathered the worst of the snow in the proper buildings of towns and villages, the majority of their time was in the wild as usual.

“And that is why we should hold a competition,” Leonnius announced, vigorously rubbing his hands against his thighs. “Whoever gathers the most pelts is the victor.”

Mydei sipped his spiced wine. He preferred to avoid wines and spirits but he made exceptions for the cold. And only for a specific blend of wine, spices and honey Ptolemy found in a book stolen from the Library of Garbaniphoro. “What brought on this proposal?”

“This blizzard has raged without pause for almost two months. There’s no telling when we’ll finally be free of it,” Leonnius bemoaned. “None of us have frozen to death but we’re hardly limber.”

“How selfless of you,” Perdikkas teased with an arched brow. “And this has nothing to do with Peucesta thieving your blanket in the night.”

Leonnius gaped at Peucesta. “That was you?”

Ptolemy was equally offended. “And you tried to frame me?”

Peucesta looked from one to the other, shrugged, and continued to wiggle his gloved fingers over a nonexistent lyre.

Phainon’s head bounced between the two of them as he tried to follow the conversation. He had made an admirable effort to learn Kremnoan since he joined the detachment but it was a difficult language to grasp. The sounds were harsher and throatier than common tongue. While grammatically similar, the two dialects shared few words.

But his head perked up and he pointed at his chin. “No,” he said in Kremnoan and then switched to common, “that was me?”

“What?” They both rounded on him at the same time.

Phainon’s hands jumped in surrender. “I woke up with the extra blanket. I rose early for my swordsmanship practice so I gave it to Ptolemy since he seemed cold. I didn’t realise it was yours.”

Leonnius huffed and slurred his next words together as quick as possible into near incoherence, “First Mydeimos and now Peucesta. Who else will be favouring him next?”

“You forgot to add your own name there,” Hephaestion remarked dryly.

It was easy to see why Peucesta had caved. Even with Phainon huddled as close to the fire as he could get without it jumping to his furs and wools, he still shivered so pitifully. Nearly four months in Aidonia and two during its worst freeze in recent memory had not been enough time for Phainon to acclimate to the harsh winter. If anything he had gotten worse.

“If you want limber then I can have you run a message to Aidonia where you beg for safe refuge in the city,” Mydei drawled and Leonnius swaddled

himself further in his himation like it would hide him and Mydei would miraculously forget his existence. “But the idea isn’t half-bad.”

It would be good for morale to have something to pass the time. They likely wouldn’t hunt enough for the entire detachment but anything was better than nothing. The fires of competition would keep them warm for a little while.

The detachment were enthusiastic and separated themselves into groups. Ptolemy was the most sought after for his traps but he sided with his cavalrymen and the men swiftly turned to those most proficient with a bow.

Phainon nudged Mydei, crouched on the ground to string his bow, with his boot. “No one interested in partnering with Your Highness?”

Mydei rolled his eyes. “Only if you remove yourself from the list.”

“Us on the same team? Where’s your healthy spirit of competition?” Phainon teased but his smile was all mirth and no surprise.

“I prefer my competition alive. I fear you will freeze to death if I take my eye off you too long.”

Team decided, they set off with a brief remark for Leonnius to not run off into trouble alone. Leonnius mockingly saluted and Mydei lingered on his intact legs before Phainon dragged him along.

Hunting was a different challenge in the snowy landscape. Many animals entered hibernation or migrated to warmer climates. The constant snowfall covered most tracks and the dead foliage left little cover to hide from the more skittish prey.

Mydei crouched behind a rocky outcrop and drew the bowstring back. The deer had yet to notice them. He hadn’t wielded a bow in some time but he breathed and let his body remember as he adjusted his aim. He loosed the arrow and it pierced through the deer’s head. It let out a death throe and then collapsed to the snow.

Phainon watched him tie a strip of red fabric to the deer’s leg with Mydei’s name on it. “I wasn’t aware you could wield a bow.”

Mydei glanced at the nearest red fabric tied to a tree in the distance, then tied another one on a branch overhead as he memorised the location. “Any weapon a member of the detachment can wield is just as capable in my hands.”

A steel body forged for war. It showed in how quickly he became proficient with every weapon every member of the detachment had eagerly tutored him in. They claimed it was a gift from Nikador.

Mydei arched a brow at the coil of rope Phainon on Phainon’s hands. “But I wasn’t aware you knew how to tie snares.”

A few had already been hidden along their route. Although there was no telling if they would catch anything, Mydei had admired the skill of the knots and camouflage.

Phainon chuckled. “My dad taught me. And Ptolemy has been helping me expand my repertoire.”

Mydei had noticed them in conversation at times—and, upon reflection, seen the rope—but he failed to realise the connection. Hunting competitions were frequent and often came with coins in the betting pool, so it was unusual for Ptolemy to teach his tricks. That made the current list of favour: Mydeimos, Peucesta, Ptolemy.

Although, Hephaestion always spared his time if Phainon requested a spar, when he usually evaded persistent requests unless they came from Mydei or flared into a challenge for a real duel. He had grown soft the first time Phainon soothed a frenzied stray and then regaled him with tales of Snowy. Perhaps he could be added too.

Even Perdikkas had taken days to explain, to the best of the detachment’s knowledge, how Mydei’s immortality worked. Alongside the best kinds of treatments for which injuries. Not that Mydei required treatment for anything other than the black tide or potent poisons. But Perdikkas, and

apparently Phainon, had certain salves and concoctions at the ready to speed the repairs and numb pain.

That meant Leonnius was the last man standing.

“What’s so funny?” Phainon asked.

Phainon’s face was completely flushed from the cold. The tip of his nose, the highs of his cheeks, the curve of his ears. If Mydei plucked off his thick hide gloves and fur lined boots, he was certain his fingers and toes would be just as icy. He even sniffled as his nose ran.

Mydei’s lip curled even further at the sight. “Nothing for you to concern yourself over. I was just thinking about how you’re bound to lose.”

“And here I thought you wanted to be on the same team so we could be victorious together,” Phainon said with a mocking sigh, a large puff of white, and shake of his head.

Mydei smirked. “Competition is much livelier when you can watch your opponents confident facade crumble.”

“Then shall we keep going so I can witness it first hand.”

There wasn’t much further for them to go before the ground took a steep incline to form a mountainside. It would be unwise to venture into the mountains but he recalled Perdikkas had been eager to locate a local flower that sprouted from cracks in the stone and clambered up rocks.

The majority grew too high but they followed alongside the mountain and plucked any flowers that bloomed within arms reach. They even located a cave with a number growing inside but their bounty was still scarce.

“Shame,” Phainon said through trembling lips. “He mentioned how they were good for stemming bleeding and…” Phainon’s head swivelled. “Did you hear that?”

Mydei assumed he meant the strange thump. But he wasn’t sure what it was or where it came from. It didn’t sound like an animal. Too large.

Somewhere overhead.

The sound rumbled nearer and nearer and a sudden shadow stretched stark across the snowy forest floor. Phainon’s arm looped around Mydei’s chest and yanked him backwards. His back slammed into Phainon’s front and the cave plunged into darkness.

“Avalanche,” Phainon explained, breath hot against his nape, and he freed Mydei from his hold. “Sounded like when the wind blows and the snow tumbles off the roofs.”

The cave entrance had been completely buried. Mydei kicked the snow and some of it flaked off to scatter across the cave floor but it hardly made a dent. There was too much of it. Too heavy, so that it compacted itself into a solid wall.

Mydei rolled his wrists and flexed his fingers. They were still warm, flexible. “I’ll dig us out.”

It was too dark to see more than vague silhouettes but Phainon managed to grab his wrist in one attempt. “Your fingers will freeze off.”

“They’ll heal before that,” Mydei corrected him. “At most they’ll go completely numb.“

Even if his blood froze in his veins and he collapsed of hypothermia, his body would warm again after a brief dip in the Sea of Souls.

No chill in the living world could compare to the waters where the dead gathered. That place seeped beyond skin, sapping the warmth from the marrow of bones. His body had acclimated to that kind of frigid existence. Even after years roaming far from the Sea of Souls and clawing his way free as swiftly as he was submerged, his body temperature remained exceptionally high.

“Let’s just w-wait for the others,” Phainon insisted, as though his teeth hadn’t already begun to chatter.

Everyone would gather back at the camp. When they realised Mydei and Phainon were missing, they would send out search parties in the general direction they had been seen venturing in. Mydei had already tied scraps of red fabric to the trees along their route and Hephaestion’s dogs may have been strays but they were prodigious trackers with the right training. Then they would just have to dig the two of them out.

Mydei shook off Phainon’s hand. “All right.”

It would be too much hassle to combat the cold, the uncooperative snow, and Phainon’s objections. If worst came to worst then Phainon would be too weak by that point to oppose him when he started digging.

His eyes adjusted somewhat to the darkness, enough for him to notice Phainon’s gaping lips at such an easy acquiescence. Neither of them had an actual light source. The closest was…

Mydei slid down the wall to the ground, “Never mention this to anyone.”

“That we almost froze to death in a cave because we were picking flowers?”

Phainon couldn’t see it but Mydei rolled his eyes anyway and didn’t dignify his snark with any other response.

Instead he evened out his breathing and closed his eyes as he pushed up his sleeves and exposed parts of his neck and collarbone. He felt his heart pumping in his chest, blood flowing through his veins, the heat of his immortal life.

“Mydei, you’re—“

“Shut up,” he growled and opened his eyes.

A red light washed over the dull grey stone and the white snow. His tattoos were glowing.

It took a lot of concentration to make them light up let alone keep them that way. It usually just happened. When he fought hard enough to require all of

his strength and focus. When he woke in the night from a nightmare that plunged him back into a lightless abyss or a lonely future.

Phainon sat opposite him. There wasn’t much space. If they both stretched their legs out then they would overlap.

“So th-those markings of yours…”

Mydei clicked his tongue. “If you must know, they are remnants of my time in the Sea of Souls.”

His body healed all wounds without even a mark as a reminder. The closest thing he had to a scar were these red markings where the Sea of Souls— Death and Strife and the struggle to survive—had embedded itself beneath his skin. Every time he encountered them again in force, his tattoos would shift and grow to match the life he led.

He clenched his fist and red dust trickled between his fingers like sand in an hourglass as the time passed in silence.

“H-how much… much longer until they-they come for us,” Phainon stammered between chattering teeth. It was a miracle he had any teeth left with how long they had been clattering away.

Mydei tapped his head back against the wall, one leg bent upright so his arm could rest over it. “It’s not been that long.”

But long enough it was obvious how much Phainon suffered from the cold. While they had crept through the snowy undergrowth, his features had flushed but nothing too concerning. Now his face was bloodless, even as he swaddled his himation over his head and curled into himself to preserve as much warmth as possible. Mydei wouldn’t bet a scrap of bronze on his survival let alone gold.

He sighed and unclasped his woollen himation. “Come here.”

For once, Phainon’s first instinct wasn’t to jump at Mydei’s command. Not because of Mydei’s status but because that’s just how Phainon was: a big,

white dog like the one that left for Okhema with his parents. Except he didn’t have any fur to keep him warm.

He stared through Mydei with distant eyes and shivers wracking his body. “Why?”

“Just come here.”

Phainon scooted across the rough stone floor and leaned against the wall, their shoulders brushing together but nothing more. Mydei rolled his eyes as he shrugged off his himation and closed the distance so minuscule there was no reason for Phainon to leave it at all. Mydei had already made his approval of physical contact with Phainon clear but his mind worked in the strangest ways.

He begged for scraps of attention but found excuses to avoid Mydei and spar with Hephaestion if Mydei indulged him too much. He plastered himself to Mydei’s side but had arbitrary list of touches and lines he refused to cross no matter how Mydei welcomed him at times he would shrug off others. He did all sorts of things for Mydei from his laundry to cleaning and polishing his gauntlets—a pain and Mydei knew it. The little plates and grooves were not as open to rag as a smooth blade—but he never expected anything in return.

Mydei shed his gloves with his teeth. Then he curled an arm around Phainon’s waist and felt another shiver run through him. Except he hadn’t relaxed his tensed muscles by the time Mydei shuffled under his arm, bringing it around his own waist, and tossed one end of his himation over Phainon’s shoulder. They didn’t have any firewood so their only option was body heat.

It was difficult to tell if Phainon was breathing despite how Mydei squinted at the fabric over his chest. His face had gone completely blank which, paired with the utter paleness, made him look almost like the unflattering portrait Leonnius had etched into the snow the other day.

“Yours, too.”

“Huh?” Phainon muttered unintelligibly which meant he hadn’t frozen solid. Maybe the cold had gotten his brain first.

“Use it as a blanket. Give it to me.”

He reached beneath his himation for Phainon’s, searching blind for the clasp. Phainon shrieked and whatever ice in his veins keeping him so sluggish suddenly turned to steam as his hands flew to his chest and colour surged into his cheeks.

“I can get it!”

With the fabric in the way, Mydei couldn’t confirm for himself but he knew without a doubt that Phainon’s trembling hands were fumbling for the clasp and missing.

“You’ll be a block of ice before that.”

“Keep your hands to yourself! I can do it.”

Mydei’s fingers curled. The biting cold had forced him to remove his gauntlets. Even with his gloves, the heated skin of his palms hotter than any red hot steel was too exposed.

Phainon finally unclasped his himation and pulled it free, handing it to Mydei so he could drape it over their tucked legs. The himation over their shoulders, and partially over Phainon’s head, had a gaping opening at the bottom even when he pinned it together in the middle. But when he used Phainon’s clasp to pin the two sheets of fabric together it created one big blanket. It was easier to trap the heat in when they could tuck the edges against the floor.

“There.” Mydei nodded, satisfied, and leaned against Phainon’s side.

Phainon’s head dropped against the top of his. As though making up for lost time after so many years, Mydei’s body had gotten significantly taller in the past year. Except Phainon hadn’t stoped growing either so their height difference hadn’t shrunken enough for Mydei’s liking.

“You’re warm,” Phainon mumbled, dreamy but still more lucid than he had been. “I can feel your hand through my clothes.”

“Give me your other hand.”

Again, no different than a dog, Phainon placed his paw in Mydei’s open palm. His fingertips were so cold Mydei half expected there to be steam where their skin met.

“Oh, that’s nice…”

“How did you ever manage the winters?” Mydei asked, rubbing their palms together. He knew it must have snowed in Aedes Elysiae considering the name of his dog.

“The winters weren’t as harsh.” He managed a shake of his head and a small smile. “I’ll have you know I actually enjoyed going out in the snow. It was always fun to play in with my friends.”

“Did those friends include fairies?”

His chuckle was still shaky. “You’ll never believe me about that, will you?”

Mydei did believe him but it was more fun to disagree. He snorted, “I’ve roamed every corner of Amphoreus and never seen a so-called fairy.”

Again, not quite true. In the sunlight and the wheat fields, Phainon looked much like a fairy. One who helped farmers and brought good harvests and languished in the grain stalks, sunlight turning his hair near golden, blue eyes like a perfect sunny day.

But in the winter, Phainon looked like he emerged from the snow. Not as a harbinger of famine and blizzards or the cold long nights, but the fun to be had in the snow and the warmth shared between people huddled close around a fire.

“I wanted to show them to you. They would’ve liked you.”

Phainon’s voice had grown quieter and Mydei imagined his eyes had closed. It would have been concerning but he could feel Phainon’s body temperature rising, so he didn’t bother trying to force him awake.

“What about you? You’re so warm. You could… could run around naked in the snow and watch it melt.”

Mydei rolled his eyes and squeezed Phainon’s hand until he winced. “Use your brain.” Mydei relaxed his hand, drawing circles into the meat of Phainon’s thumb. “It’s another… consequence of my time in the Sea of Souls.”

That made Phainon perk up a little. “Another boon? Like that steel body of yours.”

Mydei huffed a laugh. “Something like that. But…”

Phainon’s cheek fell back against Mydei’s head. “But?”

Mydei kissed his teeth and felt the burn of his hands where they met Phainon’s icy ones. “If you weren’t half frozen to death, you would hardly enjoy holding my hand.”

“Mydei,” Phainon whined and nuzzled his cheek against Mydei’s hair, “what about me makes you think that?”

His mouth opened, and then closed again. What made him think that Phainon wouldn’t want to hold his hand? That was a surprisingly good point for someone half-lucid and muttering into the top of his head.

“It’s—my hands are really hot.” Which sounded quite pathetic when he put it that way.

Hotter than the forges of Castrum Kremnos. Peucesta had said in much more complex verse that Mydei barely understood—not long after he emerged from the Sea of Souls and was folded into the detachment. The gauntlets were the only reason he could touch anyone without it scalding.

“Feels nice.”

“Because your fingers are icier than the river we crossed to get here.”

“No no. It’s because they’re Mydei’s hands,” Phainon insisted in that same sleepy voice and he squeezed like Mydei didn’t know where his hands were.

Their body temperature had warmed the air under the blanket. That was why Mydei felt his face beginning to warm too.

“Stop mumbling. I can’t understand you.”

No response. Mydei squeezed Phainon’s hand but his fingers were slackening in Mydei’s hold. He was asleep. Mydei shuffled, getting comfortable against Phainon’s shoulder. The others would come for them soon.

“Phainon,” Mydei whispered and waited. Still no answer. He breathed a shaky exhale. “Do you think fate can be defied? Or am I just as mad as my father for thinking that I…”

After all, his father had murdered his wife and attempted the murder of his son all in an attempt to defy a prophesied fate. A future he didn’t want to come to pass.

When would it be Mydei’s turn to make a sacrifice? What would he be willing to give? And what if it was all for nothing?

“Don’t say that about yourself.”

Mydei stiffened and tried to jerk away but Phainon’s hand tightened around his waist, keeping them stuck together.

“You—“

Did he really pretend to be asleep?

“Wasn’t pretending,” Phainon defended himself from an accusation Mydei hadn’t even loosed yet. “Just dozed off. Then I heard some upsetting slander and woke up again.”

Mydei clicked his tongue but didn’t push Phainon away when he nuzzled his head against Mydei’s temple.

His voice was low in Mydei’s ear, as gentle as the warm breath dissipating in a puff of white. “Don’t insult yourself by comparing yourself to that…” He finished with quite the Kremnoan insult. One that would have any man, woman or child lunging at his throat with a blade.

Mydei blinked once, twice, just in case he had fallen asleep. “Since when?”

He pulled back just a bit as he chuckled. “Leonnius taught me. But my point stands. You would never lose yourself.”

“How can you be so certain?” Mydei asked, unable to mask the bitterness now that he had opened the gates of his honesty. “You’ve seen me on the battlefield. The solitary lion? Or just a mad mutt?”

“That’s different. You let yourself loose but you never lose control.”

“Maybe I will one day.”

“You won’t. If something needs protecting, the only thing you would ever willingly sacrifice is yourself. Your golden blood, your immortal body, your lives.” It was only his breath against Mydei’s nose, fanning across his cheeks. He wasn’t sure the tremors in it were from the cold. “Even when it hurts.”

He was so distressed in his crinkled eyes and downturned lips that Mydei wasn’t certain if he was talking about Mydei’s pain or his own. He knew that face. The one Phainon always made when Mydei was reckless on the battlefield. Like every drop of spilled blood and length of rended flesh was just as painful for Phainon as he imagined it was for Mydei, who had long since grown immune to such trivial pains.

He let himself slump near boneless against Phainon’s side, breathing in a crisp scent of winter air. “And if I ever forget myself—“

You will be the one to kill me.

“Then I’ll be by your side to remind you.”

The light of his tattoos pulsed quicker with his heart. It was obvious, too obvious, but he kept his nose buried in Phainon’s shoulder like neither of them would notice.

“All right, Deliverer,” he scraped as much rigour into his voice as he could. “Go back to sleep if you want. By the time you wake up, you’ll be warm by a real fire.”

He hummed low in his throat. “Don’t wanna leave you alone.” But the effect was compromised by the tired slur to his words.

Mydei laughed. “I’m not alone. Or are you planning on going somewhere?”

Eventually Phainon’s breathing levelled out again. Mydei didn’t have any more to say but he pinched the back of Phainon’s hand just to catch him in the act if he was pretending again. Phainon’s brows furrowed and his lashes fluttered but he didn’t stir.

He let the light of his tattoos burn out, plunging them back into darkness, and focused on the rise and fall of Phainon’s chest, breath running through Mydei’s hair. He was still alive, nowhere near succumbing to the cold. Just as Perdikkas was still alive. And Leonnius and Ptolemy would be once they emerged from the land entombed in snow.

Mydei’s head perked up as muffled noises came through the snow. Voices. Harsh contact striking something firm.

The light broke through next as a few sheafs of snow flaked off and broke against the ground. As more and more tumbled down and the chunks grew larger, the voices came louder and the light brighter.

Mydei unclasped his himation first and cinched it shut again around Phainon’s chest. Then he took Phainon’s himation from around their legs and wrapped it back around Phainon’s shoulders.

By the time the first dog broke through the snow—a new one. Suited to the climate since they found it wandering the snowstorm with a ravaged ear, muzzle and tail—Mydei was on his feet with Phainon over his back.

Hephaestion climbed over the snow to reach him but Mydei only kicked his discarded bow and quiver towards him. “Mydeimos. Everyone else is accounted for. Water has been heated to warm you both up,” he reported quick and efficient, stooping to pick the two items up.

Mydei boosted Phainon on his back and readjusted his grip on his thighs. He clambered over the heap of loose snow, feeling it give and slide under his feet. Hephaestion caught him with a hand around his arm and let go once he found his footing again.

Once they reached flat ground, Leonnius whistled. “Did he die? Is this his funeral shroud.”

Mydei walked right past him. “He’s asleep.”

“Want me to be carry him?” Leonnius asked but immediately laughed before Mydei could even respond. “Stop running my mouth and start running my feet.”

Mydei closed his mouth again, retort stolen, as Leonnius ran off back to the encampment with the good news.

They followed the red scraps of fabric back to the encampment. The deer and the snares had already been cleared away but Mydei had little care left for the competition. The detachment welcomed them back with some compliments to their hunt—the deer was a clean kill and the snares had moderate success—although Ptolemy emerged victorious with a bear hide.

Mydei didn’t spare them much more than quick acknowledgement as he carried Phainon straight to the tent reserved for the portable water basin and let the flap close behind him. Even without the structure of a building to keep the heat in, it was warm as the steam rose from the water.

“You can stop pretending to be asleep now.”

Phainon didn’t twitch. But when Mydei loosed his hands to drop him to the floor, his limbs sprung to life and clung to him, arms around his neck and legs around his waist.

“How did you know?” Phainon pouted.

“When you stopped drooling on me. Now get off before I dump you in clothes and all. And tell me when how long Leonnius has been giving you lessons on the Kremnoan language.”

If Mydei wanted to throw this information in Leonnius’ face and watch him rush to defend himself, he needed the exact details of when exactly Leonnius added himself to this supposed list. Although, there was little purpose to a list of those among them who favoured Phainon if all their names could be found on it. And Mydei would never deny who was at the very top of that list.

Chapter End Notes

Phainon’s parents adopted Mydei and Mydei’s friends adopted Phainon. Perfectly balanced.

Mydei to Phainon: Paw Phainon: [immediately gives his paw]
