chapters.title: Chapter 9
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei inevitably encounters the black tide and Phainon’s thirst for revenge again.

Chapter Notes

Only twenty dusks later into Mydei’s fifth year of exile, the detachment stayed far from the main city where Aidonian loyalists could crush Ptolemy beneath fallen columns. A break in the snowstorm let the encampment push towards the boundaries of Aidonia’s territory, hoping to leave before the next big freeze came in.

They stopped in a half-thawed town to sell off their extra pelts and wools that would be rendered unnecessary bulk in the warmer weather outside Amphoreus’ coldest region.

Mydei lurked nearby with his hood up and arms crossed. The townsfolk tried not to stare at the scary stranger loitering in the shadows of the street and hurried past to go about their business.

With everyone including him bundled under thick winter clothing, the only thing that distinguished him from the others was the red mark below his eye visible from beneath his hood. Yet everyone just knew he was suspicious.

It’s because you don’t smile. You brood. Phainon told him once after effortlessly convincing a merchant to purchase an ornate dagger he had taken as spoils but saw no need to keep.

The same dagger he had struggled to pawn off to a different merchant just earlier that day. The only difference was that Mydei noticed the first merchant’s frantic glances in his own direction, and excused himself for Phainon’s second attempt.

If Mydei forced a smile, the situation would spiral so fast the town guards would get involved before he even had the chance to stop smiling. He would know. Ptolemy had tried that strategy with him already.

So Mydei kept his head down and waited for Phainon to finish. Then they could move on and reunite with the rest of the detachment…

Except Phainon was gone.

Mydei sighed and a woman startled nearby, glancing over and then scurrying away when he pushed off the wall. He needed to go wrangle his companion because, for all Phainon’s skill at selling items with his chivalrous but amiable charms, he also had a bad habit of being scammed.

He could only assume people didn’t run scams in a community as small as Aedes Elysiae because Phainon’s idea of value for anything that couldn’t be found in a rural wheat farming village was… frighteningly flexible. He was not allowed in a marketplace unsupervised.

Technically the coin was his to spend so long as he contributed enough to the detachment’s coffers to feed himself and maintain his weapon and armour. But there were limits to what foolery Mydei was willing to witness. Especially when someone, usually Ptolemy, would inform him that his latest antique was nothing more than a forgery and Phainon would shrug it off saying other people probably needed the money more than him anyway.

The familiar white hair was tucked beneath a hood but he recognised the himation and boots stood at a stall. Mydei didn’t soften his glare at the stall owner as he stationed himself at Phainon’s side.

The stall owner flinched but chiselled on a shaky smile and returned to whatever discussion he was having with Phainon, “It’s strange. We usually have one or two merchants from the town about half a day by horseback. But they haven’t shown up at all this week.”

While Phainon responded placatingly, Mydei kept his face flat, unimpressed, and scanned the wares. A fabric stall.

“Do you need new clothes?” Mydei asked, brows furrowed.

As far as he was aware, Phainon’s clothes were still in acceptable condition. He had grown in height and muscle since he first joined but he was still within the range of a standard Kremnoan warrior. And he took care to repair his clothes where he could in the manner taught to him by his mother. For someone once so pathetic at braiding hair, his fingers were surprisingly dexterous when it came to needlework.

“Need? Not at all.” Phainon admired the dyed bolts of fabric and his gaze lingered on a muted yellow. “But I feel a splash of colour might add some charm to the camp.”

The Kremnoan detachment hardly needed charm. While it was true the encampment heavily skewed towards blacks, browns and reds, those were simply the most practical. Did Phainon really want to be cleaning blood and gore out of whatever other colours he preferred? The stains would never come out from…

Mydei looked from the yellow in his hands to the purple tucked under his arm. His nose scrunched. “Why those colours?”

Phainon paused like the question surprised him, or maybe just the sharpness of Mydei’s tone. “They’re my favourite.” Another moment too long passed as he dragged his finger along the yellow weave. “They remind me of home. Why? Do you not like them?”

The yellow was far from the gold of the wheat fields but that could never be captured in the simple dyes affordable to the masses. This was likely the closest to be found.

But there was something more important than that.

Mydei glanced again between the yellow and purple. “Do you intend to wear them together?”

“Of course!”

Mydei took the purple bolt from under his arm and set it back on the table. “No.”

Phainon whole face crumpled in sheer heartbreak. “Why not?”

“No.” When Phainon’s expression didn’t move, Mydei pinched the bridge of his nose and sighed. “If you must, wear one at a time. But never both at once.”

That was an acceptable compromise and he immediately perked up again, purchasing both sets of fabric with his usual smile.

“A quick question,” Mydei had to ask as they walked away and Phainon hummed to go ahead. “Has your perception of colour ever been different from those around you?”

Phainon squinted at him, brows furrowed. “No. What brought this up?”

“Curiosity,” Mydei brushed him off but his eyes caught on the fabric again, one laid over top the other in Phainon’s arms. “For any potential weaknesses to exploit in our next competition.”

Phainon chuckled. “Is that so? Sorry to disappoint.”

They met up with Ptolemy and Perdikkas carrying new arrows and medical bandages. Then Hephaestion and Peucesta with some smoked ribs and cheese bread between them. Ptolemy suggested they visit the local alehouse for drinks if they had all concluded their business and none of them refused.

It was an ordinary day. Nothing unusual from any other supply run through any other town thriving in the peaceful periphery of larger city states vying for power.

That was why none of them expected the black tide to surge.

The only warning was black blotting out the sky and devouring the sun. It was mere seconds before creatures appeared as numerous as rain in a storm.

Mydei crouched in a small alleyway away from the main streets suddenly flush with people, crushing each other beneath feet and against walls as they fled. He shoved his hands into his gauntlets and Hephaestion buckled them for him.

Peucesta had no weapon on hand except a short dagger. Perdikkas possessed a sword, and Hephaestion both a sword and a shield at his back. Phainon’s sword was strapped to his waist, heavier than the others as he trained his body to throw the weight of a great blade. Mydei had his gauntlets but only Ptolemy had a spear.

Mydei flexed his fingers, testing the joints of the gauntlets in the cold. “Ptolemy, your spear.”

It was difficult to see without the daylight but it was undoubtedly panic that flitted across his features, evident in his two steps forward and an aborted third. “Mydeimos…”

But all Mydei could see was Ptolemy’s body crushed beyond recognition beneath a pillar. The only proof it was him was the blood-soaked ends of his hair, the bracer around his wrist and his spear flung away by the collapse.

He silently opened both hands flat and any further objections died. Ptolemy presented his weapon and laid it across Mydei’s open palms.

“You four return to camp and inform the others,” Mydei ordered. “Phainon with me.”

Hephaestion paused as he re-buckled his sword from his back to his waist. Mydei knew what he wanted to offer—he could wield his sword beside them. Three was better than two against any foe, let alone the black tide— but, in Mydei’s absence, he always entrusted the detachment to Hephaestion and Krateros. He held his tongue and tied his hair back.

No objections, Mydei raised a hand and the rest of them followed. “May we all walk the path of victory and meet again.”

Wherever the black tide was spreading from, it had yet to reach them. There was no time to waste and the four of them merged into the crowd pushing towards the town’s main gate.

Mydei twirled Ptolemy’s spear, getting a feel for the length and weighting, slightly longer and heavier than he was used to. This was the right decision. For those without golden blood in their veins, and potentially marked for death, it was safer to return with reinforcements.

Metal shone as it slid slow and smooth to rest below the spear, overlapping and crossed together. Just like that, Phainon held up the weight for him.

Phainon’s lips curled into a crooked smile. “Ready?”

Mydei smirked back. “For victory? Always.”

In a twisted way, it was almost nostalgic. The two of them had fought side-by-side on many occasions, from friendly games amongst the detachment to life-or-death on the battlefield.

But this was the first time they stared down such an overwhelming force since that first joint encounter with the black tide. A force that didn’t settle or scatter—it only rose inevitability. A river under endless rain about to burst its banks and flood the plain. A raging sea crashing against the coast, wearing it away and gouging its way inland.

Under that black sky that would never see the sun again, the only thing they could rely on was themselves and each other. That Phainon would watch dispatch the blade before it met Mydei’s back as he rummaged through the rubble to pull out a sobbing child who had tried to rescue her cat. That Mydei would catch any arrows assailing Phainon as he carried an elderly man on his back until his son could take over.

Mydei thrust his spear and pierced through a creature’s chest. The hit knocked it to the ground in a plume of snow and shattered ice. It thrashed, tearing more of its flesh and bleeding orange and black on the blade, yet unable to pull free. It gurgled a dying wail and stilled.

He pulled the spear out and the body skidded across the ice when he kicked it away to open more space in the main street. “That puts me at seventeen.”

Behind him, Phainon sliced through another creature. They had both shed their himations to rid themselves of the extra fabric—too dangerous in battle where a corner snagging could mean their demise—exposing his build hidden underneath. Training with the detachment had squared out his shoulders, shaped his biceps and thighs, and strengthened his core to wield the weighty blade with relative ease.

“Eighteen for me,” Phainon answered tersely, bereft of the usual competitiveness and mirth curving his lip.

That was fine. Expected even.

Mydei dodged a black tide creature’s blades arm and retaliated with a sharp lift of his spear. The limb fell clean off and the next strike was to its neck. He picked up the severed arm and launched it at a creature coming out of an alleyway for Phainon’s back.

This was Phainon’s first encounter with the black tide since it engulfed his homeland. Worse still, the black tide looked the same no matter where it went. The darkened empty sky, the monsters that emerged from it, the smell of blood and rot in the air.

Mydei jumped and spun. He kicked a black tide creature in the chest, feeling the give under his heel even before the crack echoed in his ears as its body caved to the pressure. Once from his kick and again when it flew through a house under construction.

His feet slipped on the landing but he caught himself on his spear. Curse these icy roads. And the narrow streets while he was at it. Once reinforcements came it would be difficult for them to manoeuvre in the Kremnoan formations capable of weathering the black tide.

But when no one laughed at his blunder, he knew something was amiss. Phainon would never fumble such an obvious opportunity to jab at him unless—

He was distracted. His weapon hung limp at his side as he stared into the distance. In the harsh shadows and orange lights of the black tide, a new emotion cleaved apart Phainon’s lovingly crafted mask of composure and revealed itself in every harsh line of his face and body: hatred.

Mydei barely glimpsed the set of his jaw and his eyes darkened as though the black tide had already swallowed them too. The harsh reds and oranges set the golden tattoo on his neck alight.

So we can match, Mydei.

Our markings aren’t even remotely similar. Just say you want one.

Now they were similar. The golden sun was no longer a reminder of the gentle light over his hometown. It burned hot amidst the devastation, almost pulsing, like the red flames that flickered across Mydei’s body.

Phainon darted out into the side streets.

“Phai—“

A bowstring twanged and Mydei threw himself behind an overturned cart. If he had stayed in place, the arrow embedded in the wall would have gone through his brain. The black tide touch such a fundamental part of his body. He wasn’t sure what would happen to him if it ever did.

He stood just long enough to hurl his spear up and through the house window the arrow had come from. The black tide creature collapsed and Mydei didn’t have anymore time to spare. He gave chase.

By the time Mydei rounded the corner of the alleyway, Phainon had disappeared. He needed a better vantage point.

He took off running, jumped as high as he could, and pushed off the wall for the slight boost in height. He grabbed an open window and hauled himself up before clambering onto the roof.

Rot tainted the air. Beyond a mere smell, Mydei could taste it on his tongue and feel it crawling along his skin. It searched for a way to pry him open

and burrow its way inside. To feast on whatever humanity could be found in a body like his and fester, corrupting him from the inside out. It didn’t stop at the body. The mind had to be completely corroded too.

He needed to find that pinprick of white in the darkness. He couldn’t see from here. Phainon had gotten too far away too fast. He vaulted across to another rooftop and kept his stride going when he landed so he could jump to the next.

This was too far. He was straying too far from the main street and the town gates. Where was he?

There.

A swarm of black tide creatures. At the centre, a flash of white and steel locked in battle.

Mydei leapt from the rooftops and channeled his raging blood into a fist. The ground cracked beneath him and red crystals burst forth.

He didn’t check how many were impaled by those sharp edges. He simply charged at the ones that were left.

All of those negative emotions pressing against his throat, his heart, his mind and squeezing them to impotence—he took them all and launched them at his opponents.

He lost the spear so all he had was his gauntlets and his blood as he tore through death and decay with his hands and dared it to do the same to him. Every cut, every bruise, every drop of golden blood was paid back a thousand fold.

Soon there was only one left. Sword drawn, back to him, panting with the exertion that slicked white hair to his nape.

He turned at the sound of Mydei’s steps and Phainon’s body went sprawling to the floor at Mydei’s fist whipping across his jaw.

He hissed, hand at his bleeding lip and bruising jaw. His eyes were thin rings of blue around a greedy, feral black.  “Have you lost your mind?”

Mydei stalked towards him and Phainon had just enough time to get half way to his feet before Mydei grabbed him by his tunic and yanked. Mydei was still the shorter of the two but he hauled Phainon forwards right off his feet, putting an uncomfortable arch in his spine. When Phainon struggled to even his stance, Mydei kicked his legs to keep him there.

He deserved more than a split lip and bruised jaw but Mydei only shook him like the insanity would rattle out through his ear from brain. “I could ask you the same thing.”

They were supposed to fight beside each other. To watch each other’s backs and ensure they both made it back to the detachment alive.

But Phainon had run off without a second thought.

Phainon grabbed at Mydei’s wrist and any sense Mydei knocked into him was gone again. “He’s here. That black-robed swordsman. I saw him.”

Mydei’s teeth ground together. If they shattered they would just grow back. There were things he wanted to say, practically fighting to be the first to spew at him with fire and acid, but when he parted his lips there was no sound.

This was still an area about to be drowned under the black tide. Maybe Phainon saw the black-robed swordsman among the ruins that looked like his past. But they would drown in monstrous insanity before they found him.

Mydei scowled and shoved him away. He stumbled one step and recovered with a warrior’s grace.

Still, the space between them was enough to draw words like blood as he spat, “I didn’t realise you took yourself for a Kremnoan. Valorous death before glorious return.”

And he couldn’t keep the mockery from his voice. One that he had kept safely within the confines of his mind and his heart that knew better than that war cry. Strife and the endless gluttony for glory was nothing but a dead end.

He tore off a pointed end of crystal and hurled it. Phainon tipped his head but it was pointless. Either way, it skimmed past him and impaled a black tide creature through the head. More of them poured from the alley.

Mydei kissed his teeth. “Follow me or stay behind. Your hatred will weigh you down and ensure you drown in the coming tide. The choice is yours, Deliverer.”

He didn’t wait for an answer before he ran back the way he came. He needed to make it back to the main street so he could scatter the black tide and let his warriors push into the town with a sense of cohesion that could hold against the onslaught.

Over the chittering of black tide creatures and collapsing rubble hitting the ground, he may have heard footsteps echoing his but he didn’t turn to check. It could have just been the black tide finally finding a weakness to claw its way inside his mind.

Left. A shadow. He threw himself to the floor, tucking his shoulder and rolling back to his feet. His legs tensed as he prepared to throw himself at the black tide creature that had tried to take him by surprise.

A steel blade pierced its chest. It howled as the blade yanked free and the next swing came for its head, silencing the painful sound.

Phainon flicked the blood from his sword. Mydei glanced over him from the neck down for any major injuries. None. He kept running.

The black tide had advanced towards the open gates. It would be difficult to push them back but the line had to hold if he didn’t want the detachment swarmed the moment they funnelled into town.

Mydei’s tattoos pulsed and a number of small crystals formed in his palm. He tossed them towards the smaller streets that connected to the main one. They exploded on impact and blockaded the extra entrances off. The black tide would have to come straight for them.

White and gold in his periphery. He flexed his fingers and lunged for the nearest horde.

He had just finished ripping it to shreds when the klaxon sounded overhead. Not a signal of retreat but a declaration of war.

The detachment pressed in behind him and there was no day or night under the blackened sky, only the ache of his body and a growing pile of inhuman corpses at his feet as the battle raged on. If there was someone at his back, he didn’t know.

Eventually, the incursion began to slow and the detachment advanced. The same way a cut bled quick, then sluggish, and then stopped completely, the black tide lulled. It was just for now. A temporary respite before it inevitably erupted again.

But it was enough for the detachment to claim victory.

They organised search parties and dispersed throughout the town to sweep it for survivors as quickly as possible. Once there were no humans left to find amongst the corpses of monsters, they returned to the encampment.

Krateros reported no casualties—Ptolemy was alive. Mydei still had the chance to apologise for his lost spear and replace it with a new one—as Perdikkas purified Mydei’s wounds with the waters blessed by Phagousa. They found the vials in one of the Titan’s abandoned temple. While Krateros rattled on with the battle report and even once silence fell, Perdikkas kept quiet. He was too busy glancing furtively between Mydei and Phainon on opposite ends of the medical tent.

As soon as Mydei’s bandages were wrapped and he was dressed in a fresh set of garments, he strode out the tent and neither of them stopped him.

His face always rested in anger. Usually various members of the detachment would tease about his bad mood after a stellar victory and offer him a drink. But whatever expression he wore chased even the boldest of the detachment away.

His ears throbbed. His head ached. He hadn’t told Perdikkas. If he had, there was nothing the physician could do. It wasn’t the type of physical ailment that could be healed or his body would have done so already. It was all in his own head.

But he had over exerted himself. His arms and legs itched. Not the skin but the veins beneath it, all along the extremities where he had drawn blood to create those crystals. The blood replenished quicker than the sensation faded.

He paced his tent.

He wanted more. More battle, more bloodshed to lose himself in. It was the only time he could take the restraints of everything—duty, responsibility, fate—wrapped around him like chains and pull with all his might. Every unpleasant thought and memory could be sharpened into a weapon.

Then maybe his head wouldn’t be so full.

Phainon charged into battle with hatred his only guide. A death wish. Phainon broke one of the detachment’s laws and left his comrades vulnerable. A valorous death still left nothing more than a corpse. Phainon abandoned him. Phainon could have died within arms reach.

“Mydeimos,” someone called from behind the tent flap.

He inhaled, tensed his whole body and held it, then exhaled and relaxed. “Enter.”

Leonnius walked in first but the flap closed behind Peucesta. Leonnius’ neck was wrapped, likely around the same cut that just peeked over his jaw. Peucesta upper arm was bandaged but his forearms and fingers were hale enough for him carry and place a full chalice of honey brew without it

spilling, and to pluck at his lyre. Just twice to test the tension of the strings and he nodded before setting it aside.

No music from Peucesta. They were serious.

At Mydei’s open surprise, Leonnius ran a hand through his hair and it still fell perfectly arranged afterwards anyway. “Hephaestion and I swapped.”

“I’m his overseer,” Peucesta added.

Mydei sat on the kline. “What do you want?”

Leonnius dropped himself cross-legged to the floor cushion without spilling either chalice in his hands. He offered one to Mydei. “To hear the latest gossip of course. How are you looking to settle your grudge?”

Kremnoans returned favours tenfold and grudged a hundredfold. But once the matter was settled it was settled. If any ill feeling arose then they were put to rest as soon as possible through whatever means necessary. Every warrior needed to be able to trust the one beside them, in front of them, behind them. Petty grudges had no place among comrades on the battlefield. Especially as their life of exile, fraught with turmoil, could claim any one of them at a moment’s notice. To have a close relationship abruptly ended while wrought with resentment would mean a lifetime of regret.

“It’s not a grudge,” Mydei grumbled as he swirled his chalice, more red than he preferred. Leonnius always skimped on the goat milk; claimed Mydei’s taste buds would never mature otherwise.

Leonnius whistled. “Something you won’t settle with a duel. Who was at fault? You or him?”

“Him.”

He threw his head back and cackled. “Maybe I shouldn’t have agreed with Hephaestion’s plan. The look on that poor puppy’s face must be something.”

Mydei rolled his eyes but didn’t argue. He sipped his drink, leaning his chin against the hand braced at the elbow on the kline.

Once Leonnius finished laughing, Mydei set the chalice down, thumbing the smooth face slowly. “He abandoned my side to satiate his need for revenge.”

The smile slid from Leonnius’ lips. He set his honey brew aside. “That’s serious.”

Mydei let his silence agree.

It wasn’t Leonnius who spoke next. But Peucesta.

“Then will you no longer entrust your back to him?”

Mydei’s head jerked up to Peucesta’s dark eyes, always seeing and observing for the inspiration and verse that would outlive them all. “What?”

Leonnius shrugged, finger running the rim of his chalice. “Brothers in arms need complete trust in each other if they all want to make it home alive. He betrayed your trust. Are you going to do anything about it?”

It was no secret that out of everyone within the detachment—who had spent five years raising, training, teaching Mydei while also battling, eating and drinking, sleeping alongside him—Phainon had supplanted them all. He was the one Mydei trusted the most. The one Mydei wanted at his side not only in battle but when they marched by day and gathered around the campfires by night.

And the others suspected that might change.

Mydei poked his chalice. It swayed, tilted, and the liquid sloshed. But it didn’t spill and the chalice fell back into place like nothing happened. “No.”

“It’s your life,” Leonnius said, no judgement as he sipped his honey brew.

Mydei waited for him to drain the chalice before he glanced between the two and asked, “Did you ever expect another answer?”

They shared a look. Amused. Mydei knew their reply.

Leonnius grinned and raised his empty chalice high like a toast. “No.”

Peucesta played a song while Mydei finished his drink. It was a ballad of two brothers who went on to claim glory together. Only once the song ended did they leave him.

He needed to wash off, adorn his spare set of gauntlets, celebrate with his men already so rowdy outside. Yet he couldn’t bring himself to move from the kline.

Over the sounds of drunken cheer, footsteps shuffled on the grass back and forth in front of his tent. Yet no one asked permission to enter.

“Phainon.” The steps stopped. “Just come inside.”

The flaps parted and closed again behind Phainon as he skulked in, head and shoulders bowed. Under different circumstances, Mydei might have joked that the others must have given him quite the chiding. But it would fall flat. Besides, Phainon would have looked the same, even without the intervention of their friends, the moment hatred stopped fogging the forefront of his mind and his rationality returned alongside remorse.

Mydei motioned for him to sit and he did without hesitation. On his knees, still curled inwards at the neck and shoulder even when he tried to keep some dignity in his stiff back. It was as though he had received some terrible news or knew he was about to.

They both sat in silence. Phainon loved to speak, using his whole body to convey every word, so it was surprising that he remained absolutely still. The others must have warned him that Mydei didn’t take kindly to those who didn’t accept their deserved punishment outright.

Mydei blinked slowly as he realised that he had never been… angry with Phainon before. The closest he had ever come was annoyance but the difference between that and raw fury was as vast as the entirety of Amphoreus.

Mydei calmed the last embers of his anger with a deep breath. They smouldered, prepared to blaze again at the slightest provocation, but it didn’t feel like smoke to suffocate the both of them when he exhaled and spoke, “Your actions spoke enough, so heed my words. Seek revenge for the dead but don’t be so eager join them.”

“I won’t,” Phainon swore but his head remained bowed. “I… lost myself. In the heat of battle and my hatred. You have my deepest, most sincere apologies, Mydei. I don’t have the words to tell you how much I regret betraying your trust and leaving you in battle.”

“I’m not your keeper,” Mydei jabbed.

Phainon’s shoulders shrunk into himself and Mydei silently cursed. He meant what he said but perhaps the circumstances and his tone were too harsh for Phainon to brush it off.

But he then lifted his head and met Mydei’s eye and there was still shame but it merged with his resolve to no longer evade in cowardice. “No. But I abandoned your side once. I refuse to let there be a second time.”

Mydei tilted his head, considering as he gazed down at Phainon sat upon his knees while Mydei lounged on the kline. This sort of position didn’t suit them.

He sighed and crooked his finger, telling Phainon to rise and then join him with a pat of the cushioned seat. Phainon hesitated but Mydei arched a brow like a dare and Phainon quickly sat beside him. Back straight, legs together and hands tucked in his lap.

Unlike Phainon, Mydei had never hated anyone. But he had also never lost so much at someone else’s hands like Phainon. Perhaps animosity towards his father should have gone hand-in-hand with his pursuit of revenge for his crimes against Mydei and his mother. But all he felt was the resolve to carry through his responsibility, and an exhaustion he felt down to his soul. If anything, the only thing Mydei truly despised was…

Mydei rolled his eyes at Phainon’s scolded posture and nudged his thigh with his foot. “Hatred is a valuable weapon in the right hands. Use it as a whetstone to hone yourself until you can reach your goal. But exercise caution before you shatter yourself against it.”

… Fate. Everything true black-robed swordsman had attempted and in-part succeeded to take from Phainon was the same as what fate endeavoured to take from Mydei. His home, his friends, his family. So he knew how to take fear and contempt and use it as just another weapon. The same as his spear, his gauntlets, his immortal body.

Phainon nodded vigorously. “I will take your words to heart, Mydei.”

“I think your brain would be better.”

“Both would be best,” Phainon chirped and when he glanced sidelong at Mydei they shared a smile.

Mydei nudged him again with his foot. “Phainon, know that, if you do one day join the ranks of the dead, the one seeking revenge on your behalf will be me.”

Phainon’s eyes widened but Mydei didn’t know what he found so shocking. If Phainon died—a thought Mydei had hardly even entertained before today, and still scarcely believed—then who else would tear the entirety of Amphoreus asunder in search of retribution except Mydei.

But that was its own kind of curse. This thirst for revenge and the hatred that came with it. One that, if permitted, carved its way through bone and left something hollow behind—a mere spectre of living. If Phainon didn’t want Mydei to live by that same curse, then he would simply have to live a long life.

Mydei tipped his head into his knuckles and smirked. “And next time the opportunity for your revenge arises, speak to me and I will gladly be another weapon for you to achieve your goals.”

“Mydei…” Phainon breathed, the slightest tremble to his voice under so many layers of emotions. He shook his head. “Just having you at my side is enough.”

The chalice was empty but Phainon didn’t need to know that when Mydei lifted it to his lips the same moment he kicked at him. A playful thing that still aimed for Phainon’s neck but he easily dodged and grabbed him by the ankle, laughing the whole time. And Mydei gave himself away when his laughter echoed in the empty chalice.

That made the two of them, once again, the same. No matter what, Phainon would be the one entrusted with Mydei’s back.

Chapter End Notes

PhaiDei may have their fights but they (and the Kremnoan 5) will make sure they talk it out before the end of the chapter.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei spends the night hunting mercenaries and stargazing with Phainon.

Chapter Notes

In Mydei’s seventh year of exile, several city states began to fear the growing numbers and strength of the Kremnoan detachment. Through contracted mercenaries and rogue armies, they hoped to dispatch the eyesore that marched across Amphoreus once and for all.

Rather than try to flee or evade their enemies, Mydei blew their campfires out at sunset and hunted the mercenaries through the mountains surroundings Aenionus. Terrain they had spent the last several days memorising under pretence of marching through. There was no city for Peucesta to lure them into before they set it ablaze.

Nothing but the moon and stars to illuminate the way, it was almost nostalgic as Mydei sprinted through the forest after a fleeing figure.

His body had grown. No longer short and scrawny but tall and broad with muscles he kept amassing to match his brutal style of combat. Every day Phainon struggled to decide between telling him to stop or continue building more. A bit hypocritical considering the Phainon’s deliberate exercise regime, designed with accumulated knowledge from the entire detachment, to noticeably strengthen segments of his body.

It had only worsened since Mydei finally adopted more Kremnoan styles of clothing; body finally suited to the loose garments hanging off one shoulder and exposing his torso. There were all sorts of benefits: freer movement, fewer layers in the heat, less fabric to repair or replace. The biggest boon

arose on the battlefield as the sight of his bare body marked in red tattoos, his unruly mane and his golden claws inspired terror in his enemies.

But to be quick and evasive rather than bulky and unyielding was still familiar from a childhood where he sensed more than he thought. He knew how to lighten his steps, weave in and out of the trees, use the foliage to his advantage so they would never quite know how close he truly was.

Then he struck.

He dove down from the trees and kicked the mercenary to the ground with a boot to their ribs. They hit the floor hard but still tried to roll with the momentum. Mydei was already on top of them before they could recover, his spear driven through their chest. Then he was gone again before they could wheeze their last breath to curse him.

After days of scouting he had chosen this area. Except for the one mountain pass that led to and from Aenionus, there was nowhere else to flee when the mountains penned them in on all sides. It was the perfect hunting ground.

The Kremnoan detachment dressed in their darkest garments, distinguished only with a single strip of red fabric tied around their right arm. They prowled through the darkness in search of their prey with all the animalistic barbarism others accused them of, and would continue until the sun broke over the mountains.

It was far from an honourable battle. But the mercenaries had no interest in honour when they lurked in the shadows for days on end as the detachment roamed the mountains. A scavenger stalking a lion, not for the carcass of the prey but for the moment the lion was vulnerable enough to butcher. Observing. Waiting for the weakest moment before they would strike.

This was the chosen battlefield of their enemies. It was only right for the detachment to meet them upon it.

He leapt over a creek and his feet grazed  the grass when a flash caught his eye. He threw himself to the ground just as a blade flew over his head.

Close. Maybe it would finally be an opponent with skill and not just surprise.

He rolled away and to his feet as the great sword plunged into the earth where he had first dropped flat. The moon gleamed off the hilt and edge. He squinted. He knew that great sword—had sparred against it and been saved by it. He would recognise it anywhere even as the tip pierced through his back.

“Phainon.”

His assailant yanked his sword from the ground and paused. He stepped out the shadow between two trees and lowered his hood, revealing white hair and bright blue eyes. “Mydei! I didn’t realise it was you.”

Mydei took Phainon’s offered hand, letting himself to pulled to his feet. “Is that so? Just when I thought you had finally seized your opportunity to dispose of me for good.”

At eighteen, Phainon had stopped growing taller sometime in the early half of the year, and, as though his body couldn’t remember how to be static, put on even more muscle in his shoulders, biceps and thighs. Mydei was still growing fast but two years difference and nine years of neglect means difficult to dispel. A fact Phainon always took advantage of by draping himself over Mydei’s shoulder at every opportunity.

Even now, his arm slung over Mydei’s shoulder while the other hovered over his own heart in mock offence. “The end of our relationship requires something more fitting. Something remarkable that the poets of Amphoreus would write epics about for eras to come.”

“And how would you accomplish that small feat?”

His smile grew, ever more mischievous, and he leaned closer with a secret shared just between them. “A duel declared in front of the entire Kremnoan detachment. It would continue day and night until I finally found the answer to that immortal body of yours.”

Mydei’s tenth thoracic vertebra ached like it had already shattered once before. But that wasn’t enough to deter him from the idea of that duel between them nor the thrill that Phainon had envisaged it, hardly different from his own fantasies, too.

Mydei grabbed at the wrist dangled over his shoulder and squeezed like he meant to shatter the bone. “Good luck with that. I’ll wear you down before you get anywhere close.”

Phainon kept his hand in place and chuckled. “That’s very confident of you.”

The rustle of the undergrowth alerted them to a presence and they both fell silent. Too strong and too low to be the wind when the branches overhead hadn’t even swayed. Mydei flicked the dagger from his belt into the bushes with one quick movement. A quiet squeal. Not human but, when they parted the bushes, a rabbit.

“Huh.” Phainon plucked the dagger out and cleaned it with a flick before spinning the hilt to face Mydei. “Good throw.”

Mydei sheathed the blade with a mild hum. “I have always been better at game hunting than you.”

“Hey now. I give you an honest compliment and you give me lies in return.”

“That’s why you stole one of my rabbits during our hunting competition.”

“You will never let that one go, will you?” Phainon said with a forlorn little sigh and shake of his head. “How long has it been? A year? That was an honest mistake, I swear it upon my honour as a warrior.”

Mydei had actually forgotten all about the incident until now. It was nothing of note, simply routine hunting competition during an easy spring, but Mydei would swear Phainon stole one of his rabbits to supplement his own kill count and edge out Mydei for the victory. Phainon had always denied it.

The results had hardly mattered considering they were technically on the same team the entire time.

Still, he rolled his eyes and shrugged Phainon’s arm off just as it was returning to its chosen perch on his shoulder. “If Nikador strikes you down before morning, we shall know why.”

“Ah ha!” Phainon cheered, entirely too loud considering the night hunt. He was triumphant even as Mydei walked away and he trailed behind. “So if I live then I must be telling the truth and you can no longer bring the matter up.”

“It means Nikador happened to be asleep.”

Phainon took the sharp reply in stride and laughed, leaning forward into Mydei’s peripheral vision, eyes crinkling when their gazes met. “Then I will declare it before every battle. Surely Nikador must watch at least one in our lifetime.”

Mydei paused. First under the guise of listening for any close movements. Then in consideration as he gazed at the full moonlight and pinpricks of starlight through the canopy. Simply watching as the always did, seeking to capture stories to scatter across the night sky.

“It would have to be a grand battle,” Mydei murmured. “One that could shake the earth and the skies.”

When he glanced over again, Phainon had a hand on his great sword and the other his hip. He was already smiling at Mydei, too gentle for a conversation about their weapons levelled at one another, but it was a language shared between them. “Then I’ll save my declaration for the day we finally duel with our all.”

Mydei’s lip curled and he twirled his spear, balancing it across his shoulders as he picked any direction to start in. Just to get moving. They had stood around long enough his sweat was cooling dewy on his skin.

“Acceptable. And I will continue to bring the matter up until then, lest you forget.”

Phainon sped up to walk at Mydei’s side, mindful of the spear but bypassing it to brush their shoulders together. “Oh Mydei, like I’d ever forget anything about you.”

There was no reason for them to stay together—two people made more noise than one, they were both capable fighters on their own, they covered more ground apart. But every time he glanced around, he caught sight of a red armband and white bangs peeking from beneath the hood moving in tandem with him through the darkness.

The mercenaries had realised the hunt was on after the first dying cries echoed through the night. Few had the courage to stand against the detachment without a well-timed ambush. The ones that did were the first to perish in the opening wave of the bloodbath.

The rest of them hid amongst the undergrowth, burrowing into caves and clambering up trees where they could lash out with an advantage and boost their meagre chances of survival. Others hoped the detachment would simply miss them and move on, leaving them to flee. Only to be caught by the groups stationed on either end of the mountain pass.

Although the two of them had a habit of competing with numbers, that was reserved for the black tide or hunting competitions rather than human lives. There was no celebration or witty remark when Phainon’s great sword pierced someone’s chest or Mydei’s spear cut through their neck. No regret either. Only a quiet resolve and acceptance that Death had come to the mountains of Aenionus. If not for the mercenaries then it would be the detachment.

Their encounters began to dwindle until several hours passed without a hint of an enemy. They searched through tree hollows, empty fox dens, small caves but all turned up empty. There were only other detachment members, still roaming, but the smoke occasionally rising from the trees meant they were settling down for now.

They wandered along the river. Mydei even challenged Phainon to delve into the water and check a small cove nestled into the wall. A child would have been lucky to fit inside but Mydei stood at the bank, hanging over the sunken river, while Phainon stood calf deep and peered into the opening because they had raced over who could climb a tree fastest and Phainon lost.

“Feel free to borrow my spear,” Mydei said with just a tinge of mocking and a thump of his spear against the ground.

Phainon’s great sword would just about fit but the spear would be more flexible if anyone were hiding inside—they definitely were not—yet he waved over his shoulder. “Keep that for yourself.”

The grass rustled behind him, quiet beneath the gurgle of the river but not low enough to escape his senses. One person. Kremnoan military training.

“Your Highness. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon jerked his head into the cove roof and he reeled back, hissing Kremnoan curses near silent under his breath but Mydei could read his lips well enough. A snicker escaped Mydei’s pressed lips and he arched a brow when Phainon shot a glare at him as he rubbed his sore head.

Then it settled into an amiable smile when he glanced over Mydei’s shoulder. His knees and waist bent, about to kneel or at least bow, but the splash of water up his thighs stopped him.

His expression turned a bit more sheepish at that and he waved instead. “Good evening, Krateros.”

It was far from evening but to say goodnight would be an even greater blunder. Phainon generally sought approval so long as the other person was worth his respect and it wasn’t being maliciously withheld. Krateros was one of the few people Phainon wanted approval from. He certainly knew how to select a challenge for himself.

“What brings you here, Krateros? Where are your men?” Mydei asked as he offered Phainon a hand and hauled him onto the bank.

“We found someone cowering inside a fallen tree trunk.” Krateros kissed his teeth. “These mercenaries are nothing but cowards. To disgrace themselves by fearing death at the hands of their enemy.“

Mydei hummed and Phainon paused as he squeezed the water from his clothes. Not to catch Mydei’s attention but mere curiosity at the sound, neither agreeing nor disagreeing with Krateros’ sentiment.

Mydei nudged him with his foot and pointed at his drenched lower half again, telling him to focus on the task at hand, before he spoke to Krateros, “I assume the smoke curling belongs to our own men.”

Krateros checking Mydei up and down for injuries or anything else he needed to address, and then lingered on Phainon. “Yes, while they are taking a reprieve from the battle they also remain vigilant for any mercenaries the campfires may draw out.”

“So long as they keep their weapons at hand and honey brew from their tongue, they can do as they please.”

Krateros looked between the two of them again, confusion pinching his brow. That was fair considering, while the rest of the department gathered into small parties, Phainon and Mydei had split off alone at the beginning of the hunt. In the vast mountain range, they had somehow ended up back together in hardly any time at all.

“You two…” He shook his head and masked the confusion behind an authoritative cross of his arms that only grew more intimidating with every grey hair he collected with time. “Have either of you taken a rest since the hunt began?”

“Not yet,” Phainon said, slow and brows furrowed.

Although they weren’t at rest, they were hardly at work either. More so at play.

“See that you do,” Krateros advised, too gruff for his words and stiff shoulders. “To… dry off. The water will weigh you down. And the night is cold.”

Mydei’s lip quirked as Krateros walked back the way he came. Perhaps Krateros would never be fond of Phainon but Mydei didn’t think Krateros was fond of anyone except for Mydei himself. Even then, was any of that fondness addressed to him or to the crown Krateros envisioned he would one day wear, and the woman he had failed in the past.

If Krateros knew Mydei’s own treacherous thoughts directed at their dynasty and homeland—that the so-called false prophecy and voices of traitors in Eurypon’s ears were nothing but truth—perhaps he would have agreed with Mydei’s father and tossed him into the Sea of Souls himself.

They wandered without even the facade of searching for more mercenaries until they found a rocky outcrop in the open, cushioning it with their chlamys to rest.

Mydei unwrapped his jerky rations and offered some to Phainon, the same way Phainon offered his waxed leather flask of pomegranate juice, despite both having their own full rations. Phainon took the jerky from Mydei’s fingers with his teeth. Mydei let Phainon tip the juice into his mouth before taking it back for himself.

Phainon chewed slowly when he usually gobbled his food so quick Perdikkas had to dislodge his food before he choked and Mydei challenged him to name a single thing he tasted except for the obvious salt.

Then he uttered, more a question than a proud declaration of intent, “Valorous death before glorious return.”

Mydei stilled. He slowly swirled his own flask like it was a chalice. “Going into battle against your dinner?”

Phainon didn’t rise to the bait he simply rested his arm over his propped knee, fiddling with a length of smoked jerky and gazing unseeing at the

trees. “While the rest of the detachment adopt it as their motto before they charge into battle, I’ve yet to see you use it.”

“What of it?” Mydei drawled as his heart quickened and he tore into a length of boar meat just to feel something that wasn’t his tongue between his teeth. “To constantly use the same speech would lessen its effect.”

Now it was his turn to hum noncommittally. He chewed thoughtfully at the jerky and didn’t grab another, only dusting his hands off. Mydei finished his food in silence despite his appetite disappearing as quick as the cold night descended once the sun vanished into the horizon.

Phainon raised his flask to the moon and stars. “May victory always be yours.” He tilted his head into a smile in Mydei’s direction. “You use that one all the time, no?”

“All the time is an exaggeration.”

“Then, you use that one and subtle variations the majority of the time.” Phainon tapped his finger at the stone beneath him to a deliberate rhythm, following the steady beat of his thoughts. “But that, too, is a traditional Kremnoan sentiment.”

“And what of it?”

“It just feels as though… you’ve never been fond of that idea. Valorous death before glorious return.” And then, as though Phainon hadn’t cracked Mydei’s head open on the rocks and read his hidden thoughts, second in secrecy only to one deception, illuminated in moonbeams and starlight, Phainon smiled like the sun. “Is that right, Mydei?”

His mouth opened and even moved but no sound escaped. But words should never be used where actions sufficed.

His hand shot out and Phainon’s eyes widened, reflecting black and gold, but didn’t move even when Mydei’s glove pressed against his lips and his claws dug into his jaw. No blood. Just the threat of Mydei’s gauntlets drawing gold to smear across his round cheeks and sharp jaw balanced

between adolescence and adulthood. Maybe some light bruising beneath the tips, thumb on one side and four fingers on the other.

“Speak of this to no one,” he growled with all the ferocity of a cornered animal.

Phainon’s brows creased and he would have tilted his head if he were able. But Mydei’s hand kept his head firmly in place and his mouth shut. He couldn’t answer.

Mydei let go but Phainon still didn’t speak, just stared at Mydei with eyes as deep as the pit of the sea Mydei had once crawled through. Brighter, lighter, even in the darkness of the night. Rather than weigh him down and drag him into a watery grave, it sought to lift him like wind beneath feathered wings during a warm, clear day as Phainon searched his every feature with something working behind his eyes.

“So,” Phainon began cautiously, hand loosely cupping his jaw where Mydei had grabbed. “You… don’t entirely agree?”

Of course. Phainon had never let anything go in his life. The same as following his every step, sticking to him, completing chores and favours— just another thing he was so dogged about.

Mydei crossed his arms and squeezed. The same as prying teeth, the word was dragged slow and bloody from his mouth. “No.”

Phainon only hummed blithely, massaging the redness that would likely darken to bruises. “You never mentioned that before.”

A harsh laugh tasting like iron came next. “I never mentioned that I—“ he clenched his jaw. Never before had he voiced it out loud. But it wanted out so badly he could feel it knocking the back of his teeth, “—oppose the most central creed of Kremnos.” He pushed his bangs back, clawing at his scalp. “Oddly enough, I never saw fit to mention it in conversation.”

There was no offence in Phainon’s expression. He only offered his flask. Mydei had his own. He took it anyway and threw a mouthful back. Tartness

washed down the back of his throat and left a bitter aftertaste with no milk to dilute it. He dragged his arm across his mouth as he passed the flask back and Phainon took a sip too. No words. Only their breaths falling into rhythm as they watched the stars.

When he was ready to spit something other than vitriol and panic, Mydei spoke. “Strife is nothing but a dead end.” He chuckled as hollow as the sentiments that united his detachment. “Valour? Glory? I’ve clawed my way out the Sea of Souls and listened to the longing cries of the dead countless times. There is no valour. No glory. No eternal battlefield. Nothing worth discarding your life for.”

On instinct, Phainon’s head swivelled but he stopped himself and forced himself to look at the tree tops curling with smoke where the detachment rested, the mountains in the distance that sealed them off from the rest of the world, the sky above them that connected Amphoreus’ lands—its past, present and future.

“Then what is it like?” Phainon asked, casual yet  soft where he was usually loud in his cheer. “Tell me, Mydei, what it was like for you.”

No one had ever asked before. Not like that. Not in a way that wasn’t probing for imagery of an endless battlefield of past heroes. Their only interest, drunk on battle or honey brew, was an exhilarating tale. One he gave them in the form of creatures slaughtered at the hands of a child.

Mydei’s exhale trembled like his soul had never quite thawed, even after seven years. “Light, sound and warmth were all unknown. The only constant were the monsters. Not as monstrous as creatures of the black tide. But they knew I was… not the same as them—smaller, weaker. When they hunted me down and my body stitched itself back together, it would begin all over again.”

He knew Phainon had given up the facade of not looking, reliant on the barest tip of his head and his eye peering out the corner. But Mydei didn’t want to know what kind of expression he was making. To some extent, he already knew. The pure anguish at Mydei’s anguish, like he would take any beating, any impairment, any pain if it would spare Mydei the same pain.

But there had to be more. Sympathy. Worse: pity. Maybe realisation that violence was as much a part of him as his own blood. That he was nothing more than another monster from the Sea of Souls constrained to a human body. What else would explain his resistance to the Hand of Shadow and his undying body?

He didn’t want to see something that could change the easy rhythm between them he always took for granted. Miss a beat, a step, and they may never align again.

Yet he wanted to be seen. For someone to understand even a sliver, as slim as a newly waxing moon in the night, and there was no one who understood him better than Phainon.

He squeezed his arms tighter, carefully not to tear fabric and flesh with his claws as he held himself the way people usually held others or were held by them. “No pain in this world could ever compare to what I already endured. And in the places where the dead gather and wait for passage along the West Wind, they speak to me. It’s nothing but frigid ruins brimming with sorrow.”

Only two voices had ever given him reassurance. The rest clamoured for him to join him. Give up on living, just as they were forced to do, and sink to the bottom of the Sea of Souls where he would never again wake to a warm sun.

All those souls dressed in Kremnoan garbs or armour who took one look at his own clothing and the mark of Strife over his chest. They gathered around him, a legion of the dead who elevated him to the fore of an endless battle that would never come, no matter how they hoped. Warriors who still hungered for glory in a place it would never be found. As though, stripped to their barest selves, that voracity was as much a part of them as anything else—more than the desire for life.

Pinpricks stung his arm and he let go before blood could bead through the tiny holes in his sleeve. He dropped his chin against his tucked knee, eyes lowered to the drab stone. “What could be more courageous and venerable than fighting for a future to live by?”

One where his friends yet lived. Even if they turned their backs on him once they inevitably realised the truth of his disdain for Castrum Kremnos and its crown, so long as they had the chance to live,  he could accept the most bitter loss.

The shuffle of fabric, and the air warmed with Phainon’s presence. His feet slid into view beside Mydei’s own without touching. “But once you become king would it not be possible for you to create change.”

He shook his head. “If their minds were so easily swayed, fear would have done so already. This ideal has been ingrained throughout Kremnos’ entire thousand year long existence. The cycle of Strife and the Kremnoan dynasty keep each other aflame.”

A wildfire blazing out of control. A destructive force of nature whose strength was never to be doubted. But it would one day consume everything and then itself when there was nothing left to burn. Not a soul left to throw itself onto the pyre in the name of honour.

But a corpse was still nothing more than a corpse. When the soul departed for the Sea of Souls and the body became carrion, a glorious death made no difference.

“To claim the throne and lead the detachment home,” Mydei recited the purpose handed to him. The voices of his friends who still lived but should have died and bestowed their final words onto him echoed in his mind. His hands clenched, scraping through fabric to the stone. “Would be a death sentence issued by my own hand. Perhaps not immediately but their future and the future of their children will end in blood.”

Because they would rather expend their lives fighting for their homeland, a valorous death for a glorious irrational outcome, until the black tide swallowed them all than even attempt to adopt a peaceful way of life. Even if an eternal day burned just over the horizon, the final haven of Amphoreus, the Kremnoans would refuse safe refuge and fight until their final breath.

Honour, Courage, Tenacity, Sacrifice were not inherently detrimental values. Mydei strived to uphold them with every draw of his weapon, knowing he could never expect his warriors to follow them if he did not. But even Nikador knew they were most formidable when balanced by Reason.

Phainon waited for him to say more. Mydei kept his lips thinned but he closed that final distance so their feet bumped at the ankle bone; their thighs and shoulders pressed together.

“This view of the stars…” Phainon said with a smile clear in his voice. Not the big showy one, or the overly polite one. Not teasing or goading. An honest one. “It’s nostalgic.”

To Mydei, the night sky was simply the night sky. So long as it wasn’t the Evernight or the lightness abyss, the moon was the moon and the stars were the stars. To Phainon, being beneath a starry sky reminded him of a time when he was young and gazed up at the same sky. Home. And he could pretend everything was unchanged.

Phainon pointed. “That’s my favourite constellation.”

His finger drew through air like he could touch the sky itself and leave proof of his existence there. Maybe he could. Stars were named after heroes. Perhaps, one day, a constellation of a hero wielding a great sword would be named after Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. It would be fitting. Phainon would not only engrave his name into history but the very sky itself.

Mydei’s body was stiff, prepared for the nonexistent threat that had set every part of him on edge, alight, and faded away like nothing because it was Phainon beside him.

He leaned back on his hands and squinted at a cluster of tiny, distance lights. “What is it?”

“Leon. The lion.”

Mydei squinted harder. “I fear your eyes are different to mine.”

“Here.” Phainon threw an arm over Mydei’s shoulder and tugged him close, the lines of their torsos squeezed together so Mydei could follow the line of his finger. “See. It starts over there and then—“ he dragged his finger through the stars, “—goes like that and ends—“ he flicked his finger, “—at the tail.”

He repeated the motion. Just as he must have done—or had someone do for him. A mother, a father, a best friend—in the wheat fields untouched by Strife and bloodshed. Now Phainon was an adult dusting off the memories of a young boy as he tried to follow the stars and take the two of them to a safe and peaceful home. Somewhere simple.

“I still don’t see anything.”

“Come on, Mydei, use some imagination. Or must I check with Ptolemy if that word exists in the Kremnoan dictionary?”

That excuse had become unusable only two years into Phainon’s time with the detachment, unless Mydei felt particularly audacious. Phainon’s brain was built for knowledge and so much exposure to the language meant he absorbed it quickly.

He huffed but did nothing to elbow Phainon from his shoulder. “The only star I need to be aware of is Cynosura.”

“The star to help navigate the poles? How pragmatic of you,” Phainon chuckled with a small shake of his head. “But I refuse to believe that you don’t possess a favourite. There has to be one you’re drawn to. What about the heroes of old scattered across the night sky? Surely one of their tales must call out to you.”

Of all the ballads Peucesta sang, epics and poems of old heroes, none of them had ever particularly resonated with him. The rest of his friends had at least one or two they would request Peucesta recite for them, but Mydei only listened and appreciated the skilled voice and coordination of his

friend, holding a weapon more powerful than any spear. One that thrived in war and peace.

Mydei stared at Phainon’s bright eager eyes and the stars glittering across them. “Is there a dog?”

He perked up and held up two fingers. “There are actually two.”

Phainon flopped onto his back, one arm behind his head while the other remained free to gesture at the sky again like some strange, forgotten ritual to summon Aquila. Mydei laid down next to him to stand a chance of seeing the thing that had Phainon so enamoured.

“Canis Major,” he stated as he traced it with his finger. “And Canis Minor. Big dog and small dog.”

Mydei hummed, considering, but the angle wasn’t good enough. He shuffled closer, head laying on Phainon’s sternum while he gazed up. “Show me again.”

He could hear and feel Phainon’s heart beating fast but he obliged in drawing both constellations out again. Mydei could almost see them if he squinted and tilted his head just so against Phainon’s chest.

“Canis Major is my favourite,” Mydei concluded anyway. “But it could provide useful knowledge to hear about the others.

They stayed like that—Mydei’s head pillowed on Phainon’s chest and Phainon’s arm draped across his shoulder. He pointed out the stars and recited stories he had read in books, learned from home, or heard from Peucesta and Ptolemy—until the sun reached through the mountains. Mydei saw nothing but Phainon’s pale skin against the dark sky, outstretched hand just within reach if he dared to grasp it, and heart steady beneath his ear.

Chapter End Notes

PhaiDei chose their favourite constellations based on each other. Neither of them noticed. They’re losers.

This chapter (and next chapter I’m ngl) slightly delayed because of irl stuff. Not bad. Just things that consume more time than I thought they would unfortunately.
