chapters.title: Chapter 11
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei has one last night to resolve himself to fulfil one prophecy in an effort to subvert another.

Chapter Notes

In Mydei’s tenth year of exile, the awe disappeared from the voices of those who uttered the name Castrum Kremnos and only the fear remained. The renowned mobile fortress that heralded Strife and defeat at the hands of the fearless warriors it housed had become the home of something else: a Mad King and Mad Titan—there was no match more perfect.

The Kremnoan detachment’s ranks swelled with their infamy. Exiled Kremnoans flocked from across Amphoreus to join and many chose to exile themselves from Castrum Kremnos, fleeing the Mad King, to pledge their loyalty to the Crown Prince and pin their hopes of restoring Castrum Kremnos to its full glory onto him.

As time passed, the dreams and memories, the feeling that he had done something before or the relief in feeling as though he hadn’t, began to get more distant. Hazier. As though the desperation that had forced him to peer beyond the veil of the world had, after ten long years of sleepless nights, grown weary.

Or perhaps unnecessary. Perdikkas ground herbs by the fire. Leonnius ran around the encampment to snatch food from every cooking pit. Ptolemy polished his sword. Peucesta strummed a song about a hero finally returning home. All of them alive and thriving at Mydei’s side.

None of them would live forever, but in the years since Mydei had rewritten their deaths with his one hand, Fate had never come for them again. As

though Fate were not a predator on a relentless chase for its prey, but a mere snare in the road that Mydei guided them past.

Only one snare remained.

“Mydeimos.”

He blinked slow, eyes burning from how long he had simply stared at the scene in front of him. One from a dream if only his dreams weren’t so terrible.

Hephaestion offered him a new chalice and Mydei placed his down on the grass—empty. Not that he realised until now—and took it. The lowlight, more shadow than fire so far from the campfire, made it near impossible to see the colour of the liquid but Mydei knew it would be the same as always: mixed to perfection.

Hephaestion sat at his side. “Why so distant? Has the mark of a decade finally disillusioned you to the greatness of your companions?”

Mydei spun the chalice stem between his fingers. “Not at all. I was merely thinking about something.”

“The strategy to take Castrum Kremnos is sound. We all agree,” Hephaestion immediately reassured him of the conclusion they had come to in the war tent just the day prior.

But it wasn’t the battle that would come with the dawn that had captured Mydei’s thoughts.

“Hephaestion.”

“Mydeimos.”

Mydei raised his chalice to the full moon, pink liquid dyed milky. “You are my dearest companion. In my absence I would entrust my detachment, my warriors, my people to you.”

Hephaestion stayed silent. Not because he was waiting for Mydei to continue, potentially a cost to his grand compliments, but due to his gaping lips and wide eyes. The chalice almost slipped from his hand.

“I… I’m aware,” Hephaestion finally scrounged together some composure after Mydei’s highly effective opening strike. “And honoured by how you honour me.”

Mydei hummed. He could leave the conversation there. Hephaestion might think him a bit strange but the events of the night and the next day would leave little space for him to linger over it. If it ever came up again, it could be blamed on the nerves.

But Mydei was never one to back down after deciding on a course.

“Have you ever considered what may have been if we had never found Aedes Elysiae?”

If Mydei had never found Phainon. If Phainon had never joined the detachment.

Hephaestion was still his dearest companion but it was no secret that Phainon was more. It wasn’t the detachment Mydei entrusted to him—but his own back.

Never in six years had Mydei caught even a speck of bitterness or gloom. Not when Mydei discussed the detachment’s next location or aim with him, nor when Hephaestion and Phainon nursed strays back to health together. Not during encampment training regimens and sparring sessions nor when they all shared honey brew together.

Hephaestion was the same as all Mydei’s memories of a future that would never come to pass. It was Mydei who was different: less dependant on him militarily and emotionally. After all to the them that should have been, their closest companions began to leave one by one until only the other remained.

Not only were the six of them still united, a seventh member had melded into seamlessly.

Phainon, who was more to Mydei than even his dearest companion. Who Mydei relied upon to keep him sharp physically and soften his rough edges emotionally. A distinctly non-Kremnoan touch, without all the expectations that Mydei wholeheartedly wished he could make true. But refused to just the same.

Mydei asked if Hephaestion had ever considered it, yet Mydei had no need to imagine—he already knew.

Hephaestion only shrugged. “Perhaps once or twice. But never in much depth. Only as a passing thought that…” He chuckled and tucked his hair behind his ear. “Of relief. That the Sea of Souls had gifted you such a name as Aedes Elysiae.”

Mydei blinked at him. “Relief?”

Now Hephaestion smiled, just as sheepish as that little laugh, so far from the wild grin of the battlefield Mydei had learned from him, and the colour to his cheeks wasn’t only the distant firelight. “Yes. Not that you were unhappy for those first four years. But your happiness always had a weight to it. As though you could never fully enjoy the moment.”

Mydei pressed the chalice to his lips, if only to stop himself from doing the same with his fingers and tracing the edges of his smile. Hephaestion had no reason to lie but it was something Mydei had never noticed about himself. How obvious was his dissatisfaction?

“In that unknown wheat farming village with the unknown boy you met, it was as though you finally discovered how simple happiness could be.”

Simple happiness. Perhaps that was what it looked like to a Kremnoan. Joy that didn’t need honour nor glory.

It was simply allowed to be, and not earned. That was why Mydei had never thought about it that way but Hephaestion was far from wrong. With

Phainon, he could be whatever he wished to be—shrewd or childish, wise or foolish, courageous or fearful. Without the burden of his titles and responsibilities of the Crown Prince or even Mydeimos. He only had to be Mydei.

Even now, he watched Phainon pluck at the strings on a lyre as he glanced between his fingers and Peucesta nodding his approval between words. And what was Mydei to do except smile.

He swallowed the rest of his drink in one and stood. “Come. Let’s join them.”

Hephaestion laughed loud and not abashed, accepting the hand pulling him to his feet. It was always Phainon who noticed him first, body attuned to Mydei’s presence, able to locate him no matter the crowd of a marketplace or the chaos of battle. He didn’t stop strumming even as Mydei tugged off his gauntlets and presented his open hands.

Leonnius whistled. “Mydeimos has finally returned to his musical career.”

Phainon missed the next note and Ptolemy winced. Yet Phainon was busy searching Leonnius’ face to Mydei’s hands, then Mydei’s face, and dropped to Mydei’s bare hands again. “I wasn’t aware you could play.”

“I have many talents.” Mydei shrugged and motioned with his hands again.

“It was Peucesta’s idea,” Perdikkas said, pestle and mortar set aside for some fig juice.

When Phainon looked questioningly at Peucesta, he lowered his warmed goats milk mixed with honey, good for his throat, and explained, “To teach him to gentle his hands.”

“Huh.” Phainon handed the lyre over and scooted over so Mydei could sit beside him on the felled log. “Did it work?”

Leonnius raised his chalice of pure pomegranate juice. “Snapped so many strings Peucesta dug a grave for them.”

So close to the fire pit, it was only natural Mydei felt his face warm. He shifted the lyre in his hands, his arms, and stretched his fingers across the strings.

“But yes,” Hephaestion showed some mercy with a smile at the corner of his lips, inclining his head. “Have a listen for yourself.”

As though Phainon’s body weren’t already tilted towards him, ears open and waiting, eyes fixed on the slope of Mydei’s face. At such an angle, the reddened tips of Mydei’s ears must have been visible through his hair, and they were too close for Mydei to hope the light and shadow of the fire could hide it.

Mydei played one song, one of three he knew. The rust fell away like an old weapon, picked up from a forgotten battlefield so that the craftsmanship below could be revealed and appreciated after so long.

At some point, he had simply stopped picking up the lyre. There was no incident to deter him when his friends had only encouraged him despite the sheer number of broken strings and shrill notes that defiled their ears.

He just knew that one day, and once upon a time, it had hurt to hold a lyre with no one to play it for.

Now, Peucesta sang along, never faltering even when Mydei strummed the wrong string with the wrong timing. The others sang along at the rhythm’s crest. Phainon swayed at his side, shoulders bumping but too gentle to dislodge his hands over the strings.

When he finished, cheers erupted from their small group of seven and everyone raised their chalices. A new one found its ways into Mydei’s hand and he raised it too, all downing their drinks as one.

No alcohol. They knew better than to drink excessively before a battle.

The lyre returned to its rightful owner, playing idle notes to accompany their conversation passing around the circle, rising and falling as the fire

simmered and jumped. Sounds that broke away in flickering embers only to merge once again at the right moment.

“How are the remedies?” Mydei asked Perdikkas.

He chuckled and shook his head. “You worry too much, Mydeimos. The remedies have improved with the herbs you recommended. But they’re still unnecessary. Hephaestion’s condition has been stable for years now.”

Across the fire pit, Hephaestion threw his head back and laughed at something Leonnius had said. An embarrassing story based on Ptolemy’s arms thrown around Leonnius’ neck.

If Mydei wanted to preserve moments like it, he must maximise Hephaestion’s odds of surviving the relapse of his illness in the coming months. Supplementing his diet and stocking every ingredient Perdikkas could possibly need, to the confusion of both, was far from enough.

Even if Perdikkas were here, he couldn’t stop destiny from taking me.

Hephaestion had said so himself, whether as a final comfort or a fatalistic acceptance Mydei didn’t know. But he knew better than to risk it.

They parted ways for the night. Mydei’s private tent had recently become a shared tent after the others complained that Phainon had gotten too large to continue sharing with any them. Mydei had told them to rearrange themselves to make room, yet it was nothing but a cursory argument and they all knew how it would end.

So it was Phainon who settled in the cot opposite Mydei’s with wishes for a good rest before blowing out the candle. Phainon’s breaths that played in Mydei’s ears as they lengthened and evened out under the influence of sleep, just loud enough that Mydei wasn’t quite alone as he closed his eyes, greeted by darkness and his thoughts.

Illnesses like Hephaestion’s, which plagued him throughout his entire life, weren’t as simple as an enemy to evade or cut down. While Perdikkas’ life hadn’t ended during that ill-fated battle against Ladon in Mydei’s fourth

year of exile, he still had yet to find any cure and Mydei began to accept there were none for Hephaestion’s condition. Instead, he needed Hephaestion to survive in spite of his relapse.

Mydei needed the Kremnoan detachment inside Okhema.

“Mydei…” a bleary voice whined, still half-asleep, and Mydei paused partway to the tent entrance. “Where are you going?”

He huffed a laugh. His footsteps had been near silent but somehow Phainon had woken up anyway. “A walk.”

He yawned, a shadow moving in the dark as he pushed himself up. “Wait a moment. I’ll join you.”

Mydei rolled his eyes. “Lie back down and rest.”

“What have we said about stones and glass houses,” Phainon retorted, too slurred to be sharp, and tossed his blanket back onto his cot.

Mydei’s frowned. “Don’t be sloppy. At least fold that.”

Even if Mydei didn’t intend to be gone long, he had smoothed the creases from his blanket so it appeared untouched. Diligent cleanliness was simply good practice when infections and infestations spread like wildfire in such close quarters, which he failed to instil in Phainon after six years.

Phainon stretched his arms overhead, yawning again. “We’ll be back soon anyway. Watch, the bedding will still be warm.”

The encampment was dark. Quiet. The only noise was the wind buffeting the occasional bird in the trees, and the woodland creatures or the night guard shifting through the undergrowth. Everyone wanted to be well rested come morning and the world held its breath so it could bear witness.

Only the two of them were awake to leisurely stroll the encampment until they found a spot far enough from the tents and patrol route for peace.

Mydei was so accustomed to Phainon at his side that he felt the privacy of being alone; two sets of footsteps and breaths falling as one. But it was better when he could turn his eyes from the full moon and find Phainon already looking his way, never shying away even once caught. His lip only twitched into a small smile, just wide enough to be a little smug and cheeky.

To onlookers, it appeared that Mydei was always spoiling Phainon, indulging his affections and whims. But in truth Mydei was the one that had been spoiled by him so thoroughly he knew no one else could ever compare.

“What was it about this time?” Phainon asked in a voice that had fully shed the remnants of sleep. Eyes just as clear; shining as pale as his hair under the full moon.

Do not shed tears for me. It’s not befitting of your status.

Mydei grunted. “The same as usual.”

Farewell, my dear friend… you must… lead us home.

Ten years of spitting in Fate’s face, yet he always knew it would come to this. Perdikkas, Leonnius, Ptolemy, Peucesta were all alive and by his side. He would do anything to guarantee Hephaestion would be no exception.

So tomorrow he would once again join hands with prophecy when he took his father’s head. A long sought revenge, but also a means to an end: so that the Goldweaver would open Okhema’s gates to them, and that the detachment would follow him through.

“The Son of Gorgo will be crowned in the blood of eternal Strife and it’s dynasty.”

Those were the words Krateros had told him when Mydei asked why his father would toss him, a new born infant, into a place for the dead. The prophecy his father had received all those years ago. A prophecy that

Mydei, in keeping with Kremnoan tradition, would slay his father. Then he would turn his blade on Nikador and end the Kremnoan Dynasty.

Mydei laughed but it rang hollow like a wind blown through empty bones. “A mere handful of words. But it was enough for my father to end my mother’s life and abandon me to the Sea of Souls. For what purpose? So the world would never be without Castrum Kremnos and Strife at its helm.”

He laughed again and did nothing to mask the bitterness with only Phainon as witness to his true feelings. To the Kremnoan detachment, who had despised Eurypon’s rule and not Kremnos’ legacy, who still claimed its name and traditions for themselves, it would be unimaginable to ever slight Nikador as the embodiment of Strife itself.

Elsewhere in Amphoreus, people spoke of Death as a peaceful West Wind that carried people to a Sea of Flowers. In Castrum Kremnos, Death was an eternal battlefield where warriors gathered across the centuries to earn ever greater glory. Strife was the creed which Kremnoans lived and died by.

Only Phainon knew of the great betrayal Mydei would enact come the end of tomorrow. Mydei would not take the Kremnoan detachment home. Even if it earned him pure disdain and vitriol where he had once known affection.

The chill pulled his skin and he shivered. The fire pits smouldered low or had gone out entirely, leaving the night wind to sweep through the encampment unperturbed.

He crossed his arms, and took in the full moon and final time before he exhaled softly. “Come. Let us return.”

He had walked off that uncomfortable tightness in his chest and spoken his thoughts aloud. It was time for him to go back to sleep and greet tomorrow. No more fleeing, no more evasion, no more wilful ignorance.

No footsteps followed.

“Mydei.”

He paused but his heart didn’t tremble when he faced Phainon even with his carefully crafted mask, aloof and confident and a leader above leaders, laid pathetically at his feet. Backlit by the moon and almost luminescent in the night, Phainon made a hazy figure that Mydei would always find no matter the darkness he would have to wade through.

No smiles. Just grave sincerity as he laid a hand over his heart and swore, “Even if victory absconds itself from your path, I will walk it with you.”

Victory that could only be achieved alongside glory and Strife. For him to part ways with one would mean parting ways with them all.

Mydei dipped his chin into his smile that went beyond the usual slight curl of his lips. A futile attempt to hide the extent of his fond grin. “Of course you will. After all, my wish has yet to be fulfilled, Deliverer.”

This time, Phainon was in step at his side as they returned together, both of their minds spoken and heard—just as Mydei knew he would be.

Some levity lifted Phainon’s solemnity when he smiled into his next complaint, “Do you ever intend to tell me this wish of yours? Or am I supposed to guess?”

At first, Mydei never told Phainon his wish because he simply didn’t possess the words. Past, present, future jumbled together. Inexplicable knowledge. An undesirable outcome. He wished to bloody his fists on Fate and emerge victorious but there was no way to explain that to anyone who wasn’t him.

But there was something else he wanted, too. Even before that wish to see the people he cared for alive and happy. One that came to him as a sunlit voice in an abyss that had seemed so endless. But that voice told him of a whole world outside of it and have Mydei a hope to cling on to. To meet again. To battle side-by-side. To see the smile ever present in that voice for himself.

Now those two wishes had become one. Mydei had become too selfish, too spoiled, in Phainon’s presence. He wanted it all. He never wanted to let

anything go.

He would tell him. He would. Once everything came to pass and the dust settled; no matter the outcome, Phainon would know everything. Mydei owed him that much when it was meeting Phainon that had given him the opportunity to experience this simple happiness for himself. Once Mydei joined in alliance with prophecy only so he could spit in its face once again, bringing ten years of exile to an end, Phainon would have already fulfilled his wish.

“Are you telling me you can’t figure out something so simple? How embarrassing for you, Deliverer.”

“Mydei, it’s been six years and you’ve never had the decency to give me so much as a hint.” He suddenly perked up and his smile turned challenging. “Give me one chance. One question.”

Mydei scoffed. “If you only mean to inquire into the details of my wish then my answer will remain the same.”

He tutted. “Give me some credit. If you fear that the question may give you away, feel free to back down and withhold your answer.”

Mydei scowled at the obvious taunt but Phainon only lifted his brows in retaliation. “Ask away.”

Phainon pulled ahead on quick feet and spun on his toes to face Mydei, who had gained the new responsibility of making Phainon didn’t fall and smash his skull open on a rock. He raised his hands to set the scene for, regrettably but not unpredictably, more than one simple question.

He cleared his throat. “Imagine, if you would, a clear spring day accompanied by a warm breeze and the gentle waves. On that day, instead of a ring, a young boy from Castrum Kremnos washed up on the shores of Aedes Elysiae from the Sea of Souls.” Phainon flourished his hand towards Mydei. “What would you have done?”

If there was no Kremnoan detachment to find him and take him in and raise him, wandering across Amphoreus between battlefields and sieges, with the expectation that he become king. Only golden wheat fields and the open seas, radiant beneath a gentle sun that would warm him in place of the flames of Strife.

A sweet fantasy. The same he had given himself over to those years ago. It wouldn’t last. When Phainon asked such a question, it was without any knowledge of the feral beast Mydei had been when he emerged from the Sea of Souls. It had taken skilled warriors, not the steady hands of farmers and fishermen, to tame him into something human.

If the Sea of Souls had gifted him not the name Aedes Elysiae but the place itself, Mydei would have fled from the beings who looked like him and hunted in numbers larger than him. If they tried to speak to him in sounds his brain hadn’t yet learned to decipher, or gone so far as to force him to stay, he may have lashed out, even killed someone if that was what it took to escape. If he made it to the forests and the wheat fields, none of them would ever find him again. If so, it was likely he would have eventually been found by the Kremnoan detachment and never returned to Aedes Elysiae.

“It depends,” Mydei said, slow and deliberate from deep in his chest, braid swaying with the tilt his head. “Would you have kept me?”

The ground dipped. Phainon’s heel met empty air and his face slackened with surprise as he fell backwards. It was only a small hole, something easy for him to recover from when he had been forced to compose himself after much worse on the battlefield, but Mydei caught his outstretched hand.

He didn’t pull him up and Phainon didn’t slip away from under Mydei, leaned over him, with his usual grace. From the arch of Phainon’s back, all of his weight was balanced in their intertwined fingers and he let the two of them stay there.

“Kept you?” Phainon’s eyes slid down to Mydei’s throat, bobbing when he swallowed and Phainon followed the movement. His lips quirked. “Sure.

People take in strays all the time. Just have to give them a collar: return to Phainon.”

Heat flushed across Mydei’s face but he didn’t dare look away—knowing it would be his loss if he did. A loss in some undeclared, unnamed competition where the first to flinch accepted defeat—he only kissed his teeth. “Bold words for the one who’s been collared.”

A small black thing. Phainon managed to pick it up in the few moments Mydei had lost sight of him in the marketplace. It had been tasteless and bland, even Phainon debated how to wear it when it would cover the sun tattoo he liked so much. The detachment felt the need to intervene and customise it with a slit across the tattoo and a golden buckle hammered into the same symbol of Strife adorning Mydei’s belt. Now Phainon hardly ever took the thing off.

The hand Phainon let hang limply by his side finally moved, grazing his collar with a mocking tilt of his head and lips. “I put this on myself, so surely the only person I belong to is me.”

The symbol of Strife gleamed in the moonlight, as bright as the sun peeking beneath and between black leather.

He yanked Phainon onto his feet and smirked as he stumbled, suppressing that heat in his face. “Whatever you say.”

An arm reached across his shoulder. A habit even when they had both reached their final heights and Phainon flaunted a mere finger’s width over Mydei.

“I would have,” Phainon murmured in Mydei’s ear, breath ghosting down his jaw and warming his neck like…

They were just behind the rows of tents. Mydei kept his voice low, “What?”

“Kept you.”

Phainon’s fingers toyed with the end of Mydei’s braid, golden tip between his index and middle finger while his thumb brushed over the bumps and dips.

“You would come to the fields with me and Snowy to hide and play instead of work. Join me in school so we could learn to speak and read and write. Swing a wooden sword and speak with the fairies and pretend to be heroes. Then at the end of the day we’d go home together to eat at the same table, sleep in the same cot, and do it all over again.”

The sweetest of fantasies, too naive for even a daydream: idyllic, peaceful.

“Warmer,” Mydei relented as though it pained him.

Phainon perked up, fist clenching the braid in his surprise and Mydei hissed at the tug of his scalp. He hurriedly let go, threw his chin over Mydei’s shoulder and beamed. “Really?”

Mydei grunted. Not affirmative nor denial, so it was essentially a yes. “Turn your mind from the past that cannot be changed. Focus on what you can grasp with your own hands.”

Phainon hummed thoughtfully. “How like you.” His hand flexed against Mydei’s collarbone, lifting so his hands could curl as though he were grabbing hold of something just ahead. “Will another six years pass before I get a second clue?”

“If you need another six years then perhaps you haven’t been looking close enough.”

Phainon hurried two steps ahead to lift the flap of the tent, letting Mydei duck inside before he followed. The tent closed with a final breeze at their back, secluding them in a low lit privacy most used to sleep. They stood at the entrance and faced each other.

Phainon’s grin grew. “I think you may be right, Mydei.”

He didn’t let Phainon’s concession shake him, only arched a brow. “Is that so.”

“Definitely. And when is a person as honest as they are in sleep? Especially with those dreams of yours.”

And when Phainon sat down it wasn’t upon his cot with its mussed blanket in a heap. Phainon dropped himself onto the cot on the opposite side of the tent— Mydei’s cot . He even had the audacity to pat the surface like he had a right to invite its owner.

Heat plunged like his stomach, spreading from the just-cooled tips of Mydei’s ears and crossing his cheeks until he could feel it down his throat. “And just what kind of truths are you hoping to extract while I’m fast asleep?”

The leaps in logic it had taken Phainon to reach this conclusion were completely irrational. But Mydei was already kicking off his sandals and sitting down. He breathed, letting the sound fill the tent where it was just the two of them tucked away in the night. When Phainon stared at him with his tail practically wagging, Mydei laid down facing the wall.

The bedding shifted and a warmth staved off the cold air they had let inside with their exit and entrance. Phainon laid against Mydei’s back, squeezing himself closer as he draped the blanket over them both.

“Who knows?” Phainon whispered. Mydei felt the rise and fall of his chest as he breathed, as he spoke, each puff of it hot against the shell of his ear. “But I’m looking forward to finding out.”

The solid weight of Phainon’s arm rested against Mydei’s waist. Mydei felt another deep inhale and then the rumble spreading through Phainon’s chest before the sound reverberated through the air.

Phainon was singing. In low tones and murmurs for Mydei’s ears alone. A sadness tinged every note. Like memories, like longing, and Mydei could smell wheat and sea salt warmed by the sun.

For nineteen years, Mydei had been in love with a man who had etched himself so deep into his soul that the Sea of Souls couldn’t wash it away; transcending all reason as it revealed every carefully penned engraving.

In his thirteenth year, he gained a name for that man—that boy—who had been by his side ever since.

Over six years, Mydei’s love that had been fact softened and bloomed. It was no longer an old mark on his soul that he carried from one life to the next. It was tending to each other’s wounds. It was knowing each other’s every move on the battlefield. It was lying beneath a great sky in a vast world and thinking of home when sharing one heartbeat.

It was Mydei’s eyes half closed with sleep as he murmured the one vulnerability to his undying body. It was the total press of their bodies together, so nothing could dare to slip between them and into the one spot that could separate them for good, which was Phainon’s answer.

The love of my life. It had been years since the words came to Mydei unbidden. But it wasn’t accompanied by the hazy impression of memories, feelings, recollections of any life except this one—anyone except him. Now, it was just this Mydei who was in love with this Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.

Chapter End Notes

The song Phainon sings for Mydei is coronal radiance. Enjoy that fun fact.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei sieges Castrum Kremnos and fulfils a prophecy.

Chapter Notes

The gates of Castrum Kremnos opened for the exiled Crown Prince and his followers. A homecoming. A welcome on behalf of the citizens dissatisfied by the current reign who witnessed the detachment enter the city disguised as entrants into the Kremnos Festival.

The city guards, old comrades before their exile, turned a blind eye to their familiar faces. If any of them held suspicions at Mydei and Phainon’s distinctive eyes beneath their hoods then they kept those silent and waved them through the gates together.

At no point in Castrum Kremons’ long history had it undergone anything that could be considered a siege. It was impossible. While other cities had high walls to repel potential invaders, Castrum Kremnos was defended by foundation and walls that, at the ruler’s whims, moved. Wars had been won through the city’s strategic movements to deploy troops from two separate locations, rain projectiles on the enemy, or reshape the terrain.

Any good siege was a two pronged attack the culminated in a single aim: crumble the walls and cripple morale so the city could be broken open and claimed anew. To attempt the same against Castrum Kremnos was a pointless endeavour when the city could simply escape elsewhere.

Invaders risked greater losses when Castrum Kremnos’ quarry and forges enabled a near endless supply of projectiles to launch from their high walls. While Kremnoan territories could be skirmished for, Amphoreus had long accepted that it wasn’t only its patron Titan that made its central stronghold impossible to assail.

The mobile fortress rarely settled in one location, and never lingered for long. The only time it settled was the Kremnos Festival; always stationary just long enough to gather strong warriors, then relinquish those that survived while the dead gathered into that blade hung over the city.

Although it was a tradition long sullied by the Mad King.

Mydei propped his spear over his bent knee and polished the blade until the reflection of even his earring sparkled back at him. Once he was satisfied, there was just enough space for him to set the spear behind him on the narrow bed, frame half rotted and mattress threadbare, where it silently settled. Then he reached across to the bed opposite and picked up the great sword without a sound while its owner was preoccupied.

Leant against the wall, Phainon peered out the window to the streets below their shabby inn. “So those are Nikador’s Titankin.”

Giant creatures of stone lumbered the streets. First carved by the hands of Nikador, they consolidated human and animal strengths in dark stone mined from the city’s quarries. The softer white stone adorned their bodies like garments and armour; unnecessary when they were blessed with the Titan’s golden blood that didn’t spill even when struck.

Mydei inspected Phainon’s blade for any faults. Nothing. The same result as his inspection that morning before they left the encampment. But being cautious in the final moments before battle could differentiate the victor from the departed.

He set it back down where he found it. Then rose to squeeze past the table and chair in the corner and join Phainon at the window. He kept a hand on his hood, hiding his hair and eyes, casting the tattoo in shadow.

Everything in Kremoan life was done with vigour, whether military training, mourning, celebration. So long as it never veered into a lack of discipline, to live life loudly was a sign of strength and tenacity.

Yet the streets were near silent. Rather than the feast and cheer expected of the city’s most sacred festival—one where the right to rule was dangled

before the people if only someone was courageous and skilled enough to earn it for themselves. A time where warriors proved their worth by bathing in the blood of those defeated at their own hands, honouring themselves and their lineage—the streets were near empty.

The number of Titankin surpassed the Kremnoans. The few people they could spot moved about with efficiency. Not joy nor anticipation. Heads down and feet swift; the open streets a means to an end rather than a place of merry making the entire city could partake in equally.

After all, the Kremnos Festival was nothing but a formality now. A place where Kremnoans clashed against more Titankin than fellow warriors, sentenced to death so their fallen souls may invigorate the Blade of Fury.

Few warriors flocked to Castrum Kremnos to participate when the chance for glory earned in blood was replaced by stone servants of Strife under the king and Titan’s deteriorating sensibilities. The festival had long lost its purpose of honour or crown. It was only a massacre: every spark of steel and spill of hot blood meant to temper the Blade of Fury.

A bloodbath that Kremnoans offered themselves to with grim determination to overcome unflinching stone, glorifying themselves in its dust and golden blood, upholding a tradition that had abandoned them.

Phainon bumped their shoulders together. “When will I be receiving the tour?”

“This is the outer city. I—“ Grew up. He brushed the strange thought away, “—would have been raised in the inner city.”Phainon stared, expectant, but Mydei only arched a brow back. “What more do you want? If you’re so curious, ask Ptolemy.”

Ptolemy had been younger than Phainon when Mydei first met him in Aedes Elysiae. Yet he found a way to sneak in and out of the Library of Garbaniphoro with stolen books in his satchels. Ones that recorded Castrum Kremnos’ history down to its hidden corners and secret passageways.

When Ptolemy tried to return the books that should have been Mydei’s, looted from a library that was his by birthright, he had only laughed, telling him to do as he wished with them. Throughout the years, they were all carefully stored in waxed leather and kept in conditions as well as could be expected in exile.

“Come now, Mydei,” Phainon trilled his name like a challenge. “You must know at least one fun fact about the place.”

Mydei flicked his forehead and he flinched away, rubbing at the reddening spot with a pout. “The only things you must know is the location of the Path of Conquest and the straight march to the arena.”

There were still preparations that needed to be completed before the detachment could launch the offensive. Until then Mydei—and by extension Phainon, who was just an infamous for his own skills as he was for battling at Mydei’s side. His exploited birthed stories that his body must be equally as undying as Mydei’s, for him to hold the position at the Mydei’s side without ever losing his life—was to stay hidden. Lest the Royal Wing Elites, Titankin, and other loyalists could discover and hunt him down.

Mydei backed away from the window and dropped into a chair. The legs were thin and unbalanced, rocking and creaking under his weight. But he let his hood fall, pushing a hand through his hair and exhaled harshly through his teeth.

The detachment had splintered apart throughout the city. Until he received the signal, there was no way for him to know if they made it into the city unscathed, remained undetected, and completed their tasks safely.

Mydei crossed his arms, holding tight to his arms, and controlled his next breath. It was a strategy he learned in the Sea of Souls, just another mark of his time there that persisted even after ten years. The closest thing he had to comfort was his own warmth and the memory of someone else holding him —his mother’s arms. Phainon’s arms—and he recreated it the best he could.

Their rations were  open yet untouched on the table. Their weapons and armour had been inspected and polished. For now, it was just him and Phainon.

Phainon with his lighthearted goading as distraction. But Mydei watched Phainon’s eyes flicker between the mundane empty streets and buildings all the way to the white and gold towers spiralling in the distance. His questions weren’t solely for Mydei’s benefit.

“Why are you so fascinated with Castrum Kremnos?” Mydei reopened the conversation.

Phainon’s head jerked up and he reeled away, guilty as he tried to mask that interest. A strange reaction. While Mydei had no love for the city that his companions and warriors still considered home despite their long years in exile, he would never begrudge any of Phainon’s fascination in its finer qualities. There had to be something to Castrum Kremnos other than the classic Strife and barbarism. Although, there was nothing Mydei could say from experience.

When Mydei stared, unimpressed, Phainon accepted he had been caught and relented with a smile through the slightest wince. “Well, this place may have held my future… once.”

Back when Phainon’s eagerness to journey to Castrum Kremnos alone and train as a warrior was Mydei’s only indication that he may have been willing to leave his peaceful home for the detachment’s harsh life of exile. But the choice was snatched from Phainon before Mydei had a chance to offer.

Mydei’s brows furrowed. “How did you even learn of Castrum Kremnos?”

In that small village untouched by Strife. There were still small worries: personal quarrels that escalated into scuffles, particularly rabid predators that ventured too far into the village, the occasional bandit or troublemaker. Small concerns that required nothing more than a few loosely trained but strong, healthy men to pick up their weapons. If not for the black tide, the flames of war may have been forever unknown to Aedes Elysiae.

Phainon chuckled, relaxing against the wall again so he could fulfil his role and watch the sky. Not that he took his eye away from Mydei. “I was fishing one day but, oddly enough, nothing was biting. I almost fell asleep before something finally caught the line! When I yanked it out,” he said with a swing of his arms, pulling in a fishing line, “it was a gold ring with a funny little symbol on it. The village elders told me it was the symbol of Strife and must have come from Castrum Kremnos. Through the Sea of Souls for it to end up in Aedes Elysiae. Later, Cyrene told me lots of stories about how it was full of only the strongest and most honourable of warriors.”

It was far from an incorrect assessment but, while a nice change from the slander rambled by the rest of Amphoreus against the city and its Titan, Castrum Kremnos was hardly a city worth romanticising. It was a city of war and conquest. Needless battle and bloodshed that created many Aedes Elysiae’s, villages razed to the ground, for the sake of glory.

Mydei arched a brow. “I fear you were misled.”

“Perhaps a little.” Phainon glanced out the window and shrugged, too small and too casual to be genuine when everything Phainon did was so big. “Not that it mattered in the end.”

Castrum Kremnos was far from Aedes Elysiae. Geograhically, across space long since subsumed by the ever advancing black tide. And by the oppressive air of the grand architecture in the distance, gold glowing molten as it speared the sky, distant from the slums they resided in for now. Perhaps Phainon saw old houses and golden fields ablaze anyway.

“This city could never even hope to deserve you,” Mydei said.

The corners of Phainon’s lips curled and his eyes practically sparkled when he hummed. “That must be why I fled the monotony of my training regimes to join the detachment of that infamous solitary lion.”

He smirked with a small shake of his head. “Now they’re too good for you.”

Phainon cocked his head but it wasn’t the look of an overeager puppy when his hair swayed, daylight flashing off the askew symbol of Strife buckled to his collar, and he smirked. “Then I’ll just have to prove myself.”

Mydei stood and Phainon didn’t back down when Mydei reached for his throat. His claw hooked into the black leather and tugged. Just enough to let air slip underneath like the easy hitch of Phainon’s breath. Enough for Mydei’s other hand to fiddle with the buckle and straighten it again.

The entire detachment had stories about Castrum Kremnos. For every subject Phainon could endeavour to learn about, there would be at least five pure blooded Kremnoans born and raised in the city who were eager to lecture him about it. Mydei knew from experience that it was easier to get them to start talking than to stop. But Phainon had wanted to hear it from Mydei.

He let the collar snap back into place. “I wasn’t raised here,” Mydei reminded him, quietly into the space between them as he gazed at the rounded symbol. “This city is as new to me as it is to you. But,  supposedly, the outer portions of the city were constructed by convicts. So the workmanship is… questionable at times.”

He peeled away to slouch against the wall, the width of the window between them. Phainon examined the room with new appreciation despite it being just as damp, gloomy and cramped as before. Then peered out the window to do the same with the surrounding buildings. Everything appeared the same to Mydei but he watched Phainon out the corner of his eye, knowing Mydei would have to watch the sky because Phainon had forgotten, and smiled.

Against the evening sky, red smoke curled up from the buildings. Another trail of smoke rose, and another, and another, and even more where Mydei couldn’t see them from this inn’s mediocre, at best, vantage point. The smoke vanished not long after it appeared. Extinguished. The detachment was ready. The red smoke amongst the grey confirmed Mydei’s suspicions.

Although the detachment entered the city quietly, Kremnoans would never accept a homecoming without their heads held high and their intentions

declared from the depths of their stomach. At the sight of red smoke, the scattered groups merged back together at the wide open boulevard paved right to the arena entrance.

Their empty flag and the blare of their klaxons whipped in the winds blown down the Path of Conquest.

An army of warriors led by Royal Wing Elites and Titankin emerged to meeet them. Both armies were raised on Kremnoan tactics, arranged in similar formations and armed with similar shields and weapons—the first to crack would shatter.

Mydei flexed his fingers, a greatsword flashing out the corner of his eye, and his hand clenched into a fist as he smirked. This battle was no different from the rest. The outcome depended on cohesion of his army and disruption of the other. To be the spear that scattered enemy lines and the shield that defended his own was a simple task with his undying body and such a persistent white shadow at his back. He roared a battle cry and charged.

His tattoos pulsed as he shattered a Titankin with one punch to the torso and another to its jaw, red crystals floating among the grey stone. Before its torso could turn to dust, he grabbed it and lifted it as he spun. An arrowhead pierced through and stopped just short of Mydei’s eye. It clattered to the floor as the stone crumbled.

He scanned for the archer as he bent low to scoop the fallen arrow. There. A Titankin tall enough to shoot from behind two rows of enemies. He launched the arrow at its head but it knocked it out the air with a twist of its bow. He scowled but it wasn’t unexpected when the thing had been staring straight at him.

A Royal Wing Elite thrust their spear and Mydei easily side stepped. He caught the polearm, half a mind towards snapping it and the other towards stealing it, but his body was already moving. His knee coming up and hand swinging down. A bowstring twanged and he knew it was aimed at him. No time to move. He would take the hit.

Metal gleamed and a great sword cleaved the arrow from the air. Mydei snapped the polearm. One hand on the shaft attached to the blade, the other hand shot out and grabbed the warrior by the tunic. He spun and kicked the Royal Wing Elite towards the detachment and kept spinning as he pulled his arm back. He flung the spear tip at the Titankin archer and pierced it through the head.

At his side, Phainon looked him over once while Mydei did the same to him. Nothing to find, their eyes met and they nodded—two whole breaths spared—before resuming the battle.

At least three ordinary people were required to subdue one Titankin, so Mydei and Phainon took responsibility for the bulk of the stone beasts while the detachment clashed with their fellow warriors.

The madness of the Titankin was exposed when the creatures broke away from formation to overwhelm the two of them even at the cost of leaving their human comrades exposed. It made them easy prey for the detachment and they pushed through the first legion into the Hall of Strife where the next legion defended the entrance to the Kremnos Arena.

Mydei caught a Titankin’s great sword and his feet slid against the floor as it pushed all its cumbersome weight upon him. A burst of red crystals shattered the stone blade and engulfed Mydei’s fist as he punched through its arm at the shoulder. He lunged for its throat and crushed the stone in one hand, head falling and fracturing in a white plume.

The doorway was near. The quantity of warriors had been exchanged for a glut of Titankin and better quality Royal Wing Elites to better fit the limited room. But they scattered and perished just the same under the assault and the detachment seized the opportunity.

Krateros kicked a warrior off his spear, hair stuck to his sweat slick skin and blood that wasn’t his own, eyes dark with the thrilling frenzy of battle when he found Mydei. “Go! Everyone, gather in a defensive formation. Protect His Highness!”

Krateros’ battalion gathered around him and blockaded the doorway to the arena from the remaining warriors and Titankin. Behind their row of shields and helmets, it was only Mydei and Phainon sent to press onwards.

At the heart of the city, Kremnos Arena stood poised between the pit of roiling lava below and the Blade of Fury above. A forge for warriors, heated and struck and tempered for the sake of Strife.

Stood at the centre, his father awaited his arrival, accompanied by a final handful of Titankin. Undoubtedly the best.

Phainon swiped at his forehead with his arm, sweat dripping from the ends of his hair, but his smile was free of exhuastion. “Four against one. How much would you bet on me?”

Mydei drew his spear from his back and discarded the cloth bound around the blade. “Nothing. Unless it’s you and I competing, everyone bets on you. I wouldn’t make any money.”

Phainon chuckled. “To think I’m worth so little to you.”

All four Titankin aimed at Phainon. This time not from madness but careful control, so that it was Mydei and Eurypon left to face one another. There were no words to exchange as they each levelled their spears. One of them would be conquered and one of them would be crowned in blood.

While Eurypon’s mind as a leader had deteriorated to madness, his body was still fastidious as they clashed. Even years onwards, long enough for Mydei to reach adulthood, it was obvious how he emerged victorious from a Kremnos Festival of the past and held steadfast to the crown ever since.

Both body and mind were honed for combat. Quick and precise strikes. Keen eyes that noticed any and all vulnerabilities. The courage to risk his life for the advantage.

To think this man had dishonourably poisoned his wife and thrown his child into the Sea of Souls.

But for all Eurypon’s skill, Mydei had spent every waking moment of his childhood battling with his life as forfeit. Every day in the Sea of Souls and the wilds of Amphoreus forged his body of steel from merely armour into a weapon. At first a feral child who could only lash out at everything before it could destroy him first, and into a disciplined warrior who commanded armies.

He had waged battles on every terrain, under every disadvantage and advantage, and emerged victorious to stand before the King of Castrum Kremnos. Not for his crown but for the vengeance owed to his mother and to himself, and for the future he wished to see.

For others, risking their lives took courage and restraint to overcome fear. An opportunity to earn a valorous death enough to suppress the inherent desire of all things to keep living. For Mydei, Death was something he had experienced as much as he had forced onto others. His oldest companion, second only to pain.

An aging body of a bygone king couldn’t compete. To the end, Eurypon epitomised Castrum Kremnos—past strength that waned in the present and would inevitably crumble against the onslaught of the future.

Mydei disarmed him with a flick of his wrist and kicked him to the ground.

It was all so familiar. The same spear tip poised at the same face laughing as the end drew ever closer. The same burning sky as the fortress blessed by Nikador fell to a siege for the first time in its thousand year history. The same end to the same prophecy.

“A fierce fighter…” Eurypon praised in a voice hoarse from battle. “I did not expect such heroism from a feeble Okheman. Fulfil your duty as the victory, warrior, and tell me your name. I seek an honourable death from you.”

A father brought low at the feet of a son he couldn’t recognise. The rest of the city knew of the Kremnoan detachment, many hoping for their return home to herald the return of Kremnos’ former glory. Yet Eurypon lacked

the wits or the attentiveness to his citizens to realise that the detachment and its leader were not Okheman—but Kremnoans finally seeking justice.

“As if you have any honour!” Mydei spat. “Listen closely. I am the leader of the Kremnoan detachment—Mydeimos. I’m here to finish you, father.”

The same speech and the same dreaded realisation as Eurypon The Mad King realised that his true madness was believing someone so undeserving could ever transcend prophecy.

For the first time, his voice trembled as he gasped, “It is you. The beast spurned by all. So, you did defy death. The prophecy was true—you will bring an end to my Kremnoan dynasty.” His fists clenched into the ground and he jerked forward, spear tip drawing blood. “Then swing your blade! Take my crown, coronate yourself with an old king’s blood, and inherit it all. Become the new rightful king of Kremnos.”

Mydei scowled and stamped his foot onto Eurypon’s stomach, wheezing out a pained breath, to keep him in his place. “No, I don’t want the crown. Listen—if there’s only one end for the kings of Kremnos, then the crown means nothing to me.”

More Strife. Another dead end drawn long like the dying breath of a wounded animal. But it would be Mydei’s blood splattered across the wall.

“All I want is your life. To avenge mother and my comrades!”

Eurypon cackled low and breathless beneath Mydei’s foot yet still so arrogant. “But the walls of Kremnos will not fall with me. Do you truly think you can escape Fate’s grasp, my son? The son of Gorgo is destined to be crowned in blood!”

Mydei glared down the length of his spear, capturing blood and insanity in its polished edge. “Father, in some ways you and I… are more similar than I would ever wish to admit.”

Eurypon scowled and opened his mouth to retaliate but Mydei patience for this farce had worn thin. He brought his boot down upon his chest and drew

a long line of blood across his throat.

An old king. A coward. Finally in the dirt where he belonged.

“But you and I will never be the same. To subvert Fate you sacrificed your wife, threw your newborn child into the Sea of Souls, and tried in vain to enslave a Titan by desecrating the body of a god—when you should have resisted Fate’s inescapable grasp with the strength of your own mighty will. And now Fate’s reckoning is upon you.”

The same ending to the same story. A prophecy.

So it should have been the same too when those sneering words faded away in a gurgle of blood and the Blade of Fury pulsed in acknowledgement of all the souls that had joined it. When Mydei crouched down and pulled the signet ring from the old king’s finger and clenched it tight, hoping it would crumble to dust and take Castrum Kremnos with it. Mere relics of the past.

But the ring, bloodstained and unscathed, mocked him.

The Kremnoan detachment, the entirety of Castrum Kremnos, behind Mydei. But no one at his back. At his side. His dearest companions another bloodstain on the steps of history and Fate.

Yet when he turned, a lone figure stood tall by the exit to the arena. White hair streaked in gold and red. Blue eyes that never looked away. The scent of wheat and salt which made Mydei think of home that needed neither the golden fields nor the sea. Just the memory of them etched into his soul by his hand entwined with another’s.

The spear fell from his hands and Mydei ran. Impulsive, undignified. But if Phainon—who had seen him at the highs of his victories and the lows of his despair. Had clashed against his vicious brutality and held him gently afterwards. Had found the edges of his mask shaped like a crown and watched him bleed when it pulled free, only to stymie it with steady hands —never strayed from his side, then what need did he have for dignity. Not a king, a prince nor The Undying. He was just Mydei.

There was no surprise on Phainon’s face. No boisterous, victorious grin. Just the softest of affection as he opened his arms wide and welcomed Mydei in. Mydei’s rough voice and stony demeanour. Mydei’s temperament honed for battle and not for peace. Mydei’s burning body too hot to hold. Mydei’s nightmares of a world that had happened but only to him. Mydei’s lips that clashed against his.

It was Mydei gathered in Phainon’s arms, hands held over his tenth thoracic vertebra, and Phainon kissed him back like he had been the one waiting since before they had ever met.

Lips dry and dusty from battle, tasting of sweat and blood, where they moved with adrenaline and six years of longing from each other’s side.

Mydei pulled away and Phainon tried to chase, eyes still closed and arms holding him tight, but Mydei set his hands on Phainon’s shoulders and his eyes fluttered open. He didn’t let go, holding Mydei aloft over that finger’s width of height different he so loved to gloat about.

One of Mydei’s hands traced the long line of his throat and over his jaw with the very edge of his claws. Shivers and raised skin followed as Phainon’s eyes flitted between Mydei’s hand and his gaze, too wide and hungry to settle in one place.

He cupped a cheek flushed from more than exertion and leaned in again. He stopped just short their lips meeting, heavy breaths mingling together. When chuckled lowly into the small space between them, Phainon licked his lips like that was a kiss.

Mydei smiled, entirely too fond for his next words, “I want that duel.”

Phainon’s eyes dipped from Mydei’s eyes to his lips and he was already leaning in again. “Okay. Right now?”

“We need to be—“ Phainon managed to push past Mydei’s arm and land a peck. Mydei bit his lip in retaliation, “—further from the city. I didn’t kill Nikador.”

“Wanna try?” Phainon tilted his head, gazing through his lashes with nothing but amorous confidence. Mydei swatted the back of his head and he tossed his head back and laughed. “Another time then. If it’s the two of us not even a Titan can hope to emerge victorious.”

Mydei scoffed but felt his ears burn and Phainon’s grin knew it too. “Ridiculous,” Mydei chastised and kissed him on the forehead, watching his brows rise and his eyes widen, tail practically wagging. “Now put me down.”

“But what if I want to carry you out the city in my arms?”

“Then I will gouge out your eyes and leave you here,” Mydei threatened as he placed a kiss on one eye, thumbing a small cut bleeding gold at the edge, and then the other.

Although Mydei’s feet touched ground, Phainon’s hands slid up his back, around his shoulders, and searched for Mydei’s hands. He let him grasp one but shook the other free, once again unfurling his fingers to find that ring.

Phainon hummed, taking Mydei’s wrist in hand like a consolation prize. “What is that?”

“The signet ring.” He jostled the ring to show the emblem, the etched lines pooling blood. “Every ruler of Kremnos adorns it upon their ascension, either through combat or marriage.”

Branded in Strife’s name until it came time to brand another. A vicious cycle.

Phainon stared at it, wide eyes tracking the gold moving between Mydei’s fingers. There was nothing particularly eye catching about it. A bland chunk of gold that had seen more bloodshed than anything else. Since Mydei refused to take the crown, he had no need for such a symbol and refused to place it upon his thumb.

He stretched out his arm, held over the arena’s edge where the rising heat of the lava below grasped hold. A final warning.

He opened his hand and the ring glowed molten as it fell. There was no splash. But he knew the moment it sank into the lava because his next breath came easier as the weight of a thousand year old dynasty melted away.

There was nothing more for them here. When Mydei raised an empty flag and loosed the same battle cry he had unleashed at the battle’s beginning, now from the arena’s exit, all of Castrum Kremnos knew who had emerged victorious. The prince had been crowned in the blood of the Mad King.

It was something worth celebrating as the final loyalists were rounded up and given their honourable deaths. As though madness had beget madness, the Titankin had grown sluggish with Eurypon’s death. Less quick, less strong, less brutal. They were easy to subdue.

Then the detachment mourned their losses in song, feast and honey brew as the citizens joined them to celebrate the end of one reign. None of them yet knew that a new dawn for Kremnos under a new king wouldn’t rise with the next sun.

While cheer filled the streets finally befitting a festival, Mydei returned to the arena and gazed up at the Blade of Fury. Mydei had avenged his mother and opened the way for the detachment’s future in Okhema while Eurypon’s body had been strung from the arena’s walls for all to witness.

Yet the only true winner was Strife. It had feasted on their battle, ever stronger for all the warriors who had given up their souls. An executioners blade over Kremnos.

Around his waist, Phainon’s arm squeezed reassuringly. Wordless but saying all he needed to. Mydei laid his hand over Phainon’s and squeezed back.

“Mydeimos.”

He glanced back as though he wouldn’t know that voice in his dreams, in death and then the next life. Hephaestion, alive after battle, still healthy in the colour of his cheeks and steady feet, smiled.

Mydei’s heart quickened as he turned to face his five friends. Phainon’s hand stayed, steady and grounding. A gesture that didn’t go unnoticed by their five companions.

Hephaestion tilted his head in the arch of his brow. “Are congratulations in order?”

The two of them exchanged a glance. Phainon shrugged. Mydei inclined his head towards the others. It was such a familiar exchange it almost distracted him from what he needed to say next.

Phainon smiled and practically purred, “Perhaps.”

They cheered and a flurry of words came next. A betting pool. Coin. Some brief congratulations may have been scattered amongst the talk of profits and losses.

“You can skip them. We have more pressing matters.” Mydei crossed his arms but he knew any attempts at stern leadership were lessened by Phainon practically draped over him. Mydei didn’t shrug him off. “The red smoke from earlier.”

While the detachment had signalled the completion of their own small tasks with smoke, the role he had entrusted to these five alone had been hidden amongst them, only distinguished by the mineral that dyed smoke red.

Instructions to gather a handful of their most trusted men and search the forgotten corners of the city for evidence of the black tide. Red for confirmation that the incursion had already begun.

Ptolemy, who guided them with his unique knowledge of the city’s history and layout, stepped forward. “The black tide’s invasion had begun. In the city’s catacombs and corners where regular citizens would fail to notice. Not with its usual destructive surge but—“

“Filtered through the strength of a Titan,” Mydei concluded and the Blade of Fury pulsed again. Like the beating heart of a Titan in its death throes. “Come morning, I will…”

The words lodged themselves in his throat. The serrated edges of blades he had swallowed for ten years, accumulating and knowing it would be all the more painful the day he could no longer chew them down, grit his teeth and grin through it.

Phainon’s hand moved from his waist to his lower back. Mydei shuddered at the heated press of his palm spread against that one spot and his words came easier.

He held his head high. “I will enter into self-imposed exile and take all those willing to follow as I join hands with Okhema. I’m certain you all have your grievances that I left the old king’s blood to nourish the earth rather than crown myself. Speak them now.”

The five exchanged glances. There was… nothing Mydei could read. Mydei leaned more of his weight back into Phainon’s hand. Those silent conversations between them all were a natural consequence of the time and hardship they endured together. Now he was an outsider to their conversation.

They silently nominated Hephaestion and he smiled weakly. Some grime stained the skin in front of his ear that he missed cleaning up after the battle, yet this was the most off balance he appeared all day. Not when faced with enemies or the black tide in his homeland—but meeting Mydei’s eye.

“Mydeimos,” he said and inhaled deeply, until his chest expanded and his shoulders rose. “We already knew.”

Mydei blinked. He might have even swayed but Phainon was so close, against his side, at his back, it was impossible to falter. “What?”

He tucked his hair back. It fell loose again and he dragged his fingers to fiddle with the ends. “There was no need for you to say as much. Your actions spoke your intentions well enough. It was easy to see how happy you were without the burden of prince, let alone king.”

Hephaestion glanced meaningfully between Mydei and Phainon. At the minuscule distance between them and Phainon’s hand at Mydei’s back.

Mydei let his mind slowly run over the words again. “You never spoke of this.”

At that, Hephaestion’s smile softened. “We waited for you to resolve to tell us yourself. There are many burdens on your shoulders, Mydeimos. Some of which were placed by our own hands. It was only after seeing you with someone closer to your own age, acting more like a carefree child than you would have ever felt free to show us, that we realised our mistake.”

His eyes burned and his throat bobbed, as though the sting was just another thing he could swallow down and sequester away. “You weren’t…”

Outraged. Disgusted. Betrayed.

Hephaestion took a step forward, hesitated on the second, but he took in Mydei’s face and closed the distance. His face was too blurred for Mydei to discern his expression but his hand was gentle when he lifted Mydei’s in his palm.

He bowed his head and Mydei’s fingers grazed his forehead. “You are our prince, Mydeimos. But first and foremost you are our most cherished friend.” He lifted his head, so close it was impossible to deny the smile curving his lips. “Why wouldn’t we want our friend to be happy?”

Ptolemy thumped his spear against the ground, drawing everyone’s eye as he lifted an empty hand to the sky in a toast. “You faithfully served the detachment all these years.”

Perdikkas raised a hand. “Spilled your blood in place of our own.”

Peucesta raised a hand. “Carved yourself into the image of a king when you were only a child.”

Leonnius raised a hand. “Never faltered with your feet against the earth and the rust-scented wind at your back.”

Hephaestion raised a hand. “A simple happiness isn’t a bad thing. And neither is a selfish one.”

In his entire life, Mydei had never shed tears. As a child, the Sea of Souls took them away before they could fall. By the time he emerged into the living world, his mind and body had been numbed by pain and hardened by Death beyond the ability to shed tears.

Hephaestion laid a hand against his chest. His heart. “We will follow you wherever you wish to lead us. Not because of your regal blood or your undying body, but because our love and loyalty belongs to a friend.”

But his eyes watered and tears fell hot down his cheeks.

“I wanted to fulfil your wishes. To bring you all home,” Mydei’s voice stayed steady, heedless of the tears, but it had lost any semblance of authority as it shrank into itself. “But to do so would be a death sentence for you all. More than that desire to fulfil your wishes, I wish for you all to live.

He tried to scrub at his face but the metal gauntlets would only draw blood in place of tears. A hand on his chin angled his face and those same hands wiped at his cheeks, his jaw, beneath his eyes and was followed by the press of lips, quick and light everywhere tears had fallen. Phainon pulled him into an embrace.

Then another at his back, at his sides, surrounding him in warmth as his tears escaped him. First in silence and then as quiet sobs that had waited nineteen years to be heard. And they all held him through it until his cries quieted to hiccups, quiet sniffles and then finally to nothing.

From the ground that had spent a thousand years stained in nothing but blood, his tears bloomed seven lilies stained red in the name of his friends still by his side.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 13
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon finally have their long-awaited duel.

Chapter Notes

Discontent thrummed through the detachment and the citizens of Castrum Kremnos. But Mydei kept his head high as he marched all those willing to follow him out of the city gates.

The moment Mydei announced his departure from Castrum Kremnos in self-imposed exile that morning, their ranks that had endured for ten long years finally fractured.

The black tide lurked about the city like weeds, too persistent to ever be completely gouged from stone. Confronted with the proof of Nikador’s madness, the inability to safeguard Castrum Kremnos and its citizens, some accepted Mydei’s decision to leave the city as sound.

Others resolved themselves to remain. To be chased from their homeland was too disgraceful; they would rather combat the black tide until it eventually, inevitably, consumed them. Mydei accepted those losses and the disdain that scored itself into his back as they scorned his retreat.

But there was one spot their eyes were never permitted to touch. Phainon’s hand remained firm over Mydei’s tenth thoracic vertebra.

By the time they returned to the encampment, Castrum Kremnos was nothing but a blur on the horizon. Unmoored without its ruler, the stronghold drifted away; nothing but a burial ground for those who refused to leave the husk of a dynasty, now the home of a Mad Titan to sow Strife from.

In the days prior to the siege of Castrum Kremnos, the encampment had been suffused with an undeniable anticipation. But it was stifled beneath their ingrained military discipline. Every warrior knew the importance of preparing for battle, so their excitement hung in the air like the moment before lightning struck.

Now that the storm of conquest had passed, any exhilaration waned under the deluge of responsibilities and uncertainties. Manage the wounded, notate the sudden influx of exiles, distribute resources.

It was far from the glorious return home imagined by the detachment, or the grand liberation envisioned by the citizens. But Kremnoans weren’t only steadfast during combat. This was another part of war—its aftermath. Another chaotic battle ground everyone tackled with resolute focus.

Only a half a day was needed before Mydei was presented with the final numbers of the Kremnoan detachment. It had more than doubled in size. A list lacking many familiar names, and filled with unknown ones.

People who raised Mydei: taught him language, battle strategies, how to wield many weapons. Who had clothed and fed him and bled for him as much as he bled for them. Now they had parted ways. While they chose to return to their homeland, the detachment had become a new home for many people and Mydei would lead them towards the dawn.

“Your Highness,” Krateros called out in that tone; donning the role of a disapproving teacher once more.

Mydei faltered and Phainon stumbled at the abrupt stop, caught by the hand around Mydei’s waist. By the cross of his brows and pinch to his face, it was obvious that Krateros was displeased about something.

There were many reasons to be disgruntled when the encampment was so cramped with people who had yet to fully settle after two days. The detachment shared roots with the former citizens of Castrum Kremnos but ten years was long enough for the detachment to create its own systems and rhythms better suited to a life of wandering.

Mydei waved Phainon to go ahead. Hephaestion needed help calming the dogs down, stressed over the sudden influx of unfamiliar scents and movement about the encampment.

They had adapted well for those first couple of days. Until Leonnius delivered the message to Mydei that one of the newer detachment members had seen them as nothing but mangy strays and gone to kick one. Members of the original detachment had intervened and prevented any significant damage but the dogs were shaken. While they often played with or obeyed Mydei’s commands, it was Phainon who was the more reassuring presence for them.

He glanced from Mydei to Krateros and back again before tilting his head in silent question. Mydei shrugged and flicked his fingers again for him to go. Phainon’s smile didn’t waver under the blunt dismissal; he only pointed at his cheek. Although Mydei rolled his eyes, he kissed the spot right above his finger.

Too greedy, Phainon tried to turn his other cheek for another and Mydei finally shoved his face away. He watched Phainon glance out the corner of his eye, blue crinkled with as much mischief as joy, and Mydei narrowed his eyes in warning.

Phainon turned his face into Mydei’s palm. One kiss through Mydei’s gauntlets wasn’t enough for him and he left a quick, sharp bite. Mydei gaped, speechless at the lingering feel of blunt teeth through the leather, and Phainon pulled away with a little smirk.

Then he ran off with laughter in his footfalls.

Mydei tried to rest his face into its usual unimpressed stare, one that bordered on anger no matter his true feelings, but knew it was a futile effort with the heat in his cheeks. A small bit of colour, but unmissable when Krateros observed him so closely with keen eyes.

“Is there an issue?” Mydei asked, already running through the list of things he needed to oversee, delegate or do himself; ready to slot in whatever problem had risen to Krateros’ attention.

“I believe this conversation should be had in private,” Krateros insisted cryptically.

They retreated to Mydei’s tent. For the first time since Phainon began to use it as his own, both cots were tidy on their respective sides. After all this time, all it had taken was Phainon insisting the two of them share a bed, leaving his untouched while Mydei’s was perfectly made, as always, by morning.

If Krateros noticed he didn’t dare comment as Mydei lowered himself onto the kline. Rather than lift his legs to lounge against the end, he invited Krateros to sit.

Mydei reached for the table and poured them both a drink. Just water for now. They didn’t have the luxury of indulging in honey brew with so much work to be done.

When Krateros kept his thoughts between him and the chalice at his lips, Mydei prompted him to speak, “Is this private enough?”

Krateros nodded but took another breath as he set his chalice down. “Your Highness, I taught you many things as you came to understand this world.”

Mydei kept his back straight and shoulders square, a diligent pupil if not for the languid swirl of his drink. “And I remain grateful for your teachings.”

“There was one thing I always told you to bear in mind.” Whatever hesitance he previously possessed vanished as his expression hardened into a challenge. “What was it?”

Many teachings had passed from Krateros to Mydei over the years. There were only two things Krateros was so austere about: Kremnos’ five tenants, and…

“A lion should never dwell amidst its prey.”

There was no relief or approval when Krateros nodded. “Never reveal your vulnerabilities to anyone.” He crossed his arms and his forehead creased

with something between a troubled frown and a glower. “So what is it you intend to do with Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Mydei’s brows rose. “Is that any concern of yours?”

“It is,” Krateros answered without hesitation. “It shall remain as such so long as I continued to serve you and that boy remains at your side.”

“If Phainon is considered a boy then so must I.”

“I see that in many ways you are. And are still in need of guidance.”

The chalice landed on the table with a harsher thud than Mydei intended, water almost sloshing over the rim. “Our relationship is a private matter.”

“You are the Crown Prince,” Krateros refuted, voice rising. “You have already rejected the crown and led your people from the high walls of their homeland. Do you intend to shirk more of your responsibilities? I once vowed to your mother that I would give my life to protect your reign only for the crown to stay on the old kings fallen head.”

At the mention of his mother, any outrage Mydei felt swelling in his chest cooled, flames doused in ice water. He rested his weight against the kline, temple against his knuckles. “Did my mother really have such expectations of me? Did she wish for me to commit patricide, to steal the throne, and continue this endless conquest?”

With Phainon at his back, it had been so long since he was last submerged in the Sea of Souls and he intended to keep it that way. He could still perfectly recall the utter devastation on Phainon’s face the first time he witnessed Mydei crumple to the ground as a corpse. Years and numerous injuries had passed since then but any time the heat of battle urged him to be more reckless than usual, a flash of white in his peripheral restored his rationality.

But if Mydei were to die tomorrow and found himself adrift in the Sea of Souls, a voice or sometimes a golden figment reaching out to him and guiding him back to the world of the living, what would she say?

There was no way for him to know without taking a dagger to this throat then and there. All his mother had ever spoken of were the virtues of strength and endurance, and the great things Mydei still had left to accomplish. Did she mean patricide and the crown? Or a new path away from that vicious cycle consuming itself with every turn?

Even Krateros did not answer.

Mydei sighed, “Do not mention this matter again. We will not dishonour the fallen by placing words in the mouths of the dead.”

If the day ever came, then Mydei would ask for himself. Not because it would shape the outcome he sought and the sacrifices he would make to take his people there. But because he owed it to his mother, who had stayed his weary soul every time he had need of her since childhood, to know her true self. Even more than the revenge he already delivered to her.

“Even so,” Krateros continued, slow where he had just been so quick to anger, “the Kremnoans followed you, their prince, out from their homeland and are soon to arrive at the mercy of their worst enemy. They look to you for reassurance of their future. For evidence that their decision was not the wrong one.”

There had been no command. Quite the opposite when Mydei renounced the throne, his ultimate authority over the Kremnoans, for a self-imposed exile. Those willing to join were welcome.

He had plainly spurned the crown and its title, yet the detachment still referred to him as the Crown Prince. As though he hadn’t tarnished that crown with his own hands and wished for it to rust to nothing. While his companions accepted him first and foremost as their friend, the same couldn’t be said for the rest of the Kremnoans.

When people spoke to him it was with deference, often going as far as reverence, belonging to his title. He would prefer if they used his name alone, but the older, more traditional Kremnoans were scandalised enough when Mydei refused kingship. It would take time to completely wear away tradition.

However, even if his title faded from their lips and history itself, he would never abandon those who looked to him for leadership. With or without a crown, it was his responsibility to safeguard the future of his people.

“If anyone has any objections, they can voice them with a duel. Either of us will be more than willing to meet them with our weapons raised.”

That should have been the end. If two parties came to opposition in ideals, it was only natural for that to be resolved through the clash of steel.

The twist of Krateros’ expression said otherwise. Strange for a man so committed to Kremnoan tradition. “There are many objections. Or has your newfound vulnerability made you deaf to them.”

A newfound vulnerability. Whether Krateros was referring to Phainon’s person or the love between them, he was wrong in every aspect. None of it was new, but something tenderly nurtured over the years that had only now blossomed in full. None of it made Mydei weaker, vulnerable, but stronger with something behind him to be protected, and to guard his own back. Not as an exchange, but from their own free will.

“It’s not like a Kremnoan to grumble over such matters,” Mydei grumbled himself. “If they seek an answer then they will have to present the challenge themselves rather than shy away in unbecoming gossip.”

It was the exact behaviour Kremnoans mocked other city-states for, particularly Okhemans with their silver tongues and endless need to wag them. For Kremnoans, if one word was sufficient then why use ten?

“Fraternising so intimately with outsiders only intensifies their unease, and concerns that you prize the opinions of outsiders more than your own people.”

Even better, words should ever be used where action would suffice. Yet Mydei had been forced to listen to Leonnius report such drivel passed between the former citizens of Castrum Kremnos.

When Phainon introduced himself as Phainon of Aedes Elysiae to every new face it was impossible to pretend the dearest companion of the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, and one of the leading figures of the Kremnoan detachment, was very much not Kremnoan.

Phainon had only laughed at Leonnius’ report. Then tried to conspire what other bland, uninspired insults they could spark themselves and watch spread like wildfire in a dry prairie. The six of them had been less impressed but Phainon read the silent look they shared and immediately refuted the idea they hunt down the bad actors responsible for such slander.
