Mydei scoffed with as much disdain as when he first heard the first of many insults. “Phainon? An outsider? What a terrible joke. Six years of blood and steel given better than any Kremnoan, only to be denounced as an outsider.”

“Only those within the detachment have witnessed his feats for themselves. To those who lived in Castrum Kremnos until a mere few days ago, all they have are rumours of his prowess. But does his disposition really speak of a battle-hardened warrior?”

He could converse in Kremnoan fluently yet never lost his country accent or fully adapted to utilising the back of his throat for the language’s harsher sounds. He kept his more modest sense of dress that covered him from head to toe. He lacked a military cleanliness instilled from young.

The biggest transgression of all: he clung to Mydei constantly, as though he would die if they shared the same space but not the same air. Like a consort clung to the powerful arm of a king. Mydei’s blood had boiled so quick his tattoos flashed a dangerous red when Leonnius repeated that one.

To the obstinate people who valued the traditions of Castrum Kremnos above all else and descended from their lofty fortress from necessity rather than choice, this was a problem. Which meant it became Mydei’s problem.

Mydei clacked his gauntlets, feeling on his palm the remnants of a playful bite that hadn’t even pierced his gloves. “He should not be made to bear the burdens of the detachment.”

Krateros scoffed. “You claim he is Kremnoan in all but blood. Now your actions and words speak otherwise.”

“It has nothing to do with his lineage.”

“Yet you would have Hephaestion or I bear the detachment in your stead.”

“Neither of you would be forced to demean yourself to prove your worth to people salivating over your every move, hungering for a vulnerability to exploit,” Mydei hissed with a flash of teeth and his tattoos, blood rising to the surface, crystals threatening to pierce his skin.

Krateros didn’t flinch, as though Mydei were an unruly kitten and not the solitary lion with blood and gore between his maws. “He need not bear responsibility. He only need remove the ones forced upon you by your shared follies. Is he incapable of even this? Is he not your equal? If the idea offends you so, it’s shameful to do things by half measures. Your intentions must be clear beyond doubt if you seek to provide stability.”

Of course they were equals. They could never be anything else.

But, as Mydei considered Krateros’ words and noticed the slight purse of his lips paired with the tinge to his cheeks that were far from anger alone, Mydei realised the, embarrassing, solution he was so insistent upon. Mydei had been too prepared for insults, the same friction between them over the rarely spoken matter, and missed Krateros’ true intentions.

He huffed a laugh through his nose and his face eased into a small smile. “I understand.”

Krateros eyed him skeptically. “You do?”

Mydei picked up his chalice and downed the rest of it in one, dragging a hand across his mouth. “I have heard the complaints of you and legion, and shall work to rectify them immediately.

Words should never be used where actions sufficed.

In the field that had hosted Castrum Kremnos just a few days prior, Mydei and Phainon stood opposite one other, armour and weapons aflame under the rising sun. At the edges where grass plains met the forest, the entire Kremnoan detachment gathered as witnesses.

Phainon flowed through his routine stretches, loosening his muscles to swing that hefty great sword. “So when I win do I become king?”

Even without any intervention, Mydei had every intention to fulfil their shared wish: a duel at the peak of their abilities, acknowledging and saluting each other in their full glory, as they both strived for total victory before the entire detachment. A duel to shake the earth and the heavens and earn Strife’s gaze.

Just not now. The same as the direct acknowledgement of the love that had flourished between them over the years, Mydei had first intended to wait until circumstances calmed before he brought the matter up for discussion. Unfortunately, his emotions trumped his reason towards the end of the battle and he let everything spill free—from a soul rending love to heart wrenching tears, and had never felt so light for his confession.

Once again, circumstances altered his plans. This duel doubled as proof of Phainon’s status as Mydei’s one and only equal, and Mydei’s declaration of intent. If anyone harboured doubts or questions, they only need to witness and remember this duel to have their answer.

“There’s no longer a King of Castrum Kremnos for you to win the title from,” Mydei reminded him as he felt the pull of his shoulder blades from his own stretches.

“So what do I get out of this exactly?” Phainon asked with an arched brow, as though he would walk away if Mydei told him nothing. As though he hadn’t already revealed his hand years ago at the mention of a full fledged duel between them.

Mydei smirked. “If you can defeat me, I guarantee the spoils will be worth the effort.”

“Funny,” Phainon said. No laughter but grin so carefree across his face. “I thought the spoils had to be agreed upon before the duel.”

Mydei laughed under his breath and showed some small mercy, “In Kremnos there are two duels where the spoils go unsaid. If, after six years, you’re still completely unaware of that then you must be beyond all hope, Deliverer.”

“Oh, is that a hint? You only ever use that little nickname when you’re thinking about wishes. If I win, will you finally tell me what your wish is?”

That elicited a full laugh. “Deliverer,” the nickname rolled off his tongue in a lazy drawl, “think harder and you’ll have your answer.”

His brows twitched in consideration but there was no sign he found the answer. He simply set a hand upon his great sword and Mydei kicked up his spear in answer. They circled each other as the duel commenced.

“Mydei,” Phainon said before the first clash could mark the end of all conversation that didn’t come as the sing of metal.

He didn’t allow Phainon’s words to distract him, searching for an opening he knew from experience didn’t exist. “What? Chickening out?”

Phainon’s lips, distractingly, quirked. Mischievous, sly, almost triumphant and Mydei reassessed his stance for any vulnerabilities—there were none— but Phainon only said, “I never stole your rabbit.”

It took a moment, but when Mydei realised he tossed his head back and laughed. “Looks like you may have just sealed your fate.”

Then the battle truly commenced.

The weight of Phainon’s great sword should have put him at a disadvantage against Mydei’s quicker, longer spear. But Phainon swung a sword with one hand that some men struggled to lift with two. It was effortless, never letting the unwieldy momentum take him anywhere he didn’t want to go

when he swung and recovered quick enough to parry Mydei’s dodge and jab.

Six years wasn’t a long time to spend mastering a weapon. Even for Kremnoans, it took a lifetime for someone to claim mastery and most never made it to that pinnacle. If there was no one better at wielding an immortal body as Mydei, then no one could compare to Phainon’s prowess with a great sword. A skill forged and tempered with two goals: revenge on that black-robed swordsman from Aedes Elysiae, and to stand as Mydei’s equal.

Every strike was proof of his efforts. Beyond any doubt, Phainon was Mydei’s one and only equal in this world. That’s the way it always had been, and always would be.

Mydei blocked the next blow and felt the metal protest under the force. His arm tingled at the collision, from the sheer might and intention behind Phainon’s every move. He shifted his weight and met Phainon’s strength with his own, pushing him back just enough to slip free. Then closer while his arms were off balance. He drew his arms back for a swing aimed right for Phainon’s chest. Blue eyes eclipsed by black widened and Mydei’s grin sharped. A dare.

Phainon dropped low and lunged. The spear nicked his forehead and dripped gold down his nose, down his cheek, but it was nothing compared to the damage if Phainon’s shoulder hadn’t caught the spear shaft. The twist of his body. His raised arms where Mydei had thrown him off. He was already prepared for another—

He swung. Mydei tried to dart back but something hooked his ankle and he stumbled. He wouldn’t rebalance in time so he dropped limp the ground and the great sword sailed overhead. Before the blade could fall upon him, he rolled to his feet.

Panting, sweating, covered in the most minuscule of cuts bleeding gold already beginning to staunch. They took the time to breathe.

Mydei’s fingers ached more when he unclenched them than when they tightened again around his spear. “You tripped me.”

Phainon smiled, which meant yes. Not that Mydei had any doubts. “Would that be a problem?”

“I simply didn’t expect you to rely on such underhanded tactics.”

He barked a laugh, rough with adrenaline and exertion. “What is it you always say about that conspicuous body of yours? It’s your greatest weapon. Surely you of all people should understand someone using their own to the fullest.”

“By tripping me like two children in the marketplace,” Mydei jabbed, sharp as the twirl of his spear, raising it ready.

Phainon yanked the tip of his great sword from where it rested in the earth. “If only all the men sent down the Sea of Souls by Mydeimos The Undying had realised that they only needed a child to bring him low.”

He arched a brow. “Admitting to being a child now?”

His grin grew. “I prefer to think of myself as an exception.”

The reprieve was over and they charged at each other again. No matter what Mydei brought to the fore of his flurry of attacks—speed, strength, strategy, dexterity, deception—Phainon matched him blow for blow. Like a dance, one would lead and the other would follow only to snatch the initiative back for themselves. A constant give and take. Push and pull. A challenge in every spark of steel and heavy breath to keep up don’t fall behind stay as an equal.

That was why duels were the final stage of Kremnoan courtship. Mydei flaunted the pinnacle of his every attribute with his life, honour and legacy at stake, and Phainon responded with a demonstration of his own. There was no better way to learn everything about a person than when they were on the other end of a blade.

But for the two of them it was nothing more than a formality. What was there for Mydei to still learn about Phainon? He already knew the shape of his arms and legs, his body, from eating, bathing, sleeping beside him. He

knew Phainon’s sharp mind and tenacity from their many sieges and defences at each other’s side. He knew his courage to step outside the safety of the easy path to join a nameless army of exiles and face down Death. He knew he burned with as much hatred as love. He knew he wanted Phainon and nobody else.

When Mydei’s spear finally snapped and Phainon’s great sword shattered under the force of their blows, they spared a single breath to toss them aside, shards glowing under the crescent moon.

Mydei bared his teeth and Phainon flashed his back as they reverted to their basest instincts. Conquer or be conquered. It was the very root of Strife and Mydei had never been so starved and so glutted by it.

He raised his hands ready and Phainon lunged empty handed to grapple at him with nothing but themselves. Phainon swung a punch and Mydei snatched his wrist with reflexes honed through experience of such close combat. Phainon jerked his arm back and hauled Mydei with him right into a head butt. White burst behind his eyes and warmth trickled over his lip. Nose bleed. He kicked Phainon in the chest but he was so disorientated behind his watering eyes it was only enough to make Phainon stumble.

Mydei licked away the blood, smearing gold over his upper lip and teeth.

This was it. The weapons had been so, so close. That had been the duel he thought he wanted: both warring at the zenith of their prowess. A show of sparks closer to lightning, erupting into a wildfire through their veins.

But here, now, finally, it was everything and more. Nothing between them. No weapons, no masks, no responsibility or duties or titles. They were stripped raw and still couldn’t bear to look anywhere else as they collided in a blazing heat that would consume anyone other than them.

The duel lasted for fourteen days and fourteen nights. Something taken straight from a dream, a hope, a wish. Better. Because their years at each other’s sides made them so.

It ended with Phainon’s every pant of breath and drop of sweat and blood falling against Mydei’s face. Phainon’s arm across Mydei’s bare chest, his legs pinned on either side of Mydei’s waist, his hand around Mydei’s throat.

Phainon’s eyes were black, his fangs bared, every inch of him the same flushed mess as Mydei but only one of them emerged victorious. It wasn’t Mydei, and the defeat stung in the places that never outgrew the desire to hoard glory, finally relearning what it meant to lick his wounds. But he had never been so thrilled to be thrown into the dirt and thoroughly defeated.

“Yield,” Phainon hissed, as rough as his raw, bloody knuckles trickling across Mydei’s exposed throat.

The tension that Mydei carried with him in every waking and sleeping moment dissipated as he relinquished everything to the man above him. “I yield.”

Phainon’s dropped like the dead right over Mydei’s body: skin slick with blood and sweat, muscles still twitching having forgotten how to rest, hearts beating in a lingering rhythm of their battle.

The sun was rising, a warm hand stretching over the trees and grass towards them. Their discarded weapons gleamed in the distance but there was no telling where Phainon’s ended and Mydei’s began.

It was the same sunlit gleam off Phainon’s near translucent hair, off his skin slick with sweat and blood over the grass and mud stains. A shine Mydei longed to see off an earring, a red gemstone inlaid in gold, and a gold tipped braid.

He grunted at the weight. His body was undying, not beyond fatigue. “Get off, you’re sweaty.”

“Can’t move,” Phainon bemoaned in a slur. Then immediately jerked his head up, chin propped over Mydei’s collarbone. “I won.”

“Is there a hole in your head?“

He grinned lazily, pure satisfaction in the crease of his lips and eyes, blue slowly returning to his eye. “It’s nice to hear, don’t you think?”

Mydei forced his arms to move, trembling with muscle fatigue, and he pushed Phainon’s messy bangs back. Neatly hidden by his hair was a thin line across his forehead where Mydei’s gauntlets scratched him. Mydei wished for it to heal, for every wound and scar and trace of a troubled life to disappear from Phainon’s body. He silently hoped this one would stay even knowing it wouldn’t.

“Congratulations, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, you have bested me.” He laid a kiss on his forehead, lips coming away tinged a thin layer of gold. He licked it clean. “Half of my honour, my life, my soul is now yours.”

As though his honour had any meaning with no one to share it with. As though the life he had now wasn’t owned to encountering Phainon amongst the wheat fields that day. As though Phainon’s name hadn’t been etched into Mydei’s soul the day he was born.

Phainon tipped his head, begging for another kiss that Mydei gladly laid upon his nose. He chuckled weakly. “That almost sounds like a marriage proposal.”

“It is.”

Phainon stopped laughing, stopped breathing. His body tensed before it remembered it was too exhausted for that and went limp again. “Oh I passed out from exhaustion. This is a dream.”

His chest rumbled under Phainon’s cheek with the beginnings of a laugh, too tired to form as more than a purr. “It’s flattering to know you’ve dreamt of such a thing.”

“All the time.”

“You never mentioned anything.”

“Mydei, you kissed me for the first time three days ago. Or however many days ago now. I lost track of time.”

Seventeen. But the fortnight had blended together into one long event; somewhere beyond the passage of time as a dream was finally realised.

Mydei scratched at Phainon’s scalp, his head nuzzling into the sensation of the same claws that had viciously tried to tear victory from his chest was reduced to soemthing so gentle and doting. “To me this was always… an inevitability. Phainon, you are my wish. Not just a duel but everything you would be happy to share with me, and for me to share with you.”

A home that was constantly on the move but would eventually settle beneath the light of an eternal dawn. Warmed through with more love, from Phainon, from his dearest friends, than he thought he would ever be permitted to have.

“Oh,” Phainon murmured, more a puff of air against Mydei’s neck.

While Mydei ran his gauntlets through Phainon’s hair and slowly down his back—massaging at that spot Phainon complained ached whenever he overexerted himself under the weight of his great sword—Mydei dredged up past memories from the Sea of Souls. But they didn’t come with the taste of Death like stagnant water pouring down his throat. It was warm, comforting, in the shape of a voice he had come to hear every day and would for every day to come.

He spoke of two words that kept him company for four years through the terror of knowing beyond doubt that the people who meant the most to him in the world would perish while he was helpless to save them.

And a boy he stumbled across in a wheat field at a quiet edge of the world and how everything had fallen into place.

“Mydei,” Phainon said, so anguished for all the pain Mydei had managed to keep hidden throughout the years, “all this time… you never revealed this to anyone…”

Phainon’s head was still laid over Mydei’s chest, his heart, not from exhaustion but simply because he had no wish to move. Even the hand that had idly drawn patterns over Mydei’s stomach—including Phainon’s own name at one point, not that Mydei stopped him—had stilled while Mydei revealed the secret buried in the deepest part of him.

“Who would believe such a thing?” Mydei said with a quiet laugh, tinged with a hint of that self-deprecation, that loneliness, he should have outgrown.

Phainon’s head lifted, no need to search for Mydei’s eye when there was nowhere else he would be looking. The pinch of his brow was too distressed to be truly aggrieved at the long held deception, and rest of his expression was hardened with resolve. “I would have.”

“You would,” Mydei agreed easily, yet he rapped a knuckle against his temple. “But everything was so complex. These feelings and memories I couldn’t discern.”

Sometimes, back then, treading the worn path of some Mydei before him along the course of Fate, it was difficult for him to know where he ended and someone like him began. Meeting Phainon, sparing his friends—the more he diverged from that set route the more he shed that eerie sensation of someone else living through him, him living through someone else.

But he was never certain until the moment he realised that his love for Phainon was his and his alone. From the memories and experiences they shared between them.

The sun had risen but no one from the Detachment dared to fetch them, letting them languish in the warm grass marred by their duel.

Mydei kissed the crown of Phainon’s head warmed by the day. “Harbour no doubts. That love was a thought and a feeling. But over those six years what grew were my own feelings. Not for some distant memory of a past or future Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, but the you who was by my side through it all.”

Phainon’s breath hitched and he lifted himself up, hands on either side of Mydei’s torso. He blocked out the sun overhead but Mydeu could still see it, reach and grasp it, in the radiant smile Phainon reserved for him.

“Me too,” Phainon breathed. “To me, it was always going to be you, even if I didn’t know it before we ever met or even the first time I saw you. Not the Crown Prince, or Mydeimos The Undying. Him, too,” he chuckled and Mydei’s lip curled. “But even if you were just Mydei who appeared in the wheat fields of Aedes Elysiae like a stray kitten and stayed.”

It wasn’t some grand revelation. Mydei’s heart quicken anyway. He knew Phainon felt it when he lowered himself back down to snuggle against him.

Mydei’s hands wrapped around his shoulders. “You were far from subtle.”

“And you never acted on my lack of subtlety.”

Mydei shrugged, fiddling with the short hairs at his nape. “Why rush? I enjoyed what we had. I never longed for more when you were always at my side.”

“But now you’re in a rush to… get married?” Phainon asked, more curious than uncertain.

He snorted. “There are many people in the detachment who would protest at the mere idea we rushed anything.”

Phainon’s hand returned to Mydei’s torso, draw swirls, flowers and hearts. “So those six years were courtship? Is there some sign unique to Kremnoans? None of you ever mentioned that to me.”

“Courtship is just a process for two parties to learn enough about each other and decide if they would equally benefit from pursuing marriage.”

Phainon pinched his side. “Just when I was beginning to think you had a knack for romance after all…”

“We don’t have to be wed straight away. It would be more difficult that way considering the current circumstances,” Mydei admitted.

The detachment was being held together by sheer vigour. It would take time to march to Okhema, and then even more time to get his people to acclimate and settle.

When they were to be wed, it was the only thing Mydei wanted on his mind for days, weeks, months or however long it took to organise. It would come second to nothing and no one. A grand affair, combining whatever traditions from Kremnos Mydei was willing to keep and whichever Phainon longed for from Aedes Elysiae.

“Consider the duel a statement of intent.” Mydei took Phainon’s hand in his —a hand that had held him and held a weapon for him—and kissed his ring finger. “Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, I intend to marry you. If not today then someday.”

Phainon’s fingers twitched. Then he turned their hands so he could lean down, dry lips lingering on Mydei’s ring finger, a second kiss in the words, “Another inevitability.”

Mydei chuckled. Is there anything more fitting for us?”

Because Mydei knew they were destined to meet each other. Somewhere, somehow. Never so early that their roughened edges had a chance to grow around each other like they had never been apart—rather than clashing, sanding, until they fit together. Even if their love never came to fruition, Mydei wasn’t privy to a time when love hadn’t been nurtured somewhere between the two of them.

Phainon lifted his head, eyes still heavy with the weight of a duel that said everything that could ever need to be said between them, but smiled like he had never felt exhaustion and declared anyway, “I love you.” His arms wrapped around Mydei, back arching so they could slide between him and the soil, hands folding over his tenth thoracic vertebra. “Honour, life, soul— we’ll share in it and protect it.”

A shaky breath of disbelief, relief, escaped through Mydei’s lips. He bumped their foreheads together and closed his eyes. “You succeeded after

all, Deliverer.” But that title that once fit better than anything not longer felt so fitting off his tongue. “Phainon.”

Every impossible wish fulfilled by Phainon’s hands.

Chapter End Notes

Went from six years of something to actually getting together to a marriage proposal less than three weeks later. PhaiDei are truly iconic.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon arrive in Okhema to greet a new future and some old faces.

Chapter Notes

Word of the Kremnoan detachment’s movements journeyed quicker than their feet. Between the detachment’s route and the holy city, the only major city, although reduced to the remains of one, was Janusopolis. The fallen walls and temple neutrally became the neutral ground chosen by Okhema’s Goldweaver.

On the other end of the crumbling bridge out of the ruins awaited a legion of warriors. Unmistakably Okheman by their armour, and the woman at their head. Dressed in a white chiton adorned with gold laurels creeping across her body and head like her blessed blood and fine hair had bloomed jewellery. Mydei halted the detachment at the sight of the infamous Romance demigod.

Despite the Kremnoan detachment outnumbering the Okheman legion, the Goldweaver remained steadfast as she assessed first Mydei and then Phainon with dull eyes. Her golden threads strung so thin they were near imperceptible between half-fallen pillars.

Although his recollections of her were vague and hazy, he knew there was no chance she would turn them away. The Flame Chase Journey she had dedicated hundreds of years to only lacked two demigods. All of Amphoreus knew that two amongst the Kremnoan detachment’s ranks bled gold—who better to bear the Coreflame of Strife than the heir to its dynasty.

A tent had been set up prior to their arrival, offering some privacy for their discussions. Inside, a young child with red hair garlanded with flowers smiled in greeting, at once childlike yet restrained. Burdened. Phainon grinned back with a little wave and the child’s smile grew at the reciprocation.

While the Goldweaver took her seat beside her young companion, Mydei crossed his arms and loomed over the table. “Lady Goldweaver, if these negotiations will drag on then I will need to order my men to set up camp.”

The Goldweaver didn’t flinch at the tone and face that scattered enemies; if anything, her lip curled into the slightest bemused smile. “That depends entirely on whether we can reach a satisfactory arrangement.”

With the fall of their city and the long days of marching, the Kremnoan detachment’s endurance was beginning to wear thin. It was different now. Both when they moved or rested, the detachment was no longer so carefree, billowing like clouds drifting through the sky wherever the wind sought to take them.

Their numbers had swelled with those unfit for a life of wandering— children, wounded, elderlies, or simply those unaccustomed to the life and less adaptable than the others. Their resources were thinner, stretching to meet their physical needs. Compounded by the anxious uncertainty of their future, morale was exceedingly low. The detachment needed somewhere to settle.

However, if the two forces came to arms, the sheer numbers and discipline of the Kremnoan detachment led by Phainon and Mydei would force the Okhemans into a retreat. If they launched an attack against the holy city, the Goldweaver’s threads would prevent them from storming the city walls. From there, it was questionable whether the detachment’s current ranks could endure a protracted siege.

Peace was their best option.

The child stared up at Mydei with such hopeful eyes. “We don’t want to see Chrysos Heirs fight.”

“We…” He sighed and pulled out the chair opposite the Goldweaver. “Would also like to avoid unnecessary Strife.”

Phainon took the seat beside him and the girl’s smile was relieved. Grateful, when she glanced between the two of them.

The Goldweaver hummed, light and airy, but as elegant as the cross of her arms over the table and the slight smile of a casual conversation, not the negotiation between two armies eager to kill. “Then allow us to keep this brief. The refugees of Aedes Elysiae hold you and your warriors in high regard. They speak of how you fearlessly plunged into the black tide and rescued as many civilians as possible.”

“Kremnoans do not fear death nor the black tide,” Mydei confirmed, already aware of the only thing the detachment had to offer. “Make no mistake, we believe in the value of an equal trade. In exchange for safe refuge, the Kremnoan detachment will act as the holy city’s spear and shield against the incursion of the black tide.”

The black tide was a horrifying perversion of nature. If Mydei were able, he would keep his people far away from it. But he meant what he said: the detachment would never accept pity and charity, their pride as warriors wouldn’t allow it, not from anyone, let alone their age old enemy.

The main virtue of the Kremnoans was their military might. If not for the presence of the Goldweaver and her defences wound around the city, the Okhema would have fallen to Kremnos’ siege long ago. That same undeniable strength, which earned them scorn for their savagery from the rest of Amphoreus, was the one thing of value they could hold steadfast to after the fall of their city. And offer with pride.

While the detachment’s days of conquest were over, the familiar lifestyle of military training and excursions would hold them together in such turbulent times.

“Prince Mydeimos, I do not take the solitary lion nor the blazing sun at his back for fools,” the Goldweaver rebuked, her small smile falling into something too disinterested to be anger, despite her scathing tone.

So do not take me for a fool.

Phainon nudged Mydei with his knee beneath the table and he tapped him back; a signal for him to go ahead.

Phainon’s lips curved into a warmer smile, amiable yet sincere, as expected from a face that often looked stranger without a smile and even rested in one. “Lady Goldweaver and…” He met the young girl’s eye again. “Forgive me for not asking sooner, but what would your name be?”

The girl laughed. “We are Tribbie. And there’s no need to call Agy that.”

“So long as we remain on amicable terms, Aglaea will do fine,” Aglaea agreed but her expression unsoftened. She hadn’t yet received what she truly came for.

Unperturbed by the strange phrasing, Phainon bowed his head. “It’s a pleasure to officially meet you, Lady Tribbie and Lady Aglaea. I am Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. As you can probably guess for yourselves, you have my most sincere gratitude for sheltering the refugees of my hometown.”

Aglaea tilted her head, blond locks swaying like the golden threads about the tent, only visible when the candle light glinted off them just so. “As long as the holy city is able and the refugees have no intention of disturbing the peace, it will offer sanctuary to as many people as it can hold.”

But the Kremnoan detachment was not the same as other refugees. They weren’t half a displaced village of farmers or fishermen. They were a fully armed and armoured legion of Okhema’s worst enemies asking for access to the city. Far from a headless viper in its death throes from the fall of Castrum Kremnos, their Crown Prince marched at their head for them to follow. Once they were inside the city walls, the only obstacle left to a full siege was the Goldweaver.

Even without a siege, there were other risks. Friction between Kremnoans and Okhemans was already guaranteed and would hinder attempts to assimilate Kremnoans into the city. It could spark civil discontent, protests

or even riots, that challenged Aglaea’s questionable decisions. To provide the detachment refuge was an enormous risk.

Mydei nudged Phainon—Mydei’s turn again—but it was a pointless gesture when dull eyes flicked to him before he could even inhale to speak; the Goldweaver’s threads read their every move. Their persistent presence at the edge of his peripheral, perhaps moving or perhaps not, since his arrival was a power play.

There was no need for such theatrics. He had Leonnius collate rumours on the Goldweaver and had Peucesta recount every poem that venerated, or even slandered, her as soon as he resolved to relocate the detachment to her city.

Whether all the tales were true—he highly doubted it. In the same manner rumours about him were highly exaggerated—was irrelevant. Rumours told him what people believed to be true and the kind of power they attributed to the cold, ruthless woman, the very antithesis of the passions of romance, did not arise from nowhere.

“Lady Aglaea, with your vast information network, you must know the traditions behind Castrum Kremnos’ lineage of kings,” Mydei said.

“I know all about Kremnos’ archaic traditions.”

He huffed a small laugh. “Then you and I are in agreement. I took my father, the old king’s, life with my own hands. Yet I refused to crown myself in his blood—to continue Kremnos’ history of conquest while we fought against the maddened Titan of Strife and the black tide in the city that was now mine. Because needless Strife will only bring an end to Kremnos, my life and the lives of my people.”

To shed lives like trees shed leaves, all in the name of conquest, honour and glory. Eventually the tree would be left barren to wither.

Mydei squared his shoulders and tipped his head back. Not in arrogant condescension, but confidence from one ruler to another. “I have no intention of entering your city through deception only to raise arms against

the only place my people will be safe from the black tide for the foreseeable future.”

Aglaea levelled that same stare back at him. Unwavering poise. While Mydei laid his intentions bare, she searched for any signs of deception. When she straightened back into her chair and raised the back of her long, delicate but deadly fingers to her chin, he knew she hadn’t found any.

Tribbie turned from Aglaea to Mydei. “But you know there’s something else we are also waiting for.”

“Of course. Mydei and I…” Phainon glanced at Mydei for one last confirmation, the final chance to escape.

But Mydei was never one to submit to fear and he only quirked a brow at Phainon, as though questioning whether he had forgotten that.

Phainon laughed under his breath, short and breathy but fond. “We have already decided that we will be willing to join your efforts in the Flame Chase Journey.”

Aglaea wasn’t yet satisfied when she tilted her head. “The decision to dedicate yourself, mind and body, must be entirely your own. It is no game. Once made, your life and your loyalties will belong to the Flame Chase.”

Mydei smirked. “So long as it doesn’t jeopardise the future of the Kremnoan legion, you can have this undying body as your own.”

Finally, her expression gave. Just the slightest bit, as imperceptible as her threads, but Mydei was adept at reading people he engaged on the battlefield and the table wasn’t a large enough distance to disguise the softening at the very corners of her heartless mask.

“Then we are in agreement,” Aglaea concluded. “Okhema welcomes the Crown Prince and the Kremnoan detachment in exchange for your assistance against the black tide and services to forward the Flame Chase.”

The holy city was still a few days march from Janusopolis. Despite the proximity, both armies refrained from mingling during marching or resting hours, with very few exceptions. Mydei and Phainon frequently conversed with Aglaea and Tribbie about the state of their men, immediate plans for the day or night, and the expectations held of the Chrysos Heirs.

Leonnius ran messages at Mydei’s behest and refrained from stumbling on his swift feet when an Okheman expressed mocking surprise he could understand the common tongue enough to pass word.

Ptolemy attempted to organise a small hunting competition. It ended with accusations that the detachment used deception to be victorious and a full conflict nearly erupted over wounded pride.

Perdikkas volunteered his concoctions when a number of Okhemans were injured while seeking shelter in a dilapidated temple that then collapsed over them, only to be spurned as though he offered poisons and not cures.

Peucesta discussed a famous Okheman epic with some of their musicians; a fruitful conversation marred by other Okheman’s overhearing and scorning him for believing a Kremnoan could hope to understand the higher literature of the holy city.

Hephaestion’s polite conversation openers were frequently repudiated with insults aimed at his more delicate face and physique for battle. Yet the same warriors were too cowardly to accept his suggestion of a friendly spar.

By the time they reached Okhema’s gates, it was abundantly clear how great the challenge of assimilating into the holy city would be when neither people were willing to meet halfway. While some Okhemans and Kremnoans had overcome their initial hesitance to engage in productive conversation or exchanges, the vast majority remained steadfast in their segregation. Old blood stained; it would take effort to scrub it clean.

Still, his friends didn’t question his decision when they gathered around the fire pits with honey brew. Like a lost spar, they took the defeat in stride and concocted a new angle of attack with a thrill for the challenge.

Provisions had been made by Aglaea for the detachment to reside in the city barracks. While space, resources and the citizens’ morale had been prepared for the sudden influx of their worst enemy—a group of barbarians who drank the blood of their victims—the barracks were stationed on the outskirts of the city. Out of sight unless someone came searching for them.

Unease permeated the cramped quarters, still within Okhema’s high walls where it was difficult to flee and easy to be cornered. But it was the first time they had a real roof over their heads and walls at their sides to keep the wind out since they departed from Castrum Kremnos.

Healers from the famed Twilight Courtyard arrived to treat the injured and check for any infections or diseases that could trigger an epidemic in the city. Mydei silenced the Kremnoan cries of outrage at the implication they would ever allow themselves to wallow in filth.

Even once their initial indignation quieted, it was far from calmed.  They hovered over the healers in crowds practically brimming with bloodlust ready to overspill if a single mistake was made. Never mind that the piercing stares caused the healers’ hands to tremble.

The Chrysos Heir with pink curls and a strange floating creature smiled at Mydei appreciatively when he ordered the Kremnoans give them space to work. Only Perdikkas and his physicians were permitted to observe, help if the healers needed the extra hands and, more importantly, act as a familiar presence to reassure the patients. Perdikkas was fascinated with the glow at Lady Hyacinthia’s hands and she was more than happy to explain as she made swift work of any lingering aches and pains from their long journey.

Despite the strange bugs Lady Aglaea insisted were perfect for communication, Leonnius ran laps from the barracks to Marmoreal Palace as Mydei’s messenger with a golden tassel from Aglaea in case anyone dared be too persistent with their questioning of the Kremnoan moving through the emptier streets. While he passed word to Mydei, it also gave him the unique authority to tell stories to the children; things about the city to ease the nerves they grit their teeth and buried but never went away.

While Mydei walked back and forth around the barracks, putting out fires of discontent and anxiety everywhere he went, Ptolemy recited the basics of Okheman courtesy and had him repeat the most crucial points back. Over the chatter, Peucesta plucked at his lyre with the beginnings of a new song intertwined with the familiar rise and falls of the old ones, evoking memories of honey brew, the campfire and a distant home nestled inside their new one.

A short distance from the barracks, Hephaestion conversed with the Okheman warriors that lingered nearby. Some were, tentative, acquaintances he had made over the past few days who came with a genuine interest in how the detachment was settling. Others were not officially stationed nearby but lacked the confidence to leave the Kremnoans unchecked.

Beside Mydei at every step was Phainon. Never too close but never far enough Mydei couldn’t find him with a quick glance around the room.

Even now, Phainon awaited him at the entrance to the barrack. His smile grew as Mydei approached and he offered a hand. “Ready to go?”

So that Mydei could uphold his image of independence from Aglaea, she retreated to manage her own affairs upon their arrival through the city walls. She only requested his and Phainon’s presence at Marmoreal Palace once the situation and sufficiently stabilised. It was a chance to meet the other Chrysos Heirs, discuss the Flame Chase Journey and the needs of the Kremnoan detachment.

But Leonnius was a traitor who failed to informed Mydei that Marmoreal Palace was a bathhouse.

Mydei had no qualms with stripping off his dirtied travel garments and slipping into the thin bathing tunic. The issue was…

“Stop pouting,” he told Phainon without halting from folding his clothes.

He squeezed tighter around Mydei’s middle, head over Mydei’s shoulder so he couldn’t ignore the push of his lips even further as he whined, “Mydei,

all these people are gonna see you in this.”

“It’s hardly any different than my usual clothes and you have no qualms about those.”

“It is,” he sulked with another squeeze. “The whole detachment dresses like that.”

“It’s a bathhouse. Everyone will be dressed like this. ”

“But…”

“Phainon, what would you have me do? Bathe fully clothed?”

“Is that an option?”

“Use your brain and tell me.”

Everyone turned out to be an exaggeration. Tribbie had mentioned that Chrysos Heirs were famous in Okhema and attracted more public attention than they often sought, so a changing room was reserved exclusively for their use alongside a private bathing area.

The Hero’s Baths were the most decadent scene Mydei had yet to witness in his life as a prince; although it was a title more in name than riches. Not only did it hang in the air over the rest of the bathhouse, it had a sweeping view of the skyline cast in eternal daylight by Kephale’s protection.

Golden water flowed down from a cracked pearl overhead and into the baths. Waters that shimmered with the blessed of Phagousa.

The other Chrysos Heirs were already in the baths, drinks and food at hand. Tribbie waved from her seat on the edge, drawing the attention of the two other red haired girls she had told them about during their travels: Tinnon and Trianne. Lady Hyacinthia, accompanied by the strange creature she had introduced as Ica, also raised her hand in greeting with a soft smile, as steadfast as the one worn by the man at Mydei’s side.

The man clinging very adamantly to Mydei’s side, arm slung around Mydei’s waist so Mydei’s unclothed side was pressed against the bathing garments over Phainon’s torso, so thin it was practically bare skin to skin.

They had yet to meet the last Chrysos Heir, seated at the edge furthest from the others where she watched them with wide eyes. Ptolemy had warned that Okhemans could be more… averse to skinship between comrades.

At that, they had both turned to look at Phainon across the barracks, a child on his lap and another hanging off his arm as they listened to Peucesta’s song. With those senses of his attuned to Mydei’s every move, Phainon’s head immediately perked up and swivelled.

He cocked his head in silent question, whether Mydei needed him at that moment, and Mydei waved his concerns away. Phainon nodded and blew Mydei a kiss. Peucesta’s next word warbled with suppressed laughter. Ptolemy and Mydei’s shared look right betrayed the truth: it was hopeless.

Departed their fearsome reputations, none of the Chrysos Heirs hesitated in their presence. The two of them sat so close, thighs and shoulders together, despite the luxurious size of the baths probably helped soften the image of two incarnations of Nikador who ravaged the battlefield.

The others laughed, suggested ideas, and shared their troubles freely. Even when Mydei’s words sounded perfunctory as usual, none of them were offended by it.

The water also did wonders to relax the atmosphere. Waters blessed by Phagousa were a necessary precaution to hoard away in case of encounters with the black tide, but he never encountered it in this quality nor quantity. All the fatigue seeped out of his heated blood into the waters and steam.

“How are the detachment’s arrangements?” Aglaea asked.

“They remain anxious,” he admitted with slight shrug. No one expected them to feel at ease immediately. “The barracks are too small for everyone to stay comfortably.”

Aglaea plucked a grape from a floating platter and toying with it between her fingers. “I’ve already gathered the paperwork for the construction of more barracks to accommodate your numbers. Your soldiers will also receive a stipend for their services.”

Efficient. The mind to anticipate issues and resolve them swiftly was a trait he valued within the detachment, and he made an effort to promote those who demonstrated the ability to ease his burdens rather than add to them.

Even without the Coreflame of Romance at her fingertips, it was obvious how Aglaea maintained power for centuries despite the tumultuous opinions of the Flame Chase over the years. She was rather terrifying, and that only heightened Mydei’s opinion of her.

“We can move some of the injured to the Courtyard for now,” Hyacinthia suggested. “It won’t be much. But it would alleviate some numbers.”

Mydei shook his head. “Being separated would only make everyone more anxious. Thank you for taking the effort to come to the barracks, Lady Hyacinthia. Perdikkas had much to say about your capable hands.”

If it weren’t for the heat of the bath already flushing her cheeks, he was certain she would have blushed to accompany her bashful smile. “Just Hyacine is fine. And I’m happy to be of service to all who need it.”

“In that case,” Mydei began, more tentative than he would have liked, and Phainon squeezed his hand under the water, “one of my men has been plagued by illness since young. I fear the change in conditions may result in a severe relapse in the coming months.”

The shy preening at the compliments disappeared as quickly as it came, replaced by a look he recognised from Perdikkas’ face whenever Mydei entered the physician’s tent dripping gold behind him. Solemn when confronted with an issue that could take lives and they held the power to solve, but never cold and distant.

Only earnest as she nodded. “A stress induced flareup of a chronic illness. Would you mind me asking for their name?”

If he sighed with relief, it was silenced by the lapping water. “Hephaestion.”

“Hephaestion,” she repeated slowly, committing it to memory. “I didn’t treat anyone by that name today. I can come to the barracks again tomorrow for a check-up. If I want his medical history, Perdikkas would be the one to ask, right?”

Mydei smiled. From their limited interactions, he quite liked Hyacine; her positive attitude doing nothing to detract from her wisdom and dedication. “That’s correct. If tomorrow doesn’t fit your schedule then there’s no need to rush to trouble yourself.”

Hyacine laughed. “I wouldn’t call it trouble when there’s a patient in need.“

“I will be happy to lend my aid wherever possible,” Castorice offered but she frowned. “Although, I lack the same abilities as Lady Hyacine, Lady Tribbie, Lady Trianne, Lady Trinnon, or Lady Aglaea.”

One of the first things they had discussed was a brief warning about Castorice’s unique constitution due to her connection with Death. It explained the physical distance between her and the others, and the self-doubt evident in her words.

“Thank you, Lady Castorice. Everyone has unique skills and abilities; they only require the correct circumstances to apply them. Mydei turned back to Aglaea and the original conversation. “It would also be beneficial to organise joint training exercises once tensions cool. The more controlled exposure the legions and guards have to one another the better.”

Aglaea considered it for a moment before suggesting, “Perhaps a week’s time. If the situation remains unstable then we can reconsider the exact date.”

Across several quints that bled into hours, they discussed the future. One where the Kremnoans assimilated into Okhema. Where they pursued the Coreflame of Strife that was Mydei’s by birthright and tradition before he left it behind in his homeland.

While Phainon refrained from speaking much on matters of the detachment, leaving them to Mydei unless prompted with a nudge, there were a number of discussions that revolved around him. An education in the Grove, where another Chrysos Heir resided and, Aglaea explained with scorn, was too self-absorbed to deign to greet them. The kind of education Mydei was unable to receive without accusations of falling to Okhema’s persuasions, which would damage his relationship with the detachment.

There were ideas for public relations campaign with Phainon’s boyish charms and heritage rooted in Aedes Elysiae, whose refugees had successfully assimilated into the city, at the fore. A good middle ground to show Okhemans that not all Kremnoans were lower than even the most savage of animals.

The conversation ended as Aglaea, rather ominously, revealing she had their measurements and would prepare garments befitting her two new Chrysos Heirs. He wouldn’t deny the Goldweaver, as renowned for the quality of her garments as her ruthlessness.

For now, the changing room had clean chitons for them to redress in. They were white with a few accessories, simple yet pure gold, to hold the fabric in place but were otherwise plain and unassuming. When Mydei finished pinning his in place, Phainon was still fumbling with the drape, head and eyes down. So he couldn’t anticipate Mydei’s hand threading through his hair as he leaned in to press a kiss to his temple.

His fingers froze around the clasp, eyes widened and lips parted. Mydei chuckled and began to pull away but that brought Phainon back to life. He grabbed Mydei’s hand in his own while the other cupped the back of Mydei’s neck, keeping them in place.

“What was that for?” Phainon asked, entirely too fond, eyes roaming across Mydei’s face like the answer would be written there. It was, because Mydei was just as disgustingly lovestruck.

So he didn’t shy away even when the intensity of Phainon’s gaze on Mydei, always on Mydei, made heat rise to the tips of his ears. “It was a thank you. For everything.”

A tenderness that made Mydei appear as more than a fearsome warrior prince, something gentled, for the better, by Phainon at his side. A silence so Mydei could do his job as prince, as king in all but name and crown and a ring he destroyed, despite his time in the detachment and his status as Mydei’s equal and parter earning him the right to speak.

For so much more than could ever be put into words but Mydei would spend a lifetime trying.

“Not that I don’t appreciate it. But,” he dragged the word out and his smile didn’t reach the peak of its usual coyness. Too soft, even as he teased, “I think you missed.”

“Have you ever known me to miss?”

Mydei could launch a spear across two battlefields and still perfectly impale an enemy’s head.

Phainon hummed thoughtfully. “Nope.” He lowered Mydei’s hand from his hair, dragging down the side of his neck, over his exposed collarbone, straight to his chest. Phainon’s heart beat earnestly under Mydei’s palm. “You got me right here in one clean shot. I won’t ever recover.”

“Sap.”

“Your fault,” Phainon murmured, eyes flicking down to Mydei’s lips and they were dilated black when they came back up. “So take responsibility.”

“I already offered to be wed,” Mydei reminded him.

His ears burned down to his cheeks but he leaned in and Phainon met him halfway for a short kiss turned long when Phainon stepped closer and Mydei hauled him further in. Although they shared a tent and a cot, they were too exhausted from managing the detachment’s present and future while still marching by day to do more than succumb to sleep at night.

The bath had cleansed away that exhaustion, and left them alone for the first time in weeks.

As always, Mydei had to be the first to pull away while Phainon chased. Mydei stopped him with a press of their foreheads together.

“Goldweaver…” Mydei managed between pants. “The surprise…”

Phainon licked his lips, seeking the lingering taste of Mydei on them. That expression beneath his half-lidded eyes was completely at odds with the way he so pathetically begged, “One more?”

“Greedy,” Mydei chastised and gave a final kiss. “Now stop fiddling with the chiton. Let me do it.”

Long flowing fabrics didn’t suit life in a farming village or on the move, especially not with such expensive decorations and soft material. It was easier for Mydei to control the drape and pin it in place for Phainon, smoothing it out to fall beautifully over his broad shoulders, muscled chest, trim waist and down his legs.

“How do I look?” Phainon asked with wide, overly innocent eyes.

Mydei knew what he was really asking and leaned in for another kiss, breaking away quickly before Phainon could turn it from something chaste into something more. He kept their hands intertwined.

“Adequate. Let’s go.”

“Wait a moment. My pocket.”

Phainon retrieved his pouch from his travel garments and began to tie it around his waist like always, before he paused. Then he peered up demurely and Mydei sighed, holding out a palm for Phainon to drop the pouch so Mydei could tie it for him.

A Garmentmaker waited for them outside and led them through the halls of Marmoreal Palace. People didn’t spare the effort to be discrete when they stared, mind spinning rumours about the solitary lion and blazing sun that had come to reside in their holy city.

But Mydei was never one to waver under the gaze of others and neither was Phainon. In fact, he donned his second most charming smiled—the most charming one was reserved for Mydei alone—and waved at them like this were a casual stroll through the marketplace of some unimportant town that knew neither of their names.

They arrived at a closed door, a private room, and the Garmentmaker left as soon as it was clear it had delivered them successfully to the location. They glanced at each other in silent question and both shrugged.

Phainon reached for the door and Mydei didn’t stop him, stepping aside to give him space. The door swung open and Phainon froze.

Thoughts of betrayal flashed through Mydei’s mind. But that didn’t make sense. Aglaea needed two more Chrysos Heirs. Even if the detachment’s arrival swung public sentiment away from her, her grasp on power was far from fickle enough—

Phainon stumbled into the room and their joined hands, squeezed bloodless, bones creaking, dragged Mydei in behind him and he knew his face was just as stunned.

Age lined their skin and hair but the sight of the two who had welcomed Mydei into their home was unmistakable.

Phainon released a shaky breath, “Mum. Dad.”

Audata’s hands cupped over her mouth fell away as she took a step weighed by hesitance and disbelief. “Phainon… my boy.”

In Hieronymus’ arms, Snowy panted away, tongue lolling and tail wagging, and he yipped and squirmed at the sight of his long lost owner.

Phainon’s hands slackened around his and then let go as he ran to the mother and father he hadn’t seen in six years. They welcomed him with open arms and, together, fell to their knees.

“You’ve gotten so big and strong.” Hieronymus chuckled wetly. “I can hardly believe it.”

Phainon lived life loudly. His joy, his love, and even his tears. He wailed and sobbed like, in the arms of his parents, he had returned to the child Mydei had once stumbled across in the wheat fields.

Mydei leaned against the wall. Perhaps he should have left them to their private moment but any movement would draw extra attention to him when the family huddled on the floor were so consumed by sheer happiness to the point of tears. Reunited with his parents, Phainon didn’t need Mydei for support the same way Mydei needed him.

Mydei wanted to be there for him anyway.

Once Phainon’s cries tapered off into sniffles, he turned back. He really was an ugly crier—swollen eyes, snot, flushed face—but Mydei couldn’t help but smile.

“Mydei…” Phainon whined, more pathetic than his usual theatrics but asking for the same thing.

That brought everyone’s attention to him and his first instinct was to push down his smile, square his shoulders, and bear the weight of the gazes that fell to him with expectations. But the moment passed and Mydei relaxed again when those eyes on him didn’t feel uncomfortable.

Phainon smiled through the tears. “Come here.”

“Mydei…” Audata had the same smile as her son. Had given it to him during long days in a home they thought would last forever but would have to start anew here. “To think you’re the same Mydei. You look even bigger than Phainon.”

Phainon sniffed, teary yet somehow so indignant. “Actually, I’m still taller.”

Mydei pushed off the wall and rolled his eyes. “Not when you’re down there.”

A finger hooked into his chiton and tugged. “Then get down here.”

Mydei let Phainon pull him to the ground, his arm catching Mydei’s waist before his knees could strike the floor too hard, and their small huddle opened to let Mydei inside. It was warm. In the same way Aedes Elysiae had been warm. Small and cosy. Peaceful. He never wanted to leave.

Audata reached across, too many emotions to name in the squeeze of her hand over his leg. “You’ve been taking care of each other.”

“Of course!” Phainon tugged Mydei closer into his side, every bit of space eliminated in a well-practice instant, like a needless apology for pulling his hand away when he ran to his parents. “And for the rest of our lives too.”

A blink of confusion, then their eyes widened.

“I…” Mydei cleared his throat but didn’t dare shrink away from their questioning gazes. “I hope it’s all right that I didn’t… ask for your blessing.”

Audata sniffled. Her tears came renewed and Hieronymus hugged her against his side in the same way his son always reached for Mydei.

He placed a kiss to her cheek and rubbed her shoulder soothingly. “Our boy is getting married. Our Little Snowy.”

“Not yet,” Phainon interjected and his hands grappled uselessly at the air, not quite sure where to go. “I’m still… still your Little Snowy—“

“What are you waiting for!” Audata suddenly yelled and she swatted at his hands. Mydei’s equal, tied with him for the most fearsome warrior of the Kremnoan detachment, in all of Amphoreus, yelped. “If you find a good man who wants to marry you then you marry him! You think good men grow like wheat!”

“N-no but-“

“Snowy’s already so old! Don’t you want him to see you get married?”

Snowy barked, as though on command. Mydei scratched behind his ears and he rolled over. After the bath, Mydei’s hands were still bare of his gauntlets and he scratched all along Snowy’s belly without fear.

“Well-“

“You always used to talk about how cute Mydei was! And now—“

“Okay!” Phainon finally burst with embarrassment, flush disappearing down his neck and underneath his chiton; the red a lovely contrast against the white. He burned hotter when Mydei arched an amused brow. “We get the idea. We’ll… discuss a date.”

Hieronymus ruffled Phainon’s hair with a chuckle. “Your mum is just happy for you, Phainon. As am I. For both of you, Mydei.”

Mydei scratched at the inside of Snowy’s thigh and his leg thumped. He projected his voice past the mumble it instinctively pulled into at the blatant approval, “Thank you.”

“You must be awfully busy,” Audata said, acknowledging without naming the duties that awaited outside this room. Phainon nodded, eyes still low to the ground. “But come for dinner whenever you’re free and we’ll be happy to see you. You must have a lot to say about your time away from home.”

Phainon perked up and his grin returned brighter than ever. “We will.”

“Mydei, feel free to bring people with you,” Audata offered.

In truth, proper courtship was something of a gap in Mydei’s education. It had been wholly unnecessary compared to the much more crucial skills and knowledge he had needed to learn as a child. By the time he came of age where the proper process of courtship would be applicable, none of the detachment felt the need to teach him. They were much too preoccupied betting on his relationship with Phainon and, supposedly, any attempts to educate him was ruled out as cheating.

The only thing he had known was the story of his parents, who underwent ten duels and tied as equals in every instance before deciding to wed.

Still, Mydei was fairly certain that the two families meeting was standard.

It was instinct to clack his claws together, fingers forming a loose fist. But he was stripped of his gauntlets. Instead, he gripped Phainon’s hand when he asked, “Would five be too many? Perhaps six?”

“You spent six years feeding Phainon’s appetite, six people for one night doesn’t compare,” Hieronymus jested and Phainon made no attempt to defend himself. But Hieronymus’ smile softened after his playful chuckle. “You and any of your friends and family are always welcome.”

With their address scrawled on a strip of parchment and carefully tucked away in Phainon’s pouch, they parted ways outside Marmoreal Palace. By the time they returned to the barracks, the Kremnoan detachment had settled down to rest after their long journey. The few Kremnoan guards stationed at the entrance saluted as the two of them passed by.

The sun never set in Okhema. It was the blessing of Kephale stood tall over the holy city with the Dawn Device over their shoulders.

His body knew it was time to slumber but the sky was no different between when they first arrived in the city and now. As though no time at all had passed. No matter how different Mydei felt with every step forward lighter than before.

The only thing that betrayed the hour was the empty training grounds. A sky full of daylight and yet it felt as though the only people awake were the two of them.

“Your parents are doing well.”

“Yeah.”

Mydei arched a brow at the lacklustre response. The entire walk back, Phainon had been oddly distracted as he stared ahead in a daze; only

Mydei’s arm around his waist prevented him from walking into walls.

He first assumed the emotional exhaustion had intensified the physical kind, accumulated after so long and too deep in his body for even Phagousa’s blessing to wash away. But Phainon had been the one to forgo sleep at the barracks for the training grounds.

“Phainon.”

“Yeah?” Phainon still stared ahead when they had long since stopped walking.

There was nothing but a blank wall and a rack of training weapons. What was so interesting there, or in the confines of Phainon’s mind, that could whisk Phainon’s attention elsewhere?

Mydei pinched Phainon’s chin, turning his head so there was nowhere else for him to look. His eyes, his ears, his mind on Mydei alone. “A warrior who allows themselves to be pressured into the rhythm of others will inevitably face defeat.”

Don’t rush. Everyone from Krateros to their five companions to the old detachment and now Phainon’s parents wanted them to be wed as soon as possible. All for their own reasons but the outcome was the same.

If the day they were married wasn’t the happiest day of both their lives then it was pointless.

Phainon sucked in a deep breath. “It’s not that. It’s-it’s something else. Just don’t be upset with me.”

He pulled his chin from Mydei’s fingertips and Mydei’s brows creased, deepening still when Phainon avoided his questioning gaze. He waited as Phainon rifled through the pouch he insisted he bring with him. It was the kind of pocket everyone possessed and kept close: coins, a dose of emergency anaesthetic, whatever other valuables they could need at a moment’s notice.

“Found it,” he muttered to himself.

When he straightened, he breathed through the lingering nerves and steadied himself with newfound resolve. There was something held tight in his fist. Too tight for Mydei to get a glimpse.

“Close your eyes.”

Mydei closed them, waiting in darkness but every sense as attuned to Phainon as Phainon’s were to him. The rustle of fabric as Phainon moved, the skim of something across Mydei’s cheek rose up towards his forehead, and then a cool weight dropped around his neck.

“Open them.”

Phainon’s smile was even, pretty and tame, which meant the nerves had returned and he simply chewed them up and swallowed them down. “I found it a while ago I just… I wasn’t certain how to go about returning it to you.”

Finally, Mydei looked down. Hung from his neck was a thin chain, something almost delicate if he not for the markings of Kremnoan forgery, ensuring it was as resilient as his regular jewellery. At the end of the chain was more gold. A ring.

When Mydei cupped it in his palm, stamped on the surface was the emblem of Strife. But it was more than that.

“I really did fish it up one day. As a child. And then the priests and Cyrene told me about Castrum Kremnos. It felt… like a sign? Like something important. So I kept it close all these years. At first as a reminder of what I wanted to do with my life and I thought I might be able to reunite it with its owner when I eventually got to the city. Then… then you arrived and I joined the detachment and I kept it because… I’m not certain honestly. Because it felt right and—“

“Breathe,” Mydei told him even when his own breath was caught in his lungs.

Phainon paused to take a deep breath, searching Mydei’s expression the entire time. When Mydei gestured with a lazy hand, he continued, “I thought it was just interesting jewellery people liked to wear. I didn’t realise it was more than that until…”

“Until you saw me take a similar one from my dead father’s finger,” Mydei finished as Phainon’s strange reaction that day, an observation buried under all the emotional highs and lows, finally made sense.

He nodded meekly, fingers twined in front of him and the same colour to his cheeks as his bitten lip. “Then a lot was happening and I didn’t know when or how to return it to you after all these years. So I promised myself it would be safely in your hands once we were inside Okhema.”

Then he didn’t say any more. He simply peered up at Mydei through his lashes. A scolded puppy when Mydei hadn’t even said anything yet because…

What was there to say? What words could possibly be enough?

Words should never be used where actions sufficed.

Cold metal pressed against Mydei’s lips as he kissed his mother’s ring returned to him from the Sea of Souls by Phainon. Phainon who had been connected to him in so many ways before they ever met.

Then he grabbed Phainon by his chiton and kissed him too.

There was so much he wanted to tell Phainon through the press of their lips, their shared breath, his hands clenched until they trembled. When Phainon’s mouth and hands moved against him just as desperately, he knew Phainon understood and hungered to say the same things back.

But there were things that had to be said in words, too. Ones hidden so deep even Mydei hadn’t unearthed them until that moment. Once, he would have left them half-uncovered and half-buried, only there for him to acknowledge in passing but never aloud.

Now, they spilled freely, easily, like rain softened the earth and made life bloom. Not because he owed anything to Phainon but simply because Mydei wanted him to know.

When he pulled away it was to murmur against his reddened lips, “Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, I lied.”

Phainon’s eyes widened with a thousand questions and the faith that Mydei would answer. Too enraptured to look away.

“Half my honour, half my life, half my soul. It’s more than half.” Mydei laughed at his own past foolishness. To think it would only ever be half. “All of it—all of me is in your hands. Always.”

The past, the present, the future. Beyond something Mydei could ever hope to comprehend but knowing all he needed to ensure Phainon grant his selfish wish.

From the Sea of Souls, to the wheat fields, to the wilds of Amphoreus, to the Dawn of tomorrow. The memories had been engraved into Mydei’s soul and he could only hope to press every word, every touch, every memory even deeper. So deep it could never be removed and Mydei would always remember Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.

Chapter End Notes

And they all lived happily ever after forever. The end.

Thank you everyone who read to the end my self-indulgent fic about Mydei saving his friends and falling in love and getting a chance to fully experience love and happiness.

This was my first multi chapter fic and it go wildly out of hand but I enjoyed every moment of carving this little world out. I’m exceedingly happy with how it turned out.

If you’re curious about how out of hand it got this is the comparison with the first draft because I still look at this and laugh and know I

always will

I’m honestly sad it’s over. But alas all things must come to an end and this fic was never about the flame chase etc. I do have a couple ideas for extra stories in the same setting but I’m not gonna promise anything because I am both sad but also a bit burnt out from this fic.

Anyway, I was overwhelmed by the support for this fic. Especially from all my lovely regular commenters (you know who you guys are). It made such a difference to my motivation to get this fic out as quickly as possible.

So everyone, thank you so much! I hope you all enjoyed reading as much as I enjoyed writing it!!

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Extra Story One - Family Dinner
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon’s two families come together for the very first time over dinner.

Chapter Notes

Jumpscare POV switch to Phainon!

The very first time I’ve written Phainon’s POV without making him suffer immensely. Hurray!

It was strange to once again have a place to call home. As a child, Phainon never thought he would be without one. Life was contained to Aedes Elysiae: the golden wheat fields he would sow and harvest alongside his parents, the sea he would fish from with the other villagers and his friends, the small wooden house warmed by one hearth the four of them would gather around forever.

Even once Phainon grew a little older and the world expanded beyond the reaches of the wheat fields through Cyrene’s stories and the weathered treasures washed upon the shore, he always believed Aedes Elysiae would be home.

He could outgrow his childhood house, get married, have children of his own. He could venture into the world of heroes immortalised in song, the starry sky and people’s hearts. He could leave his small village for Castrum Kremnos and train to be the warrior that could protect those he cared for and fulfil their wishes.

But his heart would always belong in Aedes Elysiae. The place he could always return to.

Until it was consumed by the black tide and black-robed swordsman. Those peaceful days were destroyed, twisted into monstrous affronts to nature and burned to bloodstained ashes.

Yet his unmoored heart was given new direction. Perhaps, if Phainon had followed what remained of his friends and family six years ago, Okhema would have become as close to a new home as he would have found in his lifetime.

Instead a boy arrived in the wheat fields and heralded the arrival of the wider world. Six years of wandering, never settled, never stagnant, always on the move towards something just beyond the horizon, and Phainon found home. One with shields for walls, impenetrable when stood together. Fire pits for hearths, dug in the evening and covered in the early mornings. Foundations embedded in the people, moving and shaking but never crumbling.

At one point, Phainon may have considered that first meeting fate but now he knew better. Mydei had entrusted the truth to him. The truth of this future he had guided them towards: small back grown broad to shoulder his burdens, wreathed in the dawn only he could see until the moment it rose to envelop them all.

So Phainon had long outgrown the need to have a house to feel at home. If Mydei decided the weight of kingship in all but name was too great for him, then Phainon would be the one to pack their belongings and carry them through Okhema’s gates as they returned to a life of self-imposed exile together.

But he wouldn’t deny there was a comfort to that old idea of home. A nostalgia when he opened the front door, footsteps ringing with a wind chime echoing the sound of his childhood alongside the words from his lips:

Mum, dad, I’m home.

Their house in Okhema was larger than his childhood home in Aedes Elysiae. It had a small but proper courtyard to spend time in the open-air

with privacy. A bathroom connected to the city’s aqueducts. An andron with more than one kline so his parents could entertain guests, and a large kitchen to match their hospitality.

As a student enrolled in the Grove of Epiphany, his lodgings and meals were provided. It was the house he spent the most time residing in due to the demands of his studies, yet it was a mere empty shell he was forced to occupy. It was always the streets of Okhema he ran back to at the slightest free time in his schedule.

Here, the aroma of his mum’s cooking had been changed by time and the ingredients available. But it still waved away the fog of his memories, returning him to those simple days, enveloping him in the warmth of a life that didn’t truly know peace because it didn’t yet know strife.

Except now he entered the kitchen without any chastisement from his mum to remember to at least wash his hands before attempting to thieve food ahead of mealtime. It was routine when he cleansed his hands, glanced at the ingredients waiting to be prepared, and took up a suitable knife.

Today was an important day. A wariness flitted across his mum’s face but she didn’t object when Phainon began to carve into the raw catfish. This would be the first time they cooked together in the two months since Phainon first arrived in Okhema alongside the Kremnoan detachment. All she knew was the child who refused to touch raw meat and crafted barely edible salads.

Phainon laughed away her anxieties. “You worry too much. I may not have had easy access to a kitchen per se but you learn to make do with what you have.”

A crease of skepticism at the corner of her eyes but it eased as he nimbly sliced through the fins and cut cleanly around the head in preparation to remove it later. For now, he kept it for a better grip as he worked to remove the skin. Familiarity in every pass of the blade, feeling the memory of scorching hot palms cupping the back of his hands. A chest pressed against his back rumbling with the evidence of the voice low in his ear.

His cheeks warmed with blood and the ache of his sudden grin. He cleared his throat and blinked twice, shaking off the ghost of sensation before he lost a finger to distraction and his mum never trusted him with a knife again. “I also happened to have a good teacher.”

“Ah.” He didn’t look up, sliding the knife just under the skin to take as little flesh as possible with it, but she did nothing to mask the smile in the high lilt of her voice. “Would that be one of the friends we’re meeting today, or your betrothed?”

The knife slipped. No longer a clean strip of tough skin as he sheared a deep chunk of meat with it and he could hear Mydei’s disapproval at the lifted scraps. He squeaked wordlessly as any composure he previously regained vanished, a rock throwing ripples across still waters.

She tittered behind her fingertips. “Is there a need to be embarrassed? Is that not what you are? Betro-“

“Stop,” he wailed and withdrew the knife before he could butcher the fish entirely. Mydei would know it was him with one experienced eye.

If he had been chopping anything other than raw fish he would have dropped his head into his hands. All he could do was tuck his chin against his collarbone as he slumped to rest on his hands splayed across the countertop.

Betrothal. The intent to be wed, one day. An inevitability.

The idea that Mydei wanted that future—something utterly definitive, fixed in ink and blood, when everything between them had been nurtured in their transient lifestyle gallivanting the wilds of Amphoreus—with Phainon was almost unbelievable. It was something Phainon had never even contemplated when every day, every moment, was spent basking in Mydei’s presence coloured like the warmest dawn leading him into pleasant dreams.

This dream Mydei had fought so hard to ensure was their future. Alone, even when Phainon thought he was at Mydei’s side, his back, with every step.

A cool touch grazed his cheek. Although he was accustomed to a warm palm others and the cold itself flinched from, he leaned into the gentle hold on instinct, tilting his head to meet his mum’s eye.

She brushed her thumb along his cheekbone. “Oh dear, I recognise that look on my Little Snowy. You’re all grown up but you still make the same face when you get lost in your thoughts.”

He huffed a weak laugh and nuzzled into the soothing touch. “Am I that obvious?”

“You’ve always opened your heart to the world. It’s not a bad thing.”

Content, Phainon hummed. Every reminder that six years away from his parents hadn’t changed him beyond recognition was a relief. “Mydei says the same thing.”

Not exactly. He was every bit the stray cat Phainon first thought him as upon their initial meeting. Every affectionate lick or cuddle was accompanied by the flash of claws and fangs.

Earnest to a foolish fault, Mydei had called him. Too soft and sweet to be a genuine insult, not when Mydei finished, so someone will have to stay by your side to stymie that bleeding heart of yours.

She took her hand back, Phainon letting it go with only the slightest noise of protest, and shook her head as she grabbed a new knife to finely slice the cabbage. “That’s because Mydei has a sharp eye and sharper mind. I couldn’t have picked a better husband for you.”

Phainon poked the hilt of his knife, more fearful of any potential missteps with the short blade than he felt when loosed upon the battlefield with a greatsword in hand. “Back to that again?”

“Happiness begins in the home.”

He successfully withheld a flinch in all but the upward jolt of his head, eyes wide. “I am happy. Elated. The sight of Mydei—no, just the thought of him

—makes my heart sing praises to Mnestia for blessing humanity with concepts of love and beauty.”

Did he give off the impression otherwise? If there was even the slightest hint that he was displeased with the current state of his life then Mydei would know. He would have picked it up with the speedy precision of hunting hounds scenting blood. These were the types of things he knew about Phainon before he even realised it himself.

“The only thing I have to despair over is that our responsibilities keep us more separate than we’ve been since we first became companions.”

Which was no secret. Phainon whined about their long periods of separation, head propped on Mydei’s chest and Mydei’s bare hands running through his hair, whenever their busy schedules permitted them a moment of true privacy. A tricky task considering Phainon’s commitment to lectures and classes at the Grove while Mydei was confined to Okhema, particularly the barracks along the outskirts housing the rest of the detachment.

He dragged his finger back and forth along the countertop and quietly admitted, “I simply hadn’t prepared for us to… be betrothed so soon.”

Six years. Not of skirting around the love burning steady between them like a well-tended hearth and not the flames of Strife that surrounded them. They simply enjoyed each other’s presence, revelling in the ways in which they already came together with their soft curves and harsh edges while the rest grew around each other with age and shared experience.

Marriage wasn’t something he ever seriously considered. It had only crossed his mind as a child who hadn’t yet considered paths other than the one treaded by those around him: marriage, children, a long and peaceful and happy life.
