He had never truly yearned for anything more than they already were for those six years before Mydei poured more love than Phainon ever thought he deserved past lips and into his heart. As much as Phainon already harboured there for Mydei.

And he still hadn’t thought of marriage. Mydei was the crown prince with the future of his people on his shoulders. Phainon was a village boy who had been lucky enough to have the opportunity to stand at his side, and fought with every breath to prove that offer wasn’t a mistake.

As soon as Mydei confirmed that his words at the end their duel were truly a proposal to be wed, it was all Phainon could think about. He wanted that. He wanted that more than anything. Even if it didn’t come with a house, children, nor a long and peaceful life—it would be a happy one.

He just hadn’t been prepared for how much he wanted it.

He hung his head with a sigh, “Every time I think of us together in that sense, permanent and irrefutable, it reminds me of all the distance forced between us now.”

His eyes squeezed tight. Phainon missed him. He missed Mydei so fiercely his heart ached and every pulse of it carried that yearning down to the tips of his fingers. The simple acts of living—sleeping, breathing, cooking— were plagued by Mydei.

He constantly searched for gold and red in the corner of his eye only to be disappointed when it was someone else, sometimes just a figment of his imagination. They were drawn to each other like rivers to the sea and Phainon had always been more than willing to drown. After so long, every separation felt like a part of himself was missing.

A muffled sound opened his eyes again. A giggle, slipping through his mum’s lip pinned between her teeth even as she continued slicing the cabbage.

Phainon frowned. “This isn’t really a laughing matter.”

She patted his cheek and went back to chopping. “I can see that you two will be very happy together.”

He picked up the knife to resume skinning the catfish. The skin was too tough to eat and Mydei wrinkled his nose if any of the muddy flavour

remained. Phainon was certain Mydei wasn’t aware that his nose wrinkled whenever he smelled or tasted something unpleasant. It always filled Phainon with the urge to kiss the tip of his nose.

He smiled to himself as he imagined that peck and the way Mydei’s nose would only crease more but he would never pull away. “There is no one else.”

His feet had carried him to every corner of Amphoreus but even if he had stayed forever in Aedes Elysiae, taken Mydei home like a stray from the wheat fields, kept as a house cat without the need to grow into a lion, the truth would be unchanged: there was no one else anywhere in Amphoreus. It could only be Mydei.

The gentle smile Phainon had first learned from his mum, one she wore for him and his dad and Snowy, was reflected back at him now. “Then let me thank the man who makes my son happier than I’ve ever seen him. And even taught him how to feed himself for a change.”

Not just himself, but everyone he cared about. After all, this was the day his parents would be officially introduced to those Mydei considered family.

With all the skills and care handed to him over the years, he helped prepare every dish alongside his mum, his dad who returned to the marketplace, and Snowy who snuck scraps, as the day passed through the ends of Entry Hour to the beginning of Descent Hour.

His parents had made it clear that their home was Phainon and Mydei’s home, so there was no need for either of them to knock before they entered. Mydei was always sure to knock anyway. While his parents finished setting up the andron, Snowy followed on Phainon’s heels to welcome their guests.

At the front was Mydei. Dressed in a white chiton loose around his chest and thighs but cinched tight around his waist with the belt taken from his usual outfit. The black and gold emphasised the trim cut of his waist while a swathe of red embroidered in gold draped over his shoulder.

It was a gift from Agalea after too many complaints through the golden threads of Phainon occupying his hands throughout his sparse time in Okhema by clinging to Mydei’s side and laying them over his half-exposed chest. It was an attempt to hide Mydei from the gawking civilians, lacking the detachment’s cultural laxity towards clothing and desensitisation to bare skin.

The material was expensive. Tailored to fall loose enough to expose that red tattoo of Strife where Gorgo’s ring rested on its chain, teasing the top of his chest with an invitation for Phainon to slip his hand right under, but tight enough to prevent any flowing fabric from hindering his movements. Yet Phainon could have sworn he saw the vibrant red of his markings—heated blood. The colour of passions: both war and love—showing through the white. Another tease.

The cross of Mydei’s arms, fabric pulled tauter across the expanse of his chest, didn’t help. He cleared his throat and Phainon swallowed, eyes drifting up past ring, then the gold and blue of his necklace, to meet that amused gaze beneath an arched brow. His hair was brushed and his usual braid interlaced with golden chains and blue jewels.

“Hi,” Phainon croaked.

Mydei’s lip curled into a smirk as he assessed Phainon from his usual unkempt hair to his simple, short tunic. “Hi.”

Then he looped a hand around the back of Phainon’s neck and tugged him into a kiss. At the first press of their lips—soft, tacky with something vaguely sweet—Phainon forgot where he was and why.

He slid his arm around Mydei’s waist, not to pull him close but just to hold him, and returned all the affection Mydei bestowed him so freely. The most precious gift. Invaluable, irreplaceable. Yet Phainon always found himself so hungry for more. And he knew Mydei would indulged him because, in this, they were still equals. Equally greedy.

It made the world beyond the soft fabric and hard muscle beneath his hands, the fragrance of pomegranate hazing his mind, and hot breath against his

lips—everything simply disappeared.

And come back with the sharp clear of someone’s throat.

Mydei pulled away just enough to tip his head back over his own shoulder, still clutching to Phainon’s neck with one hand while the other wound under Phainon’s arm. Phainon peered over his other shoulder.

Their five friends stared back at them. Well, Ptolemy had turned away with a bashful smile tilting the one edge of his lip Phainon was privy to. Perdikkas had a hand sealed over Leonnius’ mouth but Phainon could imagine the incoming whistle or crass comment based on the crease of his eyes alone. There was a glaze to Peucesta’s eyes, a look that only arose when his thoughts drifted to poetry and lyricism.

The slight curl to Hephaestion’s lips was amused even as he raised the ceramic amphora in his hands. “Is now the time for you to invite the rest of us inside?”

Phainon counted heads and his brows furrowed. “No Krateros?”

Mydei released him, lips glossy with whatever Phainon had tasted on them, and patted his chest on his way past. “We settled on one mouth for them to feed for every year we fed you.”

A few chuckles arose from the others as Phainon finally shuffled out the doorway to let them inside.

Although Mydei played it off with humour, the true meaning behind the absence of Mydei’s sour-faced, strict teacher was obvious: no need to overwhelm Audata and Hieronymus to that extent. Although his parents had hidden their nerves well, Phainon’s perception was honed on the battlefield where even the slightest of movements in his enemies differentiated life from death.

His mum had been more frantic as she obsessed over the exact flavour every dish, which hadn’t paired well with his dad fumbling like he had never watched water boil over the fire before. They were so nervous it

almost infected Phainon, but the only reason his hands had to tremble was sheer eagerness to see Mydei again after ten long days without him.

While Mydei had marched ahead at the entryway, he waited patiently beside the doorway to the andron. Out of sight so Phainon could take his hand— bare. Adorned with rings both thick and thin. A decorative vambrace down each wrist—and lead the way into the room.

His mum jumped from one of the kline’s arranged in a half circle, table laden with food between them, and hurried over to wrap Mydei in her arms. “Mydei, how are you?”

From the side, Phainon blinked as Mydei only rumbled a laugh and returned the embrace as though it were natural, replying with a light jest, “Lured in by the aroma of your cooking.” He stepped back, Phainon taking his mum’s place by slinging his arm around Mydei, and motioned behind him. “These are my companions.”

Hieronymus rose to join them. “Hello, Phainon tells us you watched over him during your travels.”

“I’m certain there are many stories he’s yet to tell you,” Hephaestion said with a bright smile and Phainon felt a shudder pass through him. He offered the amphora. “We prepared honey brew for the occasion. Thank you for welcoming us into your home despite all the troubling rumours.”

Hieronymus took the amphora with a light laugh. “You must be Hephaestion. As for those baseless rumours, everyone from Aedes Elysiae who stands here now thanks to the Kremnoan detachment knows not to heed any of them.”

“Cast them from your mind,” Audata reassured them, “as we do. And finish introducing yourselves.”

Alongside their introductions, there were other gifts they presented as gifts for his parents’ hospitality. A basket of figs and plums, a jar of honey, a bolt of silk, and meat carved from spit-roasted pig prepared and cooked by Mydei’s own hand.

“This is very generous of you,” Audata said with a furtive glance between the gifts in her arms and across the table. “We’re grateful but there was no need to trouble yourself.”

“Nonsense. This much is nothing,” Ptolemy insisted with a dismissive flap of his hand. “After all, Phainon would never have come into our lives if not for you.”

“Then where would our dear Mydeimos be,” Leonnius said, so exaggeratedly mournful Phainon was surprised he didn’t have tears to accompany it.

“Besides, we never gave you our proper thanks for welcoming Mydei into your home all those years ago,” Hephaestion delivered what should have been a killing blow with that suave smile and tuck of his hair behind his ear.

Audata only shook her head, exasperated as she struggled to string the words together, “When we welcomed Mydei into our home… and all of you now, we—we never intended to treat you as guests.”

The lax air around them shifted into something sharper. An old instinct that prickled at any violation of hospitality, a warrior’s hand always ready to draw their weapon at the slightest sense of danger. Experience had prepared them for the worst when the safety promised between a guest and host collapsed.

It was usually around the time soldiers surrounded them with blades poised to maim for ransom or simply kill and be rid of the Kremnoan scourge blighting Amphoreus.

Not that his parents could sense their sudden discomfort, the five of them searching for reassurance in Mydei. Who appeared unthreatened but equally confused, glancing from Audata to Phainon. He subtly shook his head, just as clueless.

But Peucesta’s voice rose above the unease, “There’s no need to mark debts amongst family.”

Everyone held their breath for a different reason as Peucesta’s word fell, weighty, upon them.

A smile brightened Audata’s face. “Yes! Exactly! Thank you, Peucesta. Phainon was right when he told us you have a way with words.”

Peucesta returned her smile with a small one of his own. “I see where Phainon learned his own earnest words from.”

“And his lovely smile,” Hieronymus added with an enamoured grin of his own towards his wife.

Audata swatted at him. “And you gave him your shamelessness.”

“Lucky him,” Leonnius chirped, once again relaxed as he teased Phainon with a particularly pointed grin. “He may not have caught Mydei’s eyes without it. Did he ever regale you with the tale of how we first met?”

Perdikkas snickered and Phainon flushed as both his parents looked at him, curious for the bait Leonnius dangled before them. Phainon’s wide eyes silently pleaded with Mydei but he snorted, squeezed Phainon’s wrist draped over his shoulder and remained otherwise silent.

“Not that one, no.” Hieronymus motioned to the klines. “How about we discuss it over our meal? The food’s getting cold.”

“Phainon, get changed into something more pleasant,” his mum ordered with a dismissive wave of her hand out the room.

He frowned down at his clothes. It was a tunic: simple but hardly something to till the fields in. There was nothing wrong with his clothes. If anything, a simple glance around the tool confirmed Phainon fit right in. The only person who stood out was Mydei. Not that he would complain about getting to see Mydei overdressed.

Mydei huffed a laugh. “I’ll lend a hand before you offend our eyes.”

Across the room getting comfortable on a kline, Leonnius’ mouth opened but Phainon interrupted him with an accusatory jab of his finger, “Not in

front of my parents!”

Leonnius’ mouth slowly closed. Then opened again with an overly pleasant smile and tone, “The first time we met, your son drew his blade on me and accused me of being deviant.”

Phainon dropped his head against Mydei’s shoulder and whined, “Mydei, I’m being persecuted by our friends.”

“As the only other witness to this event, I can attest that this is exactly what you did.” Mydei mercilessly left him for dead even as he petted his hair.

Phainon lifted his head with a prominent pout, the kind that tempted Mydei to kiss it from his lips if only they were somewhere more private. “Well, I refuse to stand here and be subjected to it.”

His hand casually slung over Mydei’s shoulder crept across to rest over his collarbone. Phainon was almost entirely draped over him and something preened in the back of his mind at the possessive hold Mydei only leaned into. His grip tightened so he could haul Mydei backwards out the room with him and he wished they could walk through Okhema the same way.

“I told you I would come with you. Cease your tugging,” Mydei demanded but didn’t struggle as they exited into the courtyard.

Phainon hummed, feeling it pass from his chest through Mydei’s body and into Phainon’s hand on the other side. “More delicate treatment requires a fee.”

Mydei scoffed. “What an inattentive lover.”

“Bold words after you so mercilessly abandoned me to the mercy of our companions.”

“I never claimed to be any better.”

Any insult to Mydei, even in the soothing cadence of Mydei’s own voice, blazed through him like sparks in summer fields parched by drought. Almost lightheaded as he seethed on instinct, exhaling smoke and not air.

Everyone in the Grove knew better than to speak ill of Mydei or anything Kremnoan in front of him: he returned their ignorance with hours of lectures, and accompanying notes delivered to their hands the following day. Anaxa always rolled his eyes at Phainon’s essays for class and scolded him for not using even a fraction of the efforts he spent on his extracurricular debates.

He bit his tongue before he could habitually jump to defend Mydei against his own words. Instead he angled his head upwards and watched Mydei’s gaze, kept steadfastly ahead, flit down to his beseeching eyes. Lower, to his lips.

“Again?” Mydei asked, exasperated but only in that usual push and pull for a question he already knew the answer to.

“We were interrupted earlier.”

“Yet you had more than enough,” Mydei dismissed even as he leaned almost imperceptibly closer.

Phainon licked his lips. “Quite the opposite, I haven’t had my fill yet.”

“There’s plenty of real food if you would stop with the delays.” Mydei was so close, breath hot against Phainon’s upper lip.

Close enough he gazed up through lowered lashes. “That won’t be enough to sate me. I only want you, Mydei.”

The very corner of Mydei’s lip curled, not quite a smile nor a smirk. Something in between and wholly satisfied. A taunt that itched Phainon’s mind and he responded by kissing it from his lips. That hand draped over his chest reached up to grip Mydei’s chin, angling Mydei’s neck into a more comfortable position where Phainon rose from his slouch to meet him.

Just a taste. A quick flick of his tongue along Mydei’s bottom lip.

Phainon pulled away before Mydei could shove him off and scold him for something too indecent in his parents’ home. He slid his arm down to

Mydei’s waist and sidled up next to him so they could walk to his room.

The taste lingered in his mouth and he licked the roof of his mouth. “What’s on your lips?”

“Nothing now that you licked it all off like a slobbering dog.”

Phainon smiled. “Then I’ll put more on for you, so what was it?”

He huffed but answered, “A concoction of beeswax, honey and olive oil.”

He squinted at Mydei’s lips. With the balm removed and Phainon’s saliva cooling, they had lost their lustre, but that wasn’t the only difference. “Did that concoction also contain a pigment?”

Mydei’s expression remained unchanged but the very tips of his ears coloured, stark against both light and dark tones of his hair. “A slight one.”

So slight Phainon had failed to notice, too enthralled by the rest of Mydei’s decadent appearance belonging to a crown prince rather than a warrior if not for those indisputable muscles. But now he could see where the colour had rubbed off with the balm, except for the smear at the corner of Mydei’s lip.

When Phainon’s bedroom door closed and Mydei scanned the room from the kline on one side to the shuttered window on the other, Phainon took the opportunity to lean in and lick the remainder of the pink clean.

“You—“ Mydei spluttered and shoved his face away. “Insatiable mutt.”

Phainon licked his lips again, knowing Mydei felt the edge of Phainon’s tongue graze against his palm when he shoved his face even further away before letting go.

“Have you considered a bolder colour? Bright red would suit you.”

As vivid as his markings. So that it would stain Phainon’s own lips with the same smear of colour. Matching, as Mydei left kisses across his cheeks, down his neck and arms. Against every bit of exposed skin he could find.

The outfit Aglaea had prepared for The Deliverer was modest even by Okheman standards but he could always forgo the long white coat if it meant wearing the shape of Mydei’s mouth like a brand instead.

Or maybe Phainon could paint his lips and add his own markings to Mydei’s body.

Mydei scowled, as though he had pried Phainon’s brain open and witnessed the thoughts fly through unfettered. “You speak as though you don’t have a brain. And here I thought you were averse to sharing.”

Phainon’s brows furrowed. “What does sharing have to do with this? Isn’t it quite the opposite?”

The long-suffering look on Mydei’s face was so judgemental Phainon joined him to question his own intelligence in the brief moment before Mydei alleviated him of his misery.

“How can your mind be so innocent and still so…” His nose scrunched. Phainon imagined a peck that tinted it red. “Perverted. Next time you walk past one of this city’s brothels, take a note of the colour they wear on their lips.”

Phainon tilted his head, forehead ceasing as he tried to recall something he paid such little attention to it was barely even a passing memory. Nothing. But he had enough mental acuity to deduce from Mydei’s unimpressed look.

“Ah.”

“Now cease with the delays and change into something more presentable.”

“What’s wrong with this outfit?” Phainon despaired with another glance down and over his shoulder down his back.

“Nothing,” Mydei reassured him despite reaching for the belt. “It’s presentable. The colours don’t hurt my eyes.”

“It was one time.”

One time Phainon had ignored Mydei’s dissuasions and attempted to wear both yellow and purple in tandem. Ptolemy had sprayed the honey brew from his mouth while Leonnius cackled. The next morning, Peucesta had silently handed Phainon a full set of clothes with both pain and pity in his eyes.

Mydei plucked the fastening from shoulder; nothing to stop the fabric from sloughing off Phainon’s body and leave him bare. “But consider that this dinner is… as much about us as the meetings between our families. Perhaps more.”

All along, Phainon had considered this dinner to revolve around everyone except for him and Mydei. They were the only two people in the room who knew everyone by more than name and second-hand experiences retold with nostalgia.

So he had forgotten why Mydei’s five companions, more family than friends, and Phainon’s parents were meeting at all.

Phainon frowned at his own foolishness. “You’re right.”

“Fine words to remember,” Mydei agreed as he opened the wooden chest beside the full-length silver mirror.

From it, he retrieved one of the white chitons embroidered with golden vines and laurel leaves, alongside a blue swathe of fabric, both gifted by Aglaea. While Phainon may have struggled when he first arrived in Okhema, he had quickly grown comfortable with the long finery far removed from life in a farming village or self-exile. There was no reason he couldn’t dress himself.

But he didn’t object when Mydei raised the fabric over his head, only stooping low so Mydei could ensure the layers fell correctly when he let go. Mydei fixed the chiton and blue decorative chlamys into place with a golden pin shaped like the sun, and cinched Phainon’s waist with a gold belt adorned with a blue jewel.

Then he swept Phainon’s discarded tunic across the thin layer of dust atop the rarely used jewellery box. He cast an assessing eye over Phainon, stood exactly where Mydei had left him, before retrieving the pieces he thought best.

An armlet that, like Mydei’s own, emphasised the size of Phainon’s bicep trained to lift his greatsword, but paired it with daintier bangles than Mydei’s vambraces. No rings and no necklaces. But he clipped a single earring into place: gold and a red jewel.

Mydei stepped back to admire his work and Phainon twirled to help him.

Although he still complained, “This feels slightly excessive.”

Mydei arched a brow and gestured a hand down his own conspicuously decorated body. “Is it now? Before you answer, recall those fine words from earlier.”

“You’re right.”

He hummed approvingly. “I am.”

“But you are aware my parents have no particular investments in seeing me the lover of a wealthy prince?”

Mydei crossed his arms but stared Phainon right in the eye, unblinking and unflinching as he answered, “Of course.”

Which meant he was lying.

But Phainon’s heart only swelled. How could it not when Mydei made himself look so gorgeous every person of age would beg for the chance to kiss his feet let alone be betrothed. And he did it because he still felt the need to make a good impression on his parents. Two people whose affections had begun when Mydei was just a scrawny, unkempt child Phainon had brought home by the hand.

It was so endearing, Phainon couldn’t contain his grin. “Mydei, my parents were content for me to join you in exile if it made me happy.”

Mydei blinked slowly, working hard to keep an indifferent, implacable mask in place. Flawless if not for the smallest crease of his nose.

Phainon tangled their fingers together and left a small kiss on the tip of his nose, watching it scrunch more and compel him to leave another. Then he took one of their joined hands and pressed it against his chest.

“I mean it, Mydei,” Phainon murmured. “The only thing you ever have to bring home is you.”

Mydei rested their foreheads together, eyes like the dawn burning through Phainon to brand him from the inside out. “I’ll take you at your word.”

A short kiss. Chaste and sweet even when there was no more honey on Mydei’s lips. Phainon’s eyes fluttered half open and he parted his lips to ask for another one.

He choked on the request when Mydei hooked a finger in his collar, turned and pulled.

“Enough stalling. You would need to hide here for months before the others run out of your embarrassing stories.”

Phainon chuckled bashfully as he stumbled after Mydei, leading him around by the leather collar buckled by the symbol of Strife. “You noticed?”

“You’re far from subtle.”

“Speaking of. When were you going to tell me that you visit my parents’ house when I’m not around?”

That was the only explanation for the ease with which his mum and Mydei had hugged in greeting earlier. Casual, as though they had done it any number of times.

“I came for dinner a few times in the past,” Mydei said nonchalantly.

Phainon pouted. “You see my parents more than you see me. I used to see you every hour of every day and now I’m lucky to see you for a few hours a

week. I’m deprived, Mydei!”

He rolled his eyes at this old bout of whining. But Phainon meant it as much as the first, second and thirtieth time!

“If you’re so desperate to see me daily then graduate sooner and return to Okhema.”

Apart from removing himself from the student roll, it was the easiest solution when Mydei was prevented from enrolling due to the political optics. It would only splinter his relationship with certain sections of the detachment who would see an Okheman education as indoctrination and a betrayal.

Unfortunately, as brilliant as Phainon was, it wasn’t so easy to accomplish. He sighed, “Anaxa knows my intentions and has chosen to prolong my torture.”

Mydei snorted. “Torture? Have you attempted becoming a better student?”

Just as Mydei crossed the threshold of Phainon’s bedroom and into the light of the courtyard, Phainon snagged his wrist and they paused. Gaze lowered to the floor, his grip tightened and Mydei silently waited, head tilted back over his shoulder where sunlight glinted off his earring.

Phainon worked his jaw before he admitted weakly, “I miss you.” And the rest of the words broke free. “I miss you so much, Mydei. All of the time. Just the thought of you makes my heart ache.”

It was unbearable. Phainon would rather fight a thousand of Strife’s Titankin than be separated another week. He laid in his empty dormitory and sought comfort in the memory of steady breathing on the opposite end of a military tent. Then the warmth of a body snuggled close to him, which he had only gotten to enjoy in full so briefly before they arrived in Okhema.

In the safety of the Grove of Epiphany, now another student who learned about the world rather than experience it under their nails and cutting skin,

he longed for the days where he charged into battle and the black tide. It was danger but never dangerous when the two of them were side-by-side because Phainon never once doubted they would overcome everything in their path.

He pushed a hand through his bangs, eyes clenched shut. “I caught your scent on the clothes I met you in two weeks ago and couldn’t bring myself to move for hours, consumed by the last time we were together. I couldn’t sleep that night without them close by, as though they were a substitute for you in my arms.”

A laugh hollowed out by self-deprecation escaped him. Mydei remained silent. No doubt lost for words after such a pathetic admittance.

“Me too.”

Phainon’s eyes opened wide. He didn’t blink, taking in the sight of Mydei glowing radiantly in the eternal daylight, illuminating the flush of his cheeks.

His eyes softened, creasing at the corners like the slightest upturn of his lips. “I miss you too, Phainon. More than words can describe.”

“Oh.” And Phainon laughed again but it was quietly bemused, ghosting down the muscles of Mydei’s back as he slumped his forehead against Mydei’s shoulder. “The two of us are… two halves of the same mess.”

“This should be the easiest of trials we’ve gone through.” Mydei sucked in a harsh inhale. “Yet it feels like the most difficult.”

Phainon laid his agreement in a kiss upon Mydei’s bare skin. “I know we aren’t parting ways forever. But it feels the same as an eternity. I’ve never felt such a temptation to be selfish as when I dream of taking you in my arms and leaving everything else behind.”

“Since when do we flee from our troubles. Unless you’ve chosen to adopt an Okheman mentality,” he teased.

“No,” Phainon replied in a harsher language that scraped the back of his throat, “Kremnoan is a better match. Sometimes, I just wish…”

A hand reached back to pet his hair and he nuzzled his forehead against Mydei’s shoulder as he replied, “I know. It will be easier once everything settles down. You adapt so expertly in battle. You can adapt to this, too.”

“Just…” Phainon dredged a weighty exhale from the depths of his chest. “Come here.”

“Everyone is waiting,” Mydei reminded him but turned without a struggle.

He stepped into Mydei’s awaiting arms, the lines of their bodies merging into one as Phainon slumped entirely against him. He buried his nose in the crook of Mydei’s neck and cradling his hands over Mydei’s single weak spot entrusted to only Phainon.

Warner than the Dawn Device, forges and the hot baths. Sweeter than any of them, scented with honey and pomegranate.

For the first time in weeks, Phainon breathed and Mydei did the same. As though all their anxieties could be so easily expelled within the safety of each other’s arms, where they chose to stay for a little while longer.

By the time they returned to the andron, the conversation had moved on from how hopelessly enamoured Phainon was from the moment he first met Mydei, to the point he drew a sword on Leonnius before fully comprehending the situation. Instead Ptolemy regaled them with the history of a city they had once visited, but which one amongst dozens Phainon wasn’t sure.

Everyone indulged equally in food, honey brew and nostalgia.

From the floor, Hephaestion petted Snowy, half asleep draped over his lap but head popping up when there was a particularly raucous round of laughter. “They made me a very wealthy man when the betting pool finally closed.”

Heaping his dish with a salad mix of cabbage, coriander and rue seasoned with honey vinegar and silphium, Ptolemy clicked his tongue and shook his head. “After six years, you emerged the greatest victor from that fiasco.”

Perdikkas sighed and bemoaned, “What sane man would have guessed they would officially begin courting so shortly after the fall of Castrum Kremnos? And even bet substantial coin on it?”

Hephaestion threw his head back, almost bumping Peucesta’s leg where he lounged on the kline behind him, as he laughed and lifted his chalice. “Mydeimos may act rational and stoic, but he is a man as hot-blooded as any. The rush of long-awaited victory can drive men to do many things. But I must admit, even I was stunned by the speed of your betrothal.”

The others cheered their agreement and raised their chalices.

On the kline reserved for the two of them, Mydei rolled his eyes but lifted his chalice of pomegranate juice and goat’s milk. “If you reveal all your secret insights into my nature, you may find your future winnings shrink.”

He threw his drink back and Phainon leaned forward to pour him another chalice of the his favourite beverage, mixed by Phainon’s own hand to ensure the ratio was just right. While Phainon was there, he scooped more of the olive relish onto both their dishes. When he reclined back, Mydei shuffled into his prior position leaned against Phainon’s side.

“Well someone else here has their own insights,” Ptolemy said and his foot nudged Leonnius’ leg, sharing the same kline.

Leonnius shrugged but the twist of his lips was particularly menacing paired with his scars and narrowed eyes. “Hephaestion said it best. Our dear Mydeimos rarely loses control of himself. Almost every instance is brought about by Phainon. After letting himself loose once, I just knew—ah. Peucesta, how would you say it?”

He thumbed at his lips, cleaning away the grease of the pig meat and smear of soft goat’s cheese, topping the same slice of bread freshly baked by

Audata. “When a man of great restraint indulges once, he continues to indulge as though he lacked restraint all along.”

Leonnius snapped his fingers. “That. So I assumed it would be a brief courtship. Laid to rest by their swift betrothal.”

Phainon blinked at this new information his friend had never told him. “You bet coin on that?”

Leonnius’ grin sharpened. “I made coin on that.”

“The more popular option would be a courtship as drawn out as… whatever it was you were doing for those six years,” Perdikkas sighed, a hand to his head like the mere thought gave him a headache. One he sought to cure with a long sip of his drink.

Mydei’s eyes narrowed and his smile was so overly pleasant it was more terrifying than any stoicism or wild smirk in battle. “Considering how much coin you claim to have won, you must have bet on Phainon’s victory.”

Sensing danger, Leonnius chuckled weakly. He looked to Ptolemy but his friend only glanced away; as the other four did, finding themselves preoccupied by their food and drink or Snowy’s fur.

Leonnius threw back the rest of his honey brew and slammed the chalice down with the fearful grit of a man facing their own death. “It could have been anyone’s victory. I decided on a coin toss. Far from Nikador’s battle-honed senses or even Cerces’ reason, perhaps it was Zagreus who favoured me in that moment.”

The long, low hum from Mydei’s chest betrayed nothing. “I hope the gamble was worth its weight in gold.”

Another weak laugh and Leonnius poured himself a full chalice that disappeared just as quick as the first.

“I heard the poems about your duel but I thought they were exaggerated,” Audata said with awe as she stared at the two of them cuddled together like

two chimeras on the kline.

Hieronymus patted his own thigh. “Our Little Snowy—“ a few knowing looks and sniggers at the nickname but Phainon ate his catfish, flavoured by the fig leaves it was wrapped in as it baked. Face serene, “—has always been stubborn.”

Peucesta nodded. “I composed those poems myself.”

“Oh!” Audata clapped her hands, delighted. “We’ve been told how talented you are with any number of instruments and lyrics.”

“An Okheman writer reached out for collaboration. The songs have spread quicker than anticipated.”

“Not to say all of his compositions are… true to life,” Hephaestion warned her.

Phainon laughed and shared a conspiratorial smile with Mydei. “It’s more interesting that way, no?”

It was the reason Mydei and Phainon had given Peucesta permission, along with this anonymous writer, to interject tales as outlandish as they wished to make them. The more preposterous the better.

Perhaps it was wrong of him as a student of the Grove dedicated to the pursuit of truth and knowledge, but it was so entertaining to witness what people were willing to accept as true when Mydei was a figure larger than life. A warrior born from legends, destined to be immortalised in the stars alongside other great heroes.

The conversation flitted between all kinds of stories as wild as the lands they had been realised in. Each spanned the six years of the detachment’s most triumphant highs and Mydei or Phainon’s own most embarrassing lows.

Five warriors, born and raised for the battlefield, previously unknown to the two farmers who had never held a blade sharper than a kitchen knife or

scythe, and Mydei and Phainon the only familiarities to bridge the two—yet it was so effortless.

Phainon hadn’t even realised he harboured doubts until the disbelief slipped into relief that not even a hint of awkwardness weighted the air, uplifted by carefree laughter and simple conversation. He hadn’t expected anything dramatic to occur, certainly not violent, but oil and water never mixed. Everything from age to past life experiences to the present made the two halves of Phainon and Mydei’s lives so dissimilar they were hardly recognisable as paths through human life.

Yet everything had blended together. Less like oil and water, and more like two separate amphoras of wine poured into one as the fruits and spices blended together into a more delicious flavour and aroma than either could hope to accomplish alone. The type to warm him through entirely with a single sip.

While Phainon offered to whisk Mydei away from Okhema and the Kremnoan detachment to live a life only for themselves, and meant every word of it if Mydei had agreed—he knew Mydei would never abandon his responsibilities. It was outside of his nature: one that cared too deeply for the people who turned to him, gazing at his back for inspiration and reassurance of the future, to ever betray the hopes entrusted to him.

Besides, that was simply a quiet, selfish wish. This life was infinitely better. More than a wish, it was dream too wonderful to even dare to wish for. And was now safely within their joined hands that would never let go.

Dinner ended with a dessert of honey pancakes, served alongside a platter of the gifed figs and plums. Action Hour was slowly coming to an end, Snowy fully succumbed to slumber on the rug beneath the central table, but Peucesta asked if Audata and Hieronymus would like to hear a song. At their enthusiastic agreements, the plucked strings and trilling voice of Peucesta resonated through the room.

After one full song to admire Peucesta’s craft, Leonnius requested another for the rest of them to join him. Since Phainon’s parents knew no

Kremnoan, Peucesta selected one of the recent popular songs in Okhema: a tale of Mydei and Phainon’s exploits told in common tongue.

While everyone joined along, eyes distracted away from Phainon and Mydei, he placed a kiss against Mydei’s temple and dragged his lips down the shell of his ear. “How are you?”

Although Mydei abstained from alcohol, his cheeks were flushed with the warmth of the room and his eyes dazed with unadulterated joy, he almost appeared intoxicated when he nuzzled further into Phainon’s side.

“Disappointed,” Mydei said. Phainon blinked, lips parting wordlessly now that his scripted reply was inapplicable. “You made a mistake skinning the catfish.”

With the voices of their family singing, Mydei’s words almost snuck free from Phainon’s mind but he replayed them to the rhythm of the ballad.

He slumped his head and laughed into Mydei’s hair. “Apologies. I became distracted.”

“What have I told you about distractions?”

Phainon’s heart swelled so large he struggled to breathe through his overwhelming affection with no where to go but he swept Mydei into his arms, pulling him onto his lap, so it might pass through Phainon’s skin and settle beneath Mydei’s own.

“They belong in neither the battlefield nor the kitchen.”

Mydei tucked his head under Phainon’s chin, words brushing down Phainon’s neck to warm the metal mark of Strife. “So what exactly did you let yourself be distracted by.”

“What else but the same as always: my beautiful husband-to-be,” he practically purred in Mydei’s ear, lips and voice brushing the skin.

It was directly in front of his eyes and he watched the blood flow upwards, tinting the very tips. Phainon tucked the hair back to expose the reaction in

full and Mydei swayed to bump against him chastising but didn’t shrug him off. His ear was almost as red as his hair. Phainon wanted to bite it.

Mydei cleared his throat. “It appears you’re still in need of more lessons.”

“Or someone who will feed someone as hopeless as myself,” Phainon countered with a pretty flutter of his lashes.

“Lessons it is,” Mydei said flatly. “Until you are no longer so helpless.”

“What if my stringent teacher never deems me acceptable? My lessons will continue?”

“I expect nothing less.” It was almost scathing but the way Mydei peered at him through his lashes, lips tugged to bare teeth in a wild grin…

And Phainon smiled. “For the rest of our lives, Mydei?”

“For the rest of our lives, Phainon.”

Chapter End Notes

I am back in this verse and they make so so happy!!

I debated having the extras match the main story and be in Mydei’s POV buuuut one of my extra story ideas doesn’t really work unless it’s Phainon POV. And I’m an all or nothing type of person.

So enjoy these opportunities to read how pathetically down bad Phainon is (which will likely have to wait until after PhaiDei week because I need to actually finish prepping for that sorry).

I wasn’t sure whether to post the extras as a separate thing or not. But I figured it would be easier for people who want to read them to find it here than anywhere else.

And yes the “anonymous writer” is Castorice. Her and Peucesta are bonding over their love of PhaiDei fanfiction.

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Extra Story 2 - Honourable Words
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and the Kremnoan detachment are tasked with an excursion against the black tide.

Phainon is the last person to find out.

Chapter Notes

Remember everyone: Communication is key in all relationships— romantic or otherwise.

Ordinary life revolved around nature’s rhythms. There was reassurance in the celestial bodies that told them when to eat, work, sleep; and the changing seasons that dictated what type of work they performed in cycles of sowing and harvesting, peace and strife, work and rest.

Even once Phainon’s life expanded beyond fields to be tilled, planted and harvested along the beat of nature’s dance, life in the Kremnoan detachment wasn’t so different. They marched great distances, confronted armies, and sieged cities from spring to autumn. In winter, the detachment settled down like beasts hibernating through the cold conditions least suitable to their transitory lifestyle, and lurked in wait for the snow to thaw and the hunt to resume.

Although the last bastion of humanity as Amphoreus crumbled, disfigured by the black tide into something indistinguishable from the wild days of Phainon’s adolescence, Kephale’s blessing made Okhema exempt from much the Titans’ natural laws. Warm days and clear skies blended together into one eternal day on the cusp of spring becoming summer.

But life in the Grove of Epiphany was an entirely different existence. Day and night blended together as Phainon was crammed into the libraries,

studies and research laboratories with nothing but oil lamps to illuminate the miserly gloom. The one boundary preventing them from completely merging was his class schedule.

The seasons were even more indistinct. The leaves sheltering the Grove from wind and rain never changed their verdant hues, as evergreen as Cerces’ knowledge nurturing humanity.

Four months into Phainon’s student life and he was finally given a proper break. Something related to Cerces absconding with Mnestia for two weeks in order to personally understand the Romance espoused by the Titan. But the reason was of little importance. What was of utmost important was that he had two whole weeks with no classes, no field trips, no research studies.

One final, blunt reminder from Anaxa that he would not be available for any questions, no matter how dire they were perceived to be, and Phainon was free. He sprinted from his seat with a quick farewell to his disgruntled professor and straight to the dromas stable.

None of his fellow students nor professors attempted to stop him. Sightings of a white blur dashing through the Grove had become commonplace in the past months, so the others watched with amusement, encouraging cheers, and some slight concern when he leapt down a few levels rather than follow the tree’s inner spiral. It was less than a day’s ride to the Holy City. There wasn’t a moment to waste. He wanted to make the most of his two weeks.

Two weeks. Such a thing used to mean little to him. Days in the detachment passed much the same, stretching into weeks, months, years. But it was far from a dull monotony.

Morning meant hurrying to meet Mydei in his private tent or by the cooking fire pits, until he eventually claimed one half of Mydei’s tent as his own and they greeted the day together. Midday meant sparring, hunting or any other competition to be had with Mydei and the others. If they were on the move then it meant marching to the beat of a rowdy song that carried them forward.

Evenings were the time to settle into camp, bathe in local waters, and prepare dinner at the campfires where they gathered for food and honey brew, song and dance, laughter and good company. The clamour lasted until the moon was high in the sky, bidding them to crawl into their sleeping cots in preparation for a day that would be just the same as the one passed.

Now the thought of two weeks was enough to make his heart race; tight in his chest but so light he feared how easily it would be crushed when those two weeks came to an end and he was forced to return to the Grove.

It was certainly a more luxurious life, less physically demanding, than he was used to: he didn’t have to catch and clean his own meals, his bedding was softer than thin cots on hard ground, he was never required to wield a weapon. But those were never things he disliked about life in a farming village and the wandering wilds. They were enjoyable in their own way. He could understand the merits of either lifestyle, and why some were more suited to one than the other.

What vexed him more than anything else was the separation. If he spent two weeks with Mydei—his betrothed. The title alone made him giddy, lightheaded, and was often the cause of others catching him laughing under his breath in the library—and the gold thread, stretched across the plains and forests between them, was wound tight around them, Phainon feared for his resolve to disentangle themselves.

It wasn’t the type of fear that kept him away. He may be on the path of a scholar now but he was first and foremost a warrior, a Kremnoan one, an honour that he had rightfully won long before a fourteen day and night duel began the process of setting it in stone. He grappled with fear, charged towards it with heated blood, conquered it so the spoils could be paraded.

Heartache was much more potent than any fear but that too failed to keep him away. It was a pain he was willing to withstand as proof of where his heart truly laid. He trembled with it as he passed through the city gates, dromas thankfully trained to slow upon entering civilisation because Phainon’s mind was elsewhere entirely at the first touch of the Dawn Device bathing him in Kephale’s light. He yearned to see the same light

warming flawless pale skin, brightening hair the same gold and auburn as his childhood, glinting off golden jewellery, including signet ring.

Unfortunately, he was slowed by the people bustling back and forth across the stables. He was a frequentest visitor by now and he had yet to see the space so lively. But the arms laden with boxes and saddles, carts stacked with crates and sacks, and the garments of those around him—all of it was familiar.

The Kremnoan detachment preparing to depart.

He dismounted with a reassuring pat of the dromas’ flank as he scanned for the most familiar faces amid the myriad flitting past in long strides. “Ptolemy!”

Scroll in hand as he barked orders amidst a huddle of his men, Ptolemy’s head jerked up. As Phainon slipped through the crowd, Ptolemy’s eyes widened and he flinched away. It was far from his usual smile and hearty pat on the back. His feet shuffled as though he were about to commit such a transgression as fleeing, despite standing in the open before his men.

Phainon checked over his shoulder but there was nothing that could provoke such a reaction. Certainly no Krateros, Hephaestion nor Mydei coming to scold Ptolemy for somehow fumbling his orders. Next he looked down at himself. There was no offence to be taken from his clothes: Mydei had complimented the soft blue tunic in the past and his trousers were plain enough to avoid clashing.

He raised his hand in a small wave and smiled through the awkwardness. “Ptolemy.”

Only to be met with rapid blinks. Perhaps an eyelash had tumbled, or an inopportune wind had stirred the red soil into his eyes. He may have been gone for the past month and a half, too busy with a workload thrice as heavy as other students to visit, but if that was enough time for Ptolemy to forget his face then he was due a visit to the Twilight Courtyard.

“Phainon,” Ptolemy finally said, as though it were squeezed from his lungs in a weak wheeze that happened to take the shape of his name. “You’re in the city.”

He nodded and maintained an amiable smile, even as the warriors around Ptolemy averted their eyes. His skin prickled with various gazes on him from all around the stable. “Something about a festival to Cerces and Mnestia. The Grove’s activities are on hold for the next two weeks.”

“Right,” Ptolemy said, eyes on Phainon but too hazy to do more than peer through Phainon as he gnawed his bottom lip. “Wait here.”

A flick of his hand rallied his men to follow him a short distance. The braying dromases and horses were loud as ever but Phainon glanced out the corner of his eye and many of the men lingered where they had previously hurried like their lives—worse, their honour—was at stake if someone noticed them hesitating. The Kremnoan shouts had dimmed into a muttering din too quiet for Phainon to parse.

Still, the stable’s noises combined was enough to muffle Ptolemy’s exchange with his men. With his back to Phainon, Ptolemy’s face and lips were impossible to read. He could only rely on the faces of the others: stern, stricken, stressed.

It was foolish to jump to conclusions, to make assumptions—not enough evidence, Anaxa would berate him, and toss his research essay plan into the fire—but he could feel the beginnings of his hypothesis snapping into place. He didn’t like the end unfolding.

Under the eyes of so many he had fought and bled with to earn a mutual respect, he resisted the urge to clench his hands or shuffle his feet. All were signs of doubt that reflected poorly on him but, more importantly, Mydei as their prince who had chosen Phainon. Most certainly not a prince, not even Kremnoan, and now wavering somewhere between a warrior and scholar in his lifestyle.

Ptolemy passed on his scroll and his men scurried away as he returned to Phainon. His shoulders had relaxed but his face was carefully blank. Unlike

Leonnius’ outrageous tongue befitting a trickster more than a messenger, Ptolemy was never a talented liar, so he had opted against a shaky, false smile. For his face to be so utterly unreadable was impressive, which meant he was serious.

Phainon breathed once. A steadying one usually taken on the cusp of battle. “Or perhaps I misheard and it was a festival to Nikador that unshackled me from the Grove library.”

An unasked question. An opening for an explanation regarding what exactly the Kremnoan detachment was doing in the stables when it was already abundantly clear. So it was really an entirely different question that weighed the air between them more than the bellowing klaxon and suffocating smoke of war.

Ptolemy’s face was unchanged and his voice flat, “You should speak with Mydeimos.”

Worst of all, Phainon’s traitorous heart fluttered at the mention of his name, spurring images of sun lighting the horizon gold and red with the dawn he hoped they would greet together. It burned down the back of his throat as his jaw tightened. “Where is he?”

“The barracks.”

Tersely, Phainon muttered a brief thanks, one Ptolemy only returned with the bob of his throat before he bowed his head. Neither said farewell as Phainon departed from the stables through the backstreets.

The barracks, stables and armouries were all connected by a number of streets constructed for soldiers to move cargo and themselves in high volume while bringing minimal disruption to civilians. Away from the prying eyes edged too sharp to be wariness alone, it ordinarily made them a more private avenue through the city.

Today was an exception. The backstreets were perfect straight lines, spaced just over two carts’ width, with no branches: people either walked towards him or behind him but there was nowhere to duck away and hide. As he

strode towards the barracks he kept his chin and shoulders back, smile unfaltering, as though he were oblivious to the startled second glances. No one attempted to stop him. They parted for him as he stepped into the barracks.

Mydei wasn’t inside. Only Hephaestion, issuing commands to the few Kremnoans inside that ensured his attention flicked to the new shadow darkening the doorway. His words locked behind his stiffened smiled.

Then eased into surprised cheer. Another much better liar. Hephaestion had a talent for sniffing out what people wanted to hear and handing it to them with a smile. “Phainon! Back from the Grove so soon?”

Hephaestion’s arms opened and Phainon accepted the half-embrace, one hand occupied with a scroll. The strength of the hand clasped over his shoulder as they parted more than made up for its absence.

“A festival for Cerces. I have two weeks off,” Phainon gave him the short version. “Have you seen Mydei?”

For one lingering moment everything was almost normal. They embraced, they smiled pleasantly, they spoke without stammering. But the others held their breaths and then absconded with a tilt of Hephaestion’s head, scuttling like they couldn’t get away fast enough.

Hephaestion furled his scroll, wooden ends clacking together, as he sighed, “In the training grounds around the back. I’ll get him. You two should speak in a more private setting.”

“I appreciate it.” And Phainon meant it.

Whether they liked it or not, they were both public figures. Mydei had much more experience in that regard: he had accepted it with graciousness at the same age Phainon was still crying over a scabbed knee from mistaking a hill for flat ground. A duty, a title, an isolation he should never have been forced to shoulder when youth was about exploring new things, failing with little consequence, and laughing it off among good friends fumbling their way through a big world in much the same way.

That may be Phainon’s opinion but he had always approached Mydei’s status in the detachment with the solemnity it deserved. With the same reverence Mydei upheld his title and all the expectations that came with it, even when he was a short, wide-eyed malnourished child. It was a balancing act of humility, to learn and defer to those older, wiser, than him, and staunch leadership befitting their venerated Crown Prince.

He would never be petty enough to jeopardise his position. Not when they were wanderers, and certainly not when tensions were high in a city where the detachment felt every shaded corner held an enemy poised to strike. Phainon may have entertained the wild thought but he never honestly expected to be stabbed by an unknown assailant with a grudge written in blood dried from an age-old rivalry between city-states.

But he had never even thought to consider the idea that the dagger would be lodged in his back by the person he trusted most.

Only a few moments later and the barrack door opened again. Phainon didn’t dare lift his head from the slip of light stretched across the floor, bending around a broad silhouette, before the door shut the daylight out. Footsteps so adept at falling silent made themselves known across the stone.

When was the last time they had seen each other? Six weeks ago. Anaxa had begun to assign him workloads heavier than all his peers and insisted he had to be able to accomplish at least that much before he could graduate early.

Six weeks yet Phainon lifted his head and it was as though no time had passed. The red garments set him apart from the city’s sun-bleached stone. A flame that flickered with the wind against Mydei’s strides and a beacon that drew Phainon in with the same mindless devotion people reserved for Kephale’s light. Loose, wild, untamed—garments suited to prowling the backstreets like a lion waiting to be released from its urban cage. Eager to meet the wilds and bloody his maw, gold dyed red like the ends of his hair hanging loose around his shoulders.

The braid was still the same. The one Phainon had created with his one hands stir last time they were together. Too distracted by Mydei below him, fiddling at Phainon’s hair with an absentminded comment about growing it out, he had made a mistake parting the hair into equal strands and failed to notice until he was clasping the bottom of a lopsided braid.

When he offered to try again, Mydei had only laughed him off and plucked the end from Phainon’s hand. With only a few nudges, Mydei had begun to wear more pigmented lip tints in private; not quite a red but more noticeable than the teasing hint of pink, especially when it clung to Phainon’s bare skin.

The stain was still there. Curved around the golden clasp. Phainon had watched, wide-eyed, when Mydei brought the braid to his own lips and kissed the metal warmed by Phainon’s fingertips, lids low as he held Phainon’s gaze with a smug victory over his dumbstruck reaction. Then he yanked Phainon in for a proper kiss and everything was forgotten as Phainon was helpless, never even attempting a half-hearted struggle, when Mydei wanted him close.

As helpless as he was now. The same hair, the same clothes, the same sharp angles and surprisingly soft curves. As though nothing had changed.

The difference was in the finest details. Mydei at his most relaxed was reserved for Phainon and four walls that shut out a world beyond the two of them. Only then was Mydei at ease; as much as he could ever be in a world that had gutted and bled him dry over and over again since his birth.

Now, Mydei stood with the stiff shoulder and facade of the crown prince. The one that stood too far ahead to reach for. His broad back a shield, a flag and a spear point protecting those behind him, held aloft as an ideal to strive towards, guiding the way forward.

He was guarded. His eyes sharp and unflinching as he waited for Phainon to meet his eye and one of them was trapped by the shield wedged between them but Phainon wasn’t certain who. There was nothing to be gleaned from his expression nor body language, yet it told Phainon all he needed to know.

Phainon’s heart trembled. It always did at the sight, at the thought, at the lingering scent on stolen fabric, of Mydei. Even whilst Mydei gave him the same look he gave everyone else.

“The detachment is preparing to leave,” Phainon launched the first assault like spears thundering against shields, striking fear into their enemies and scattering their tight formation into something easy to defeat.

Mydei blinked slow, unmoved, because he never flinched whether his body was the spearhead or the shield to be struck. “It is.”

“Where?”

“A black tide expedition.”

Finally, the question with such an obvious answer it had greeted his arrival in the city with the detachment’s movements and the startled reaction of his friends. To hear it in Mydei’s own words would be the final death knell. Perhaps his months in the Grove meant something after all, because his body was unwieldy with the curiosity—the overwhelming need to to ask:

“Without me?”

His voice wavered but it was too late to pluck the words from the stagnant air between them. He swallowed like they were still nestled safe against his trembling vocal cords, but his throat burned with the empty air plunging heavy into his stomach.

Mydei breathed, so deep it was almost a sigh when he exhaled and answered, “Yes.”

The smile on Phainon’s face was weak. Worthless and unconvincing. He longed to tear it from his face and throw it to the floor so it would shatter at Mydei’s feet so his stoic mask would crumble with it.

He forced a breath, shuddering hot through his clenched teeth. “Why?”

A slow blink. The eyes of a predator, calm and composed as they stalked disorientated prey. But Phainon bristled and his lips pulled with the urge to

bear equally sharp teeth. Maybe that would rouse some passion—love, anger, hatred. Anything that Phainon could recognise.

“Focus on your studies. And your family.” Mydei motioned to the window. The world outside was so bright it felt too far from the darkness crushing the room to be real. “Audata and Hieronymus will be happy to see you.”

The disbelieving laugh was so caustic it burned his tongue. “You’re leaving?”

“Preparations still need to be completed.”

“When?”

That made Mydei hesitate. Finally a hint of someone real behind the unflinching military general. But he crossed his arms and his voice was beyond steady. It was flat with the boredom of someone who wanted a conversation to end. “Parting hour.”

“You had no intention of telling me.”

A rhetorical question Mydei didn’t bother to answer. He only tipped his head, lopsided braid swaying, arms tightening around himself, and blinked slow while Phainon—

“You’re going to leave me behind.”

Broke. Just a bit. At the very ends where he wanted to close his lips back over his teeth into a shape he hadn’t yet decided. A thin line. A scowl. A pained smile. The break in his voice fractured his expression. He didn’t know what face he was making, just that it wasn’t indignation. This was weakness. One he hadn’t wanted to show.

But, for the first time since stepping into the barrack, Mydei saw him. Not through the veneer of a prince nor a warrior gazing hazily across a ravaged battlefield. Mydei looked with the fleeting emotions that pierced through the surface: there and gone in the brief moment before Mydei regained his composure.

Then he turned and there was nowhere to look except Mydei’s back. “Wait for me to return and we can discuss it further.”

“I have two weeks,” Phainon blurted out. It wouldn’t change anything. He said it anyway. “I wanted to spend it with you.”

Too pitiful to be a request. Resigned.

“Go home, Phainon. And… look out for Hephaestion while I’m gone.”

Phainon’s head jerked up, eyes wide. “What do you mean?”

There barracks were empty. Mydei nothing more than an apparition sent to shatter him and dissipate, lingering only in the faint scent of pomegranates. He waited for the sweet fragrance to fade and long after.

Akin to a scolded child, he tucked himself against the wall where the daylight couldn’t scald him to action. Head dropped between his knees and arms looped behind his neck, he made a miserable sight. Not because he thought, for even a moment, that Mydei would return and take pity on him if only he appeared pitiful enough.

He just wanted to pathetically wallow where no one would find him.

“You stayed put.”

At the remark of equal parts surprise and humour, Phainon slowly raised his head. The daylight burned but he kept his eyes open and let it. “You too.”

Hephaestion chuckled and nodded to the open spot beside him. Phainon patted the threadbare mat and he sat with another short laugh, less humorous when it was tinged with something heavier. “My condition has been less stable in the past weeks. Lady Hyacinthia insists on watching me more closely and Mydeimos ordered me to remain.”

Four months, almost five, had passed since the detachment arrived in Okhema. Mydei had yet to tell him every fragment of the past—fragmented like a smashed mural he never pieced together in full. The edges didn’t quite line up and there were shards missing, but what was thrust into his

hands, his head, was enough for him to know the broad strokes and what he needed to do—but this detail Phainon knew.

“How…” he picked at the mat’s fraying edge and swallowed. “How do you feel?”

Hephaestion glanced over but Phainon avoided his gaze, unravelling thread with the same focus as someone who wove it, and he shrugged. “Fatigued at times. Shaky at others.”

He lifted his sword hand. It was plagued with a slight tremor. If he were in any many other professions, it would be hardly noticeable and even less consequential. For a warrior, it decided life and death.

“But it’s manageable,” Hephaestion assured him and let his hand fall limp with a harsh slap. “And yet Mydeimos is so…”

Of course he is, Phainon didn’t say. Because Mydei had never told Hephaestion or any of the others that this shattered mural existed, let alone what he found amongst the rubble. You’re supposed to be on your deathbed.

It explained why Mydei had ordered Hephaestion to stay behind. Ever loyal and reliable, Hephaestion had no issue with obeying Mydei’s commands with ease instead of questions, bitterness, outrage.

It didn’t explain why Phainon received the same order.

“I should be glad.” No false joy in Hephaestion’s voice. The softness was real and drew Phainon’s eye, only to find Hephaestion already gazing sidelong at him with a knowing smile. “It means he cares.”

Phainon’s nails scraped stone through thinned fabric as his fist curled into the mat. “That may be so. For the one he dared to show his care to face-to-face.” His eyes stung. It wasn’t the daylight that forced his eyes shut tight. “I never would have agreed to enrol in the Grove if I knew it would come to this.”

The long periods of separation were manageable. Their reunions—always too short. Never enough to soothe his longing. Never enough time—were like dreams that made the waking world bearable. The division that sundered his flesh and never the distance between them was temporary.

But Phainon had been under the impression that nothing would change in spite of the vast time and space between them. He was wrong. Not only had Mydei decided Phainon was no longer worthy to stand by his side as his equal in battle. But Phainon wasn’t even worthy of being told as much to his face.

“Come now. You two have always shared an understanding. Don’t tell me, now that you’re the target of his stone-faced ways, the two of you have become mere strangers,” Hephaestion cajoled. A voice reserved for a campfire, honey brew in hand and the night air refreshingly cold and crisp.

Phainon pushed a hand through his hair and laughed weakly. “Time changes all. Separation makes it more likely for our respective changes to diverge.”

Amidst his wallowing, he missed the flit of shadows and fabric until it whipped towards him. A sharp smack whacked him between the shoulder blades and he jolted forwards into his knees. He gagged at the unexpected force.

“If you intend to sulk with deaf ears then I’ll leave you to do so in privacy,” Hephaestion berated, so stern it bordered on a glare. “But while alone with your thoughts consider: when Mydeimos has ever felt the need to use deception. To shame his enemies?”

He dropped his forehead against his knees and his skin stung beneath his clothes as he breathed, pain sharpening his mind. “No.”

“Then when?”

“Never.”

That was the answer every Kremnoan would give. Only Phainon knew about the truth nestled deep inside Mydei’s heart that had festered in the

open cuts of a child afraid to lose what little he had and the fresh scar tissue of a child that had already grieved that loss—in the past, in a premonition, set to become the future. Were those deceptions? Only in the same way this had been: withholding the truth.

But, ever since they collapsed in a field after a duel no one else could endure much less revel in as they did, Phainon had never once blamed Mydei for the silence throughout the years before he was ready to end it and spoke through a rising sun.

Time changed all. Except Mydei, apparently, because he still chose to protect the people he cared for in the same way he always had.

The one who had changed was Phainon. Nervous when he had always been self-assured of his place at Mydei’s side that had become so physically distant he lost sight of it.

“I’m supposed to guard his back,” Phainon murmured. “He shouldn’t have to shoulder every burden alone.”

“Well, no Kremnoan would dare defy the will of the crown prince,” Hephaestion said and Phainon raised his head to ask for advice from one of two people even Mydei deferred to. But Hephaestion smiled, sly where it creased his eyes and he tilted his head. “Except you never treated him much like a prince. Do you intend to change that?”

Phainon huffed a laugh and smiling came easier than it had since he arrived in the city. “I wouldn’t be fit to be his betrothed if I did.”

With a firm slap of his knee, Hephaestion stood. “Then let’s find you some armour.”

The next laugh came even lighter with his disbelief. “Is that not defying the prince’s will?”

“You said so yourself: the two of you are set to be wed. In that sense, am I not doing what I’ve always done?” When Hephaestion offered a hand,

pulling Phainon to his feet, it was with a roguish smile befitting a winning strike on the battlefield. “I’m only obeying my prince.”

There was no shortage of supples in the armoury to scavenge a set of greaves, a chest piece and a plumed helmet suited to Phainon’s proportions. From there, he slipped in amongst the Kremnoans loitering around the barracks. Their duties were fulfilled and sparring an inadvisable use of energy they would soon need to march, so they merely chatted and leisurely prepared their travel packs as they waited to depart.

Some sent him second glances and likely deciphered who was beneath the helmet when a few strands of white hair and his bright eyes were still visible. They promptly turned away, mouths shut with the slightest upward tilt at the corners to seal their silence.

Since Hephaestion was staying in the city and Ptolemy was too terrible a liar to obfuscate Phainon’s identity for long, Phainon hid himself among Peucesta’s men. Once Mydei confirmed with each of his generals that their warriors and supplies were accounted for, Peucesta winked at him and issued the order to march away from the safety of Okhema’s walls.

Feet pounded against the earth in one swaying mass of dark leather and glinting metal, setting the rhythm beneath the booming tenor of Kremnoan war songs interrupted by jaunty music more crass than valorous. Peucesta’s battalion was especially raucous with the detachment’s best musician at their fore to lead the chorus to near defeating heights where Phainon nestled in the centre.

It thrummed in his ears, his head, his body. He grinned and sang along in a language he learned but never perfected. It made his voice stark amidst the tongues that formed around the rough edges of Kremnoan first and common second. All the men around him knew exactly who he was and chose to sing, sway, and march with him anyway.

In the Grove, there was no shared rhythm. Every scholar flitted through their own research, flicked parchment at their own pace, stewed in their own thoughts after every class and symposium. In the detachment,

loneliness was squeezed from existence. There was simply no space between the press of bodies and voices for it to find and fester within.

Even once night fell to smother the heat and noise in their temporary encampment, he ate and drank with the others around the fires, listening to their stories and jeering laughter or comments while occasionally throwing in his own. There were any number of tents he could have chosen to spend the night in, falling asleep to the wind knocking against the breathing and snores of his tent mates.

But the weather was mild and the earth dry, so he laid beneath the night sky. The breeze stirred the smouldering remains of their fire pits and carried the embers upwards to join the stars. Once a familiar sight, they were impossible to find in Okhema’s sky where the Dawn Device eclipsed the small pinpricks of light.

The Grove’s planetarium was for study alone and failed to compare. The stars were much too large, too close, only ever as far as the domed ceiling, even if Phainon snuck inside when the room was empty and laid down with the memory of someone beside him. A heartbeat matched to his own while they drew constellations like carefree children out past their curfew.

He reached and his index finger sketched two outlines across the sky: a lion and a dog. His hand fell limp into the space beside him. Empty.

They were still too close to the city. If Phainon exposed himself, Mydei could send him back assured that, unless the earth suddenly cracked open or the Dawn Device crumbled, he would safely pass through Okhema’s gates. No sharing a fire nor a tent. They were less than fifty paces away but it may as well have been the distance between the Grove and Okhema when Phainon still couldn’t crawl into the same sleeping cot, curl around Mydei’s back, and fall asleep together.

The grass rustled with more than the wind and he knew better than to hope but his head swivelled a little too fast. Not that it made a difference when fabric dropped over his head and obscured the silhouette with the rest of the world.

He caught the fluttering edge and flipped it over his head. The blanket settled warm around his shoulders, thoroughly heated by the fire without catching, with the same ease Perdikkas sat beside him with two chalices of honey brew. When Phainon accepted a drink it came with the bitter undertone of pomegranates but neither spoke a word as they watched the stars in silence.

The black tide surge was over a week away from Okhema by foot. It was plenty of time for Leonnius to sneak away after delivering a message from the front to the rear, Perdikkas to check his constitution from sleeping and eating rough after being pampered in the Grove, Peucesta to recount his newest, half-complete poem that was a collaborative project with Okhema’s famed anonymous writer.

By the third night, reclined against a tree as he whittled a fallen branch into a sword just the right size for a newborn and too small for anyone else, even Krateros found him. He didn’t comment on Phainon’s failure to remain at Mydei’s side nor drag him there as punishment for disobeying direct orders. He only nodded and strutted off again.

After three days of travel they were beyond the point Mydeimos was likely to send Phainon back alone, and it would be foolish to split his forces just to provide Phainon an escort. But Phainon had yet to think of a way to reveal himself. If this were an elaborate prank or a dramatic theatre performance then he would have no qualms trouncing into his tent and dramatically stripping his chlamys.

What kind of face would Mydei make once he did? Certainly not a smile, and Mydei was more likely to punch than kiss or hug him. A troubled frown? Mounting outrage? Nothing at all when every thought and emotion was wrapped in chains and hauled out of sight?

The overcast third day led into rain through the fourth day. Not the light spring showers that were more refreshing than a hindrance, but the heavy rains of summer slipping into autumn. The storm had started in the night and soaked the earth, footsteps over footsteps dredging it into heavy, muddy tracks that slowed their progress.

The songs lost their cheer, gloomy with the downpour beating the noise down and drowning it in thunder. Compared to the frigid winter months they hibernated in Adonis, these conditions were almost pleasant, even if his skin prickling in the damp cold disagreed.

It was expected when the messengers bolted down from up ahead, as quick as the lightning, outracing the next strike, and one broke away to speak to Peucesta while the other ran past to the battalion behind them. Mydei must have decided to find shelter off the main road and wait out the storm—

“Retreat and into formation! Strife Titankin have ambushed the fore!”

The fore.

The warriors around him began to draw back. It was standard. Not out of advanced military tactics to regroup and recompose themselves, nor any kind of long-standing tradition. Echoing down the legion was an announcement of battle, of bloodshed, against more than any chance encounter: these were the extensions of their own mad Titan of Strife.

Their movements were orderly but their faces were dark. Displeased. Precisely because they were forced into retreat—not by an enemy but by their prince.

Only Phainon had yet to move. The others shifted around him, flowing downstream like a river while he withstood the pull, resisted it, as he pushed forward to snag Peucesta’s arm. The next battalion had already shifted into the space abandoned by their own but the warriors parted around the disruption and Phainon kept them trapped in the centre: the calm amidst rushing rapids.

He was anything but calm as he shouted over the thundering skies, armoured footsteps, and his heart. “Where’s Mydei?”

It was all so loud. Darkness rolled in on all sides and rain dripped down his chlamys to soak through where the wind lifted to expose his ordinary garments. The winds and the water chilled him, hands shaky when they were empty of a sword to hold onto.

Lightning flashed across Peucesta’s face, illuminating it in pale lines meeting harsh angles. “Holding the frontline.”

The rest went unsaid but Phainon heard it as clearly as the war cry of a solitary lion. Phainon threw his travel pack and chlamys to the ground, ripped his sheathed greatsword free, and ran.

The trodden earth was slick beneath his soles and slid from under him. He staggered against the muddy surface trying to drag him down, finding his balance, and didn’t slow again. While the others shuffled into a retreat, Phainon sprinted for the frontline held by an army of one.

Because it was always Mydei alone at the fore. Whether the slim back of a malnourished child or the broad shoulders of a warrior, in actions rather than words, this was how he chose to demonstrate his care.

A lightning flash illuminated the empty stretch of road darkened by long silhouettes and shadows. A stark white creature loomed over a lone figure not even half its size. The lightning faded and the gloom plummeted down upon them in a crash of thunder echoed by a Titankin’s roar.

An anguished cry. A death knell. The white figure crumbled around the gauntleted hand plunged through its stomach. The scattered ashes of its head had yet to touch the ground before Mydei spun and lunged for the nearest Titankin in the horde descending upon him.

Phainon needed to move. To do something. Anything. Mydei had already ripped another head free and used it to bludgeon the weapon from a third Titankin’s hand before punching it through the neck. He pummelled Titankin to the ground like children knocked wooden towers yet more swarmed. Each more committed to Strife’s ideals—valorous death before glorious return—than even Nikador’s human followers who threw away life for honour.

The consequences of Phainon’s disobedience were irrelevant when inaction meant Mydei fighting, bleeding, suffering. And believing he had to do it alone.

But something was wrong. Mydei fought in two ways: controlled precision or unrestrained aggression. Always the former until he let himself loose into a frenzy of the second, born by an intent to kill honed like an executioner’s blade over a lifetime.

When an axe skimmed Mydei’s side, an arrow lodged into his shoulder, a fist caught him in the throat and he coughed gold across the blackened earth, it was careless. Mindless. Instincts dulled and rusted.

Mydei fought with desperation.

It was unlike anything he had seen as Mydei tore through the horde. No savageness, brutality, or self-assurance. When lighting illuminated his features for a fleeting moment, the feral flash of his fangs were nowhere to be seen. He was akin to wounded prey determined to down a predator if it just clawed and bit enough.

Against the darkness and rain and overwhelming numbers slowly, too slowly beginning to dwindle, Mydei slipped. The most juvenile mistake he had ever made in battle. One knee. He was already halfway upright. But it was enough for a shadow to fall over Mydei’s unguarded back.

That distance between them closed like nothing. The Titankin swung and Mydei jerked around in realisation.
