Metal clashed. The kind that scraped bone and teeth. The Titankin paused with surprise. It was brief but that was all Phainon needed. He shoved his greatsword against the Titankin’s sword and it staggered but Phainon chased in two long steps and drove his blade through its chest.

He glanced over his shoulder. Mydei was already looking at him. Eyes wide, sparking as bright as the golden blood smeared across his cheek and lip despite the dimness that felt just a little lighter than a moment before, he blinked in disbelief and—

They lunged at the same moment. They brushed past one another and the emotion was snuffed from Mydei’s profile like it never existed. But there were more urgent concerns.

In a single swing, Phainon decapitated the Titankin that had aimed for Mydei’s back. Mydei returned the favour with a Titankin knocked down and crushed beneath his heel.

Phainon heaved a breath. This was a warmup, far from enough to wind him. It was something else he braced for as he turned.

Mydei’s face was carefully blank. The most terrifying it could ever be. More than fury or tears because at least Phainon could read the crease of his brow and eyes, the tilt of his lips, the flash of his teeth, and know what he was thinking. What he was feeling. This was the face of Mydei shutting Phainon out the same as anyone else.

Still, they knew better than to argue on the battlefield. They naturally stepped into place. A fraught ceasefire. The narrow slip of air between them tingled with the promise of lightning. A stormy onslaught. Yet, back-to-back, they eviscerated the last of the Titankin to the same rhythm in their swing and steps.

The rain and thunder were no longer adversaries disrupting the familiar beat to their dance. Just like a red streak covering his weaknesses when his swing took too long to redirect, or Phainon earning an extra breath for Mydei to recover from overcommitting with his whole body—it all melded together.

As though nothing had changed from their long days in exile that he wished were longer still. Never ending. Years stretching into lifetimes.

But their exile came to an end, and so did the battle. That past reverie splintered in the ragged breaths between them. No enemies left to face, they could only turn on each other.

“Why are you here?” Mydei asked lowly, as level as his facade hiding all those messy thoughts and emotions he wanted everyone to believe he didn’t possess.

Phainon’s fingers twitched. He wanted them all. To pry them from Mydei’s head and inspect them and understand him. Fully, wholly, undeniably. So

Mydei would never feel the need to deceive him again.

He sheathed his greatsword and steadied himself with a breath. “You entrusted your back to me.”

That one weak spot. The only one and he was the only one who knew of it. It was his to protect and he would sooner let a blade through his back than Mydei’s own.

“I told you to stay in Okhema!” Mydei snarled. Roared, like Phainon had simply failed to hear him the first time.

Before Mydei had bared his fangs and fury.

His aching fingers hands tightened around his sword hilt and his next exhale came short from his tight chest. Mydei’s hand was where it had always been, around his lungs, his heart, precisely where Phainon had cut himself open and invited Mydei inside, but this was the first time Phainon had ever felt it squeeze.

“I’m your betrothed. Not one of your generals or foot soldiers,” Phainon reminded him through clenched teeth, in case Mydei had truly forgotten beneath that furious haze dampening the golden clarity in his eyes.

His chest heaved and his voice thundered over the storm. “So you should be the last person to betray my trust!”

“Trust? Betrayal?” Phainon almost laughed but he only sneered. “Look at your own deception in hiding the expedition from me!”

They prowled closer. Neither backed down. They were so close Phainon could see the rain clinging to Mydei’s dampened lashes and almost felt it drip down his own cheeks.

“And you donned petty disguises and hid your presence in the detachment for days.”

“You would have demanded I return to the city otherwise. What lie would you have told me then?”

“I never lied.”

“You simply withheld the truth. The same as you always have.” This time Phainon laughed. Bitter and ugly but Mydei had crushed him to pieces in his fist and scattered the remains like a worthless amphora, made to hold love and breaking under scorn, and he had to know that. “I thought fear didn’t exist in the Kremnoan language.”

A mockery of a joke Mydei had told him years ago when the language was still unknown to him. The others had laughed while Phainon confusedly tipped his head before letting the matter rest.

But it did, as Phainon learned. A meaning tricky to grasp over the years. Fear existed in many words, so inextricably connected to other concepts— of cowardice, of shame, of betrayal—that fear itself was absent except in unspoken scorn. Fear did not exist because it was not allowed to exist.

And yet Phainon had been confronted by cowardice, shame, betrayal. All of it born from Mydei’s fear.

He grabbed Mydei by his tunic and dragged him inwards. Closer. Nowhere to hide when Phainon demanded in a low growl, “What are you so terrified of, Mydei?”

Bones creaked in both their hands he snatched Phainon’s wrist tight enough to bruise and hauled them even closer. The vein in his neck throbbed with his hastening pulse, as quick as Mydei’s tattoos burning and fading and burning again.

The rain ran down his throat, under his collar, and he swallowed against the premonition of where Mydei’s bared teeth would pierce when he ripped out Phainon’s jugular. It already belonged to Mydei: marked by an emblem of Strife on a collar. Until he dropped the leash and was surprised when Phainon thrashed.

“Do I seem afraid to you?” Mydei ground out through his clenched jaw.

Lips pulled into a snarl. Eyes narrowed in a glare. Face flushed from more than the cold.

“Yes.”

He scoffed and slapped Phainon’s hand away. “Then you lost your eyes somewhere in the library.”

Mydei’s feet shifted, about to turn away. Again.

Phainon snatched his shoulder and yanked him back. Mydei tried to shrug him off and push him away when Phainon reached for his arm. They scrabbled, hands grappling to push and pull, fighting against the slick mud and the storm as much as each other.

A palm thrusted at Phainon’s nose and he side-stepped, blocking with his forearm before that jab could turn into a swing at his jaw. He darted forwards and he missed Mydei’s tunic when he jerked backwards. But the momentum lifted his necklace off his breastbone and Phainon seized the jewel encrusted golden plate at the centre.

A win. Except Phainon choked at the pressure around his throat as Mydei grabbed him by the back of his collar. Flecked with mud and golden blood, neither relinquished their hold. Stalemate.

Phainon panted, throat bobbing against the constrictive leather. “You were relieved to see me until you decided on more deceptions. Or did I misread that too?”

“It isn’t fear,” Mydei insisted again and his hand trembled around Phainon’s wrist. Suppressed rage. The after tremors of battle. The cold. Or—

“It’s only you and I here, Your Highness,” he said mockingly. “No one else will hear that their immortal Crown Prince feels fear just like an ordinary mort—“

Mydei slammed their foreheads together. The crack echoed in his ears and his eyes danced with lights as he stumbled, but the hand in his collar cupped

his neck and caught him before he could fall. His brain rattled around his skull, skin and bone throbbing where their foreheads pressed together. He blinked the light away and the rain couldn’t soothe the heat of Mydei’s body, his gaze, burning through Phainon.

“If you die out here, the one carrying your corpse home to your parents will be me!”

The world shrank down to golden eyes. He couldn’t look away. There was nowhere else he could possible look beyond Mydei’s eyes—the cusp of dawn, the heat of war, the flames of the hearth—and that desperation returned to his slitted pupils. They dragged heavy across Phainon’s face, holding his gaze only to flit down over his cheeks, his lips, and back again. Like he was afraid to forget Phainon’s face if he ever became a sallow corpse.

He didn’t know what he expected, if anything at all, when he dug his fingers into Mydei’s cracks so the truth would finally bleed out of him. He never could have guessed that this is what he would find. Mydei was frightened after all. Terrified that Phainon will perish.

It was so simple. Every deception in Mydei’s life had been born from the fear that those he cared for would die for his sake. So simple and yet Phainon had failed to see it.

“You’re too reckless when it’s for someone else’s sake—“

“I don’t want to hear that from you,” Phainon quipped back on instinct when his mind was still reeling from the crack of bone and, more electrifying than a lightning strike, Mydei’s admittance.

Hair damp, nose red from the cold, and Phainon’s mind still reeling, Mydei’s glare fell flat. “My body is immortal. Only one of us comes back from the dead.”

“And I’m the one who stands vigil over your dead body while you do!”

So Mydei was fearful that he would, one day, have to find Phainon, blood and life staining the earth gold. Only one of them had guarded a prone body or a deathbed. Even if Phainon knew Mydei would return, there was always the possibility that this time would be different.

“I have many lives to give. You have only the one.”

“You don’t know that!”

“Have you lost your mind?”

Through the cold numbing his skin, the back of Mydei’s necklace dug awkwardly into his hand. He let the jewel fall between his fingers but one thing remained cradled in his palm. Phainon’s eyes followed the thin gold chain up where it laid around Mydei’s neck and he had failed to notice. Then back down to the signet ring shining in a the rain pooled shallow in his cupped hand.

“You think Death could keep me from you?” Phainon croaked, voice rough from his shouts. He should be better than this. Than losing control. But Mydei has always tested his self-restraint, just never like this. “I would drag myself from the Sea of Souls and slay Thanatos at its gates if they tried to stop me.”

Finally, Mydei paused enough for the damp air to cool the fury loosen in puffs of fire and smoke meant to choke them both. His voice was breathy, raw like Phainon’s own, “You truly did lose it.”

“Don’t act like I’m selfish for holding you to your word. Honour. Life. Soul —“ Phainon’s hand lifted and, having basked in the heat of Mydei’s body and his own, the ring was warm against his lips, “—you promised all of it to me. I have no intention of letting anyone else have any of it.”

Dumbstruck, Mydei mumbled, “I… did…”

“You did,” Phainon repeated as the fight left them. “And I promised mine back to you.”

For the first time in the long years they had known each other better than anyone else in this world, they both had spoken and been unable to hear one another.

Exhausted from more than battle, now they were nothing more than two people stood drenched in the rain.

Phainon smoothed his thumb over the symbol of Strife, whispering under the rain, “Unless, you had a change of heart.”

Mydei heard him anyway. “No. I just…”

His face twisted and he ran a hands through his hair, gripping darkened strands as he tried to grasp hold of the words escaping him. Hazy with confusion. Lost.

Slowly, Phainon asked, “Was it because of Hephaestion?”

“No. Yes,” Mydei corrected himself, words quick when he usually considered his answers beforehand like a man being taken to an executioner’s platform. “Not entirely.“

Troubled by his own uncertainty, his brows pinched, hand tightening in his hair, and he cupped his mouth, sealing away any more unwarranted answers.

“Take your time,” Phainon reassured him and lowered the signet ring back to his chest. “We should return to the others and set up camp for now.”

Phainon reached—and hesitated. But their relationship wasn’t one of hesitances, so he grasped Mydei’s hand and intwined their fingers. Mydei glanced at their hands and squeezed and Phainon felt it around his heart beating steady for the first time in days.

They were utterly soaked by the storm still raging around them but Phainon breathed and felt it warm him through. They would be all right. They always were and this time would be no exception. There never would be so long as Phainon had a choice.

By the time they returned, the encampment was already partially pitched. While Mydei disliked formality, his tent was one of the first to be constructed. They could have dragged their feet straight inside but Mydei’s sharp whistle cut through the din of rain and chatter.

All eyes turned to them and silence lingered over the encampment. Phainon smiled, lifted their joined hands in a wave, and cheers erupted in a crash louder than thunder. Their companions were the loudest as they peeled themselves away from the others.

Leonnius clasped Phainon’s shoulder but addressed the situation first. “I saw the two of you back-to-back and knew the Titankin would be handled in no time.”

“Any injuries?” Perdikkas asked with an eye towards any golden smears, but they were all too thin to be much threat. “Physical. Since emotional isn’t my area of expertise.”

Mydei swung their joined hands for them to see again and answered, voice still rougher than usual, “None.”

“None,” Phainon echoed.

Peucesta smiled. “All passions are ignited one the battlefield.”

Ptolemy’s head swivelled between each of them, face dazedly slack. “So…”

“We all knew,” Leonnius confirmed for him and a firm pat to Phainon’s shoulder.

“Not all,” Mydei corrected gruffly and Phainon nudged their shoulders together with a small smile Mydei returned at the corner of his eyes.

Ptolemy frowned. “I—how should I feel about this exactly?”

“Motivated,” Peucesta said.

“Do you mean demotivated?” Ptolemy retorted skeptically, knowing Peucesta was never one to mix words.

“Motivated,” Perdikkas agreed.

“Motivated to work on keeping a straight face,” Leonnius teased with a sharp smirk.

“Hephaestion knows, doesn’t he?” Ptolemy asked and the silence was answered enough. He sighed. “He’s not even here and he knows.”

Perdikkas offered a consolatory pat of his back. “Sulk when the lot of us are no longer tempting illness with the rain.”

The four of them were still partially protected by their chlamys, waxed leather repelling water, but Mydei and Phainon had discarded theirs for the sake of easier movement in battle. They were akin to a drowned cat and dog, and the others scattered to find them dry linens amongst the supplies while they retreated to Mydei’s tent.

When Mydei parted the flap, Phainon followed him inside so they could shelter from the frigid winds. Leonnius returned with a basin of water and cloths. Without dry tinder to light a fire, the water was still cold but they had suffered worse than cold cloths to wipe themselves down with. It was a worse fate to have nothing at all. The fresh garments Perdikkas returned with were dry, as was the bedding in the chest Ptolemy carried inside.

Swaddled under all three blankets Perdikkas had insisted upon, there was no need for a furnace when Mydei’s body burned hot enough for the both of them. He was better than a blanket. There was weight behind his warmth as he laid atop Phainon’s chest and let Phainon wrap him up in his arms, hand resting over a knob in Mydei’s back.

His breath brushed hot through the tunic and his words sank through fabric into Phainon’s skin. “When Hephaestion died, he was my dear companion. The only one I managed to keep by my side. Unlike the rest, it wasn’t circumstance—noble self-sacrifice, nor battle—that took him from me. But sickness. His own body, and that is something beyond my power to change.”

Phainon combed his hand through Mydei’s damp hair. “Hephaestion is in good hands. His health has been entrusted to a stable life in the city, and the healing hands of the Courtyard.”

Mydei squirmed against him. Not to force distance between them but, cheek nuzzling against Phainon’s chest and leg slotting between Phainon’s own, to get closer. “Then I found myself thinking, Hephaestion was my dear companion and now I have a person dearest to me—more beloved than anyone else could ever hope to be. If fate truly wanted to be cruel, perhaps they would take them away as the cost of the others’ survival.”

Phainon’s heart ached at this weight Mydei had suffered in silence. He never wanted to be a burden to anyone but least of all to Mydei. Yet, so long as Mydei cared for him so deeply he could lose blood and bone and that tenderness could still never be gouged out, there was little Phainon could do except swing his sword for the sake of them both, hold Mydei just like this afterwards, and hope it was enough to lighten his many burdens.

He knew because he was the same way. Mydei could shatter him, destroy him, scorn his doubts, his irrationality, his mistakes that were born from an affection so deep it would remain in every broken fragment of his being. Loving someone so much was its own burden to some but Phainon embraced it, yearning to feel its weight every morning and night.

Besides, he wouldn’t be Mydei if he chose to destroy Phainon out of anything other than misguided love.

He kissed the crown of Mydei’s head, tasting rain as he promised, “I’m not going anywhere.”

“You should,” Mydei said. “This life… you have the potential for more than this endless slaughter scraping out another day for the holy city.”

The conversation had circled back around to this. For him—and him alone of every person he had grown alongside in the detachment, including Mydei —it was a tangible option for him to discard his greatsword, the aches and pains of battle, the threat of death. He could turn away from being a warrior and walk the path of a scholar. Mydei wanted him to but…

“I don’t want to attend the Grove,” Phainon admitted quietly.

In their first month, it hadn’t been much of a discussion. There were good reasons Aglaea had insisted he enrol: connections, credibility, knowledge and skills to challenge the Council of Elders. It meant reputation, which could all be directed towards advocating for the detachment.

Phainon splayed his hand flat across Mydei’s back, his weak spot, and felt the breath shudder through Mydei into him. “The most alive I’ve felt in months is whenever I’m at your side, especially in battle.”

“The separation will pass. The knowledge you accrue will not,” Mydei argued, no matter how reluctantly.

“I was considering… slowing down. There’s no need to graduate at the same pace as everyone else. I can divide my responsibilities and time the way I want.”

The only reason he insisted on graduating ahead of schedule was so he could cut their separation short. He thought he could survive condensing it down and shortening the ordeal. But so long as he could see Mydei for more than one day a week, then he didn’t care if it took twice as long to graduate.

Mydei propped his chin on Phainon’s chest and tilted his head with a slight wrinkle of his nose. “Is that possible?”

“I can discuss it with Anaxa.”

Despite his prickly attitude and habit of shooting alchemical bullets at his students, Anaxa was willing to restructure classes and coursework to help him graduate sooner. This should be fine too. Although he may have to endure a bullet between the eyes and a lecture about commitment before Anaxa revealed he had a plan prepared already because Phainon was never subtle about where his heart and mind laid.

“You told me to go home to my family,” Phainon recalled from their argument in the barracks. “Mydei, you are my family. You know that, don’t

you?”

A small hum and a carefully neutral face. Inconclusive, if not for the lingering wrinkle to his nose.

It was so endearing, a habit Phainon was certain Mydei was clueless he possessed, that Phainon smiled and was helplessly drawn in. He kissed Mydei’s nose and the wrinkle deepened before easing away as Phainon whispered, “I want to get married.”

Mydei searched his features, perhaps finding what he was looking for or perhaps not, before he leaned closer. His breath warmed Phainon’s upper lip as he brushed their noses together. “Don’t rush.”

“I’m not,” Phainon insisted in the space between them so narrow each word was practically a kiss. “I’ve simply had a change in priority. I want to wake up beside you every morning in a home we share. I want our clothes mixed together in one chest. I want—I want everything. I want it all. With you, Mydei. Honour, life, soul. These things don’t last forever so why are we wasting time waiting?”

He kissed him. Slow and languid. The kind of kisses he wanted them to share every morning when they awoke and every night before they slept— for the rest of the time they had left, whether it ended with the evernight or the new dawn. And all those feelings were given right back to him as Mydei kissed him just the same. forehead, lifted their intertwined hands to lay another kiss on his palm and then the back of his hand, down to his ring finger.

When Phainon pulled away, it was only to take the ring swaying against his chest and lift it to his lips, whispering breathlessly, “Marry me, Mydei.”

Mydei leaned down and his lips brushed the ring between them as he held Phainon’s eye and murmured, “I will.”

The ring rattled on its chain as he let it drop and pinched Mydei’s chin, coaxing him the rest of the way into a proper kiss that made Mydei’s tattoos

flash on the other side of Phainon’s closed lids. Fire lancing through Mydei’s body and Phainon’s just the same.

Phainon panted against his lips. “My love, my life, my soul—it’s all yours, Mydei, and nothing will ever take it from you. So don’t shoulder your burdens alone. Tell them to me plainly. No more secrets.”

Mydei licked his reddened lips. “Next time… my first instinct will always be otherwise,” he admitted shamefully and heaved a deep breath. “But I will be honest with you. You deserve nothing less.”

His eyes prickled but tucked Mydei’s bangs behind his ear, the back of his fingers caressed his cheek, as he smiled, shaky but truthful. “That’s all I want. I just want you, Mydei.”

“You have me.”

“I know.”

Tomorrow they would wake up. Maybe the rain would have passed in the night. Maybe the storm would continue to hound them through the day. No matter what, tomorrow they would march towards the world’s decay that all with good sense fled from. They would wage war for their lives and the lives of those behind them.

But, in some distant tomorrow, when they returned to the safety of the holy city where the day brightened eternity, they would fall asleep just like this in a bed, a home, a life they shared, and dream of an even more distant shared tomorrow.
